items.title: Using MarketForge
items.text: MarketForge turns historical market-data archives and external recordings into canonical trade and order-book datasets. Forge selects and tracks inputs, prepares processing jobs, and records their outcomes. The Engine interprets events and writes publication files that can be inspected with the CLI or Python.

items.title: Start with a first dataset
items.text: Install and prepare a testing workspace, then follow the Bybit BTCUSDT trades and depth quick start. You will verify the managed copies, inspect the normalized rows, and check the initial depth snapshot against its recorded boundary.

items.title: Choose a task
items.text:
If you need to… Start here Find an instrument, browse current statistics, or inspect a ranking Explore markets Download archives or add a recording Acquisition and external recordings Inspect raw availability and manage copies Raw storage Process data Normalize, merge, or convert Run acquisition, normalization, and merge together Historical pipeline Read an existing publication Inspect datasets or use a notebook Look up exact syntax, fields, or formats Reference

Read the concepts to understand the evidence behind a result. Use the worked examples when you want reusable inputs, or troubleshooting when a step fails. Contributors can start in Development.

items.title: MarketForge concepts
items.text:
Use these pages to interpret selections, rows, dataset identities, and handoffs across operations.

  • Identity and provenance
  • Time, selection, and coverage
  • Depth observations and reconstruction
  • Ordering and reconciliation
  • Execution, publication, and lineage

items.title: Depth observations and reconstruction
items.text:
A snapshot or bounded initial observation establishes the starting state allowed by the profile's declared scope. Updates change levels within that scope. Absolute operations set the level, while relative operations have source-specific change semantics. Read the profile and stored codes before interpreting zero quantities or resets.

flowchart TB
    S["Boundary state"] --> O["Ordered observations"]
    O -->|"index span"| R["Canonical level rows"]
    O -->|"empty span"| Z["Zero-row observation"]
    R --> B["Next book state"]
    Z --> B

The event index can establish an observation whose canonical row span is empty. It cannot fill in a missing observation. Reconstruction starts at the applicable initialization or carried boundary, follows source or causal order, and applies exact row spans. A segment identifies a separately reconstructable history. A bounded feed can establish only its declared levels, and a sequence domain can reset at an initialization. Depth index and segment formats · Verify the first Bybit snapshot

items.title: Execution, publication, and lineage
items.text:
Preparation resolves a recipe to concrete inputs and freezes the evidence needed for execution. Validation can reject a malformed or incompatible job before processing. A successful execution outcome can still be followed by a failed validation or registration step.

An Engine publication is committed on disk. Forge verifies that committed evidence before a separate registry transaction where registration is supported. A failed registry operation can leave valid files available for registration-only recovery. Inspect the operation's intent and outcome before starting another attempt. Conversion currently verifies completed output without registering it in Forge. Operation lifecycles · Forge artifacts

Publication-level selection records the intended upstream inputs. An exact file-level contribution records evidence that a source contributed rows or events to that primary file. A dataset's integrity status summarizes the applicable processing and validation evidence. It does not guarantee continuous historical coverage or external source completeness. Dataset lineage procedure

items.title: Identity and provenance
items.text:
The provider distributes bytes. The execution venue supplies the market context. A recording can identify a product, publisher and native instrument ID even when many venues use the same symbol. In MarketForge, Bybit spot BTCUSDT and the Bybit linear perpetual BTCUSDT have different canonical identities. Catalogue declarations

Identifier Scope and relationships Source object key Stable within the registered source and request scope. A managed archive row identifies the local copy and retained digest Canonical instrument ID Qualified by instrument namespace. Effective-dated specifications determine quantity and contract interpretation Stream ID Distinguishes instrument, content and source context. One logical stream can span parts. One combined part can contain many streams Stream rank Integer tie-breaker or rank binding inside a prepared job and its output. Repeated parts of one stream can share its rank Engine job and publication IDs Normalization carries separate job and dataset IDs. Physical merge identifies output through the merge job ID. Interpret each field at its wire boundary Registry publication ID One database registration for the committed Engine publication and namespace Registry file dataset ID One registered primary file. A publication can have several. Recipe selectors state which type they accept

Preserve native identity and effective historical evidence alongside canonical fields. A catalogue observation made today can be operationally applicable under an explicit inference policy without independently proving the historical specification. Historical specifications · Inference policy

items.title: Historical applicability
items.text:
An instrument identity survives changes in its trading terms. Suppose a contract’s lot size changes at midnight. A current catalogue tick size or quantity step applies to the observation collected today. A retained historical specification has its own provenance and applicability interval, which is what makes it usable for an archived record. A request that crosses a terms change may need separate processing inputs or specifications.

Keep the native provider identifier and recorded interval with the canonical instrument. Use the specifications guide to record applicability or inspect inferred evidence before preparation.

items.title: Registry identity
items.text: Numeric catalogue and file IDs belong to one PostgreSQL registry. Two environments can use the same integer for different objects. Use the registry that produced a recorded ID, and preserve the retained UUID for managed execution recovery. Run evidence

items.title: Ordering and reconciliation
items.text:
Choose ordering according to the dependencies of the data. Source observations can arrive in native order with regressing event timestamps. Chronological merge orders by event time and applies the recorded stream rank as a tie-breaker. Causal merge preserves the physical timeline sequence and any depth events needed to reconstruct market rows.

Normalization can reconcile overlapping native archives. Source preference, stream and member identity, duplicate handling, timestamp policies and explicitly permitted event exclusions affect that outcome. Inspect the retained integrity and reconciliation evidence before treating fewer output rows as benign. A row suppressed by policy differs from a rejected source record, a skipped instrument or an accepted observation that emitted zero level rows. Runtime settings and policy keys · Merge Engine architecture

items.title: Time, selection, and coverage
items.text:
Historical recipes select with timezone-aware intervals. The useful interpretation depends on the next boundary.

Boundary Selection and evidence Acquisition Provider archives whose nominal intervals overlap the half-open request. A selected archive is downloaded as a whole Normalization Selected raw archives or archive members. The output can extend outside the requested window because the worker processes whole inputs Merge Requested Engine event window in signed Unix nanoseconds. Causal depth can include reconstruction rows outside the market window Conversion Entire selected merge publication, including its causal context. The recipe interval is a selection constraint, and explicit whole-publication approval can permit a wider overlapping publication Dataset discovery File or stream metadata filters on stored envelopes. Row filters act separately on a chosen timestamp column

Event timestamps describe source event time. Nullable system timestamps describe receipt or recording where the source provides it. Native order can encode dependencies even when event timestamps regress. Observed first and last timestamps describe measured extrema, often inclusive. A contiguous sequence of nominal archive intervals or matching extrema alone cannot prove every event was observed. Check source coverage, sequence semantics, integrity observations and applicable reconstruction scope. Ordering · Publication schemas and time fields

Profiles define how source records are interpreted. Ranking policies define eligibility and comparison. Live has a separate configuration root and loader.

The workspace root anchors all managed configuration paths, even when storage.data_root points elsewhere. Named lookups use the relevant library. Acquisition map, plan, and download use a saved name, with an optional .toml suffix. Normalize, merge, and convert accept explicit recipe paths where the operation synopsis indicates; pipeline recipe commands use a saved name. Global --config selects Forge settings and follows the caller’s working directory for a relative path. Active lookups diagnose a legacy source without its migrated counterpart. Retained paths in historical evidence keep their original names and checksums.

items.title: Validation stages
items.text:
TOML parsing, schema validation, reference checks, preparation and execution succeed independently. For example, a merge recipe can point to a valid normalization recipe while the expected publications are still absent. An import validator also checks its local file selection. A registration validator uses the selected registry to check its declared bindings.

mf acquisition validate bybit-btc-20261027
mf normalize validate docs/content/examples/bybit/acquisition.toml
mf merge validate MERGE_RECIPE
mf convert validate CONVERSION_RECIPE
mf acquisition import validate NAME
mf pipeline validate bybit_spot
mf normalize profiles validate bybit.spot.spot.trades
mf markets rank validate turnover

Acquisition and registration offer editor commands. Normalize new opens an editor after creating the file. For pipeline, merge and conversion recipes, use nvim on the managed file after creation. Creating a named recipe uses an exclusive write. Edits apply to subsequent preparation. A prepared run retains its submitted request, evidence and settings.

Conversion additionally checks an optional installed instrument catalogue at data/catalog/instruments.json against historical instrument evidence. The generated catalogue and job bindings are execution artifacts. The installed Engine manifest lives at .bin/manifest.json and verifies the selected binaries. These files have separate contracts from the editable TOMLs.

The Forge TUI System actions Config show and Engine runtime use the same reports as the CLI. Recipe actions use the same managed libraries and validators. Existing editor actions hand off the selected source file.

items.title: Acquisition and raw import recipes
items.text: Save acquisition recipes in data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/acquisition/. Commands accept the managed name with an optional .toml suffix. Each [[requests]] entry selects one archive collection for the shared interval. Unknown fields are rejected.

items.title: Scope and provider options
items.text:
Field Accepted values and constraints version Integer 1, the default. interval.start, interval.end Required timezone-aware datetimes. Start must precede end. The interval includes start and excludes end. requests Required array of tables with at least one entry. requests[].exchange Required. Historical adapters use binance, bybit, bitget, okx, or gateio. Structural validation accepts any string matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$. requests[].instrument_type Required. spot, perpetual, future, or option. requests[].market_category Required. spot for spot, linear or inverse for perpetuals and futures, option for options. Adapter support varies. requests[].data_type Required. trades or order_book_l2. requests[].scope.kind Required. instrument, family, or base_coin, as required by the adapter. requests[].scope.identifier Required nonblank provider-native identifier. Adapters accept letters, digits, underscore, dot, colon, slash and hyphen. Reserved identifiers ., .., and ANY are rejected. requests[].source_options.feed Gate.io L2 only. incremental (default) or snapshot. Omit source_options for other requests.

Choose supported combinations from historical sources. Gate.io's feed changes archive selection and source identity. Choose the recording format required for later processing. Discovery applies each provider's archive calendar to select overlapping whole files. See time, selection and coverage.

items.title: Complete example
items.text:
This OKX request selects inverse dated-future trades for the BTC-USD family over one UTC+8 calendar day.

version = 1

[interval]
start = 2026-09-01T00:00:00+08:00
end = 2026-09-02T00:00:00+08:00

[[requests]]
exchange = "okx"
instrument_type = "future"
market_category = "inverse"
data_type = "trades"
scope = { kind = "family", identifier = "BTC-USD" }

For an instrument-scoped Bybit recipe, see the acquisition tutorial. For Bybit options, set both instrument_type and market_category to option and use scope = { kind = "base_coin", identifier = "BTC" }.

items.title: Common validation errors
items.text: Diagnostic Correction Invalid TOML or unexpected field Fix the reported line or field. Use [[requests]] for each request and put its fields under that entry. Missing timezone or unordered interval Add Z or an explicit offset and set end later than start. Invalid source options Keep source_options only for a gateio request with data_type = "order_book_l2". Unsupported combination during mapping Match the exchange, instrument type, market category, data type and scope against the historical source matrix. Structural validation leaves this check to the adapter.

items.title: Application HTTP/storage settings
items.text: Application settings govern the raw storage root, HTTP concurrency, retries and request pacing. Per-run --requests-per-second is capped by provider budgets. See application settings and acquisition commands.

items.title: External import configuration
items.text:
Field Required Accepted values / default version No Integer 1; defaults to 1 source_key Yes Nonempty source identifier source_kind No recording, purchased, other; default recording root Yes Nonempty source directory path files One selection method required List of root-relative filenames patterns One selection method required Root-relative file patterns max_files No Default 1000; accepted 1–10000 data_type Yes trades or order_book_l2 format_profile No Optional profile reference [identity] Yes Explicit execution venue and instrument identity [interval] No Optional timezone-aware half-open interval [specifications] Conditional Optional locally; required when the instrument is unknown to the catalogue during raw-only import

At least one nonempty file or pattern selection is required.

Unknown fields are rejected.

The source root must resolve to a directory during import input selection.

The format_profile field does not independently establish profile validity or normalization readiness.

items.title: Import Identity Fields
items.text: Field Required Accepted values identity.exchange Yes Lowercase registered execution-venue code identity.market_category Yes spot, linear, inverse, equity, option identity.instrument_type Yes spot, perpetual, future, equity, option identity.symbol Yes Nonempty native symbol

items.title: Important rules
items.text:
The market category and instrument type must be compatible.

The symbol cannot be:

UNSPECIFIED

The exchange cannot be:

external

The actual execution venue must be declared.

The provider or source origin is separate provenance.

items.title: Import Specification Fields
items.text:
The supported specification declaration can include:

[specifications]
as_of = 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z

base_asset = "BTC"
quote_asset = "USDT"
quantity_type = "base"

tick_size = "0.01"
qty_step = "0.000001"

The required fields depend on whether specifications are supplied and the selected quantity type.

items.title: Required relationships
items.text:
If specifications are supplied, both base and quote assets are required by the import configuration.

At least one supported observation timestamp or historical validity interval must establish the specification's time context.

If quantity type is contracts, an explicit positive contract value and its denomination are required.

Historical validity requires both start and end boundaries.

Exact decimal fields must use supported exact representations.

items.title: Validation constraints
items.text:
For example:

  • Tick size must be positive when provided.
  • Quantity step must be positive when provided.
  • Minimum and maximum quantity values must be nonnegative when provided.
  • Minimum quantity cannot exceed maximum quantity.
  • Contract value must be a positive finite decimal string.
  • Historical validity must use an ordered nonempty interval.

items.title: What if a value is unknown?
items.text:
Do not fabricate it.

For raw-only import, omit genuinely optional information where the schema permits it.

For full normalization readiness, obtain the required historical specifications from trustworthy source evidence.

items.title: Selecting Files with Patterns
items.text:
When a directory contains many files, writing every filename manually can be inconvenient.

MarketForge supports file patterns.

For example:

root = "./recordings"
patterns = ["*.csv"]

This selects matching CSV files in the root directory.

items.title: Why use patterns?
items.text:
Suppose your recording directory contains:

recordings/
├── trades-2026-09-01.csv
├── trades-2026-09-02.csv
├── trades-2026-09-03.csv
└── notes.txt

A pattern such as:

patterns = ["*.csv"]

selects the matching CSV recordings.

It does not select notes.txt.

items.title: Recursive patterns
items.text:
MarketForge also supports recursive ** path matching.

For example:

patterns = ["**/*.csv"]

This can select CSV files from nested directories.

items.title: Why be careful with patterns?
items.text:
A broad pattern may include files that do not share the same source format or instrument identity.

For example, a recording directory might contain:

BTCUSDT/
ETHUSDT/

If your import recipe declares only BTCUSDT but selects files from both directories, the source identity would be incorrect for some inputs.

Use narrow patterns and inspect the resolved selection.

items.title: Are absolute file entries supported?
items.text:
No.

The entries inside files and patterns must be relative to the source root.

For example:

files = ["/home/user/recordings/trades.csv"]

is not accepted as a root-relative file selection.

Instead, declare the root separately:

root = "/home/user/recordings"
files = ["trades.csv"]

items.title: Can file selections traverse outside the root?
items.text:
No.

Parent-directory traversal is rejected.

For example:

files = ["../other-data/trades.csv"]

is not accepted.

This helps keep the selected input files within the declared source collection.

items.title: Understanding Source Root Resolution
items.text: This is an important difference between external import and some other MarketForge configuration types.

items.title: External import root
items.text:
For external import recipes, a relative root such as:

root = "./recordings"

is resolved relative to the current command working directory.

For example, if you run MarketForge from the repository root:

/home/user/projects/marketforge/

then:

root = "./recordings"

resolves to:

/home/user/projects/marketforge/recordings/

items.title: What if I invoke MarketForge elsewhere?
items.text:
The same relative root can resolve to a different directory.

This is why the command's working directory matters for external import.

items.title: How can I avoid ambiguity?
items.text:
Use an absolute source root when you want the recipe to identify one fixed location independently of the current working directory.

For example:

root = "/mnt/market-data/recordings"

items.title: What does import new do?
items.text:
When you create an import recipe from an existing file or directory, MarketForge resolves the supplied source path.

The generated draft stores that resolved root.

This helps avoid ambiguity in the initial declaration.

items.title: How is this different from registration recipes?
items.text:
The full raw-data registration workflow has its own source-root resolution rules.

Those declarations can resolve repository-relative roots independently of the command invocation directory.

Do not assume that every MarketForge configuration type interprets relative paths identically.

items.title: Import File Limits
items.text:
An import pattern could potentially match thousands of files.

To avoid unexpectedly large selections, MarketForge limits file enumeration.

items.title: Maximum selected files
items.text:
The relevant field is:

max_files = 1000

The default is 1000.

The accepted range is:

1–10000

items.title: Why is there a limit?
items.text:
Imagine accidentally selecting:

*

inside a directory containing many unrelated files.

Without a limit, the import operation could attempt to preserve far more data than intended.

The file limit provides a safeguard.

items.title: Pattern traversal limit
items.text:
Pattern expansion also stops after inspecting more than 100,000 filesystem entries.

This prevents unbounded directory traversal.

items.title: Does max_files limit file size?
items.text:
No.

It limits the number of selected files.

A single large archive can still require substantial storage.

items.title: Does the importer select files randomly?
items.text:
No.

The selected file paths are resolved into a deterministic sorted order.

This helps make the import operation reproducible.

items.title: What if no files match?
items.text:
The import selection fails.

MarketForge does not treat an empty selection as a successful import of an unspecified dataset.

items.title: Symlinks and Source Safety
items.text:
External imports must preserve the correct source files without escaping the declared root.

MarketForge therefore checks source paths.

items.title: Source files must stay inside the root
items.text: The resolved file paths must remain within the declared source directory.

items.title: Selected symlink files
items.text: Symlinked source files are not accepted as managed-copy inputs.

items.title: Directory traversal
items.text:
The selection rejects paths that escape the source root.

Recursive pattern traversal does not follow symlinked directories.

items.title: Why enforce these rules?
items.text:
Without path checks, a broad pattern or unexpected symlink could cause MarketForge to import files outside the intended source collection.

The importer must know exactly which physical files belong to the declared input.

items.title: Are source directories modified?
items.text:
The import workflow preserves the original source files.

It copies or reuses the selected bytes in managed raw storage.

The source files remain separate from the managed copies.

items.title: What about files changing during import?
items.text:
MarketForge checks source-file stability.

It does not accept an input as stable merely because the filename remains the same.

The importer compares relevant filesystem information before and after hashing or copying.

If the file changes during the operation, import can fail.

This prevents a source file that is still being written from being accepted as one immutable recording.

items.title: Application settings
items.text: Forge reads an explicit global --config PATH relative to the caller's directory, or the workspace's default data/.config/forge/marketforge.toml. If the default is absent, Forge uses built-in settings. A legacy default without its migrated counterpart produces a migration diagnostic. An explicit missing path is an error. Select the workspace with --project-root, then MARKETFORGE_PROJECT_ROOT, then discovery from the current directory. A workspace has forge/pyproject.toml and engine/. Storage path values are resolved from the workspace. The recipe libraries continue to live under its configuration directory.

items.title: Fields and defaults
items.text:
All fields below are optional. Unknown keys and unintended type coercions are rejected.

Path Type and constraint Default and meaning version Integer, exactly 1 1, application schema storage.data_root Nonblank path string "data", root for managed raw bytes, publications and runs presentation.mode progress or silent progress, terminal progress preference presentation.color auto, always, or never auto, color policy presentation.editor Nonblank string Omitted, editor resolution uses the environment or available fallback http.requests_per_second Finite positive number 2.0 requests per second http.max_concurrent Integer 1–64 4 concurrent requests http.timeout_seconds Finite positive number in seconds 30.0 http.max_attempts Integer 1–10 3 attempts

items.title: Inspect effective values
items.text:
The terminal view shows each effective setting and its source. JSON retains the existing settings fields and adds setting_sources, keyed by dotted field name. A null source means a built-in default.

mf config show
mf --json config show

Provider-specific rate limits can further constrain HTTP work. Database DSNs use separate credential resolution. Engine resources use historical runtime settings. Settings model · Path resolver

items.title: Catalogue declarations
items.text: Catalogue commands accept one TOML table per declaration. The file describes a venue, a canonical instrument, or its specifications. The registry assigns numeric identities and retains evidence independently of the declaration file. See the registration procedure and CLI syntax.

items.title: Venue and instrument
items.text: Declaration Path Type and requirement Rules Exchange code Required string Lowercase token beginning with a letter, followed by lowercase letters, digits or underscores. Maximum 32 characters. external is reserved. Exchange name Required string Nonempty printable display name without surrounding whitespace. Instrument exchange Required string Registered execution venue code. Instrument symbol Required string Nonempty, no whitespace. UNSPECIFIED is rejected. Instrument market_category Required enum spot, linear, inverse, equity, option. Instrument instrument_type Required enum spot, perpetual, future, equity, option. Spot, equity and option must agree with the category. Instrument base_asset, quote_asset Required asset tokens Declare currency or asset identity explicitly. Instrument settlement_asset Optional asset token Omitted when unknown or inapplicable. Instrument status Optional token Defaults to active.

items.title: Specifications
items.text:
The canonical instrument key has the form exchange.instrument_type.market_category.symbol. Use the identity already registered in the target catalogue. The specification declaration requires provenance and positive tick_size. Asset fields, when supplied, are assertions checked against the registered identity.

Path Type and requirement Rules and meaning instrument Required string Canonical instrument reference. provenance Required nonblank string Evidence description. as_of, fetched_at Conditionally required timezone-aware timestamps Retrieval time. Supply at least one for current observations. If both are supplied, they must agree. An omitted alias inherits the other. valid_from, valid_to Optional timezone-aware timestamps Supply both for historical applicability. Start precedes end. Dates can be TOML offset datetimes or datetime strings. quantity_type Required enum base, quote, contracts. contract_value, contract_value_asset Conditionally required decimal string and denomination Required for contracts. Positive finite size and explicit denomination must be paired. Spot and equity forbid contract sizing. tick_size, qty_step Exact decimal. Tick required, step optional Finite and positive. Tick is the price increment. Step uses the declared quantity unit. min_qty, max_qty Optional exact decimals Finite, nonnegative, and ordered when both are given. Units follow quantity_type. min_notional, max_notional Optional exact decimals Finite and nonnegative. When denominations agree, the minimum cannot exceed the maximum. min_notional_asset, max_notional_asset Optional strings Denominations for applicable notional bounds. base_asset, quote_asset, settlement_asset Optional asset tokens Asset assertions for the registered instrument.

Use TOML integers or quoted decimals for exact decimal fields. TOML floating-point values are rejected. The current and historical examples use synthetic values. Collection and inference rules are documented in historical metadata policies.

items.title: Conversion recipes
items.text:
The editable version-1 Forge recipe selects whole committed merge publications and historical reference trades. Use mf convert new to generate a source binding. Workflow · Standalone Engine job

Path Type and requirement Default and meaning version Required integer 1 Recipe schema source.kind Required merge, normalize, or acquisition Upstream recipe family source.reference, source.path Required nonblank strings Named or explicit upstream reference and resolved path, verified on load source.sha256 Required 64 lowercase hex characters Upstream TOML fingerprint interval.start_ns, interval.end_ns Required signed 64-bit Unix ns, start before end Requested half-open bounds used to check selection scope selection.file_dataset_ids, selection.publication_ids Optional nonempty unique positive signed-64-bit integer lists. Mutually exclusive Explicit file IDs or registry publication IDs selection.expected_engine_publication_ids Optional nonempty unique list of canonical positive uint64 decimal strings Exact Engine IDs expected after resolution selection.whole_publication Boolean false. Set true to approve an overlapping wider publication reference_stream_ids List of distinct nonblank strings Empty list. Explicit trade stream IDs reference_publication_id Optional positive signed-64-bit registry publication ID External trade-only merge, requires nonempty reference stream selection conversion.target_quote Required uppercase ASCII alphanumeric currency string Target quote unit conversion.price_source last_trade only last_trade conversion.max_staleness_ns Required positive uint64 in ns No model default. The new template sets 60 seconds conversion.max_hops Integer 1–4 3 conversion.path_policy all or primary all. Planning and execution constraints remain mode-specific conversion.instrument_kinds Optional nonempty unique list of spot, perpetual, future, option, equity Omitted selects all kinds resources.workers, resources.memory_limit_mb, resources.max_open_files Positive uint64 settings in workers, MiB and files 1, 1024, 64, capped by the conversion runtime during preparation

Absence of an optional field means omission in TOML. The Engine gets the resolved bindings, resources and writer configuration in a generated job. The Forge collection and execution intent are separate artifacts. Recipe model

items.title: Ranking and historical metadata policies
items.text: Configuration for ranking policies and historical specification and identity inference. Use market workflows for procedures.

items.title: Where Ranking Policies Are Stored
items.text:
Managed ranking policies live under:

data/.config/markets/rankings/

For example:

data/.config/markets/rankings/
├── turnover.toml
├── volume.toml
├── activity.toml
└── base-volume.toml

These files contain the policies used by MarketForge's ranking system.

items.title: Create a policy
items.text:
For example:

mf markets rank new activity

MarketForge creates:

data/.config/markets/rankings/activity.toml

The generated file is a version-2 turnover policy template.

items.title: Edit the policy
items.text:
Open it with:

nvim data/.config/markets/rankings/activity.toml

Update its fields to match your intended comparison.

items.title: Does new open an editor?
items.text:
No.

It creates the template file.

Edit it separately.

items.title: Does the policy name determine the metric?
items.text:
No.

For example:

mf markets rank new volume-example

still creates a turnover template.

To create a volume policy, write the appropriate volume configuration explicitly.

items.title: Can policy names be arbitrary paths?
items.text:
No.

Ranking commands use safe managed policy names.

For example:

activity
activity.toml

can refer to the managed policy.

Do not pass arbitrary directory paths or traversal expressions as policy names.

items.title: What does global --config do?
items.text:
The global option:

--config PATH

selects application settings.

It does not select a ranking policy.

For example:

mf --config ./workspace-settings.toml \
    markets rank validate activity

still validates the managed ranking policy named activity.

items.title: What Is Turnover?
items.text:
Turnover represents monetary trading activity over a measurement window.

For example:

BTCUSDT
24h turnover: 500,000,000 USDT

This represents monetary activity denominated in USDT.

items.title: Why rank by turnover?
items.text:
Turnover can provide a useful basis for comparing activity across different instruments.

For example:

BTCUSDT
ETHUSDT
SOLUSDT

have different base assets.

Their base quantities cannot be compared directly.

However, their monetary activity can be compared when expressed in a consistent currency and supported by compatible observations.

items.title: Is turnover always directly reported?
items.text:
No.

Different exchanges provide different statistics.

Some supply monetary turnover directly.

Others provide contract volume or base volume that requires additional interpretation.

For example:

Base volume × Reference price

can produce an estimate of monetary activity.

But this is not necessarily equivalent to an exchange-reported accumulated turnover.

items.title: Why preserve the distinction?
items.text:
Because an estimated amount may be less reliable than a directly reported amount for certain research purposes.

MarketForge preserves the relevant interpretation evidence.

Ranking policies can explicitly allow or exclude estimates.

items.title: A Complete Turnover Policy
items.text:
The following example creates a ranking of supported Bybit markets using USDT as the comparison currency.

Save it as:

data/.config/markets/rankings/activity.toml

version = 2

metric = "turnover_24h"
comparison_currency = "USDT"

exchanges = ["bybit"]
markets = ["spot", "linear", "inverse"]
instruments = []

max_age_seconds = 3600
max_window_skew_seconds = 300

estimates = "exclude"
allow_partial_universe = true

manual_preferences = []

[conversion]
automatic = true
valuation = "reference_price_turnover"

max_price_age_seconds = 3600
max_leg_skew_seconds = 300

max_hops = 2
bridge_assets = []

prefer_same_exchange = true
allow_cross_exchange = false
allow_mixed_exchanges = false

source_exchanges = [
    "bybit",
    "binance",
    "okx",
    "gateio",
    "bitget",
]

equivalent_currencies = []

This is a complete version-2 turnover policy.

items.title: What does it do?
items.text:
The policy requests:

Property Value Metric 24-hour turnover Comparison currency USDT Exchanges Bybit Markets Spot, linear, inverse Maximum observation age 1 hour Maximum source-window skew 5 minutes Estimated turnover Excluded Partial universe Allowed Automatic currency conversion Enabled Maximum conversion hops 2 Mixed-exchange conversion legs Not allowed

items.title: Important limitation
items.text:
This policy is structurally valid.

However, a successful ranking build still requires suitable stored observations and eligible currency conversion references.

The example does not claim those observations are currently available.

items.title: Why allow partial coverage in this example?
items.text:
The example uses:

allow_partial_universe = true

to demonstrate how MarketForge can publish eligible entries while recording exclusions.

The generated turnover template is stricter and defaults to:

allow_partial_universe = false

Choose the behavior deliberately.

items.title: Policy Versions
items.text:
Ranking policies support two versions.

Version Default conversion behavior 1 Automatic currency conversion disabled by default. 2 Automatic currency conversion enabled by default for turnover.

items.title: Version 1
items.text:
For example:

version = 1

This uses the older policy behavior.

Automatic conversion is disabled unless explicitly configured.

items.title: Version 2
items.text:
For example:

version = 2

This enables automatic spot-price conversion by default for turnover policies.

items.title: Why does the distinction matter?
items.text:
Suppose your ranking includes BTC-denominated turnover but compares values in USDT.

Without an applicable conversion rule, the BTC amount cannot be scored in USDT.

Version 2 provides the supported automatic conversion configuration by default.

However, automatic conversion still depends on actual eligible stored spot-price observations.

items.title: What if version is omitted?
items.text:
The policy defaults to version 1.

For new policies, explicitly use:

version = 2

when you want the current version-2 behavior.

items.title: Choose the Ranking Metric
items.text:
The metric field specifies what MarketForge compares.

The current values are:

turnover_24h
volume

items.title: Turnover
items.text:
Use:

metric = "turnover_24h"

This selects monetary activity comparison.

items.title: Volume
items.text:
Use:

metric = "volume"

This selects grouped base-asset quantity comparison.

items.title: Can I rank by open interest?
items.text:
Not through the current general ranking metric schema.

MarketForge can retain supported open-interest observations, but the ranking policy currently supports turnover and volume.

items.title: Can I rank by funding rate?
items.text:
Not through the current ranking metric schema.

Funding rates are separate retained market statistics.

items.title: Does the metric determine how currency conversion works?
items.text:
Yes.

Turnover policies can use a comparison currency and supported FX conversion rules.

Volume policies instead compare quantities within base-asset groups.

These are different comparison models.

items.title: What Is the Ranking Universe?
items.text:
The ranking universe is the set of instruments that the policy attempts to evaluate.

For example:

All supported Bybit spot instruments

or:

Bybit and OKX linear perpetual markets

A ranking cannot meaningfully compare every conceivable instrument without defining which markets belong to its intended selection.

MarketForge therefore provides explicit universe filters.

items.title: Example
items.text:
exchanges = ["bybit"]
markets = ["spot", "linear"]

This restricts the policy to the supported instruments matching those exchange and market selections.

items.title: Why define the universe?
items.text:
Suppose you want a ranking of Bybit spot activity.

Including unrelated inverse futures would change the meaning of the result.

The universe makes the comparison explicit.

items.title: When are filters applied?
items.text:
Universe filters are applied during ranking evaluation.

They define which instruments are considered.

They are different from display filters used when inspecting an already published ranking.

items.title: Exchange Selection
items.text:
Use:

exchanges = ["bybit"]

to restrict the ranking to Bybit.

items.title: Multiple exchanges
items.text:
For example:

exchanges = ["bybit", "okx"]

This selects instruments from both exchanges.

items.title: All supported exchanges
items.text:
An empty list means the supported exchange universe is not restricted by an explicit exchange filter.

For example:

exchanges = []

items.title: Supported exchange codes
items.text:
The current market-ranking system recognizes:

binance
bybit
okx
gateio
bitget

items.title: Does including an exchange guarantee observations?
items.text:
No.

An exchange may be selected by the policy even when some of its instruments lack suitable statistics.

Those instruments may be excluded or cause a strict build failure.

items.title: Does selecting several exchanges automatically make turnover comparable?
items.text:
No.

Different exchanges may report different units, measurement windows, or turnover semantics.

MarketForge applies the relevant eligibility and conversion rules before assigning scores.

items.title: Market Category Selection
items.text:
The markets field controls which market categories belong to the universe.

For example:

markets = ["spot", "linear", "inverse"]

items.title: Supported values
items.text: Value Meaning spot Spot markets. linear Linear derivative markets. inverse Inverse derivative markets.

items.title: Can the list be empty?
items.text:
No.

At least one market category is required.

items.title: Are options included?
items.text:
No.

The current ranking universe does not include options.

items.title: Can I select only linear markets?
items.text:
Yes.

For example:

markets = ["linear"]

items.title: Does linear mean perpetual only?
items.text:
No.

The linear category can include perpetual contracts and supported dated futures.

Market category and instrument type are separate properties.

items.title: What if I want perpetuals only?
items.text:
The current ranking policy does not provide a general instrument_type universe field.

Use exact instrument references when you need to restrict the policy to specific instruments.

Alternatively, use the supported instrument-type filter when inspecting an existing ranking.

Remember that inspection filters do not change the original ranking universe.

items.title: Select Specific Instruments
items.text:
The policy supports an explicit instrument list.

For example:

instruments = []

An empty list means no additional exact-reference restriction.

items.title: Why select instruments explicitly?
items.text:
Suppose you want to compare a small research universe rather than every supported instrument.

For example:

Bybit BTCUSDT Spot
Bybit ETHUSDT Spot
Bybit SOLUSDT Spot

You can provide the exact canonical references returned by the stored market catalogue.

items.title: Important: use actual returned references
items.text:
Do not construct instrument references by guessing how symbols are organized.

The relevant reference can have the form:

exchange.market.symbol

or a type-qualified form when required:

exchange.market.instrument_type.symbol

Use the exact value returned by MarketForge.

items.title: Example
items.text:
After inspecting:

mf markets list \
    --testing \
    --exchange bybit \
    --market spot

you can use the returned references in:

instruments = [
    "bybit.spot.BTCUSDT",
    "bybit.spot.ETHUSDT",
]

This is an illustrative selection using the ordinary market-reference form.

The referenced instruments must exist in the selected catalogue.

items.title: Are wildcards supported?
items.text:
Not in the policy's instruments field.

For example:

instruments = ["BTC*"]

does not mean every BTC instrument.

Use exact stored references.

items.title: Can I select instruments by base asset?
items.text:
The current policy does not provide a general base_asset field for universe selection.

Use exact references if you need a restricted group.

You can filter displayed ranking results by base asset later, but that does not change the original policy evaluation.

items.title: Why Ranking Freshness Matters
items.text:
Market statistics describe observations made at particular times.

For example, one exchange may report a 24-hour turnover value ending at noon.

Another exchange may report its rolling window ending several hours earlier.

These observations may both be valid, but they are not necessarily suitable for direct comparison.

MarketForge therefore applies freshness and window-alignment requirements.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Imagine:

Bybit BTCUSDT
Window end: 12:00 UTC

OKX BTCUSDT
Window end: 08:00 UTC

Comparing the two values as though they represented the same recent 24-hour period could be misleading.

items.title: Why not just check the fetch time?
items.text:
Because a recently fetched statistic can still describe an old source window.

For example:

Fetched at: 12:00
Window end: 08:00

The HTTP request completed recently.

However, the underlying measurement ends four hours earlier.

MarketForge checks the relevant observation and source-window information separately.

items.title: Maximum Observation Age
items.text:
Use:

max_age_seconds = 3600

This sets the maximum accepted observation age to one hour.

items.title: Accepted range
items.text:
The supported range is:

1–604800 seconds

604800 seconds is seven days.

items.title: What does the policy check?
items.text:
The ranking evaluator checks relevant timestamps, including:

  • Fetch time.
  • Source-window end.

An observation can be rejected when its timestamps are too old for the selected policy.

items.title: Why does this matter?
items.text:
Suppose you build a ranking using observations collected yesterday.

If the policy requires data no older than one hour, the observations do not satisfy the policy.

MarketForge does not silently reinterpret the stale values as current.

items.title: Does a longer maximum age improve ranking quality?
items.text:
Not automatically.

A larger age limit permits older observations.

That may be appropriate for some comparisons, but it also increases the chance of combining measurements from different market conditions.

Choose the limit based on the intended use.

items.title: Source-Window Alignment
items.text:
Use:

max_window_skew_seconds = 300

This sets a five-minute tolerance.

items.title: Accepted range
items.text:
The supported range is:

0–86400 seconds

items.title: Why compare source windows?
items.text:
Suppose two turnover measurements were collected at different times.

For example:

Market A:
Window end 12:00

Market B:
Window end 11:58

A five-minute tolerance can permit this difference when the remaining requirements are satisfied.

Now consider:

Market A:
Window end 12:00

Market B:
Window end 10:00

These windows differ by two hours.

The second observation may be rejected under the five-minute alignment policy.

items.title: Does window skew control future timestamps?
items.text:
It also participates in the supported future-time checks.

For example, a source observation reporting a measurement window far into the future relative to the ranking build time is not automatically accepted.

items.title: Volume-specific requirement
items.text:
Volume ranking also requires a compatible 24-hour measurement duration.

This matters because comparing quantities measured over substantially different durations would not represent the same activity window.

items.title: Does a successful statistics refresh guarantee compatible windows?
items.text:
No.

A provider may return observations whose source times or inferred measurement windows do not satisfy the ranking policy.

The build performs the relevant checks independently.

items.title: Estimated Turnover
items.text:
Some providers report monetary turnover directly.

Others supply quantities that can be used to estimate monetary activity.

For example:

Base volume × Last price

can produce an estimated turnover.

items.title: Why is this an estimate?
items.text:
Because the last price is not necessarily the price at which every trade in the measurement window occurred.

For example:

Volume: 1,000 BTC
Last price: 80,000 USDT

gives:

Estimated turnover: 80,000,000 USDT

However, the actual trades may have occurred at several different prices.

The estimated result is not necessarily equal to the true accumulated execution turnover.

items.title: Configure estimate handling
items.text:
The policy supports:

estimates = "exclude"

or:

estimates = "allow"

items.title: Exclude estimates
items.text:
estimates = "exclude"

rejects relevant estimated values under the ranking eligibility rules.

This is the default.

items.title: Allow estimates
items.text:
estimates = "allow"

permits the supported estimated values.

Their derivation evidence remains available.

items.title: Important distinction
items.text:
The estimates setting controls the relevant volume-derived estimates.

It does not prohibit the separate ranking convention of valuing native monetary turnover using an eligible reference FX price.

These are different operations.

items.title: Strict Rankings
items.text:
By default, a ranking policy uses:

allow_partial_universe = false

This is the strict behavior.

items.title: What does strict mean?
items.text:
MarketForge expects the selected universe to satisfy the required comparison rules.

For example:

BTCUSDT  Eligible
ETHUSDT  Eligible
SOLUSDT  Missing turnover

If the policy requires a complete eligible universe, the missing observation can prevent publication.

items.title: Why reject the ranking?
items.text: Because publishing only BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT without acknowledging the missing SOLUSDT value could make the result appear more complete than it is.

items.title: What happens to an unsuccessful build?
items.text:
An unsuccessful ranking build does not publish a valid new snapshot.

The attempted publication is rolled back.

Previously published snapshots remain available.

items.title: Partial Rankings
items.text:
You can explicitly permit exclusions:

allow_partial_universe = true

items.title: What does this mean?
items.text:
MarketForge can publish eligible entries while recording why other selected instruments were excluded.

For example:

Included:
BTCUSDT
ETHUSDT

Excluded:
SOLUSDT — missing turnover
XRPUSDT — stale observation

items.title: Does partial mode accept invalid values?
items.text:
No.

Missing turnover remains missing.

Stale observations remain stale.

Invalid units remain invalid.

The setting permits eligible entries to be published with exclusions and the supported partial-refresh handling.

It does not convert invalid inputs into valid scores.

items.title: Can the result contain zero eligible instruments?
items.text:
No.

At least one comparable entry is required.

items.title: Why preserve exclusions?
items.text:
An excluded instrument is not equivalent to a low-ranked instrument.

For example:

Rank 100

means the instrument was included and received that position.

Excluded: missing turnover

means the instrument could not be scored under the policy.

This distinction is essential when interpreting ranking results.

items.title: Why Does Turnover Need Currency Conversion?
items.text:
Suppose you want one ranking containing instruments whose monetary turnover is expressed in different currencies.

For example:

Instrument Native turnover BTCUSDT 500 million USDT BTCUSDC 450 million USDC ETHBTC 2,000 BTC

You cannot compare the bare numeric values directly.

A turnover policy therefore uses:

comparison_currency = "USDT"

This tells MarketForge to express eligible monetary activity in USDT.

items.title: Does MarketForge assume USDT and USDC are identical?
items.text:
No.

USD, USDT, and USDC remain distinct currencies.

Any equivalence must be explicit.

items.title: Where do conversion rates come from?
items.text:
The current turnover-ranking policy supports:

  1. Identity conversion.
  2. Explicit manual rates.
  3. Explicit currency-equivalence assumptions.
  4. Eligible stored spot-market prices.

The ranking evaluator uses this precedence.

items.title: Conversion Precedence
items.text:
The conversion system applies the supported methods in this order.

Native Turnover Currency
          |
          v
Already Target Currency?
          |
          +-- Yes --> Identity
          |
          v
Explicit Manual Rate?
          |
          +-- Yes --> Manual Conversion
          |
          v
Explicit Equivalence?
          |
          +-- Yes --> 1:1 Assumption
          |
          v
Eligible Spot Price Path?
          |
          +-- Yes --> Automatic Conversion
          |
          v
No Eligible Conversion

items.title: Identity conversion
items.text:
Suppose the native currency is already USDT.

The comparison currency is also USDT.

No exchange-rate conversion is necessary.

items.title: Manual conversion
items.text:
A user may provide a documented rate.

For example, a manual EUR-to-USDT rate.

items.title: Explicit equivalence
items.text:
A policy may explicitly declare that a native currency should be treated as equivalent to the comparison currency.

This is an assumption, not an independently verified market rate.

items.title: Stored spot conversion
items.text: MarketForge can search eligible stored spot-price observations for a supported currency path.

items.title: What happens if none works?
items.text:
The instrument cannot receive a valid common-currency turnover score under that policy.

It may be excluded or cause the ranking build to fail, depending on the selected universe and partial-coverage rules.

items.title: Automatic Spot-Price Conversion
items.text:
Version-2 turnover policies support:

[conversion]
automatic = true

This enables automatic conversion using eligible stored spot-market prices.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose the native turnover is denominated in BTC.

The comparison currency is USDT.

An eligible BTCUSDT spot observation can establish:

BTC → USDT

items.title: Direct conversion
items.text:
For example:

2 BTC × 80,000 USDT/BTC = 160,000 USDT

The values are illustrative.

items.title: Inverse conversion
items.text:
The same currency relationship can be used in reverse when the supported source price is appropriate.

For example:

USDT → BTC

uses the inverse price relationship.

items.title: Why only use eligible spot prices?
items.text:
Ranking conversion needs a currency relationship that can be interpreted according to the supported policy.

The current ranking system uses stored spot-market references.

Derivative last prices are not general-purpose ranking FX sources.

items.title: Does automatic conversion contact exchanges?
items.text:
Not during rank build.

The build uses retained observations.

If the necessary spot prices are missing, obtain suitable market statistics through the separate collection workflow.

items.title: Maximum Conversion Hops
items.text:
The policy supports:

max_hops = 2

Accepted values are:

1
2

items.title: One hop
items.text:
A direct conversion path:

BTC → USDT

items.title: Two hops
items.text:
A bridged conversion path:

USDC → BTC → USDT

This uses one intermediate asset.

items.title: Why limit the path length?
items.text:
Each conversion leg introduces another observation with its own timestamp and source.

Longer paths can become more difficult to compare reliably.

The current policy therefore supports direct paths or one bridge.

items.title: Can I configure three or four hops?
items.text:
Not in the current ranking conversion schema.

The historical conversion Engine has a separate policy and different supported hop limits.

Do not confuse the two systems.

items.title: Bridge Assets
items.text:
The conversion policy supports:

bridge_assets = []

items.title: What is a bridge asset?
items.text:
A bridge asset is an intermediate currency used when no direct conversion is available.

For example:

USDC → BTC → USDT

uses BTC as a bridge.

items.title: Empty bridge list
items.text: An empty list allows any eligible connecting spot asset under the supported conversion rules.

items.title: Restricted bridge list
items.text:
For example:

bridge_assets = ["BTC", "ETH"]

restricts intermediate assets to the listed currencies.

The list also provides their configured preference order.

items.title: Why restrict bridges?
items.text:
You may want to avoid conversion paths involving obscure or unsuitable intermediate markets.

A restricted bridge list makes the permitted intermediate assets explicit.

items.title: Default behavior
items.text:
When the field is omitted, the supported default bridge assets are BTC and ETH.

An explicitly empty list is different.

For example:

bridge_assets = []

means the connecting-asset choice is not restricted to that default pair.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
A nonempty bridge list can contain up to 16 unique uppercase currency codes.

Duplicate bridge assets are rejected.

items.title: Exchange Preferences
items.text:
The conversion policy supports:

prefer_same_exchange = true
allow_cross_exchange = false
allow_mixed_exchanges = false

These fields control which exchanges can provide conversion references.

items.title: Prefer the same exchange
items.text:
For example, suppose you are ranking a Bybit instrument.

A suitable Bybit spot reference is preferred over a foreign-exchange reference under the supported ordering rules.

The current schema requires:

prefer_same_exchange = true

items.title: Cross-exchange conversion
items.text:
The policy can permit a complete conversion path from another allowed exchange.

For example:

allow_cross_exchange = true

This can be useful when the target exchange lacks an eligible conversion market.

However, the reference still needs to satisfy the applicable age and alignment checks.

items.title: Mixed-exchange paths
items.text:
The current policy requires:

allow_mixed_exchanges = false

This means a two-leg conversion path cannot combine legs from different exchanges.

For example:

Leg 1: Bybit
Leg 2: Binance

is not a supported mixed-venue path.

items.title: Why restrict mixed exchanges?
items.text:
Different exchanges can have different:

  • Liquidity conditions.
  • Price observations.
  • Measurement times.
  • Trading conventions.

Combining observations from different venues can introduce additional comparability problems.

The current policy therefore requires complete paths to satisfy its supported venue constraints.

items.title: Reference Exchange Selection
items.text:
The policy supports:

source_exchanges = [
    "bybit",
    "binance",
    "okx",
    "gateio",
    "bitget",
]

This specifies the allowed reference exchanges and their preference order.

items.title: Why does order matter?
items.text:
When several conversion paths are eligible, MarketForge uses deterministic preference rules.

The configured exchange order can help resolve otherwise comparable candidates.

items.title: Does listing an exchange guarantee its prices are used?
items.text:
No.

The source must still be eligible under:

  • Exchange permissions.
  • Available spot instruments.
  • Observation freshness.
  • Currency path requirements.
  • Measurement timing.
  • Other conversion constraints.

items.title: Does source_exchanges override allow_cross_exchange?
items.text:
No.

Listing another exchange as a possible reference source does not automatically authorize cross-exchange conversion.

The applicable permission settings still control eligibility.

items.title: How MarketForge Chooses a Conversion Path
items.text:
When several eligible spot-price paths exist, MarketForge applies a deterministic preference order.

The supported rules consider:

  1. Same-exchange paths before permitted foreign-exchange paths.
  2. Fewer conversion legs.
  3. Configured source-exchange preference.
  4. Freshness of the weakest conversion leg.
  5. Configured bridge-asset preference.
  6. Stable identity tie-breakers.

items.title: Why use deterministic selection?
items.text:
Suppose several exchanges provide a BTCUSDT reference price.

Without a defined preference policy, the selected rate could depend on incidental database ordering.

That would make ranking results harder to explain.

MarketForge therefore defines how eligible paths are selected.

items.title: Can a local bridged path beat a foreign direct path?
items.text:
Yes.

Same-exchange preference is evaluated before the number of legs under the current policy.

For example:

Bybit:
USDC → BTC → USDT

may be preferred over:

Binance:
USDC → USDT

when both are eligible and the policy permits the foreign reference.

items.title: Does fewer hops always win?
items.text:
Not across every possible exchange relationship.

The complete preference order matters.

items.title: Does selecting a path guarantee the underlying rate is perfect?
items.text:
No.

The conversion uses eligible retained observations and the specified valuation convention.

It does not reconstruct every actual execution-time currency rate within the turnover measurement window.

items.title: Conversion Reference Freshness
items.text:
The conversion policy has separate limits for spot-price references.

For example:

max_price_age_seconds = 3600
max_leg_skew_seconds = 300

items.title: Maximum price age
items.text:
max_price_age_seconds = 3600

sets the maximum accepted age of relevant conversion-price observations.

The supported explicit range is:

1–604800 seconds

If omitted, the setting inherits the policy's general maximum observation age.

items.title: Maximum leg skew
items.text:
max_leg_skew_seconds = 300

controls the allowed timing difference between relevant conversion legs.

The supported explicit range is:

0–86400 seconds

If omitted, it inherits the general source-window skew setting.

items.title: Why have separate limits?
items.text:
The turnover observation and the conversion prices are different pieces of evidence.

For example:

Turnover observation:
12:00

Conversion reference:
09:00

The turnover may be fresh while its reference price is too old.

MarketForge checks these conditions independently.

items.title: Can a stale reference be accepted because the turnover is fresh?
items.text:
Not when it violates the configured conversion policy.

A valid turnover observation does not make an invalid reference price suitable.

items.title: Explicit Currency Equivalence
items.text:
Sometimes users want to make an explicit 1:1 currency assumption.

For example, a policy might use USDT as its comparison currency while treating USD as equivalent.

This can be declared as:

[conversion]
equivalent_currencies = ["USD"]

items.title: What does this mean?
items.text:
It explicitly assumes:

1 USD = 1 USDT

for the ranking comparison.

items.title: Is this an actual market-price observation?
items.text:
No.

It is a user-supplied modeling assumption.

MarketForge does not independently prove that the currencies were trading at exactly the same value.

items.title: Why is this important for stablecoins?
items.text:
Stablecoin prices can differ from their intended reference currencies.

For example, USDC and USDT are distinct assets.

A 1:1 equivalence should not be silently assumed.

items.title: Does MarketForge enable equivalence by default?
items.text:
No.

The default is:

equivalent_currencies = []

items.title: Can the comparison currency appear in the list?
items.text:
No.

For example, if the comparison currency is USDT, do not include USDT itself.

Identity conversion already handles that case.

items.title: Manual Conversion Rates
items.text:
A policy can provide explicit rates when appropriate.

For example:

[conversion.manual_rates.EUR]
rate = "1.08"
as_of = 2026-11-20T12:00:00Z
source = "Documented reference observation"

This is an illustrative declaration.

It is not a verified historical EUR/USDT rate.

items.title: What does the rate mean?
items.text:
The rate represents units of the comparison currency per one unit of the native currency.

For example, with USDT as the comparison currency:

1 EUR = 1.08 USDT

under the supplied manual assumption.

items.title: Why use a decimal string?
items.text:
Financial rates benefit from exact decimal representation.

For example:

rate = "1.08"

preserves the intended decimal value.

items.title: Why require as_of?
items.text:
MarketForge needs to know when the rate was actually observed.

The timestamp must include a timezone.

items.title: Why require source?
items.text:
A manual rate can materially affect ranking scores.

The source field records its provenance.

items.title: Does a stale manual rate fall back to automatic conversion?
items.text:
No.

If a configured manual override fails the applicable freshness or future-time checks, MarketForge does not silently replace it with an unrelated spot-price path.

Review the manual rate deliberately.

items.title: What about a manual rate for the comparison currency?
items.text:
If a manual rate is supplied for the comparison currency itself, it must equal 1.

Identity conversion always takes precedence.

items.title: Legacy Manual Rate Fields
items.text:
Older ranking policies may contain top-level conversion fields.

The supported legacy fields include:

conversion_rates
conversion_as_of
conversion_source

These remain readable for compatibility.

items.title: Why retain them?
items.text: Existing ranking policies should not become unreadable merely because the supported configuration has evolved.

items.title: Should new policies use them?
items.text:
For new version-2 policies, prefer the structured manual-rate declarations under:

[conversion.manual_rates.CURRENCY]

items.title: Can I declare the same currency twice?
items.text:
No.

A currency cannot appear in both the legacy manual-rate map and the newer structured manual-rate configuration.

This prevents conflicting declarations.

items.title: Do legacy rates require provenance?
items.text:
Yes.

The relevant manual conversion information requires an observation time and source.

For legacy rates, the supported top-level provenance fields must be supplied.

items.title: Precision of Ranking Scores
items.text: MarketForge uses decimal representations and retained conversion evidence when calculating ranking scores.

items.title: Why does precision matter?
items.text:
A ranking may compare very large monetary amounts.

For example:

1,000,000,000 USDT

It may also use conversion rates with many decimal places.

Unnecessary floating-point rounding can affect close comparisons.

items.title: How are rates and scores retained?
items.text:
The current implementation preserves exact-ratio evidence from decimal inputs.

Stored rates and scores are rounded to 80 significant digits.

items.title: Does the terminal display all 80 digits?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

Terminal presentation can abbreviate large or precise values.

The displayed representation is not the full calculation precision.

items.title: How can I inspect the evidence?
items.text:
Use the ranking inspection commands.

For example:

mf markets rank show activity \
    --testing \
    --conversion 1

Replace 1 with a valid stored position or use an exact returned instrument reference.

The output exposes the applicable conversion or volume derivation evidence.

items.title: What Are Manual Preferences?
items.text:
A turnover ranking normally orders eligible instruments by their calculated scores.

For example:

1. BTCUSDT
2. ETHUSDT
3. SOLUSDT

However, the policy can also specify manual ordering preferences.

These are declared through:

manual_preferences = []

items.title: Why support manual preferences?
items.text:
A research workflow may intentionally prioritize certain instruments.

For example, you might want a particular reference market to appear before otherwise higher-scoring instruments.

items.title: How are preferences supplied?
items.text:
Use exact stored instrument references.

For example:

manual_preferences = [
    "bybit.spot.BTCUSDT",
]

This is an illustrative reference.

Use the exact reference returned by the catalogue.

items.title: What happens during ranking?
items.text:
Specified preferences can move the selected turnover instruments ahead of the ordinary score ordering.

The remaining eligible instruments are ordered according to the supported score and stable-reference rules.

items.title: Does this mean the ranking is purely descending turnover?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

When manual preferences are present, the final order includes an explicit policy decision.

The published snapshot retains the policy and ordering evidence.

items.title: Are manual preferences allowed in volume rankings?
items.text:
No.

Volume rankings reject manual preferences.

Their ordering is based on supported base-asset quantity comparisons within each group.

items.title: Can preferences contain duplicates?
items.text:
No.

Duplicate references are rejected.

References outside the selected ranking universe are also invalid.

items.title: Why Volume Rankings Are Different
items.text:
Turnover rankings compare monetary activity.

Volume rankings compare quantities.

These are different measurements.

For example:

BTCUSDT:
Volume = 1,000 BTC

ETHUSDT:
Volume = 20,000 ETH

The numeric values cannot be interpreted as one universal quantity comparison.

The assets are different.

items.title: Why not rank them together?
items.text:
Because 1,000 BTC and 20,000 ETH are quantities expressed in different units.

Comparing their bare numbers does not establish which market has greater monetary activity.

items.title: How does MarketForge handle this?
items.text:
Volume rankings group instruments by base asset.

For example:

BTC Group
    BTCUSDT
    BTCUSDC
    BTCUSD

ETH Group
    ETHUSDT
    ETHUSDC
    ETHBTC

Each group is ranked independently.

items.title: Why is this useful?
items.text:
You may want to compare trading activity across markets for the same underlying asset.

For example:

BTC Spot
BTC Linear Perpetual
BTC Inverse Perpetual
BTC Futures

When the required quantity evidence is available, MarketForge can compare their supported base-asset volumes.

items.title: A Complete Volume Policy
items.text:
Volume policies use a different configuration structure from turnover policies.

For example, save this as:

data/.config/markets/rankings/base-volume.toml

version = 2

metric = "volume"

volume_unit = "base_asset"
group_by = "base_asset"

exchanges = ["bybit"]
markets = ["spot", "linear", "inverse"]

max_age_seconds = 3600
max_window_skew_seconds = 300

estimates = "exclude"
allow_partial_universe = true

This is a complete illustrative base-asset volume policy.

items.title: What does it select?
items.text: Property Value Metric Volume Unit Base asset Grouping Base asset Exchange Bybit Markets Spot, linear, inverse Maximum observation age 1 hour Maximum window skew 5 minutes Estimated quantities Excluded Partial coverage Allowed

items.title: Why are both fields required?
items.text:
The policy requires:

volume_unit = "base_asset"

and:

group_by = "base_asset"

These establish the quantity denomination and grouping semantics.

items.title: Can I omit one?
items.text:
No.

Both must be supplied explicitly for the volume metric.

items.title: Does volume use a comparison currency?
items.text:
No.

Do not include:

comparison_currency = "USDT"

inside a volume policy.

That field belongs to turnover comparison.

items.title: Does volume use automatic FX conversion?
items.text:
No.

Volume policies reject the turnover-specific [conversion] configuration.

They also reject legacy currency rates and manual ranking preferences.

items.title: How Volume Is Interpreted
items.text:
Some exchanges report quantities directly in base-asset units.

For example:

BTCUSDT Spot
Volume: 1,000 BTC

This can be used as base volume when the reported interpretation is trustworthy.

However, derivative markets may report contract counts.

items.title: Example: Contract quantity
items.text:
Suppose an exchange reports:

Volume: 100,000 contracts

This does not directly tell us how many BTC were traded.

MarketForge needs the contract specification.

items.title: Base-denominated contract value
items.text:
Suppose the registered contract specification states:

1 contract = 0.01 BTC

Then:

100,000 contracts × 0.01 BTC
= 1,000 BTC

When the relevant specification evidence is valid, this supports an exact contract-count conversion.

items.title: Quote-denominated contract value
items.text:
Another derivative might specify:

1 contract = 100 USD

Converting that count into BTC quantity may require a price observation.

For example:

Contract count × USD face value ÷ BTC price

This introduces a price-based estimate.

items.title: Why distinguish exact and estimated quantities?
items.text:
Because a contract-count conversion using a verified base-denominated multiplier is different from a conversion that depends on a reference market price.

The latter introduces additional assumptions.

MarketForge retains the relevant derivation evidence.

items.title: What if the contract specification is missing?
items.text:
The quantity cannot be safely converted into base units under that method.

The instrument may be excluded or cause strict ranking rejection.

Do not invent a contract multiplier merely to obtain a score.

items.title: Zero Volume vs. Missing Volume
items.text:
This distinction matters for ranking.

Suppose one instrument reports:

Volume: 0 BTC

Another has no trustworthy base-volume observation.

These cases are different.

items.title: Reported zero
items.text:
A reliable reported zero is a valid numeric observation.

It may indicate no measured volume during the applicable window.

items.title: Missing observation
items.text:
A missing value means the relevant quantity is unavailable.

It does not mean zero trading occurred.

items.title: Why preserve this distinction?
items.text:
Treating missing values as zero would place instruments at the bottom of a ranking without evidence that they actually had no trading activity.

MarketForge therefore keeps missing information separate from valid zero quantities.

items.title: Does partial mode change this?
items.text:
No.

Partial mode can permit exclusions.

It does not turn missing values into zeros.

items.title: Volume Ranking Positions
items.text: Volume rankings retain both a unique stored position and a rank within each base-asset group.

items.title: Example
items.text:
BTC Group

Group rank 1: BTCUSDT
Group rank 2: BTCUSDC


ETH Group

Group rank 1: ETHUSDT
Group rank 2: ETHBTC

Each group has its own rank 1.

items.title: Why is this important?
items.text:
A BTC instrument at stored position 2 is not automatically economically comparable to an ETH instrument at stored position 3.

The relevant volume comparison occurs within each base-asset group.

items.title: What is group_rank?
items.text: It identifies the instrument's position within its asset group.

items.title: Does filtering change group ranks?
items.text:
No.

Published positions and group ranks remain fixed.

For example, filtering to Bybit perpetual instruments does not cause MarketForge to recalculate the original ranking.

items.title: What if quantities are equal?
items.text:
The ranking uses deterministic reference-based tie-breaking under its supported ordering rules.

This helps keep results stable when eligible quantities are equal.

items.title: Historical metadata inference
items.text:
MarketForge works with historical financial data.

However, exchanges do not always provide a complete historical catalogue of every instrument and its specifications.

For example, you might have an OKX futures archive containing trades from a contract that expired several years ago.

The source file may still be available.

However, the exchange's current API might no longer provide all the corresponding historical specifications.

items.title: Why is this a problem?
items.text:
To normalize the trades correctly, MarketForge needs to know the contract's economic properties.

For example:

  • The instrument identity.
  • Contract value.
  • Contract denomination.
  • Quantity type.
  • Base and quote assets.
  • Settlement asset.
  • Historical applicability.

Without this information, a raw quantity such as:

100 contracts

cannot be safely interpreted.

items.title: What if historical specifications are missing?
items.text:
MarketForge supports a controlled metadata-enrichment policy.

It can use retained catalogue information and compatible reference-contract evidence to establish operationally applicable metadata.

This is different from inventing arbitrary contract specifications.

items.title: Why is the distinction important?
items.text:
A metadata value inferred from a related instrument may be operationally useful.

However, it is not necessarily independently verified as historically correct.

MarketForge distinguishes operational inference from verified historical authority.

items.title: How Historical Enrichment Fits into Initialization
items.text:
The current initialization workflow includes historical metadata enrichment.

Run:

mf init --testing

The full initialization workflow performs several stages.

Conceptually:

Application Setup
        |
        v
Database Migrations
        |
        v
Current Catalogue Collection
        |
        v
Historical Metadata Enrichment
        |
        v
Standard Ranking Publication

items.title: What does enrichment do?
items.text:
The historical enrichment stage can:

  • Inspect registered exchange downloads.
  • Establish canonical instrument identities.
  • Preserve current API observations.
  • Resolve available historical specification evidence.
  • Examine supported contract-family relationships.
  • Append immutable specification evidence.
  • Report unresolved metadata.

items.title: Does enrichment download raw archives?
items.text:
No.

It operates on the relevant existing registered information and managed raw inputs.

It does not replace the historical acquisition workflow.

items.title: Does it copy or re-register raw files?
items.text:
No.

The enrichment stage does not create a separate raw-data registry or move existing raw files into another storage subsystem.

items.title: What if an exchange metadata scope fails?
items.text:
Previously retained observations can remain available.

Initialization reports exchange collection failures separately from historical metadata readiness.

One successful metadata stage does not automatically mean every historical archive is ready for normalization.

items.title: The Historical Inference Policy
items.text:
MarketForge currently uses a named historical metadata inference policy:

catalogue-btc-reference-v1

This policy defines how supported historical specifications are resolved.

items.title: Why use a named policy?
items.text:
Inference rules should be explicit and traceable.

For example, a future change to the inference algorithm should not silently redefine the meaning of earlier evidence.

A named policy allows MarketForge to record which interpretation rules were used.

items.title: Evidence precedence
items.text:
The current policy considers evidence in the following order:

  1. Historically verified specifications.
  2. Immutable historical declarations.
  3. Exact retained catalogue specifications.
  4. Compatible BTC futures or options reference evidence.

items.title: Why is precedence important?
items.text:
Not all metadata sources provide the same authority.
