For example, an explicit historical specification supported by exchange documentation should not be silently replaced by a value inferred from another contract.

The policy therefore gives stronger evidence precedence over weaker inference.

items.title: Can inference override conflicting explicit declarations?
items.text:
No.

Conflicting explicit declarations block preparation.

MarketForge does not resolve those conflicts by silently falling back to inferred values.

items.title: Why?
items.text:
Because doing so could replace historically established instrument rules with an assumption.

For financial data, such substitutions can materially change the interpreted quantities.

items.title: Why Use BTC Reference Contracts?
items.text:
Some derivative markets contain families of contracts with shared economic conventions.

For example, a futures chain may contain several dated BTC contracts belonging to the same product family.

A compatible contract may provide useful evidence about shared specification fields.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Imagine an exchange lists several BTC futures:

BTC Contract A
BTC Contract B
BTC Contract C

Their expiration dates differ.

However, certain shared properties may be the same.

For example:

Quantity denomination
Contract-value convention
Market category
Settlement asset

When the required compatibility conditions are satisfied, MarketForge can use a reference contract to fill missing shared specification information.

items.title: Does this mean every BTC contract is identical?
items.text:
No.

Even related contracts can differ.

For example, contract values or other economic properties may change across products or historical periods.

The inference policy therefore imposes compatibility requirements.

items.title: What must match?
items.text:
The reference and target must agree on the applicable known properties, including:

  • Exchange.
  • Product type.
  • Market category.
  • Base asset.
  • Quote asset.
  • Settlement asset.
  • Known quantity denomination.
  • Known contract-value denomination.

items.title: Can a Binance contract be used for an OKX instrument?
items.text:
Not under the described same-exchange reference requirement.

The reference must belong to the compatible exchange and product context.

items.title: Does this apply only to BTC?
items.text:
The current named policy uses compatible BTC reference evidence for supported futures and options cases.

Do not generalize this into unrestricted cross-asset specification inheritance.

items.title: What Information Can Be Inherited?
items.text:
The inference policy is deliberately limited.

It can inherit compatible missing shared specification fields.

It does not blindly replace all metadata.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose the target contract already has:

Exchange: OKX
Instrument type: Future
Market category: Linear
Base asset: BTC
Quote asset: USDT
Expiration: Known
Contract value: Missing

A compatible reference may provide evidence for the missing contract-value information under the current policy.

However, the actual inheritance depends on the available source evidence and compatibility rules.

items.title: What cannot be invented?
items.text:
MarketForge preserves instrument-specific information.

For example:

  • Expiration dates.
  • Option strike prices.
  • Call or put classification.
  • Underlying identity.
  • Exact known specifications.
  • Other contract-specific values.

items.title: Why preserve these fields?
items.text:
Two futures contracts may share an economic contract convention while expiring on different dates.

They remain different instruments.

Similarly, two options may share a base asset while having different strikes and expirations.

Inference must not erase those distinctions.

items.title: What if the reference conflicts with known target information?
items.text:
The inference is not accepted as a silent replacement.

Conflicts must be reported and resolved through the supported evidence system.

items.title: Operational Inference vs. Historical Verification
items.text:
MarketForge distinguishes several kinds of specification evidence.

Two important inference methods are:

catalogue_inferred
reference_contract_inferred

items.title: Catalogue-inferred evidence
items.text: This records information inferred from retained catalogue observations under the supported policy.

items.title: Reference-contract-inferred evidence
items.text: This records information inherited from a compatible reference contract.

items.title: Why are these not historically verified?
items.text:
Because the available evidence may not independently prove that the same specifications applied throughout the target archive's historical period.

For example, a reference contract observed today may share the target's current product conventions.

However, that does not automatically establish the target's exact historical contract value several years earlier.

items.title: What does operationally accepted mean?
items.text:
The current project policy allows qualifying inferred evidence to be used operationally when its compatibility and applicability requirements are satisfied.

This makes it possible to prepare some historical processing work that would otherwise lack required metadata.

items.title: Does operational acceptance prove the inference is correct?
items.text:
No.

The distinction should remain visible.

For example:

Evidence Interpretation Historically verified Supported by applicable historical authority. Historical declaration Explicitly supplied historical information. Catalogue inferred Derived from retained catalogue evidence under policy. Reference-contract inferred Derived from a compatible reference contract under policy.

The last two are operational inference methods.

They should not be presented as independent historical verification.

items.title: Inferred Applicability Intervals
items.text:
Historical normalization requires specifications applicable to the processed source interval.

When MarketForge creates operational inference evidence, it records the assumed applicability interval.

items.title: What does the interval represent?
items.text:
The current policy can assign an assumed interval covering the relevant registered inventory.

This makes the inferred specification operationally usable for the selected archive collection under the project's policy.

items.title: Does the interval prove historical validity?
items.text:
No.

The interval is an explicit applicability assumption.

It is not proof that the exchange historically used the same specifications throughout the entire interval.

items.title: Why distinguish observation time?
items.text:
The evidence also retains when its source information was actually observed.

For example:

Observation date:
November 2026

Assumed applicability:
Historical archive interval

These are different timestamps.

The observation time should not be rewritten to look as though the metadata was collected at the historical archive date.

items.title: Why is this important?
items.text:
Otherwise, a current specification could appear to be a historical observation.

That would make later research and auditing misleading.

items.title: What Evidence Does Inference Preserve?
items.text:
Historical inference records more than the resulting economic values.

The retained evidence includes information such as:

  • Source catalogue identities.
  • Source API identifiers.
  • Source snapshot hashes.
  • Inherited fields.
  • Inference policy version.
  • Applicability information.
  • Deterministic evidence fingerprints.

items.title: Why preserve this information?
items.text:
Suppose a contract multiplier was inferred from a compatible reference.

Later, you discover a verified historical specification.

You need to know how the earlier value was obtained.

The retained evidence makes that interpretation traceable.

items.title: Why use fingerprints?
items.text:
Fingerprints identify the relevant source evidence and interpretation.

For example, unchanged recollection of the same evidence can reuse the corresponding immutable revision.

If the source metadata or applicability changes, MarketForge can append a new revision.

items.title: Does updating current metadata overwrite historical evidence?
items.text:
Not automatically.

The historical evidence store is append-oriented and preserves immutable revisions.

This allows MarketForge to retain the history of the information used for previous processing decisions.

items.title: Does a new revision silently replace an explicit declaration?
items.text:
No.

Conflicting explicit historical declarations remain authoritative conflicts that must be resolved.

items.title: Why Are Futures Families Difficult?
items.text:
Some historical derivative archives contain several concrete contracts.

For example, a dated-futures family may include:

BTC-USD Contract A
BTC-USD Contract B
BTC-USD Contract C

Each contract has its own expiration and canonical instrument identity.

However, the archive provider may distribute their records together.

items.title: Why is this difficult?
items.text:
The archive filename may identify only the family.

For example:

BTC-USD

This does not identify every concrete contract represented inside the file.

MarketForge needs additional source-native identity evidence.

items.title: What does family membership mean?
items.text:
A family membership describes which concrete instruments are associated with a particular source family.

For example:

BTC-USD Family
      |
      +-- BTC Contract A
      +-- BTC Contract B
      +-- BTC Contract C

items.title: Does a current family listing prove historical completeness?
items.text:
No.

A current exchange API may omit expired contracts.

An archive may also contain historical instruments not present in the current catalogue.

Therefore, the current family population is not automatically a complete historical record.

items.title: Catalogue vs. Archive-Derived Family Membership
items.text: MarketForge retains different sources of family membership evidence.

items.title: Catalogue membership
items.text:
This comes from the retained instrument catalogue.

For example, current exchange metadata may identify several related contracts.

items.title: Archive-derived membership
items.text: This comes from supported identity discovery performed against registered historical archive contents.

items.title: Why retain both?
items.text:
Because current metadata and historical archives can describe different instrument populations.

For example:

Current catalogue:
Contract B
Contract C

Historical archive:
Contract A
Contract B

The example is illustrative.

The current catalogue does not automatically prove that Contract A never existed.

Likewise, discovering Contract A in an archive does not establish that every historical contract has been discovered.

items.title: Does MarketForge merge the two into one complete authority?
items.text:
It retains the relevant evidence and identity mappings under the supported policy.

However, it does not claim that the resulting family membership is historically exhaustive.

items.title: OKX Historical Instrument Discovery
items.text: OKX provides an important example of family-based historical data.

items.title: Perpetual archives
items.text: For supported OKX perpetual archives, MarketForge uses the relevant source-native instrument identity.

items.title: Dated futures
items.text:
Dated-futures archive bundles may contain several concrete contracts.

MarketForge can perform bounded identity discovery using the production Rust Engine.

items.title: Why use Rust for discovery?
items.text:
The archive may contain substantial data.

The Engine has the source-format processing capabilities needed to inspect the supported native instrument identities.

items.title: Current discovery limits
items.text:
The documented bounds are:

Limit Value Maximum bytes inspected per managed copy 256 MiB Maximum discovery time 180 seconds

These limits constrain the discovery operation.

items.title: Does discovery read the entire archive?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

The byte and time budgets can prevent full inspection.

items.title: Does discovering several contracts prove that no others exist?
items.text:
No.

A bounded scan can establish observed identities.

It cannot guarantee that every historical contract appears within the inspected portion.

items.title: Why is this still useful?
items.text:
It can identify concrete instruments represented by a registered family archive without requiring every contract to remain listed in the current exchange API.

This provides additional historical identity evidence for normalization preparation.

items.title: Historical Identity Discovery Caching
items.text:
Archive identity discovery can be expensive.

MarketForge therefore caches supported discovery results.

items.title: What identifies a cached result?
items.text:
The cache uses information including:

  • Managed copy checksum.
  • Compiled profile fingerprint.
  • Inference policy.

items.title: Why use these values?
items.text:
A discovery result depends on both the source bytes and how those bytes are interpreted.

For example, changing the source profile may change which native instrument fields are decoded.

Similarly, changing the archive contents may change the observed instrument population.

items.title: When can a cached result be reused?
items.text: When the relevant source bytes, compiled interpretation, and policy identity remain compatible with the cached evidence.

items.title: What if the archive changes?
items.text: A changed copy checksum requires the discovery result to be reconsidered.

items.title: What if the profile changes?
items.text: A different compiled profile fingerprint can require rediscovery.

items.title: What if the inference policy changes?
items.text: The discovery evidence must be evaluated under the appropriate policy version.

items.title: Does cached discovery create normalized datasets?
items.text:
No.

Identity discovery produces metadata evidence.

It does not publish normalized Parquet datasets.

items.title: Does discovery remove expired instruments?
items.text:
No.

The historical identity infrastructure retains relevant inactive and expired catalogue entries.

Archive-discovered expired identities can receive stable canonical mappings.

items.title: What About Options?
items.text:
Options require additional instrument-specific information.

For example:

  • Underlying asset.
  • Expiration date.
  • Strike price.
  • Call or put classification.
  • Contract value.
  • Settlement convention.

These properties distinguish individual option contracts.

items.title: Why can't MarketForge infer everything from the base asset?
items.text:
Because one underlying can have many options.

For example:

BTC Call
BTC Put
Different strikes
Different expirations

These are separate instruments.

items.title: What can the inference policy preserve?
items.text:
The historical specification inference mechanism preserves available option identity fields.

It does not fabricate missing strike prices, expirations, or underlying identities.

items.title: Are options fully supported for normalization?
items.text:
Not currently.

The existing Rust offline catalogue and installed normalization profiles do not provide general options-normalization support.

items.title: Important distinction: acquisition vs. current-market collection
items.text:
The current mf markets sync collection adapters omit options.

However, certain historical acquisition adapters support options archive discovery.

For example, the separate historical acquisition subsystem supports relevant Bybit and OKX options archive selections.

These are different capabilities.

Being able to obtain an options archive does not mean MarketForge can already normalize its contents.

items.title: What happens when required options support is missing?
items.text:
Initialization and preparation report the applicable limitation.

They do not invent missing instrument identity or Engine support.

items.title: Historical Evidence Storage
items.text:
The historical metadata system uses immutable evidence records.

The relevant database support was introduced through migration 0014.

items.title: Why retain evidence separately?
items.text:
MarketForge needs to distinguish:

  • Current catalogue observations.
  • Explicit historical declarations.
  • Inferred historical specifications.
  • Family membership evidence.
  • Archive-derived identity information.

These records have different meanings and levels of authority.

items.title: Does this create a second raw-data registry?
items.text:
No.

The evidence tables are not a replacement for the managed raw-data registry.

Raw archives remain tracked through the existing acquisition and storage infrastructure.

items.title: Does this replace current catalogue observations?
items.text:
No.

Current observations remain useful for market discovery, statistics, and reference metadata.

Historical evidence adds information needed to interpret older registered recordings.

items.title: Why preserve immutable revisions?
items.text:
Because financial-data processing should remain traceable.

If the source evidence changes, the new interpretation should not silently erase the information used for earlier work.

items.title: General Ranking Policy Fields
items.text:
The following table summarizes the supported main policy fields.

Field Default / requirement Meaning version Defaults to 1; supports 1 or 2 Policy schema version. metric turnover_24h Turnover or volume comparison. exchanges All supported exchanges Selected exchange universe. markets Spot, linear, inverse Selected market categories. instruments Empty Optional exact instrument references. max_age_seconds 3600 Maximum observation age. max_window_skew_seconds 300 Measurement-window alignment tolerance. comparison_currency USDT, turnover only Common monetary comparison unit. estimates exclude Whether relevant estimates are permitted. allow_partial_universe false Whether eligible subsets can be published with exclusions. manual_preferences Empty Explicit turnover ordering preferences. volume_unit Required for volume Must be base_asset. group_by Required for volume Must be base_asset.

items.title: Validation rules
items.text:
Unknown fields are rejected.

Duplicate or invalid references can be rejected.

Observation age must be between 1 and 604800 seconds.

Window skew must be between 0 and 86400 seconds.

Volume policies require their quantity and grouping fields.

Turnover and volume use different conversion semantics.

items.title: Turnover Conversion Fields
items.text: Field Default / accepted values automatic False in policy v1; true in v2 turnover valuation reference_price_turnover max_price_age_seconds Inherits general age; explicit 1–604800 max_leg_skew_seconds Inherits window skew; explicit 0–86400 max_hops 2; supports 1 or 2 bridge_assets Defaults to BTC/ETH; empty permits any eligible bridge prefer_same_exchange Must be true allow_cross_exchange Defaults to false allow_mixed_exchanges Must be false source_exchanges Supported reference exchanges in preference order equivalent_currencies Empty by default manual_rates Empty by default; explicit rate, time, and source

items.title: Important rules
items.text:
Currency codes must use the supported uppercase format.

Duplicate currency declarations are rejected.

Mixed-exchange conversion legs are not supported.

Manual rates must be positive and finite.

Manual rate observation times must include a timezone.

A manual rate for the comparison currency must be exactly 1.

Stale manual overrides do not silently fall back to automatic conversion.

items.title: Workflow priorities
items.text: Normalization and pipeline recipes select a published turnover snapshot with ranking_policy (default turnover). When no eligible snapshot exists, current preparation uses deterministic identity ordering. Grouped volume positions are excluded from normalization priorities. Editing a policy affects future ranking builds. Published snapshots and prepared ranks retain their evidence.

items.title: Merge recipes
items.text:
Forge reads managed merge names under data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/merge/ or an explicit recipe path. Choose the direct or source-derived form. Merge workflow · Engine job

Path Type and requirement Meaning dataset_ids Required in the direct form. Nonempty unique list of positive signed-64-bit registry file IDs Ordered normalized primary-file selections start_ns, end_ns Required in the direct form. Signed 64-bit integers, start_ns < end_ns Requested half-open Engine interval, Unix nanoseconds version Required in the derived form. Integer 1 Recipe discriminator interval.start, interval.end Required in the derived form. Timezone-aware TOML datetimes with start before end and both representable as signed-64-bit Unix ns Derived interval selection.source Required nonblank string in the derived form Modern normalization recipe name or explicit path selection.operation, selection.mode Default normalize, all, respectively. These are their only values Source kind and selection mode selection.data_types Optional nonempty list of trades, order_book_l2 Restrict matching requests selection.exchanges Optional nonempty list of lowercase exchange tokens matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$ Restrict venues selection.instruments Optional nonempty list of canonical instrument references Restrict instruments selection.instrument_types Optional nonempty list of spot, perpetual, future, option, equity Restrict instrument types selection.market_categories Optional nonempty list of spot, linear, inverse, option, equity Restrict categories selection.publication_ids Optional nonempty unique list of positive signed-64-bit registry publication IDs Explicitly bind competing normalized selections stream_ranks Map from stream ID to uint32, default empty Optional overrides when preparing the job. The resolved assignments must distinguish distinct streams timeline_ordering Optional causal or chronological Forge chooses causal when required by selected inputs and chronological otherwise

Forge verifies membership, one instrument namespace, and physical file fingerprints during preparation. A direct recipe uses registered file IDs, while the derived publication selector uses registry publication IDs. Recipe models

items.title: Overview
items.text:
The Rust Engine reads this configuration to admit processing work, bound intermediate buffers, size Parquet output, collect diagnostics, and decide whether observed anomalies or excluded source events permit publication.

Configuration Responsibility Normalization recipe Selects registered inputs and an interval. Normalization profile Describes how to interpret the source format and its record operations. Normalization runtime Controls execution resources, diagnostics, and policies for processing and publication.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
mf normalize config show | cpout
mf normalize config validate | cpout
mf normalize config schema | cpout

These commands use the locally installed managed normalization Engine. Schema-based operations need a build with the runtime schema capability. validate checks the complete TOML through the production Rust runtime loader. The schema explorer describes the current Engine build and shows whether settings are effective in the current configuration. See what validation checks.

items.title: Inspect individual settings
items.text:
mf normalize config get resources.workers | cpout
mf normalize config show --section resources | cpout
mf normalize config show --all | cpout
mf normalize config schema --field reconciliation.depth.overlap_policy | cpout

Use a dotted TOML leaf path with get, set, unset, or schema --field. Use a canonical table name with show --section, including nested sections such as resources.parquet, integrity_policy, and reconciliation.depth. The compact overview groups related settings for readability. Detailed views separate the configured value, the Engine-resolved value, and the default. An inactive value can still be present in the file and must still pass the loader's checks.

For automation, use global mf --json normalize config …. Output contains native numbers and booleans and a versioned result object.

For a read-only report on older managed builds that expose runtime settings but lack the schema interface, use mf engine runtime normalize | cpout. See Engine runtime commands and the normalization CLI syntax.

items.title: Configuration file and resolution
items.text:
Forge resolves data/.config/engine/normalize.toml under the workspace root, independent of the configured data root. Direct Engine invocations default to that path and accept --config PATH and --project-root ROOT. Relative configuration and scratch paths resolve from the project root, including when the TOML lives elsewhere. The root must exist and resolve to a directory. A missing current file is an error. If the legacy workspace file data/.config/historical/general.toml exists instead, the current managed path reports that migration is required.

Evidence Meaning Configured settings The values explicitly written to TOML. Effective settings Rust resolves omitted fields and converts the scratch path to a project-root-based path. Pipeline runs recursively overlay [normalize] in pipeline.toml after validating the base and validate the combined result. The overlay cannot set the operation's schema version. Execution-pinned settings Persisted Forge preparation retains the runtime TOML and its SHA-256 beside the batch. Execution with matching preparation evidence loads the retained copy and checks its fingerprint. Direct batch submission without that evidence uses the current runtime. Managed execution retains its own runtime copy and fingerprint. Pipeline resume uses the pinned stage files. Publication evidence The normalized publication keeps the effective Rust processing configuration in processing-runtime.json with its SHA-256 companion.

Editing the current file affects later resolutions. In-flight Engines use settings already loaded, and existing prepared and publication evidence keeps its original configuration. See pipeline inheritance, the prepared batch reference, and normalized publications.

items.title: Runtime configuration overview
items.text:
The field tables give Rust defaults on omission, rather than the workspace's explicitly configured values. schema_version, the four main resource fields, both Parquet targets, and each integrity rule's action are required. Optional tables can be omitted unless they contain required fields. A dash in a default column means there is no default or no optional threshold. The loader rejects unknown fields at every supported level. Rust integer types below are unsigned unless stated otherwise. Byte values use binary units.

Performance settings change resource use and layout. Reconciliation, timestamp processing and integrity rules can change event selection or publication eligibility. Treat those choices independently.

items.title: 1. Processing and performance
items.text:
Field Rust type · default Behavior and constraints schema_version u32 · required Exactly 1. An unsupported value fails load. This field versions the runtime document independently of recipes, profiles and batches. merge_fan_in usize · 8 Inclusive range 2–64. Requested maximum number of input runs merged at a time in normalization scratch sorting/reconciliation. Effective fan-in depends on memory, admitted handles and available runs. Higher values can reduce passes while increasing simultaneous buffers and handles. scratch_format ScratchFormat · json json, typed_trades, or typed_events. Selects encoding on scratch paths that use the reconciler's spools. See the format details below. scratch_codec ScratchCodec · zlib zlib uses fast zlib compression on participating scratch records. uncompressed stores raw encoded payloads with the spool framing. Final Parquet encoding is independent.

json is the generic spool representation. typed_trades enables typed trade payloads. typed_events also enables typed depth payloads on the shared-envelope spool path. Generic records such as routing or metadata still use JSON. The setting does not select a family-discovery or decoding strategy and does not require all records in an execution to have the same payload encoding. Both typed modes are accepted by Rust where the corresponding writer path is used. Compare retained scratch and timing measurements for the workload before changing either setting.

Forge-generated jobs declare event_timestamp_ns as the primary ordering key and stream_rank as the tie-break. That declaration belongs to the prepared job contract. Runtime [ordering] is an unknown table.

items.title: 2. Resource management
items.text:
Field Rust type · default Behavior and constraints resources.workers usize · required Positive ceiling on worker concurrency. The scoped scheduler spawns at most that many worker threads, capped by the number of work units. Memory and handle admission can leave workers idle. Other process threads, such as diagnostics, are outside this count. resources.memory_budget_bytes u64 · required Positive session-wide admission budget in bytes. Reservations include retained evidence, active units, buffers and finalization estimates. The budget is not an OS RSS cap. resources.scratch_path PathBuf · required Nonempty path string. An existing path must be a directory. The Engine creates scratch directories as needed during work, so the process needs write access and space on that filesystem. resources.scratch_budget_bytes u64 · required Positive byte budget shared through session resource accounting for participating scratch files. Spool writes charge storage as they grow and release it when removed. This is not a quota for the entire filesystem or the final publication.

An execution unit can represent one source task, reconciled work for a stream, or routed family work. Increasing workers increases potential overlap of decoders, writers, evidence buffers and file handles. An individual unit plus required retained state must fit even when no other worker is active. A clean shutdown drops owned scratch workspaces. A hard kill or failed filesystem cleanup can leave files. Reserve filesystem capacity separately from the Engine budget.

The workspace's configured 68719476736 memory bytes are 64 GiB, and 137438953472 scratch bytes are 128 GiB. These are examples of explicit settings, not defaults.

items.title: 3. Normalization safety limits
items.text:
All eight resources.normalization_limits leaves are optional u64 values. Each must be greater than zero and at most usize::MAX / 128 for the Engine's platform. Limits are checked at the identified subsystem boundary. Exceeding a limit produces a resource failure rather than permission to skip excess input through an integrity rule.

Field under resources.normalization_limits Rust default Enforced accounting workbook_bytes 8 MiB (8388608 bytes) Bounds the selected XLSX byte stream before workbook decoding. For an externally compressed source or selected member it limits the decoded member's XLSX container bytes, before expanding the workbook's own XML. workbook_xml_bytes 16 MiB (16777216 bytes) Bounds each expanded XML member the reader loads. Also bounds accumulated worksheet cell text in the applicable worksheet decode. workbook_rows 25000 Bounds row materialization on its worksheet parsing and decoded-row paths. Shared strings have a separate count ceiling of three times this setting. This is not an archive-wide count of market events. record_bytes 1 MiB (1048576 bytes) Bounds CSV encoded record payload, including quoting and embedded newlines but excluding the terminating record boundary. JSONL charges line bytes including the terminator before trimming. XLSX applies it to cell text. It also bounds selected metadata strings and sizes internal estimates. depth_levels 25000 Bounds reconstructed book and pending snapshot level counts, with bids and asks counted together at each applicable check. Also feeds depth workspace estimates. metric_entries 4096 Caps per-task file plus hourly and daily observation entries. Separate guards reuse the same numeric ceiling for inventories such as archive members, family or routing entries, output parts, row groups and depth segments. This can fail processing, independently of the diagnostics mode. reconciliation_bytes 64 MiB (67108864 bytes) Resident reconciliation/routing quota per applicable execution unit. Covers accounted in-memory state such as merge records, ownership indexes, and buffered events. The unit's quota is included in the session memory estimate. Spool storage is accounted separately. open_files 64 Session ceiling for participating handles with eight reserved for logging, metadata, provenance and finalization. Admission and spool fan-in account for active handles. The OS file-descriptor limit still applies independently.

The managed value reconciliation_bytes = 8589934592 is 8 GiB. The existing “1 GiB” comment describes neither that value nor the current Rust default.

items.title: 4. Parquet output
items.text:
Both resources.parquet fields are required positive u64 byte targets. Rust enforces row_group_target_bytes <= file_target_bytes; equality is allowed.

Field Effect resources.parquet.row_group_target_bytes Controls flushing buffered rows as their estimated footprint reaches the target. It contributes to each active writer's memory estimate. Depth also uses it with a 1 MiB floor in checks on certain metadata buffers. resources.parquet.file_target_bytes Controls rotation after accumulated output reaches the target at writer boundaries. Compression, row-group granularity, metadata and footers affect actual file size.

These targets are approximate sizing controls. Output size is distinct from decoded input, scratch size and in-memory row size. Writers currently select Parquet Zstandard level 3. Smaller row groups can reduce buffering and change scan granularity, while smaller parts can increase file and metadata counts. See publication layout and sizing.

items.title: 5. Diagnostics
items.text:
Field Rust type · default Behavior diagnostics.mode DiagnosticsMode · disabled disabled skips the optional performance collector. Essential results, integrity counters and publication evidence still exist. basic collects progress, phase, resource and process snapshots. detailed adds current RSS on Linux if readable. diagnostics.interval_ms u64 · 1000 Inclusive range 100–60000 ms, validated in every mode. The collector wakes on a timer or on coalesced progress notifications. Heartbeats can appear during CPU or I/O waits. This controls reporting, not worker scheduling.

When enabled and able to open its output, the collector emits diagnostic lines to stderr and writes effective-config.json, live.jsonl and a final performance.json under a performance-… directory beside the staging output. The TUI uses the progress snapshots directly. When snapshots are already enabled, the separate collector skips startup. One bounded wake channel coalesces progress; reporting still costs serialization and I/O. The modes do not change integrity thresholds or event processing policies.

items.title: 6. Integrity policies
items.text:
The integrity system records an eligible check and whether it failed. Its evaluation can be clean, degraded or failed. A failed evaluation blocks that job's publication. A degraded result can still be committed if independent processing and resource checks succeed. Forge verification and primary-file registration are subsequent operations.

integrity_policy.enabled is a Rust bool, optional and true by default. Setting it to false skips immediate rule enforcement and final threshold evaluation. Counting continues, and recorded violations still mark output degraded. Source checks, independent reconciliation/timestamp policy and resource guards continue. All seven rule tables and actions are required and validated even when evaluation is disabled. Legacy profile is an alias for enabled; legacy strings standard and strict both decode as true and are not distinct policy presets.

items.title: Shared rule fields
items.text:
Apply these fields under each integrity_policy.<rule>.

Leaf Rust type · default Effect and validation action IntegrityAction · required fail rejects any occurrence, regardless of configured count/rate allowances. degrade marks an occurrence degraded and fails if any configured threshold is exceeded. Rust requires at least one count, rate or window threshold for degrade. max_count Option<u64> · absent Absolute violation count across the job. Checked with strict >; zero fails on the first occurrence. The immediate evaluator can check count where supplied. Scheduled workers defer aggregate thresholds to final evaluation. max_rate Option<f64> · absent Finite fraction in [0, 1]. A degrade rule checks this separately globally, per source-file scope, and per stream. The denominator is eligible checks of that category within the scope. Rust uses decimal arithmetic at evaluation, so unsupported decimal precision fails evaluation. minimum_samples u64 · 0 Checks a rate only once the scope has at least this many eligible observations and a nonzero denominator. It never delays a count or fail action. windows.hourly.max_rate, windows.daily.max_rate f64 · required for a configured window Finite fraction in [0, 1]. Each configured window rate is evaluated independently against category observations within its source scope and time bucket. windows.hourly.minimum_samples, windows.daily.minimum_samples u64 · required for a configured window Sample floor for that category, source scope and window. Zero is valid, and an empty bucket has no rate.

The Engine compares violations using strict > against eligible observations times the fraction. A rate of 0.01 is 1%. Hourly and daily buckets use fixed UTC epoch-aligned event-time intervals, including for timestamps before the epoch. Counts use observations present in each bucket, without estimating missing samples or requiring calendar completeness. Eligible observations without a trustworthy timestamp fail verification of any configured window for that category, even when the unattributed observations did not violate the rule. Window thresholds provide independent checks and never cancel a failure.

items.title: Rule categories
items.text:
All seven use the shared action, count, rate and window contract above. Each eligible check counts once in its category for the applicable unit. A record may reach multiple checks. Source diagnostics carry contextual samples, and evaluation evidence identifies the category, threshold, observation counts and available scope.

Required rule table What counts integrity_policy.parse_failure A physical decoder attempt, such as a CSV record, JSONL message or XLSX row. Both trades and depth can fail while reading or parsing a source record. Unparseable timestamps may prevent window attribution. Typed resource-limit errors remain resource errors. integrity_policy.invalid_record An applicable record or event validation unit for trades or depth. Examples include invalid input field values, inconsistent sequence metadata or invalid price levels. A later failure in a different category does not erase an earlier successful check. integrity_policy.sequence_gap A sequenced incremental depth observation reaching continuity checks on an initialized book. Native sequence policy determines valid continuity and can require prior/end linkage. Unsequenced snapshots do not create synthetic sequence evidence. integrity_policy.timestamp_regression An applicable comparison against the previous accepted timestamp in source order for trades or depth. A lower timestamp is an integrity observation. Separately, temporal processing uses its own high-water checks, which can still fail. integrity_policy.missing_snapshot An incremental depth event reaching synchronization checks without initialization. The rule can govern whether the anomaly is tolerated, but it cannot initialize a book or satisfy a recovery boundary. integrity_policy.invalid_book Reserved for explicit book-invariant observations. The current normalization paths attribute ordinary level validation to invalid_record; they do not emit a general invalid_book result for every bad or valid book. integrity_policy.transformation_failure One attempted quantity-transformation batch for a trade, depth message or assembled snapshot. For depth, it is not counted once per emitted level. Missing required conversion terms or failed quantity arithmetic can produce it.

items.title: 7. Trade reconciliation
items.text:
reconciliation.trades.overlap_policy is an optional TradeOverlap enum. Its default is strict.

  • strict keeps distinct comparable trades and suppresses duplicates only when native identity and canonical equivalence support that decision. Conflicting contents under a reliable native identity, or overlapping sources without established comparable identity/reset domains, can fail. Equal timestamps alone are insufficient evidence of duplication.
  • prefer_source enables source precedence for ambiguous overlap or supported conflicts. It can charge a non-equivalent or unverified observation as excluded. Distinct reliable identities can still be retained. An ordered native-ID run has additional proof requirements and cannot use this option to discard conflicting records or make missing IDs valid.

Overlap ranges use each source's minimum and maximum accepted event timestamps. The selected source wins on supported conflicts, using accepted start time and stable identity tie-breaks. For example, if source A begins at 09:00 and source B at 09:30, earlier gives A precedence in their overlap and later gives B precedence. This is an illustration of resolution where preference applies, not a rule to crop all records from the other source.

items.title: Source preference and loss limits
items.text:
The table applies to both reconciliation.trades.prefer_source and reconciliation.depth.prefer_source. Both tables are optional. Their source-selection behavior activates only with overlap_policy = "prefer_source". Rust validates both tables even when inactive.

Leaf Rust type · default Effect and constraint selection Selection · earlier earlier or later by minimum accepted event timestamp. Stable source identity and source order break ties. on_unique_data_loss LossAction · fail fail rejects the first known-unique or unverified exclusion. mark_degraded permits only bounded exclusions and requires a positive event cap. max_excluded_events u64 · 0 Logical event cap applied to source and job exclusion totals. Strict > fails. Verified duplicates do not consume this cap. max_excluded_rate Option<f64> · absent Finite fraction in [0,1] representable by Rust Decimal. Applies job-wide to overlap exclusions divided by accepted logical source observations minus verified duplicates. A rate strictly above the threshold fails. minimum_samples u64 · 0 The optional rate applies at or above this denominator, provided it is nonzero. The event cap still applies below the floor. max_excluded_interval_ms Option<u64> · absent Maximum timestamp span from minimum to maximum event time within a contiguous run of excluded observations, tracked in native source order. A retained observation resets the run. Zero allows a zero-duration span only. The converted value must fit signed 64-bit nanoseconds.

Rate limits measure logical observations, independently of the number of canonical rows they would emit. The Engine records overlap and timestamp exclusions, known-unique versus unverified exclusions, and excluded canonical rows separately. A run of exclusions may include both causes and is tracked accordingly. A degraded publication records a permitted loss or other processing-quality signal. This evidence does not establish continuous market history.

items.title: 8. Order-book reconciliation
items.text:
reconciliation.depth.overlap_policy is an optional DepthOverlap enum and defaults to strict. A book is stateful. A snapshot initializes it, and incremental events update that state under the source's sequence contract.

  • strict rejects overlapping independent histories unless a supported boundary equivalence is proven. For example, matching authoritative snapshots at a shared boundary can be suppressed as one proven duplicate.
  • snapshot_recovery uses authoritative initialization snapshots and retained boundary evidence to publish valid reconstruction segments. It does not authorize intentional overlap exclusions of unique supplied observations. The Engine marks continuity unproven when an independent initialization cannot be linked by matching state and applicable native sequence evidence.
  • prefer_source assigns overlap ownership using the accepted event ranges and shared preference settings. An authorized exclusion is charged in logical observations even when it represents many levels or emits zero canonical rows. The resulting segments do not imply continuity across a source change.

reconciliation.depth.prefer_source.switch_boundary is an optional SwitchBoundary enum, default snapshot. snapshot waits for a snapshot to switch after an existing source. Excluded observations during the wait remain subject to loss limits. source_boundary allows a switch only with matching reconstruction state and native sequence evidence, either at the incoming boundary or via a matching authoritative snapshot. A new history still needs authoritative initialization.

Overlap recovery and timestamp recovery address different conditions. Source processing validates sequence, synchronization and book inputs. The integrity rules can fail the job on those observations, and the recovery algorithms still enforce their own proof and budget requirements.

items.title: 9. Timestamp regression
items.text: The Engine records raw timestamp anomalies in source order. Processing limits compare against a source-local accepted high-water mark, and independent integrity rules can fail on the raw anomaly first. Millisecond bounds are optional u64 values which must fit signed 64-bit nanoseconds after multiplication by 1000000. These controls do not change source timestamps.

items.title: Trades
items.text:
Field under timestamp_regression.trades Rust type · default Effect and constraint policy TradeTimestamp · strict strict rejects unresolved regressions. preserve retains native order for tolerated regressions. reorder allows bounded disorder and uses chronological output sorting. discard excludes regressing surviving observations within the configured bounds. max_regression_ms u64 · 0 High-water tolerance for non-strict processing. Must be positive for reorder or discard. A larger regression fails even when a discard cap remains. max_reorder_window_ms u64 · 0 High-water window for reorder. Must be positive and at least max_regression_ms in that mode. A larger window cannot relax the regression cap. max_discarded_events u64 · 0 Cap on timestamp-discarded logical events. Must be positive for discard. Checked per source and job with strict >. max_discarded_rate Option<f64> · absent Optional additional job-wide cap for discard. Finite fraction in [0,1] representable by Rust Decimal. Uses accepted logical observations minus verified duplicates as the denominator. minimum_samples u64 · 0 Sample floor for the optional discard rate. A nonzero denominator is required. The event count cap applies independently.

On the general reconciliation path the Engine resolves identity, verified duplicates and overlap before applying timestamp processing to surviving records in concrete source order. Ordered-run identity checks still apply, and raw regressions remain in the evidence even if reconciliation removes the offending record.

items.title: Depth
items.text:
Field under timestamp_regression.depth Rust type · default Effect and constraint policy DepthTimestamp · strict strict rejects unresolved regressions. preserve tolerates bounded regressions in native processing order. snapshot_recovery can suppress updates during a regression recovery and resume at an authoritative snapshot, emitting a new initialization. max_regression_ms u64 · 0 Bounds non-strict high-water regression checks, including preserve and recovery checks. A genuine snapshot sequence reset can reset the comparison state. require_sequence_continuity bool · true Must be true. Applicable native continuity checks remain enabled. Unsequenced snapshot sources need no synthetic sequence. require_recovery_snapshot bool · true Must be true. Recovery needs verified initialization evidence. max_discarded_events u64 · 0 Timestamp-recovery cap on excluded logical events at source and job scope. The first exclusion exceeds zero. No depth discard-rate field exists.

Stateful depth events are not reordered by event timestamp to repair continuity. The profile and decoder define whether sequencing is applicable, and an Engine-supported sortable workbook path can sort independent snapshots before stateful processing. A 2 ms tolerance alone establishes nothing about book reconstruction.

items.title: 10. Cross-setting dependencies
items.text: Kind Relationship Loader constraint Both Parquet targets are positive, with row group at most file target. All limits and configured rates are validated even when inactive. Admission Workers, writer targets, safety limits and per-unit reconciliation allowances compete for session memory. The handle limit reserves eight session handles. Fan-in is reduced on participating sort paths and can be constrained further by memory and handle budgets. Execution accounting Scratch encoding can change scratch bytes and codec work. Resident reconciliation state is charged to memory, while spool bytes charge scratch. Full disk and OS descriptor limits can still stop work. Integrity evaluation A fail action rejects any violation, while degrade needs a threshold and uses independent count, rate and window checks. Disabling evaluation leaves detection and resource checks in effect. Source reconciliation Preference settings apply to source ownership under prefer_source. Count bounds cannot be replaced by sample floors. Depth source changes need the selected initialization or proof boundary. Temporal processing Reordering requires positive bounds and a window at least as large as the trade regression limit. Discard also requires a positive event cap. Depth requires applicable sequence validation and verified initialization regardless of timestamp policy.

items.title: 11. Validation and safe modification
items.text:
Runtime validation checks UTF-8 TOML syntax, the schema version, recognized fields, types and enum spellings, rule and resource bounds, and cross-field constraints. It also resolves paths and rejects an existing scratch path that is not a directory. It does not run admission for a particular workload, test available RAM or free space, or guarantee that scratch is writable.

The direct loader can validate a complete candidate in a separate file. Replace PATH_TO_CANDIDATE.toml with your draft's path.

.bin/marketforge-normalize --runtime-settings PATH_TO_CANDIDATE.toml --project-root .

If Forge reports that the managed Engine is absent, invalid or too old for runtime-schema inspection, use mf engine build normalize. A successful config validation depends on the Rust loader actually running.

items.title: Preview and apply
items.text:
mf normalize config set resources.workers 12 | cpout
mf normalize config set resources.workers 12 --apply | cpout
mf normalize config set resources.memory_budget_bytes 48GiB | cpout
mf normalize config unset integrity_policy.parse_failure.max_count | cpout

set and unset preview by default. --apply rechecks the source file and validates the complete candidate again with Rust before atomic replacement. Forge checks the original file identity, contents and parent directory before saving. The edit round-trips TOML so unrelated settings and comments are preserved. unset removes only optional leaf settings. An omitted setting uses its Rust default when it has one. Otherwise the setting is absent.

Enter byte quantities as whole bytes or use case-sensitive binary units KiB, MiB, GiB, or TiB. A fractional unit is accepted only when it converts to a whole number of bytes. Enter booleans as true or false and enum values by their exact spelling.

Integrity-critical changes require --acknowledge-risk with --apply. The Rust authoring schema classifies field risk. The preview lists the affected settings and required acknowledgement. Resource-sensitive and processing-semantic changes are flagged in the preview. Schema identity is immutable through these commands. Coordinated changes such as adding an integrity window with both required members belong in the editor.

items.title: Edit the complete configuration
items.text:
mf normalize config edit

The command opens a private draft in the configured editor, with Neovim as the default. It requires a terminal. Review the changes and type apply to save. Integrity-critical edits require typing apply and acknowledge risk. A validation failure or declined confirmation keeps the draft and displays its path. The managed file must be a regular, single-link file, and the management commands bound file and draft size to 1 MiB.

items.title: A. Complete strict starting point
items.text:
This document supplies all required fields and uses Rust defaults for omitted settings. Resource values are explicit starting values. Workload admission still depends on the selected work.

schema_version = 1

[resources]
workers = 2
memory_budget_bytes = 8589934592
scratch_path = "data/.work/normalize"
scratch_budget_bytes = 17179869184

[resources.parquet]
row_group_target_bytes = 67108864
file_target_bytes = 536870912

[integrity_policy.parse_failure]
action = "fail"

[integrity_policy.invalid_record]
action = "fail"

[integrity_policy.sequence_gap]
action = "fail"

[integrity_policy.timestamp_regression]
action = "fail"

[integrity_policy.missing_snapshot]
action = "fail"

[integrity_policy.invalid_book]
action = "fail"

[integrity_policy.transformation_failure]
action = "fail"

The examples below are replacements or additions to the relevant table in example A. Keep a single declaration of each TOML table.

items.title: B. Smaller resource targets
items.text:
This sets 4 GiB of memory, 8 GiB of scratch, and 32 MiB/256 MiB Parquet targets. It reduces potential concurrency and writer buffering. A single large execution unit can still exceed admission.

[resources]
workers = 1
memory_budget_bytes = 4294967296
scratch_path = "data/.work/normalize"
scratch_budget_bytes = 8589934592

[resources.parquet]
row_group_target_bytes = 33554432
file_target_bytes = 268435456

items.title: C. Detailed diagnostics
items.text:
Adds work for snapshot serialization, logging and available RSS sampling.

[diagnostics]
mode = "detailed"
interval_ms = 2000

items.title: D. Source preference with bounded trade loss
items.text:
Earlier observed starts take precedence where the policy applies. Up to 10 charged exclusions can yield a degraded publication if other checks succeed. The eleventh exceeds the cap.

[reconciliation.trades]
overlap_policy = "prefer_source"

[reconciliation.trades.prefer_source]
selection = "earlier"
on_unique_data_loss = "mark_degraded"
max_excluded_events = 10

items.title: E. Count-bounded integrity degradation
items.text:
Replace the invalid_record rule. An occurrence degrades the job, and the third violation exceeds the count threshold. The rule does not turn invalid source records into valid output.

[integrity_policy.invalid_record]
action = "degrade"
max_count = 2

items.title: F. Preserve bounded depth timestamp regressions
items.text:
This changes both the processing policy and the independent timestamp integrity rule from example A. Replace the integrity rule table and add the depth timestamp table. Qualifying regressions can be retained in native order, subject to other sequence and reconstruction checks. Any fourth eligible integrity violation exceeds the count cap.

[integrity_policy.timestamp_regression]
action = "degrade"
max_count = 3

[timestamp_regression.depth]
policy = "preserve"
max_regression_ms = 2

items.title: 13. Troubleshooting
items.text: Problem What to check Unknown field or unsupported schema Check the exact TOML path and enum spelling. Use schema_version = 1 with the current loader. Ordering belongs to the job contract. Budget rejected or memory admission fails Check positive values and look at retained admission estimates for the largest unit, writer memory, retained evidence, and handle headroom. Parquet targets invalid Use positive targets with row group no larger than file. Scratch path unavailable Resolve it from the project root and check directory permissions and free space. Degrade rule rejected Supply at least one count, rate or window threshold. A configured window needs both fields. Reconciliation appears inactive Check the chosen overlap policy, source identity proof and whether the paths contain applicable overlap. Timestamp policy rejected Check policy-specific positive bounds, the reorder-window relationship, and the required true depth flags. Rust Engine unavailable Install or rebuild with mf engine build normalize. Configuration changed concurrently Inspect the current file again and build a fresh candidate. Setting appears to have no effect Compare current effective settings with the preparation and execution copies and the publication's processing-runtime.json. Check activation and the evidence in dataset verification.

items.title: 14. Complete parameter index
items.text:
The linked tables are the authoritative field entries. Shared leaves are defined once and apply to each named parent.

Section Leaves Schema, fan-in and scratch 4 Resource budgets and path 4 Normalization safety limits 8 Parquet output 2 Diagnostics 2 Integrity switch and seven rules, each with eight leaves 57 Trade and depth reconciliation, including shared preference leaves 15 Trade and depth timestamp regression 11 Total current authoring schema 103

Compatibility for retained general.toml is separate. The Rust loader accepts legacy merge.partitions_per_worker (usize, default 4) and merge.compression_level (i32, default 3) only under that filename. Normalization discards these values. See merge runtime for the operation that uses them.

Rust remains the configuration authority. See the runtime loader and schema, normalization execution, and Forge runtime resolution.

items.title: Normalization recipes
items.text:
For Engine processing settings, see Normalization runtime configuration. Source field interpretation belongs to normalization profiles.

A recipe selects registered raw inputs. Managed recipes live in data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/normalization/ and take their names from their TOML filenames. Both recipe shapes use version 1. The normalization guide demonstrates source selection. Prepared batches have their own Engine contract.

items.title: Editable recipe
items.text:
Source selection is the usual recipe shape. Forge matches complete registered archives against each request and selects whole overlapping inputs from the configured raw root. Source selection lets Forge derive the job and Engine dataset IDs and output paths.

Field Accepted values and constraints version Integer 1, the default. interval.start, interval.end Required timezone-aware timestamps. Start must precede end. The common interval includes start and excludes end. requests Required array with at least one [[requests]] entry. requests[].exchange Required registered execution venue code matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$. requests[].instrument_type Required. spot, perpetual, future, option, or equity. requests[].market_category Required. spot, linear, inverse, option, or equity. Equity must be used in both market and instrument fields together. requests[].data_type Required. trades or order_book_l2. The Engine calls the latter depth. requests[].scope.kind Required. instrument, family, or base_coin. Match the scope recorded for the archive. requests[].scope.identifier Required nonblank native scope identifier, such as Bybit BTCUSDT or OKX BTC-USD for an inverse futures family. requests[].source_options.feed Gate.io L2 only. incremental (default) or snapshot. requests[].source_key Optional nonempty key without whitespace. Required for equity. Requires instrument scope and selects the named external source. ranking_policy Policy name matching ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$. Defaults to turnover.

Use the complete Bybit TOML example for a concrete instrument, or the synthetic equity recipe for an external source with both feeds.

items.title: Source key requirements
items.text: Use the actual execution venue as exchange and the registered recording collection as source_key. For example, the synthetic recording walkthrough registers synthetic-equity for AAPL under example_exchange. Preparation requires a ready historical binding and verifies the registered profile fingerprint against the installed interpretation.

items.title: Family-scoped archives
items.text: A family request matches registered family archives. Forge supplies available instrument and specification authority, and the Engine resolves concrete archive bindings. Missing or conflicting evidence can block preparation. See family archives.

items.title: How stream ranks are assigned
items.text: The recipe selects archives. The ranking policy supplies ordering evidence from an existing published turnover snapshot, when available. Forge assigns dense ranks to the selected streams, with stable stream identity ordering for ties and unranked streams. Without a snapshot, it uses deterministic stream identity ordering. Preparation uses retained rankings and does not refresh provider statistics. See ranking snapshot resolution.

items.title: Nominal coverage checks
items.text: Preparation checks recorded archive intervals against the request and reports gaps, which can block the plan. Whole-file selection can extend past the requested interval. Nominal intervals and unknown evidence are distinct from observed event coverage.

items.title: Legacy file-ID preparation
items.text:
This shape selects explicit local archive and catalogue instrument IDs and prepares one content type. Use IDs from the intended registry and raw root. The example records IDs from a testing preview of the Bybit trades recipe. Use the corresponding local archive and instrument IDs from your registry, and choose unused Engine job and dataset IDs for your workspace.

version = 1
job_id = 4876983777293105620
dataset_id = 3120756497191505481
content_type = "trades"

[[inputs]]
task_id = 1
archive_id = 1834
instrument_id = 1999

items.title: Legacy request parameters
items.text:
Field Accepted values and constraints version, ranking_policy Same defaults and constraints as source selection. job_id, dataset_id Required positive unsigned 64-bit Engine IDs. Preparation checks collisions against known registered and prepared artifacts. content_type Required. trades or depth. inputs Required array with at least one entry. Each archive/member pair may appear once. inputs[].task_id Required unique positive unsigned 64-bit integer. Forge assigns task IDs anew in the generated order. inputs[].archive_id, inputs[].instrument_id Required positive signed 64-bit IDs. The instrument must agree with resolved archive identity. inputs[].format_profile Optional nonblank historical profile field. inputs[].archive_member Optional nonempty historical member field. inputs[].source_compression Optional historical field. plain, gzip, zip, or tar_gzip. inputs[].stream_rank Optional historical field. Unsigned 32-bit integer. output Optional explicit output paths. If present, both paths are required.

The optional historical input fields remain readable for compatibility. The current planner resolves the archive as a whole, derives ranks, and uses the installed profile catalogue and Engine content resolution. These fields do not provide overrides for those decisions.

items.title: Legacy output paths
items.text: output.staging_path and output.dataset_path are nonblank absolute or workspace-relative paths. They must be distinct, absent, and share a parent for atomic publication. By default, the publication goes to datasets/normalized/<dataset_id>/ under the configured data root, with sibling staging path .<dataset_id>.staging.<job_id>.

items.title: Validation rules
items.text: Unknown fields are rejected for both shapes. A recipe with inputs or job_id is read as explicit-input TOML. Structural validation checks fields, types, and local constraints. Preparation separately checks registered inputs, paths and checksums, instrument identity, historical specifications, and planned outputs. Persisted preparation uses the production Rust batch parser for executable plans. See preparation results and the CLI reference.

items.title: Pipeline recipes
items.text:
Save the version-1 TOML under data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/pipeline/. The name resolves in that library. The recipe compiles inline acquisition requests into acquisition and normalization inputs. Merge receives the registered file IDs from normalization. Stage resource overrides live in the separate pipeline runtime. Pipeline guide · CLI

Path Type and constraints Default and meaning version Required integer 1 Pipeline recipe schema interval.start, interval.end Required timezone-aware TOML datetime values, ordered and representable as signed 64-bit Unix nanoseconds One half-open UTC interval shared across stages requests Required nonempty list of unique acquisition requests. Exchange adapter validates the scope. Requests must also form valid normalization requests Source scope and feed selection normalize.ranking_policy Nonempty token matching ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$ turnover merge.timeline_ordering Optional causal or chronological Omission lets Forge select based on inputs

The recipe contains no raw, file dataset, or publication IDs. Forge binds the acquired revisions and normalized primary-file registrations to the stage outputs. See Forge evidence for artifacts used by resume. Pipeline model

items.title: Minimal recipe
items.text:
This recipe selects one Bybit trade archive scope. Save it in the pipeline library and run mf pipeline validate NAME before inspecting the plan. The interval selects archives, and local readiness is checked separately.

version = 1

[interval]
start = 2026-10-27T00:00:00Z
end = 2026-10-28T00:00:00Z

[[requests]]
exchange = "bybit"
instrument_type = "perpetual"
market_category = "linear"
data_type = "trades"
scope = { kind = "instrument", identifier = "BTCUSDT" }

Validation checks the recipe and request structure. Planning also checks the selected database and effective runtime. Run with current managed engines and the appropriate catalogue, specification evidence, and profiles.

items.title: Developer overview
items.text: Forge is the Python orchestration layer. It owns request selection, catalogue and registry access, managed storage, job preparation, and run evidence. The Rust Engine owns source interpretation, event processing, and operation-specific publication. Changes to a public contract must account for its writer, validator, and readers.

items.title: Locate the change
items.text:
Change Where to start CLI, TUI, registry, acquisition, preparation, or recovery Forge architecture Source decoding, canonical values, reconciliation, or depth reconstruction Normalization Engine Timeline ordering or materialization across publications Merge Engine Currency references or conversion output Conversion Engine A stored job, manifest, or registry contract Orchestration and persistence and compatibility

The system overview traces the boundaries between these components. The public reference defines the user-visible contracts they implement.

items.title: Set up and verify a change
items.text:
Use local development setup and the first contribution walkthrough to check your environment. Then choose an extension point and keep a representative fixture close to the code it exercises. The Bybit listing walkthrough shows how to carry one provider change through discovery, validation, tests, and documentation.

Use the testing guide to choose fixture and database coverage. For a failure, trace retained evidence before measuring performance. Review compatibility and contribution checks before handing off a change.

items.title: System architecture
items.text:
Follow the boundary between application decisions and event processing. Forge resolves what to process and records where it came from. The historical Engine interprets those inputs, produces physical output, and checks publication invariants. This division lets Engine processing use pinned filesystem inputs while Forge manages database-backed selection and registration.

---
config:
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 16
    rankSpacing: 18
    padding: 6
---
flowchart TB
    U["CLI and Forge TUI"] --> F["Forge orchestration"]
    F <-->|"Registry metadata"| DB[("PostgreSQL")]
    F -->|"Acquire or import"| RAW["Managed source files"]
    F -->|"Prepare and supervise"| JOB["Prepared jobs and retained evidence"]
    JOB --> ENG["Normalize, Merge or Convert"]
    RAW -->|"Normalize inputs"| ENG
    PUB["Published datasets"] -->|"Merge or Convert inputs"| ENG
    ENG -->|"Finalize output"| PUB
    PUB -->|"Verify and register"| F
    PUB -->|"Scan files and manifests"| READ["Dataset discovery and inspection"]
    DB -->|"Registry-backed inspection"| READ

Forge requests archive listings and downloads over HTTP, stores managed copies, and verifies Engine output. It is the database client for these historical operations. The Engine reads job documents and committed inputs from disk. The Python dataset API can open a committed publication directly and can enrich its views when the caller supplies registry records. CLI dispatch · Python dataset API

Boundary Ownership and implementation Request and orchestration forge/cli/main.py parses commands and loads the application context. Services under forge/historical/ resolve recipes, authorities and paths, supervise subprocesses, and retain reports. CLI JSON and exit status expose application outcomes. Source archives forge/historical/archives/sources/ validates provider requests and listings. Storage services manage copies and hashes. Manually supplied archives enter through registration and import instead of provider discovery. Catalogue and registry forge/shared/database/sql/core/ establishes metadata, provenance and file relationships. Catalogue and registration services resolve instrument and specification evidence. PostgreSQL stores metadata and paths, while files hold source bytes and committed output. Configuration and profile interpretation Forge validates recipe models and resolves configuration libraries. Rust compiles installed format profiles and validates job contracts before interpreting source records. Historical processing The Engine binaries dispatch into engine/src/historical/ and reuse format, conversion and persistence code under engine/src/shared/. Engine errors surface through exit status and operation-specific diagnostics. Discovery and inspection forge/datasets/discovery.py reads manifest inventories and physical evidence. Dataset operations use Arrow for exact batches and offer Polars previews or supported lazy projections. Registry-backed terminal inspection follows a separate CLI path.

The fixed historical pipeline runs acquisition, normalization, then merge. Normalize consumes pinned raw copies. Merge consumes normalized publications and Convert consumes an existing physical merge, with optional reference publications. The pipeline retains its plan and attempts and can resume a managed run from retained evidence. Quote conversion remains a separate operation. Pipeline guide · Prepared contracts

The separate Live binary loads live exchange and format configuration and runs its own application and stream graph. The normal start path restores definitions from PostgreSQL. Static validation exercises configuration without restoring that graph or contacting exchanges. Follow the entry point into engine/src/live/application/ for runtime wiring and engine/src/live/stream/ for processing. Live and management tests use their own Cargo features. Live entry point · Cargo features

items.title: Identity and evidence
items.text:
An execution venue identifies the market that produced an event. A data provider supplies access to the archive. A provider or a recording can have its own symbol, object key and path. The catalogue relates an observed source scope to canonical identity and historical specification evidence. A family request may discover multiple concrete derivatives. Normalize each with the correct concrete identity and effective specification. Preserve provenance when two sources describe the same venue or symbol. Catalogue workflow · Registration reference

Concept Consequence for implementation Source object and local copy A provider object's stable key and nominal interval establish discovery identity. A managed local copy adds location and hash evidence. Keep those identities separate from temporary download URLs and from the provider's current listing. Instrument and stream An instrument ID is namespace-qualified. A stream adds content and source context. A rank orders or identifies streams within a job or publication contract. Trades and depth can belong to the same instrument and remain separate streams. Publication and primary file One Engine publication can contain several primary files. Registration gives its publication and each registered file separate database IDs. Check which ID, namespace and member files a selector expects. Source records and canonical rows A raw record has provider-specific shape and units. One depth event can produce multiple canonical level rows, and some observations emit zero rows. Preserve indices and offsets that connect observations, events and rows. Requested and observed time Requested bounds are half-open where the contract specifies that form. Observed endpoints describe measured row timestamps, often inclusive. They cannot prove continuous coverage. A reconstruction event can sit outside the requested market interval where the physical contract permits it.

For Bybit BTC perpetual data, acquisition locates files for the venue, instrument scope and feed. Normalization resolves identity, interprets trade timestamps and reconstructs depth using the selected profiles. A combined merge keeps the streams distinct in one timeline. Quote conversion can use a selected trade stream as a price reference while still converting rows from both trade and depth streams.

items.title: Publication state
items.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Staged: write output
    Staged --> Failed: checks fail
    Staged --> Committed: Engine commit
    Committed --> Registered: Forge verifies and registers

This diagram shows the publication and registration boundary for managed normalization and merge. A final directory and registered rows have separate commit points. Failure can leave diagnostic artifacts or staging, depending on the phase. A registration retry uses a supported retained receipt and verifies committed evidence again. See the operation-specific paths in Historical operation lifecycles and the publication format reference.

Read the component chapters for implementation details. Forge · Normalization Engine · Merge Engine · Conversion Engine

items.title: Compatibility and contributions
items.text:
Review a change by following the contract from its producer to each consumer. Keep editable configuration, submitted jobs, committed publications and registry records distinct. An older installed executable and a newer Forge checkout can encounter a version mismatch even when both components build successfully.

Contract Producer, validators and consumers Review Application and operation TOML CLI configuration library and Pydantic models feed the Forge services Accepted fields and types, path and name resolution, defaults and explicit legacy rejection Format profiles Authors and Forge profile lifecycle feed the Rust catalogue compiler and task resolver Version, physical fields, source mapping and interpretation, installed provenance, exact outputs for sample records Prepared inputs and process results Forge serializers and Engine loaders, followed by Forge execution and result readers Normalization batch v4, merge's pinned single job, conversion's standalone job v1 and separate Forge collection. Check actual command capability and reject unsupported fields or formats Catalogue and migrations Registration and catalogue services, database constraints and current migration runner Identity and historical authority, applied checksums, upgrading an existing registry, rollback and idempotence Canonical columns and auxiliary data Engine writers and publication validators feed merge, conversion and dataset readers Physical types, exact values, indices, ownership and boundary semantics. Keep auxiliary evidence covered by the inventory Publication manifests and registry summaries Engine commit, Forge verification, publication/file registration and downstream consumption Supported versions, checksums and bounds, path safety, exact stream and file membership where available Structured CLI and Python dataset API Operation reporting and filesystem/registry readers feed scripts and notebooks Fields, status and exit codes, old manifests, scan/projection constraints and conflict diagnostics

Use the prepared contracts, profile reference, publication formats and Python API for exact schemas and supported versions. The Python discovery gate accepts normalized protocol versions 3, 4 and 5, and separate merge contracts including protocol 1 with chronological physical schema 1 or causal physical schema 2. The discovery gate also has a protocol-2 merge branch for timeline schema 1. That branch establishes the reader's version check, with further inventory and identity checks following it. Conversion job acceptance and Python publication discovery are separate boundaries. Current Python discovery recognizes normalization and merge manifests, and converted output is verified by conversion orchestration.

items.title: Follow the change across versions
items.text:
1. Identify the existing data or document that must still work. Keep a representative prior-format fixture and one for the new format.
  2. Trace the serializer, parser, operation validator, producer and actual consumer. For a version change, exercise rejection of unsupported versions as well as acceptance of supported ones. A loader accepting JSON alone cannot prove a useful publication.
  3. Review persisted datasets and applied migrations as immutable evidence. Use the existing workflow to regenerate a job or produce a new publication when the change requires it. Keep migrations additive to the applied sequence and test the prior-to-current path.
  4. Check a small positive case and a failure case where missing or changed provenance would otherwise be accepted. Use an isolated output destination. Record any remaining limitation such as a platform boundary, a skipped recorded fixture, or a difference between an installed and source-tree executable.

For example, adding a causal marker to a timeline affects the physical schema discriminator, sequence validation, merge writer, conversion reader and Python discovery.
