Compare the old and new schema branches and retain coverage for timestamp regression with correct physical order. Changing a label in terminal presentation has a smaller scope unless it changes a machine-readable field or identifier.

items.title: Prepare a reviewable contribution
items.text:
• Describe the user-visible problem, the responsible boundary and the observable result. Include a small reproduction or an exact fixture.
  • Keep changes within the affected operation or shared contract. Include matching documentation updates, and link to the authoritative contract rather than duplicating it.
  • Run the applicable Ruff, Pyright, Rust formatting/checking and focused tests from Testing. Include verified outcomes, skips and prerequisites. For diagrams, inspect the rendered site on a wide and narrow viewport in addition to building it.
  • Review the diff for unrelated changes, generated data and secrets. Include before/after behavior for an interface change and the supported rerun or migration path if applicable.
  • State what the verification establishes. For example, “portable conversion validates a prepared fixture without writing output” is a structural and planning check. It leaves publication and database behavior to separate checks.

Documentation lives under docs/content/. Keep links to supported behavior in the appropriate audience section and use the current implementation to check new examples. Repository engineering instructions

items.title: Conversion Engine architecture
items.text:
flowchart TD
    J["Prepared conversion job"] --> B["Bind publications and stream identities"]
    S["Source physical merge"] --> B
    R["Optional reference trade merge"] --> B

    B --> P["Plan currency conversion paths"]
    P --> V["Verify input payload checksums"]
    V --> C["Initialize reference state or build checkpoints"]

    C --> K["Convert events in source order"]
    S --> K
    R -->|Eligible reference observations| K

    K --> O["Write converted Parquet"]
    K --> E["Retain execution receipt"]

    O --> G["Validate output and reconcile accounting"]
    E --> G
    S -->|Original columns| G

    G --> M["Write conversion manifest"]
    M --> F["Publish converted dataset"]

The conversion engine expresses selected market-data values in a target quote currency while preserving the original merged events.

It reads a physical merge publication, evaluates conversion paths against eligible reference trades, and appends target values together with the evidence used to calculate them. The output retains the original prices, quantities, identities, event order, and depth changes.

The implementation lives in engine/src/historical/convert/. Its historical execution code handles publication binding, Parquet input, temporal alignment, partition checkpoints, output construction, validation, and publication. Currency graphs, reference-state evaluation, and monetary arithmetic belong to the shared conversion domain.

The diagram shows the composed execution lifecycle. The caller coordinates preparation, content verification, materialization, receipt persistence, and publication through separate APIs.1327

items.title: What conversion changes
items.text:
Conversion adds target values for two economic quantities:

Source value Added value Event or level price Price expressed in the target quote currency. Quote quantity, when present Quote quantity expressed in the target quote currency.

Base quantities and contract quantities remain part of the preserved source data. A missing quote quantity remains missing; conversion does not derive it from other fields.

Other source fields, including mark prices, index prices, and implied volatility where present, are preserved. Their presence does not imply that conversion creates target versions of them.

For an illustrative direct reference:

Native price:       100 USDT
Reference price:   0.999 USD per USDT
Target price:      99.9 USD

The original price remains available alongside the target price. Each successful non-identity conversion also records its currency path and the reference observations used.

A depth level receives the same kind of event-time valuation. Conversion does not reconstruct and reprice the entire book whenever a reference changes.1889

items.title: Conversion preserves the event population
items.text:
Every source event remains represented in the converted output.

An event whose target value cannot be calculated receives an unavailable status and null target values. An event outside the selected conversion scope in combined mode receives a skipped status.

Neither condition removes the original event.

A successfully published dataset can therefore contain unavailable or skipped conversions. Publication success means the output passed its applicable validation and accounting checks; the status counters describe conversion availability.192527

items.title: Module boundaries
items.text:
Paths in this table are relative to engine/src/historical/convert/.

Module Responsibility planning/prepared.rs Bind a prepared job to physical publications and embedded stream metadata. planning/catalog.rs Resolve reference selection and provide the alternate catalogue-based resolution API. planning/planner.rs Adapt the historical job to the shared conversion planner. reference/reader.rs Read physical trade observations used as references. reference/external.rs Advance and restore an external reference cursor. execution/shared/ Source readers, row-group partitions, common checkpoints, and trade reference prepasses. execution/trades/ Trade conversion kernels, sequential materialization, and parallel workers. execution/depth/ Depth valuation, external reference alignment, checkpoints, and workers. execution/combined/ Mixed-event conversion, internal/external reference alignment, selection, and workers. output/schema/ Appended Arrow fields, conversion rows, status codes, and batch construction. output/writers/ Combined batch construction and the adapter to merge’s physical Parquet writer. output/validation/ Physical validation, numeric checks, causal positions, and source preservation. output/publication/ Execution receipts, manifests, reference provenance, and publication. progress/ Phase reporting, partition counters, validation progress, and cooperative interruption.

Several small modules are reexports rather than local implementations:

Historical module Implementation owner planning/graph.rs shared::conversion::graph reference/state.rs shared::conversion::reference reference/evaluation.rs shared::conversion::evaluation shared/decimal.rs shared::conversion::decimal trades/trade.rs shared::conversion::trades depth/depth.rs shared::conversion::depth

Changes to path enumeration, reference-history semantics, decimal arithmetic, or the underlying monetary calculations belong in those shared modules. Historical adapters should remain responsible for translating persisted data into that domain.12

items.title: Execution entry points
items.text:
The public APIs expose several stages of the lifecycle.

API Responsibility prepare_conversion_execution Validate and bind prepared publication evidence, resolve references, and construct the conversion plan. PreparedConversion::verify_content Hash source and external-reference payload files against their bound checksum inventories. materialize_trade_conversion Sequentially write converted trade output into staging. materialize_depth_conversion Sequentially write depth output using external trade references. materialize_combined_conversion Sequentially write combined output with internal and optional external references. execute_parallel_conversion Execute checkpointed trade partitions. execute_parallel_depth_conversion Execute checkpointed depth partitions. execute_parallel_combined_conversion Execute checkpointed combined partitions. publish_conversion and the depth/combined variants Validate staging, reconcile the receipt, verify source preservation, write the manifest, and publish.

Progress-enabled variants expose the same operations with reporting and interruption checks.

execute_conversion_sequential has a different role: it evaluates reference availability and returns statistics. It does not materialize converted Parquet or publish a dataset.6

items.title: The caller composes the lifecycle
items.text:
For a sequential trade conversion, the call sequence is:

let prepared = prepare_conversion_execution(&job)?;

prepared.verify_content(&job, &reporter)?;

let metrics = materialize_trade_conversion_with_progress(
    &job,
    &prepared.source,
    &prepared.plan,
    &staging,
    &parquet,
    &reporter,
)?;

ConversionExecutionReceipt::new(job.job_id, &metrics)?
    .write(&staging)?;

let publication = publish_conversion_with_progress(
    &job,
    &prepared.source,
    &staging,
    &reporter,
)?;

This example assumes the caller has loaded the job, selected a fresh staging path, and supplied Parquet settings and a reporter.

Materialization returns execution metrics. The caller creates the receipt from those metrics before requesting publication. Writing staged Parquet alone does not complete the publication workflow.72527

items.title: Bind prepared inputs to physical evidence
items.text:
prepare_conversion_execution() consumes a ConvertJob containing the source publication declaration and optional external-reference declaration.

The prepared job supplies stream identities and currency metadata. Execution binds those declarations to the physical merge evidence rather than performing database discovery.

For each publication, binding checks:

  1. The SHA-256 of manifest.json.
  2. The SHA-256 of publication-checksums.json.
  3. The merge job identity and manifest entry in the checksum inventory.
  4. Checksum entries for every declared primary file.
  5. Physical file sizes, schemas, row counts, and row-group totals.
  6. Normalized-parent declarations against retained merge input evidence.
  7. Stream kind, rank, stream ID, publication ID, instrument ID, exchange, symbol, and available currency metadata.

The resulting PreparedConversion contains the source manifest, optional external manifest, conversion plan, and bound checksum inventories.

Prepared execution does not require reopening every original normalization directory or loading an external instrument catalogue. Its currency declarations come from the prepared bindings and are checked against the available publication evidence.3

items.title: Metadata binding and payload hashing are separate
items.text:
validate_conversion_input() inspects the manifest, file inventory, Arrow schema, and Parquet footers. It does not scan every market row.

PreparedConversion::verify_content() performs the separate full-file hashing pass. It checks every primary file in the source and optional external publication against the bound inventory.

Calling prepare_conversion_execution() alone does not perform that full payload verification.

Maintain this distinction when adding a new entry point: a valid schema and matching publication metadata establish different facts from verified payload bytes.314

items.title: The alternate catalogue resolver
items.text:
resolve_conversion_catalog() and resolve_conversion_catalog_with_normalization_root() provide a separate library route.

They resolve instruments through an InstrumentCatalog and normalized processing provenance, including compatibility handling for older processing-job layouts.

That route is useful when constructing conversion inputs from catalogue information. Its catalogue and normalization-root requirements are not prerequisites of the prepared execution API.4

items.title: Source modes and reference selection
items.text:
Reference prices come from explicitly selected trade streams.

Source mode Reference source Trades Selected trades inside the source publication. An external reference publication is rejected. Depth A separate trade-only physical merge. Combined Matching internal trade streams first, with external trade streams used where no internal match is selected.

External reference publications must be trade-only physical merges.

Reference selection rejects missing requested instruments, duplicate selected reference stream IDs, and ambiguous external references that conflict with internal combined trade streams.

The prepared execution path also applies these restrictions:

  • Trade conversion rejects unresolved planned streams.
  • Depth conversion requires an external reference publication and at least one nonempty conversion path using reference edges.
  • Combined conversion validates the separation between internal and external reference sets.

An entirely identity-only depth job therefore does not automatically bypass external-reference setup in the current prepared path.

The conversion kernels also require unambiguous source stream ranks. Treat stream rank as a validated binding, not a value that can be reassigned while reading rows.4311

items.title: Plan currency paths before evaluating events
items.text:
plan_conversion() translates the historical configuration into inputs for the shared planner:

  • Target quote currency.
  • Resolved source instruments.
  • Selected reference instruments.
  • Instrument-kind selection.
  • Maximum hop count.

The resulting ConversionPlan records each source stream’s identity-conversion status, selection status, and candidate currency paths.

A path describes how to express the source quote currency in the target quote currency. Each edge identifies a reference stream and its conversion direction.

Planning establishes that a route exists. It does not establish that the necessary observations will be available and fresh at every source event.5

items.title: Path policy affects the available candidates
items.text:
For ConversionPathPolicy::Primary, the historical wrapper truncates each stream’s candidate list to its first path before execution.

The event kernels then try the retained candidate paths in their supplied order. They stop after a path successfully evaluates and converts the required values.

If an attempted path fails evaluation or arithmetic, another retained path may be tried. Primary policy has already removed those alternatives.

This produces one conversion result per source event. It does not expand one event into a separate output row for every candidate path.589

items.title: Preserve exact arithmetic through the shared domain
items.text:
Target values use Decimal256(76, 28) in the output schema.

The numeric validation path reconstructs a rational conversion factor from the serialized reference prices and directions:

  • A direct edge contributes its reference price.
  • An inverse edge contributes the reciprocal.
  • Multiple edges contribute to one combined numerator and denominator.

The stored conversion_rate is a decimal representation of that factor. Target values are calculated through the shared decimal operations using the path ratio.

Do not replace this with multiplication by an already rounded stored rate. Doing so can introduce an additional rounding step and produce different target values.

The shared decimal implementation owns the exact rounding and overflow policy.212

items.title: Reference timing determines eligibility
items.text:
A conversion uses observations that are eligible for the source event.

Reference evidence carries:

  • Publication and stream identity.
  • Event timestamp.
  • Stream rank.
  • Task ID.
  • Event ordinal.
  • Native reference price.

The event kernel passes its ReferenceKey and max_staleness_ns to the shared evaluator. Missing observations, stale observations, future observations, identity mismatches, and arithmetic failures remain distinct outcomes.

The original reference price is installed in state. Converted target values are not recursively fed back as reference observations.812

items.title: Evaluate internal trades before observing them
items.text:
An internal trade reference becomes available after its own event has been evaluated.

This ordering prevents a trade from supplying its own newly observed price during its conversion.

items.title: Advance external references strictly before the source timestamp
items.text:
ExternalReferenceCursor::advance_before() consumes external observations whose timestamps are strictly less than the current source timestamp.

The first observation at or after that timestamp remains pending. Unselected external streams still advance the physical cursor position, but they do not update the selected reference state.

An external observation at exactly the source timestamp is therefore not eligible through this cursor.

Internal reference eligibility additionally follows the reference-key ordering enforced by evaluation and validation. A same-timestamp internal observation can precede a later event by its key; that differs from the external cursor’s strict timestamp rule.1222

sequenceDiagram
    participant L as Source loop
    participant A as Reference alignment
    participant E as External trade cursor
    participant K as Conversion kernel
    participant S as Reference state

    L->>A: Source event
    opt External references configured
        A->>E: Advance strictly before event timestamp
        E->>S: Install eligible observations
    end

    A->>K: Evaluate source event
    K->>S: Resolve eligible path observations
    S-->>K: Rate and evidence, or unavailable reason
    K-->>A: Conversion result

    opt Source event is an internal reference trade
        A->>S: Install original trade observation
    end

    A-->>L: Source event with appended conversion fields

The diagram describes the ordering rule shared by the alignment and kernel layers. Publication and writing occur after the result is constructed.1013

items.title: Preserve causal input order
items.text:
Conversion inherits the source publication’s ordering contract.

For chronological input, PhysicalConversionReader checks nondecreasing reference keys.

For causal input, it validates:

  • Contiguous timeline_sequence.
  • Required timestamp and reconstruction fields.
  • Agreement between reconstruction_only and membership in the requested interval.
  • Depth-only use of out-of-interval reconstruction observations.

It does not sort causal events into timestamp order.14

items.title: Retain enough reference history for timestamp regressions
items.text:
A causal source can move backward in event time while progressing forward in timeline order.

Before processing such a source, the reader performs a timestamp-only scan. It measures the largest backward distance from the running timestamp high-water mark and initializes ReferenceState with that regression window.

This pass reads timestamps, not future reference prices. Actual reference prices still enter state during the ordered traversal.

When an external cursor encounters a permitted source timestamp regression, it does not rewind its files. Historical selection is handled by the retained shared reference state.

Changes to this behavior must keep the timestamp scan, state retention, external advancement, and checkpoint restoration consistent.1412

items.title: Trades
items.text:
TradeConversionKernel resolves the planned stream, validates its publication identity, constructs the event key, and evaluates conversion.

Its output is one of:

  • Identity values with rate one.
  • Converted values with a selected path and reference evidence.
  • Unavailable values with a failure reason.

The optional quote quantity retains its nullability.

If the trade belongs to a selected reference stream, its original observation enters state after evaluation.8

items.title: Depth
items.text:
DepthConversionKernel evaluates one conversion path for the complete source observation and applies that path to the observation’s level changes.

The target changes remain positionally aligned with the original list.

Conversion is atomic at the observation level:

  1. Attempt the selected path for all levels.
  2. If a level fails arithmetic, discard that attempt.
  3. Try another retained path where available.
  4. If no path succeeds, emit null target values for every original level.

The optimized depth path writes into contiguous buffers. It records the buffer position before an attempt and rolls back appended values and validity bits if the attempt fails.

An observation with no level changes still receives conversion metadata and an empty target list.913

items.title: Target depth prices are event-time annotations
items.text:
The kernel processes the changes in the current event. It does not maintain a second, independently keyed target-currency book.

A reference-rate change can therefore produce different target prices for later updates to the same native level. It does not generate synthetic updates for untouched levels.

Replay the original depth changes using their native side and price keys. Use the aligned target values as valuations of those changes at their event time.

A continuously repriced target-currency book would require a separate representation with explicit rules for revaluation and level identity.918

items.title: Combined events
items.text:
CombinedConversionKernel dispatches each row to the trade or depth kernel while maintaining one reference alignment state.

It also implements conversion selection:

  • Selected events receive identity, converted, or unavailable results.
  • Unselected events receive skipped.
  • An unselected trade can still update a selected internal reference after its own event is handled.

This allows a combined source to retain reference trades while converting only selected instruments or event populations.

The physical materializers and partition workers use the batch conversion path. Direct single-event helpers are separate code paths and should receive their own accounting coverage when extended, particularly for skipped depth events.10

items.title: Partition by physical order
items.text:
Conversion partitions the existing physical timeline into contiguous row-group ranges.

build_conversion_partition_plan_with_count() reads Parquet metadata and records:

  • File and row-group indexes.
  • Global starting row.
  • Row count.
  • Compressed byte size.

Partition balancing is based approximately on row counts while keeping row groups intact. Requested partition count is capped by the number of row groups.

The partitioner does not create independent time windows. A causal timeline can regress in timestamp, and reference state depends on the complete preceding source sequence.15

items.title: A checkpoint represents the preceding source prefix
items.text:
Each worker must begin with the reference state that a sequential traversal would have established immediately before its first event.

The prepass captures that state at partition boundaries.

Source mode Checkpoint contents Trades Partition identity, number of preceding events, and reference-state snapshot. Depth Partition start row and timestamp, reference-state snapshot, and external observation position. Combined Partition start row and timestamp, reference-state snapshot, and optional external observation position.

Checkpoints are captured before processing the boundary event.

For external references, the checkpoint position describes consumed observations. A pending observation is not silently counted as consumed; the resumed cursor must encounter it again when it becomes eligible.

These checkpoints initialize partition workers. They do not define a persisted recovery protocol for resuming an interrupted conversion run.16

items.title: The prepass must reproduce execution alignment
items.text:
The trade prepass updates selected internal references in source order.

The depth prepass reads source timestamps and reproduces external-reference advancement.

The combined prepass reproduces both external advancement and internal trade updates. Its normal path projects the columns needed for that work, avoiding the full depth payload. A full-reader comparison entry point is also available.

A change to reference timing must update both the execution path and the matching prepass. Otherwise, partitions can start from a state that differs from sequential execution.16

items.title: Workers preserve deterministic output order
items.text:
Each worker:

  1. Validates its partition/checkpoint alignment.
  2. Restores reference state and external cursor position.
  3. Reads its assigned row groups.
  4. Runs the same mode-specific kernel used by sequential materialization.
  5. Writes partition output.
  6. Returns metrics and row boundaries.

The coordinator sorts results by partition ID and verifies expected boundaries and totals.

Parallel and sequential executions should produce equivalent decoded events and conversion evidence. Their Parquet file boundaries and encoded bytes need not be identical.17

items.title: Resource behavior and interruption
items.text:
The conversion executors use a bounded thread pool over a shared work queue.

Worker count is limited by the requested count and available partitions. The current execution code does not use normalization’s memory-budget admission system and does not spill checkpoint state to scratch.

Memory demand includes:

  • Resident checkpoint snapshots.
  • Per-worker reference state.
  • Arrow input batches.
  • Nested depth levels.
  • Per-event conversion evidence.
  • Output arrays and Parquet buffers.

The standard reader batch contains up to 65,536 event rows. Event count alone is not a bound on decoded bytes: one depth event can contain many level changes.

Treat worker count as a concurrency control, not a hard memory limit.1714

items.title: Interruption is cooperative
items.text:
The shared progress state carries an interruption flag. Readers, workers, validators, and publication code check it at work boundaries.

On a worker failure, parallel execution clears queued work, joins the worker threads, and returns an error. Already running work is not terminated as an unsafe thread operation.

Publication checks interruption immediately before the final rename.

An interruption can leave staging artifacts. It does not turn the in-memory reference checkpoints into reusable on-disk resume state.172927

items.title: Output schemas
items.text:
All output schemas begin with the complete source schema and append conversion fields.

Source mode Added target payload Trades Nullable price_target and quantity_quote_target. Depth Non-null changes_target, aligned with the original changes list. Combined trade_target or depth_target, according to the event kind.

Combined trade rows contain a trade target struct and a null depth target. Combined depth rows contain a depth target list and a null trade target.

Unavailable values remain null inside the appropriate target payload. An unavailable depth event retains one target entry per original level; it does not shrink the list.18

items.title: Shared conversion metadata
items.text:
Every mode appends these fields:

Field Meaning target_quote Requested target currency. conversion_status Identity, converted, unavailable, or supported skipped result. conversion_rate Decimal representation of the selected conversion factor. conversion_path Currency sequence for the chosen path. conversion_references Per-hop observations used by a successful conversion. conversion_failure Failure classification for an unavailable result.

Reference entries retain the source dataset ID, stream ID, event timestamp, stream rank, task ID, event ordinal, conversion direction, and original reference price.

Direction code 0 represents direct conversion; code 1 represents inverse conversion.

Identity conversion uses rate one, an identity currency path, and no reference observations.1820

items.title: Status and failure codes
items.text:
Code Status Meaning 0 Identity The value already uses the target quote currency. 1 Converted A candidate path and its eligible observations produced target values. 2 Unavailable Target values could not be produced; a failure code explains why. 3 Skipped A combined event was retained outside the selected conversion scope.

Standalone trade and depth publication validators accept the first three statuses. Skipped behavior belongs to the combined conversion path.

Code Failure 1 Missing reference. 2 Stale reference. 3 Future reference. 4 Reference identity mismatch. 5 Arithmetic failure. 6 No conversion path.

If candidate attempts all fail, the event retains the failure classification from the final attempt. This field is not a complete trace of every rejected candidate.

Some no-path conditions are rejected during preparation before any rows are written; others remain representable by the event kernels.1989

items.title: Validation has several separate responsibilities
items.text:
Publication combines physical inspection, execution accounting, and source preservation.

Each check establishes a different part of the result.

items.title: Validate the written representation
items.text:
Physical validators reopen converted Parquet and inspect the applicable schema, status representation, payload structure, ordering, reference evidence, and counts.

For causal output, timeline positions must remain contiguous across the dataset and reconstruction markers must remain valid for the event kind.

Depth and combined validation can run over files in parallel. Results are then checked in deterministic file order, including ordering or causal-position boundaries between files.23

items.title: Validate target arithmetic where implemented
items.text:
Numeric verification currently differs by mode.

Mode Numeric validation Standalone trades Checks identity equality, target nullability, positive stored rates, and reference chronology, staleness, and positive prices. Depth Reconstructs the path ratio from serialized reference evidence and checks the stored rate and every successful target level value. Combined Reconstructs the ratio and checks successful trade values and depth levels, together with event-kind payload structure.

The standalone trade validator currently does not independently recompute non-identity target values or the stored conversion rate.

Depth and combined numeric validation check the calculation against the reference evidence written into the output. They do not reopen every reference dataset and independently locate each original reference observation.

Keep those scopes explicit when describing validation or extending its guarantees.2122

items.title: Preserve original columns exactly
items.text:
Every publication path runs full source-preservation validation.

The validator projects the original columns from converted output and compares them with the input physical merge. It includes nested trade and depth payloads and aligns rows across different file and batch boundaries.

It checks:

  • Original field definitions and ordering.
  • Every original decoded value.
  • The expected appended-column count.
  • Source event order.
  • Missing and extra rows.

This establishes equality of decoded source data. It does not require identical Parquet encodings.

A prefix-comparison API exists for limited inspection, but publication uses full comparison.24

items.title: Reconcile the execution receipt
items.text:
ConversionExecutionReceipt is persisted as execution.json.

It records event totals, conversion statuses, reference updates, files, row groups, and depth-level statistics where applicable.

Its accounting includes:

events_read = events_written

events_written
    = identity_events
    + converted_events
    + unavailable_events
    + skipped_events

For depth-bearing output:

levels_read
    = levels_converted
    + levels_unavailable
    + levels_skipped

Successful identity-valued levels are included in successful level accounting.

The publication functions compare receipt values with independently reread physical output and the source manifest. Parallel execution also compares worker reference-update totals with the prepass.

Reference updates and references checked are different metrics: one counts state changes during execution; the other counts serialized reference evidence inspected during validation.2517

items.title: Publish the converted dataset
items.text:
The publication functions require completed staging output and its execution receipt.

Their sequence is:

  1. Validate the job, source manifest, and staging/final path conditions.
  2. Reopen and validate converted Parquet.
  3. Load and reconcile execution.json.
  4. Compare source and output event counts.
  5. Perform full source-column preservation checks.
  6. Build and validate the conversion manifest.
  7. Write manifest.json in staging.
  8. Check interruption.
  9. Rename staging to the final destination without replacement.

The returned ConversionPublication identifies the final dataset and manifest and reports written event and file totals.27

items.title: Publication contents
items.text:
Artifact Purpose Converted Parquet parts Original source events plus target values and conversion evidence. execution.json Execution accounting reconciled against physical output. manifest.json Source identity, conversion configuration, validated statistics, file inventory, ordering, and integrity results.

Sequential output writes parts directly under its output directory. Parallel output uses partition directories.

The manifest records relative file paths, physical sizes, row counts, and row-group counts. Its file entries do not contain output SHA-256 values.

Input checksum verification remains a separate guarantee from the metadata retained for newly written conversion files.263

items.title: Format versions and reconstruction evidence
items.text:
The conversion schema, conversion manifest, and execution receipt each currently use version 1. They are separate contracts.

Causal source columns and reconstruction-event counts are retained. Causal timestamp bounds come from the source manifest rather than assuming that the first and last physical rows provide timestamp minima and maxima.

The conversion manifest refers to the input merge. It does not embed every upstream reconstruction artifact.

Converting a chronological depth clip does not supply initialization history that was already absent from that clip. Consumers still need its original reconstruction contract.26

items.title: Current publication implementation
items.text:
Conversion uses its own atomic_publish_directory() helper.

The implementation currently supports Linux through a no-replace directory rename. Other platforms receive an explicit unsupported error. Cross-filesystem rename failure is propagated.

The helper provides atomic destination creation without overwriting an existing dataset. It does not currently perform the file and parent-directory synchronization sequence used by other historical publication paths.

The conversion publication functions also do not generate a new publication-checksum inventory. These guarantees should be described from the conversion implementation itself rather than inherited from normalization or merge.

Failures before rename can leave staging artifacts. Database registration and any higher-level run recovery remain responsibilities of the caller.2827

items.title: Progress and diagnostics
items.text:
ConversionProgressReporter separates lifecycle reporting from persisted execution evidence.

It exposes phases for source validation, partition planning, timestamp scanning, reference prepasses, physical conversion, validation, receipt reconciliation, source preservation, manifest construction, and commit.

Partition snapshots include event counts, conversion outcomes, reference activity, depth-level totals, and writer metrics.

These snapshots are monitoring data assembled from atomics. They are not a substitute for the execution receipt or final manifest.

Reported outcomes distinguish:

  • Validated.
  • Materialized but unpublished.
  • Published.
  • Failed.
  • Interrupted.

A completed materialization phase means staged payloads were written. Publication validation and commit are still separate steps.29

items.title: Diagnose the stage that owns the failure
items.text:
Symptom Start with Prepared publication pin mismatch planning/prepared.rs and the declared source evidence. Requested reference not found planning/catalog.rs and reference identity selection. Many unavailable rows Failure codes, chosen paths, reference timing, and staleness. Sequential/parallel disagreement Boundary checkpoints, external cursor positions, and prepass alignment. Incorrect depth target cardinality Depth buffers, list offsets, and batch builders. Original values changed Source-preservation validation and source-array handling. Receipt mismatch Worker aggregation, status totals, level totals, and writer metrics. Publication failure Staging/final paths and the platform-specific atomic helper.

Use event-level reference provenance to explain a conversion result. Aggregate counts can identify a pattern, but they do not identify which observation or path produced a particular value.

items.title: Add a reference source or selection rule
items.text:
Start with reference selection and publication binding.

Establish how the new source is identified, how its observations are ordered, and how its prices become eligible for an event.

Update sequential alignment and checkpoint prepasses together. Any source that can contribute observations at a partition boundary needs an explicit restore position and state contract.

items.title: Change route selection or arithmetic
items.text:
Change route enumeration and ordering in the shared conversion planner or graph.

Change monetary arithmetic in the shared decimal and trade/depth conversion modules.

Then verify the historical kernels, serialized path/reference evidence, and numeric validators against the new behavior. Preserve the difference between the exact evaluated ratio and its stored decimal representation.

items.title: Extend converted fields
items.text:
Update the schema, specialized builders, combined builder, validators, and consumers together.

Source-preservation callers currently encode the number of appended columns: eight for trades and combined output, seven for depth. A schema extension must update those checks deliberately.

Continue preserving original source columns so consumers can distinguish native values from derived values.

items.title: Extend depth semantics
items.text:
Maintain positional alignment with native changes and event-level atomicity.

If the feature requires a continuously valued target book, design its identity and revaluation rules explicitly. Appending a different target price to a later native update does not by itself provide that representation.

Test failures after some levels have already converted, because buffer rollback is part of the correctness boundary.

items.title: Change partitioning or resource control
items.text:
Preserve contiguous physical ownership and capture state before the first event in each partition.

Review checkpoint memory, reference-history retention, nested depth payload size, and per-worker writer buffers. A new worker-count heuristic should not be documented as memory admission unless it actually accounts for and reserves those resources.

items.title: Strengthen publication or validation
items.text:
Keep physical validation, source preservation, receipt reconciliation, and manifest construction consistent.

Adding output checksums, broader numeric verification, cross-platform publication, or stronger durability requires corresponding implementation and compatibility work. Those properties cannot be established by changing the manifest description alone.

items.title: Testing conversion changes
items.text:
The most valuable tests compare complete event semantics across the boundaries described above.

Area Required behavior to exercise Prepared binding Changed manifest pins, checksum inventories, stream bindings, currencies, and payload bytes are detected at the appropriate stage. Path selection Primary-path truncation and fallback candidates produce the intended result without expanding the event population. Internal references A trade cannot use its own newly observed price. External references Equal-time observations remain pending; strictly earlier eligible observations become available. Staleness Boundary ages, missing observations, and future observations remain distinguishable. Causal input Timestamp regressions preserve timeline positions and use eligible retained history. Partition checkpoints A reference update at the first row of a partition is processed exactly once. Sequential equivalence Parallel output preserves decoded values, statuses, paths, and reference evidence. Projected prepasses The combined projected prepass agrees with its full-reader comparison path. Depth atomicity A later level failure removes partial results from the attempted path. Empty depth changes Zero-level observations retain metadata and event counts. Combined selection Skipped events remain present, and skipped internal trades can still supply references. Numeric validation Altered target values are detected wherever independent numeric verification is implemented. Source preservation Mutations to original scalar or nested fields fail publication. Receipt reconciliation Incorrect status, level, file, or event totals fail before commit. Interruption and publication Interruption leaves no successful publication claim, and existing destinations remain untouched.

Use decoded Arrow values and serialized conversion evidence for sequential/parallel comparisons. File sizes, compression results, and row-group boundaries are implementation details that can vary without changing the dataset’s meaning.

For a new feature, follow one event through prepared identity, reference eligibility, kernel evaluation, target payload construction, validation, receipt accounting, and publication. That trace reveals whether the feature is implemented consistently across the complete conversion path.

items.title: Debugging historical workflows
items.text:
Start with the operation's exit status and retained structured output. Identify the latest verified stage, then compare the pinned inputs at that stage with what the next component consumed. Use the same environment, project root and recipe or submission path as the original invocation.

Symptom Evidence and next action A recipe selected the wrong inputs or none Inspect the preparation report's requests, missing evidence, candidate IDs and selection bounds. Compare file dataset IDs with publication IDs and check scope, stream kind, namespace and interval. Use explicit selectors where the recipe supports them. Preparation fails with missing historical metadata Compare the recorded venue, source scope, instrument and effective specification to the catalogue and registration workflow. Check whether the source has a concrete instrument or family assertion and which normalization tasks it contributes to. Valid TOML produces an Engine rejection Inspect the prepared or submitted JSON, and read the actual Engine validation result. Check supported schema or mode, paths, hashes and runtime limits. Merge validates via --validate-job; current conversion uses --validate. Do not pass the Forge conversion collection to the Engine. An expected option or schema is missing Run mf engine status in the Forge environment. Compare the checksum and recorded revision with the installed binary and edited checkout. Use mf engine build normalize, merge, or convert as appropriate, then generate a new preparation if the old one pinned a different executable. Normalized values or counts differ Open the exact source member and resolved task. Check profile fingerprint, timestamp/quantity units and instrument specification. Compare task counters and canonical fields with independently interpreted source records. Row counts and event counts can differ for depth. Integrity evaluation degrades or fails Read the recorded metrics and integrity evaluation in the committed manifest, or failure.json where emitted. Compare the category and count or rate to the retained runtime policy. A few displayed diagnostic samples do not bound the total count. A book looks incorrect after a boundary Inspect source observations, segment/index evidence and initialization state. Locate the first wrong event, operation or sequence relation. Compare the prior book and subsequent changes at that point. For a causal merge, inspect sequence and reconstruction markers alongside event timestamps. Files exist but catalogue inspection cannot find them Check staging versus the final manifest path. Compare the Engine outcome, verification and registration states in the run report. When normalization or merge has committed and the retained receipt is intact, use the operation's documented registration-only command. Conversion has no Forge registration path in this checkout. Python discovery or row inspection fails Inspect MarketData.discover().diagnostics, the publication manifest and primary file metadata. Verify per-file registry evidence and schema support. For Decimal256 or nested values, use Arrow batches for exact values and check the Python API's projection limits. Resource use is unexpectedly high Compare the effective runtime settings, phase diagnostics, bytes, rows and task counts with the expected workload. Look for archive expansion, reconciliation scratch, open-file pressure, or concurrency admission before changing limits. See Performance.

items.title: Find the relevant artifact
items.text:
Stage Location or evidence Prepare Use the command's reported path. Normalization retains a batch and report, merge a merge-job.json and report, and conversion a convert.json collection, per-job JSON and prepare-report.json. Dry runs can report proposed artifacts without creating them. Execute Look under the reported operation run in data/runs/ or the configured data root. Inspect execution-intent.json, execution-result.json and pinned submissions. Non-TUI subprocess capture can retain engine-stdout.log and engine-stderr.log. A TUI owns its terminal output. Validate or diagnose Read the structured Engine result wherever the operation uses one. Inspect normalization failure metadata, processing counters and relevant integrity diagnostics. Use manifest.json, checksums and the declared auxiliary inventory to establish what was committed. Inspect catalogue Use mf datasets show ID --testing or mf datasets lineage ID --testing for a registered file ID. Use the filesystem-first Python API if you have a final path.

For read-only CLI inspection of an existing registered file, substitute the actual file ID. The JSON output is suitable for checking IDs and statuses without relying on terminal formatting.

uv run --project forge --locked mf --json datasets lineage "$FILE_DATASET_ID" --testing
uv run --project forge --locked mf --json engine status

Keep exact filenames and submission hashes when reporting an issue. Use only the recovery commands the affected operation documents. A retry of execution and registration-only recovery affect different state. Never patch a committed manifest or overwrite registered files to pass a check. Historical lifecycles · Data and lineage inspection · Python API

items.text: Intended change Start at Check the adjacent boundary Map fields or units already handled by a reader Format profiles Profile compiler and runtime interpretation List or download a provider's historical archives Acquisition integration Scope identity, interval, managed registration Decode a new physical representation Readers and parsing Format classification, member selection, resource accounting Change reconciliation, ordering, or depth semantics Reader and Engine guide Canonical invariants and consumer behavior Change input selection, preparation, or CLI behavior Forge orchestration Pinned evidence, exit statuses and Engine loader Change catalogue declarations or historical evidence Catalogue and registry Historical resolution and migrations Change a physical schema, manifest, or dataset reader Publication and reader contracts Producers, validators and downstream readers

config:

---

    A -->|"decode bytes"| F["Reader"]

Start at the first boundary that cannot express the change. A Bybit column rename in a supported CSV format belongs in the profile. An unexpected archive path belongs in discovery. A new archive codec or record encoding belongs at the reader boundary. Source integration guide

---
flowchart TB

    O -->|"event rules"| E["Engine"]

When the source already decodes correctly, trace what changes next. A new input selector belongs in Forge. Changed snapshot or delta behavior belongs in Engine interpretation and must agree with the profile contract. A changed persisted format requires work on producers and consumers. Orchestration and persistence · Compatibility review

MarketForge's source integrations are internal code with explicit dispatch. Installed profiles are data interpreted by the existing compiler and decoders. A new implementation capability needs wiring, tests, and documentation even when its configuration is expressed as a profile.

items.title: First contribution
items.text:
Strengthen an existing Bybit archive discovery test so it checks which instrument Forge associates with each returned archive. This is a test-only exercise. Use the Python environment from Local development. The saved provider pages and mock transport make the exercise independent of PostgreSQL and live HTTP.

  1. Locate the implementation. The test calls ExchangeSource("bybit", http).discover(...) in forge/historical/archives/sources/exchanges.py. The Bybit branch checks the page and link scope, then constructs DiscoveredArchive records. An archive includes the source request as well as its nominal time interval and object identity.

  2. Read test_observed_bybit_directory_variants and the nearby negative-page test. The existing positive test checks that spot, linear and inverse fixtures return three distinct archive identities inside the interval. The negative test covers denied listings, incorrect scope and unsafe links. The positive test can also assert that each record preserves the exact requested scope.

  3. Run the positive and negative cases before editing.

    uv run --project forge --locked --group dev pytest -c forge/pyproject.toml \
  forge/tests/unit/historical/archives/test_source_regressions.py -k 'observed_bybit or bybit_negative'

  4. Edit the existing test. Give the request a name, pass that object to discover, and add the assertion after constructing results.

    nvim forge/tests/unit/historical/archives/test_source_regressions.py

    Replace the existing async with open_http_client(...) block with the following. The snippet starts at the test body indentation. Keep the preceding fixture read and the remaining assertions.

        request = selection("bybit", market)
    async with open_http_client(
        limiter=ImmediateLimiter(1),
        transport=httpx.MockTransport(lambda _: httpx.Response(200, text=page)),
    ) as http:
        source = ExchangeSource("bybit", http)
        results = [archive async for archive in source.discover(request, interval)]
    assert all(archive.request.scope == request.scope for archive in results)

    Keep the existing count assertion. Without it, the scope assertion would pass for an empty result. The expected scope comes from the selection supplied to the test. A different directory or market rendering must still produce a record owned by the same requested instrument.

  5. Rerun the selection and check the edited file using the repository tooling.

    uv run --project forge --locked --group dev ruff check \
  forge/tests/unit/historical/archives/test_source_regressions.py
uv run --project forge --locked --group dev ruff format --check \
  forge/tests/unit/historical/archives/test_source_regressions.py
git diff -- forge/tests/unit/historical/archives/test_source_regressions.py

  6. Review the impact beyond the assertion. archive_scope_document and archive_scope_key serialize scope for storage and later source matching. If a real adapter change alters the scope emitted by discovery, review the acquisition configuration and historical acquisition guide, and document the new behavior there. In this test-only exercise the public behavior is established by the existing contract, so the production example needs no edit.

A contribution description can say that the Bybit fixture tests now check returned archive scope as well as count, uniqueness and bounds, with the positive and negative mocked cases verified. State that the check covers adapter output and leave live availability and download verification to their respective tests. Adapter source · Fixture tests

items.title: Forge workspace architecture and action inventory
items.text:
The workspace is a Textual client of Forge domain services. The direct CLI continues to own its own parsing, presentation, JSON formatting, and exit status. Workspace forms have an explicit catalogue of supported actions and typed fields. Displayed shell commands are for interoperability.

flowchart LR
    CLI[Direct CLI] --> Services[Forge services]
    TUI[Textual screens and forms] --> Queries[Debounced screen queries]
    TUI --> Controller[Application operation controller]
    Queries --> Services
    Controller --> Lock[Workspace ownership]
    Lock --> Services
    Services --> Engine[Owned process and readers]
    Services --> Report[Existing run artifacts]
    Report --> TUI

Query workers are exclusive. Responses also carry a generation so an obsolete response cannot replace current filters. Application-owned operations survive navigation and retain the workspace lock through cleanup. Engine jobs use the async historical supervisor and retained diagnostic logs. Synchronous tooling with subprocesses uses a joined process-group bridge. Textual owns the terminal while rendering.

The shell handles navigation, selection, and query generations. resources.py adapts bounded query results to typed selections and presentation.py defines resource-specific columns and contextual argument bindings. inspection.py presents subject sections and tables with a separate raw evidence view. operation_view.py renders structured snapshots and updates available actions as the controller records results. Shared Tokyo Night styling lives in workspace.tcss.

To add an action, define its fields, workspace area, and side-effect class in forge/tui/actions.py. Connect it to a service in workflows.py or services.py. Reuse existing request models and receipts. Add a parser coverage assertion or an interaction test for new forms. There is no shell or argparse dispatch from a widget.

items.title: Forge architecture
items.text:
flowchart TD
    Entry["CLI, Forge TUI or pipeline recipe"] --> Forge["Forge operation services"]

    Forge --> Markets["Metadata and rankings"]
    Forge --> Acquisition["Archive acquisition"]
    Forge --> Registration["Recording registration"]

    Markets --> Registry[("PostgreSQL catalogue and registry")]
    Acquisition --> Raw["Managed raw files"]
    Registration --> Raw
    Acquisition --> Registry
    Registration --> Registry

    Forge --> Preparation["Preparation and evidence checks"]
    Registry --> Preparation
    Raw --> Preparation

    Preparation --> Engine["Managed Rust processes"]
    Raw -->|"Normalization inputs"| Engine
    Engine --> Publications["Publication files and manifests"]

    Publications -->|"Normalized or merged inputs"| Preparation
    Publications --> Verification["Forge output verification"]
    Verification -->|"Normalized and merged file registration"| Registry

    Publications -->|"Supported publication layouts"| Readers["Dataset and lab APIs"]
    Forge --> Runs["Run reports and retained inputs"]

Forge is MarketForge’s Python application layer. It connects user requests, market metadata, managed files, PostgreSQL records, and Rust processing jobs.

The diagram shows the main relationships. Each operation follows the applicable path through the system. Acquisition produces managed raw inputs; normalization produces canonical publications; merge consumes registered normalized files; conversion consumes merged publications and their interpretation evidence. Forge prepares these operations, invokes the appropriate Engine executable, and records their outcomes.

The implemented historical pipeline composes acquisition, normalization, and merge. Standalone commands also expose these operations individually. Conversion has its own preparation and execution workflow.

This page explains where each responsibility lives, how the components cooperate, and which parts to inspect when extending Forge. Source paths are relative to the repository root.

items.title: The application boundaries
items.text:
Forge owns the surrounding application workflow: selecting work, resolving identities and historical evidence, retaining execution inputs, managing subprocesses, checking results, and maintaining registry state.

The Rust Engine owns the processing behavior exposed through its execution contracts. For normalization, this includes interpreting source records and producing canonical data. Forge invokes Rust validation when it needs the authoritative interpretation of a profile, prepared batch, or completed publication.

PostgreSQL stores identities, declarations, source inventory, observations, publication records, and lineage. The filesystem stores source bytes, configuration, prepared inputs, execution evidence, and publication artifacts.

These boundaries determine where a change belongs:

Intended behavior Primary owner Interpret CLI arguments and select an operation forge/cli/ Resolve a recipe into concrete registered inputs The relevant historical operation Discover exchange archives forge/historical/archives/ Collect current instrument metadata or statistics forge/markets/ Bind a recording to historical identity and interpretation forge/historical/registration/ Decode a new source representation or change normalization semantics Rust Engine, with corresponding Forge contract changes where required Verify and register normalized or merged output Historical operation services and forge/datasets/registration.py Read supported publications in Python forge/datasets/ Coordinate acquisition, normalization, and merge forge/historical/pipelines/

The boundaries are implemented through ordinary Python calls, typed models, database transactions, files, and subprocess contracts. Contributors should follow the concrete service calls when tracing behavior. There is no universal operation class that implements every workflow.

items.title: Repository map
items.text:
The Python project is configured by forge/pyproject.toml. Both mf and marketforge invoke forge.cli.main:main.1

Package Responsibility Useful starting points forge/cli/ Command registration, argument handling, result presentation, and exit status main.py, commands/ forge/startup/ Application settings, workspace paths, and consoles context.py forge/catalog/ Manual exchange, instrument, and specification declarations models.py, service.py forge/markets/ Current metadata, observations, collection completeness, and rankings service.py, repository.py, providers/, ranking/ forge/historical/archives/ Remote archive discovery, acquisition, caching, and managed-copy registration operation.py, discovery.py, sources/, storage/ forge/historical/imports/ Local source inspection and copying into managed raw storage formats.py, service.py forge/historical/registration/ Bind local recordings to catalogue, specification, and profile evidence models.py, service.py forge/historical/profiles/ Discover, validate, and install Rust profiles service.py forge/historical/metadata/ Historical specifications, canonical identities, family evidence, and inference service.py, policy.py, resolution.py, discovery.py forge/historical/normalization/ Select raw inputs, prepare batches, execute Rust, and register verified output batch.py, mapping.py, execution.py, datasets.py forge/historical/merge/ Select normalized files and prepare, execute, verify, and register merges config.py, discovery.py, service.py forge/historical/conversion/ Discover merged inputs, establish conversion evidence, and execute standalone JSON jobs recipes.py, contract.py, service.py, execution.py forge/historical/pipelines/ Coordinate the fixed acquisition, normalization, and merge workflow config.py, service.py, planning.py, dashboard.py forge/historical/engine/ Build, identify, verify, and supervise managed Engine executables managed.py, process.py forge/storage/ Browse, verify, reconcile, and clean up managed raw storage browsing.py, service.py, cleanup.py, dependencies.py forge/datasets/ Publication registration, registry inspection, filesystem discovery, and Python row access registration.py, catalog.py, dataset.py, parquet.py forge/orchestration/ Common run-artifact paths and retained-run inspection artifacts.py, inspection.py forge/shared/ Configuration, database access, HTTP, concurrency, ownership, paths, and terminal rendering The corresponding subpackage forge/lab/inspection/ Dataset inspection and bounded profiling profile.py

Some package names reserve space without implementing a subsystem. In the current source tree, forge/features/, forge/tui/, forge/shared/storage/, and the evaluation, optimization, tracking, and training packages under forge/lab/ are empty.

Implemented presentation code lives in forge/shared/terminal/ and operation-specific modules such as forge/historical/pipelines/dashboard.py.

items.title: Application context
items.text:
build_context() constructs an immutable ApplicationContext containing:

  • Validated application settings.
  • Resolved project and data paths.
  • The selected settings-file path.
  • A normal-output console.
  • An error/progress console.

Startup resolves configuration and prepares presentation objects. Database connections, HTTP clients, workspace ownership, and Engine processes are opened by the operations that need them.2

This keeps configuration-only commands usable without first opening external resources.

An explicit application configuration path is resolved relative to the caller’s working directory. Storage paths inside that configuration are resolved relative to the workspace. A missing default configuration uses application defaults; a missing explicitly selected configuration is an error.

items.title: CLI handlers
items.text:
forge/cli/main.py builds the root argparse parser. Most command families expose a configure(parser) function that registers actions and assigns a service_handler.

The handler receives the parsed arguments and ApplicationContext. It loads the operation’s input, invokes the appropriate service, presents the result, and returns an exit status.

Some acquisition, configuration, and database actions retain explicit dispatch branches in main(). Follow the existing dispatch for the command being changed.

A new command should normally keep these responsibilities separate:

Responsibility Placement Command name, flags, and argument relationships CLI configuration Recipe or declaration validation The relevant model and loader Input selection and application behavior Operation service Database queries and transactions Existing repository, registry, or service boundary Human-readable output Terminal renderer or operation display Structured result Service result and CLI JSON emission

This separation lets another workflow call the service directly. The pipeline uses that ability to compose operations without launching nested mf commands.

Runtime errors handled by main() can be emitted as JSON on stderr. Argument-parser errors follow the parser’s own path. Operation handlers also determine their own success, partial-result, and failure statuses, so contributors should inspect the relevant handler before changing exit behavior.1

items.title: CLI help
items.text:
1. Register the command with its family’s configure(parser) function or in forge/cli/main.py. Provide a concise, user-facing help= description when registering it. Use description= for behavior that needs more detail.
  2. Assign top-level commands to a group in forge/cli/help_content.py. Newly registered commands without a group appear in Other Commands. Nested commands appear under their registered parent.
  3. Add concise argument help to the parser action. The renderer reads operands, choices, defaults, repeatability and mutual exclusion from argparse.
  4. Add a few examples to EXAMPLES where they help discovery. Use the complete command path, put root options before it, and prefer read-only, plan or dry-run forms for operations that can modify data.
  5. Review root, family and action help at 80 columns and through a pipe. The CLI help regression tests traverse the parser and parse the curated examples. The TUI action inventory also checks parser parity.

forge/cli/help.py renders help through the shared Rich console. Argparse continues to own argument parsing, validation and usage errors.

items.title: Explicit initialization
items.text:
Building an application context and running initialization are different operations.

The init command explicitly creates application directories, applies testing-database migrations, collects supported market metadata, attempts historical enrichment, and refreshes standard rankings. Its implementation calls the underlying services directly and retains stage outcomes.

It is a useful example of application composition, but its API-backed catalogue population does not replace manual catalogue registration for other venues and recordings.3

items.title: Configuration and workspace paths
items.text:
Forge has several configuration boundaries:

Configuration Purpose Application settings Storage root, presentation, and HTTP defaults Operation recipe The requested work, selection, interval, and operation-specific policy Engine runtime settings Processing resources and supported runtime policies Format profile The interpretation of recorded source fields Prepared JSON Concrete execution inputs and their resolved identity or publication evidence

forge/shared/config/models.py defines strict application settings. Unknown fields and unintended type conversions are rejected.

Operation models extend the project’s settings conventions while defining their own contracts. Changing application settings does not automatically change a normalization recipe or Engine job schema.4

items.title: Path resolution
items.text:
ProjectPaths resolves the project root from an explicit argument, MARKETFORGE_PROJECT_ROOT, or an enclosing workspace. A recognized workspace contains forge/pyproject.toml and an engine/ directory.

Constructing ProjectPaths does not create directories.

Location Resolution Managed executables <project-root>/.bin/ Application settings <project-root>/data/.config/forge/marketforge.toml Managed configuration libraries <project-root>/data/.config/ Managed raw files <data-root>/raw/ Dataset publications <data-root>/datasets/ Run artifacts <data-root>/runs/

Changing storage.data_root relocates data and run storage. Configuration libraries remain under the project root’s data/.config/.

Use ProjectPaths and the existing configuration-library helpers when adding a command. Reconstructing these paths independently can make a feature behave differently when the data root changes.5

items.title: Catalogue, observations, and historical identity
items.text:
Three kinds of evidence participate in Forge’s identity handling:

  1. Catalogue declarations identify venues and instruments.
  2. Current observations describe information retrieved at a particular time.
  3. Historical evidence establishes the interpretation applicable to a processing interval.

They have different responsibilities and lifetimes.

items.title: Manual catalogue declarations
items.text:
forge/catalog/models.py defines exchange, instrument, and specification declarations. catalog/service.py validates their relationships, persists them, reuses equivalent declarations, and rejects conflicts.

Instrument insertion also establishes a persisted historical authority mapping through the database schema. Contributors must distinguish the catalogue instrument’s database identity from the canonical historical identity serialized into processing inputs.6

Identity Meaning Provider-native publisher or instrument identifier An identifier interpreted within its source namespace and applicable context Catalogue instrument ID The PostgreSQL identity of a catalogue instrument record Historical canonical instrument ID The identity used under a declared processing namespace Stream identity The logical data stream represented by processing or publication evidence Engine publication ID The identifier written by an Engine operation Database publication ID The registry identity of a publication File dataset ID The registry identity of one primary output file

Resolve these identities through the existing authority and registration code. A numerical match between two identity domains does not establish equivalence.

items.title: Historical specifications and families
items.text:
forge/historical/metadata/ connects retained catalogue information to historical processing.

Its responsibilities include:

  • Establishing or reusing canonical authority.
  • Selecting applicable historical specification evidence.
  • Recording inference assumptions and source evidence.
  • Resolving supported family membership.
  • Checking that retained identity evidence still matches the source bytes and installed interpretation.

Historical specification resolution must cover the actual processing input. Normalization can select whole archives extending beyond the requested interval, so the required validity may be wider than the user’s selection.

Current observations alone do not establish historical applicability.

Family handling adds another boundary: observing instruments in an archive establishes an observed population. It does not prove that the archive contains every historical member of that family.

For supported family discovery, Forge invokes the Engine’s nonprocessing resolution contract. This is a deliberate use of the authoritative source interpreter to establish identity evidence without running normalization.7

When adding metadata behavior, preserve the distinction between explicit declarations, verified evidence, and inference. Record assumptions through the existing policy and evidence structures.

items.title: Current market metadata and rankings
items.text:
forge/markets/ collects current instrument metadata and market observations. This subsystem is separate from historical archive discovery.

markets/providers/public.py translates upstream responses into Instrument and Observation models. markets/capabilities.py identifies supported collection scopes. markets/service.py coordinates collection, while markets/repository.py persists the results.8

items.title: Collection completeness
items.text:
Metadata collection establishes the instruments observed in a particular collection scope. Retained catalogue history remains available even when an instrument is absent from a later current selection.

Statistics collection uses a successfully established metadata scope and checks instrument identity. Ambiguous, duplicate, or missing selected identities prevent that scope from being treated as complete.

Observations are retained as evidence. The collector advances the latest-value view after the scope succeeds. This allows the implementation to preserve observations from unsuccessful attempts without presenting an incomplete scope as a completed refresh.

A change to provider parsing therefore needs to consider pagination, units, instrument identity, and collection completeness together.

items.title: Rankings
items.text:
Ranking calculation and statistics refresh have separate entry points.

markets/ranking/service.py builds rankings from retained metadata and observations. It stores the snapshot, entries, exclusions, and conversion evidence within its publication workflow.

markets/ranking/workflow.py coordinates a refresh followed by ranking publication.

Turnover and grouped volume have different comparison semantics. A grouped volume result is not automatically a valid global ordering across unrelated assets.

Normalization preparation reads stored ranking positions when available and uses deterministic identity ordering for unranked streams or absent ranking evidence. Current ranking information should retain its interpretation as current prioritization evidence.9

items.title: Extending market collection
items.text:
Adding current metadata support requires reviewing:

  • Capability declarations.
  • Endpoint selection and pagination.
  • Instrument and observation translation.
  • Unit interpretation.
  • Exact contract identity.
  • Scope completion and publication behavior.
  • Relevant provider and collection tests.

Adding an archive downloader does not automatically provide these capabilities. A venue may support one workflow before another.

items.title: Historical archive acquisition
items.text:
forge/historical/archives/ turns an archive request into discovered source objects and verified managed copies.

Its main responsibilities are divided as follows:

Module Responsibility config.py Validate the acquisition request sources/base.py Define the source protocol and shared discovery helpers sources/exchanges.py Implement supported exchange discovery discovery.py Coordinate discovery and reusable scan evidence registry.py Persist source-object and scan information planning.py Inspect registry/cache evidence without acquisition operation.py Coordinate the complete acquisition operation storage/acquire.py Reserve, reuse, acquire, and recover managed copies storage/files.py Perform the physical file operations

items.title: The source interface
items.text:
The archive source boundary is defined by ArchiveSource:

class ArchiveSource(Protocol):
    version: str

    def validate(self, request: ArchiveRequest) -> None: ...

    def discover(
        self,
        request: ArchiveRequest,
        interval: AcquisitionInterval,
    ) -> AsyncIterator[DiscoveredArchive]: ...

The production implementation uses explicit exchange dispatch in ExchangeSource. Discovery support is registered in code.

A discovered object describes the actual archive scope and a stable source-object identity. Temporary signed URLs are locations from which bytes can be retrieved; they are not sufficient object identities.10

items.title: Discovery evidence
items.text:
A successful discovery scan establishes reusable scan membership. A completed refresh can supersede overlapping older scan evidence.

A failed or cancelled refresh may retain observations, but it must not replace the previously completed coverage with an incomplete result.

Acquisition planning reads available registry and cache evidence. Discovery and local-byte verification remain separate checks.

items.title: Managed file acquisition
items.text:
The acquisition service first attempts to reuse a verified managed copy.

A new transfer reserves its identity, streams to a temporary file, validates the container, computes and records size/hash evidence, publishes the file, and completes registry state.

The implementation retains enough evidence to recover certain interrupted publication steps. An incomplete transfer without verified evidence is treated differently from a fully written, validated file whose final registration was interrupted.

Container validation checks the physical archive and rejects common error responses. Market-data interpretation remains a later responsibility.

items.title: Adding an archive source
items.text:
Start with ArchiveSource and a nearby implementation in ExchangeSource. Then inspect the orchestration code that selects adapters, budgets work, and allocates coordination resources.

An extension may require changes to:

  • Request validation.
  • Exchange dispatch.
  • Supported scope declarations.
  • Discovery identity and interval handling.
  • Shared HTTP budgets.
  • Operation allowlists or coordination assumptions.
  • Fixtures for pagination, malformed responses, and stable source identity.

Return DiscoveredArchive values through the existing discovery flow so that scan membership, caching, managed-copy reuse, and recovery retain their established behavior.

items.title: Manual recordings and the shared raw-data model
items.text:
Manual recordings and downloaded archives converge on the same managed raw-storage model.

The current schema separates:

Record Responsibility historical.raw_sources Source identity and provider provenance historical.raw_objects Stable source-object identity historical.local_archives A managed physical copy, its hash, size, and state historical.raw_interpretations Interpretation revisions for supplied objects historical.raw_bindings The association between a copy and an interpretation

Compatibility views retain older names such as remote_archives and external_archives, and some Python symbols still use that vocabulary. These names should not be interpreted as separate physical storage systems.11

items.title: Importing bytes and establishing interpretation
items.text:
forge/historical/imports/ inspects and copies local files. Its copying implementation reuses physical-file and recovery primitives shared with acquisition.

forge/historical/registration/ establishes the evidence needed to interpret those files.

Registration preflight combines:

  • A concrete canonical instrument.
  • Applicable historical specifications.
  • An installed and Rust-validated profile.
  • Quantity-encoding compatibility.
  • Source inventory and bounded sample checks.
  • Optional publisher and native-instrument evidence.

The resulting binding is retained with the managed source.

The legacy raw-import route can preserve bytes without establishing a verified normalization binding. Normalization checks that the required binding exists and is ready.

A file’s checksum identifies its bytes. Its interpretation also depends on identity, specifications, and profile evidence. Reusing verified bytes under a new interpretation therefore requires an explicit binding.12

items.title: Adding a recording layout
items.text:
If an existing Rust reader and profile contract can express the source, the extension may consist of catalogue declarations, a profile, registration evidence, and meaningful verification.

A new binary representation or unsupported record semantic also requires Engine work.

Keep recording support independent of API collection unless the workflow actually needs an upstream service.

items.title: Profiles and the Rust interpretation boundary
items.text:
forge/historical/profiles/service.py manages profile discovery, validation, and installation.

Python checks local file properties, TOML syntax, declared identity, and namespace consistency. Semantic validation stages the candidate alongside installed profiles and invokes the managed normalization executable.

This lets Rust check both the candidate interpretation and its compatibility with the profile catalogue.

Installation freezes the submitted bytes, verifies that the source did not change, and publishes them under the declared profile identity. An equivalent compiled interpretation can be reused. A conflicting interpretation under the same installed identity is rejected.13

This boundary matters when extending the schema:
