  • Python profile inspection must remain consistent with the supported naming and discovery rules.
  • Rust remains authoritative for interpretation semantics.
  • Preparation and execution must retain the relevant interpretation evidence.
  • Tests must establish how a source example is interpreted.

Avoid adding a second Python implementation of normalization semantics merely to make a profile validation command more convenient.

items.title: Normalization from recipe to registered files
items.text:
Normalization connects most of Forge’s historical components.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as CLI handler
    participant Forge as Normalization services
    participant DB as Testing registry
    participant Engine as Managed Rust Engine

    CLI->>Forge: Load recipe and prepare
    Forge->>DB: Read raw inventory and applicable evidence
    DB-->>Forge: Identities, specifications, ranks, and inputs
    Forge->>Engine: Validate prepared batch
    Engine-->>Forge: Validation result
    Forge-->>CLI: Batch and preparation report

    CLI->>Forge: Execute prepared batch
    Forge->>Forge: Retain submission, settings, profiles, and executable
    Forge->>Engine: Execute retained batch
    Note over Engine: Writes publications and structured outcome
    Engine-->>Forge: Process outcome and result file
    Forge->>Engine: Validate committed publication
    Engine-->>Forge: Publication validation

    alt Required outputs verify
        Forge->>DB: Register primary files and lineage
        DB-->>Forge: Publication and file identities
        Forge-->>CLI: Execution and registration result
    else Verification or registration cannot complete
        Forge-->>CLI: Retained evidence and failure state
    end

items.title: Preparation
items.text:
historical/normalization/batch.py coordinates preparation. mapping.py resolves each selected archive, and contract.py serializes the Engine-facing job structure.

Preparation checks managed input state, physical size and checksum, requested scope, canonical identity, applicable specifications, and profile bindings where required.

It selects complete overlapping raw inputs. The requested interval does not turn preparation into a row-trimming operation.

The preparation transaction reads a consistent database snapshot. It groups work by canonical content type, assigns identities and stream ranks, and constructs the batch.

Normal preparation retains the batch and report and invokes Rust’s production batch validator. Dry-run preparation resolves the plan without publishing those artifacts or performing that final file-based validation step.14

items.title: Execution
items.text:
historical/normalization/execution.py creates an execution directory and retains:

  • The exact submitted batch.
  • Runtime settings.
  • Profile files and fingerprints.
  • A copied executable and its checksum.
  • Raw-input checksum evidence.
  • Execution intent.
  • Structured Engine outcomes and logs.

Where preparation evidence exists, execution checks that the submitted batch, runtime, profiles, and executable still agree with it.

This prevents a prepared request from silently changing interpretation between preparation and execution.

The synchronous execute() wrapper delegates to execute_async(). Pipeline callers use the asynchronous entry point and can provide a child execution directory, frozen historical configuration, a pinned executable, lifecycle reporting, and expected raw inputs.

items.title: Verification and registration
items.text:
Execution success, publication verification, and registration are separate states.

Forge checks the structured Engine result against the submitted jobs, validates committed publications, and compares publication identity, inventory totals, and retained processing evidence.

historical/normalization/datasets.py then coordinates registration. datasets/registration.py writes the publication and primary-file records together with supported raw-input or parent-file lineage.

Registration can remain pending or fail after files have been committed. Retained execution and registration evidence allows the supported recovery path to revalidate completed output and attempt registration.15

items.title: Extending normalization
items.text:
Choose the module according to the behavior being changed:

Change Starting point Recipe fields and validation normalization/config.py, recipes.py Registered-input selection normalization/batch.py Identity and historical evidence resolution normalization/mapping.py, historical/metadata/ Serialized Engine job fields normalization/contract.py, batch.py, corresponding Rust contract Process lifecycle or retained execution evidence normalization/execution.py Publication verification normalization/datasets.py Primary-file registration and lineage datasets/registration.py Source decoding or canonical record semantics Rust Engine and relevant profile contract

A recipe extension may affect several of these boundaries. Trace its value from parsing to the Engine input and then to the evidence needed for verification.

items.title: Merge and conversion have separate workflows
Merge
items.text:
Managed merge consumes registered normalized primary files.

Its direct recipe identifies file dataset IDs. A derived recipe can select inputs through a retained normalization declaration and associated evidence.

historical/merge/service.py resolves those files, verifies publication fingerprints and ownership, establishes the stream identities, assigns ranks, and writes the Engine job.

Execution retains the job, runtime, and executable. After Rust completes, Forge verifies the merged publication and registers its primary files with parent-dataset lineage.16

Contributors should preserve the distinction between a publication and the files selected from it. Several file dataset IDs may belong to one publication.

The merge preparation and verification code is the place to change input selection or publication evidence. Timeline construction and record-processing semantics belong to the Engine contract and implementation.

items.title: Conversion
items.text:
Conversion prepares quote-currency conversion work from registered merged publications and the required reference-stream evidence.

The implementation separates:

Module Responsibility recipes.py User recipe and fingerprinted upstream declaration discovery.py Select compatible registered merged publications registry.py Read publication and lineage records evidence.py Verify committed source and interpretation evidence contract.py Define the standalone Engine JSON job service.py Assemble jobs and retained preparation evidence execution.py Execute and verify prepared conversion jobs

An upstream recipe reference identifies the intended source workflow. It does not run missing acquisition, normalization, or merge operations.

Preparation emits a collection document and one standalone JSON job per selected merge publication. The Engine job embeds publication bindings, stream identities, currencies, conversion policy, resources, input paths, and output destination.

An external instrument-catalogue file is not required by that standalone job interface. If the optional preparation catalogue exists, Forge checks its consistency with historical evidence.

Conversion operates on whole selected merge publications. Selection must satisfy the workflow’s scope rules; it does not introduce arbitrary row clipping.

The current Forge execution flow runs the prepared jobs sequentially and stops after a failure. Converted-publication registration and conversion resume are not implemented in this workflow. Its receipts explicitly represent registration as unavailable.17

items.title: The historical pipeline
items.text:
The pipeline composes existing services through explicit handoffs.

flowchart TD
    Recipe["PipelineRecipe"] -->|"Acquisition request"| Acquire["Acquisition service"]
    Recipe -->|"Normalization request"| Normalize["Normalization services"]
    Recipe -->|"Merge options"| Merge["Merge services"]

    Acquire -->|"Pinned ArchiveSelection"| Normalize
    Normalize -->|"Registered primary-file IDs"| Merge

    Acquire --> Evidence["Pipeline reports and stage evidence"]
    Normalize --> Evidence
    Merge --> Evidence

PipelineRecipe translates one interval and request set into acquisition, normalization, and merge inputs.

PipelineRun owns the stage state, retained evidence, and recovery decisions. It calls the services directly.

The current sequence is fixed:

  • Acquire the requested archives.
  • Prepare, execute, verify, and register normalization.
  • Prepare, execute, verify, and register merge.

items.title: Exact stage handoffs
items.text:
Acquisition returns an ArchiveSelection containing the acquired identities and checksum evidence.

Normalization preparation receives that selection explicitly. Execution checks the expected raw-file hashes.

The next stage receives the registered normalized primary-file IDs. Merge therefore consumes the output of this pipeline run through concrete registry identities.

These handoffs are the central pipeline contract. Extending the pipeline should preserve an explicit account of what each stage produced and what the next stage consumed.18

items.title: Planning and retained execution state
items.text:
Pipeline planning reads available registry evidence and checks managed Engine availability. Exact acquired files, normalization jobs, and merge file identities are resolved at later stages.

A planned result is therefore an assessment of available prerequisites, not a completely frozen execution plan.

Execution retains the submitted recipe, resolved application settings, runtime configuration, profiles, executables, acquired selection, preparation evidence, and child execution receipts.

orchestration/artifacts.py::RunArtifacts supplies common paths such as:

  • submitted.toml
  • resolved-plan.json
  • report.json
  • events.jsonl
  • steps/<stage>/<attempt>/

The pipeline state machine lives in historical/pipelines/service.py. The orchestration/ package provides supporting artifact and inspection utilities.

items.title: Resume
items.text:
Resume validates retained evidence and requires the original workspace, storage root, and testing-registry identity.

It can reuse completed acquisition, reconcile committed outputs with registration, or create a fresh processing attempt from retained inputs.

It does not continue a partially written Parquet file from an arbitrary row offset. A retry may require fresh job identities and output destinations.

Changes to pipeline recovery must account for both publication state and registry state. An Engine process may have committed output before Forge finished recording the surrounding workflow.

items.title: Current extension boundaries
items.text:
The pipeline contract uses archive acquisition requests. It does not currently expose external recording registration, equity source_key selection, conversion, arbitrary stage ordering, or a general task graph.

Adding a stage requires explicit changes to:

  • Recipe validation.
  • Service invocation and input handoff.
  • Persisted stage state.
  • Artifact ownership.
  • Failure and retry behavior.
  • Status reporting.
  • Integration coverage.

Also inspect receipt discovery when connecting workflows. Some source-derived merge and conversion discovery paths recognize standalone execution-directory layouts. Pipeline receipts use nested stage-attempt directories, so those paths should not be assumed interchangeable.

items.title: Managed Engine executables
items.text:
forge/historical/engine/managed.py defines approved targets for normalization, merge, and conversion.

The managed build workflow constructs the appropriate Cargo invocation, builds and checks the executable, installs it under .bin/, and records installation evidence.

resolve() verifies the installed executable against that evidence before an operation uses it.

Execution services often retain a private executable copy so that the bytes used by an operation remain identifiable throughout its lifetime.

Build metadata records useful revision information, but it is not a complete source snapshot.19

items.title: Subprocess ownership
items.text:
historical/engine/process.py provides asynchronous supervision for noninteractive child processes.

It owns the child process group, drains output streams into bounded logs, and terminates and reaps the process when cancellation requires it.

joined_io() ensures that blocking filesystem work has finished before the caller releases ownership.

Execution paths are not completely uniform: standalone interactive processing and conversion also use the existing synchronous process runner. Inspect the caller before changing cancellation or terminal behavior.

When adding a new Engine operation, establish its target, input contract, validation, execution outcome, artifact verification, and registration behavior explicitly.

items.title: Storage administration
items.text:
Two storage-related package areas serve different purposes.

historical/archives/storage/ implements managed-copy acquisition, physical publication, and recovery.

forge/storage/ exposes application-level browsing and maintenance over those managed copies.

Module Responsibility browsing.py Read-only inventory browsing registry.py Selection and pagination queries coverage.py Nominal coverage aggregation service.py Inventory verification and reconciliation cleanup_plans.py Reviewed cleanup-plan contracts cleanup.py Preview and apply cleanup dependencies.py Concrete lineage and prepared-input dependencies managed_files.py Checked physical inspection and removal

Verification can change registry state when a file is missing or corrupt. Reconciliation can recover a supported reservation state.

Cleanup rechecks registry identity, dependencies, and physical file evidence before applying a reviewed action. It records per-target outcomes because filesystem removal and database changes do not form one globally rollbackable transaction.20

Dependency checks establish the managed dependencies the implementation can inspect. They do not prove that an unrelated external script has no reference to a file.

A storage extension should use the common registry and managed-file mechanisms so that downloaded and manually supplied data retain consistent maintenance behavior.

items.title: Dataset registration and Python consumption
items.text: The datasets package contains both write-side registration and read-side inspection. These have separate entry points.

items.title: Registration
items.text:
datasets/registration.py::register_files() receives verified publication evidence and an existing database connection.

It establishes a shared publication record, a dataset identity for each primary file, and supported contribution links to raw inputs or parent files.

The caller owns the surrounding transaction boundary.

items.title: Registry inspection
items.text:
datasets/inspection.py queries registered metadata and lineage for terminal inspection.

This is a database-backed view of registered state.

items.title: Filesystem and notebook API
items.text:
datasets/catalog.py::MarketData provides the filesystem-oriented entry point.

flowchart TD
    Files["Manifests and primary Parquet files"] --> Discovery["Filesystem discovery"]
    Supplied["Optional caller-supplied registry records"] --> Discovery
    Discovery --> Catalog["DatasetCatalog"]
    Catalog -->|"Select physical files"| Dataset["Dataset"]
    Dataset -->|"Select logical membership"| Stream["Stream"]
    Dataset --> Rows["Arrow or Polars row access"]
    Stream -->|"Apply stream predicates"| Rows
    Dataset --> Inspection["Lab inspection"]
    Stream --> Inspection

DatasetCatalog selects physical files using established metadata.

Dataset represents a physical file or a supported publication grouping.

Stream adds a selected logical membership and the corresponding row predicates.

Selecting a file because it contains a matching instrument does not filter every row in that file. Use the stream-selection boundary when row-level membership matters.21

Filesystem discovery does not query PostgreSQL automatically. Optional registry records are supplied by the caller.

Discovery uses publication and file evidence. It is not universally limited to Parquet footers: establishing causal-merge membership can read relevant columns in bounded batches.

MarketData resolves its own paths rather than loading the CLI’s application settings. Code using a custom data root should pass the intended root explicitly.

items.title: Lab inspection
items.text:
forge/lab/inspection/ builds on dataset handles and provides schema, column, row-group, timestamp, comparison, and bounded profiling facilities.

Metadata inspection and explicit row reads have different costs. Preserve that distinction when extending notebook representations or inspection methods.

A rich display should not unexpectedly perform an unbounded data scan.22

items.title: Database access and transactions
items.text:
Database credentials are resolved through the shared loader. Testing and production credentials use distinct keys.

The testing connection helper checks the configured database name, the connected database name, and the database-purpose marker before yielding a connection.

Connections are opened with autocommit enabled; callers establish transactions for operations requiring a consistent or atomic database boundary.

Migrations validate applied migration history and checksums and apply pending changes under database coordination.23

When extending a service, identify who owns the connection and transaction. Functions that accept a connection should preserve their caller’s transaction model.

items.title: Workspace ownership
items.text:
WorkspaceOwnership acquires nonblocking exclusive locks for the project and data roots.

Ownership is explicit. Constructing ApplicationContext does not acquire it, and a helper does not automatically establish ownership for every caller.

Operation entry points must establish the required ownership boundary before calling services that rely on it. Pipeline child services must also cooperate with the ownership already held by their parent.

Lock files remain in place; releasing ownership closes the held handles.24

items.title: HTTP and bounded work
items.text:
Shared HTTP infrastructure provides request pacing, concurrency limits, retry behavior, cooldown handling, bounded buffered responses, and streaming downloads.

Tasks communicating with the same upstream during an operation should reuse the configured client and budget.

A failed streaming body is handled by the acquisition layer together with its partial file. It must not be treated as an automatically replayable buffered response.

shared/async_work.py::bounded_map() uses a fixed worker population and bounded queues. Results arrive as work completes. Callers that need deterministic order must establish it explicitly.

These helpers make concurrency and resource behavior part of the service contract.25

items.title: Presentation
items.text:
Terminal renderers consume operation results and progress information.

The shared console configuration provides consistent color and output behavior. Operation-specific displays interpret the relevant progress model.

Pipeline presentation owns one dashboard while its child services execute. Business decisions and durable stage state remain in PipelineRun.

When adding a progress field, update the service event or report model first and then the renderer. Terminal availability should not determine whether an operation produces useful structured evidence.

items.title: Extending Forge by following one complete behavior
items.text: A useful extension starts with the observable result and follows it through the actual boundaries.

items.title: Add a CLI capability
items.text:
Start with a neighboring command module and its configure() function.

Define argument validation, load the relevant model, and call a service that can also be used outside the CLI. Keep result formatting and exit policy in the handler or renderer.

Verify both structured output and the relevant error path. If the operation mutates state, establish ownership and transaction boundaries explicitly.

items.title: Add an archive or metadata provider
items.text:
Decide which capability is being added.

Archive discovery requires ArchiveSource behavior and its acquisition integration.

Current metadata requires provider translation, capability declarations, instrument identity handling, unit interpretation, and collection-completeness behavior.

If both capabilities are needed, implement and verify both paths. Their scope models and supported products can differ.

items.title: Add a profile or recording interpretation
items.text:
Determine whether the installed Rust contract can express the representation and semantics.

If it can, contribute the profile, declarations, registration example, and verification.

If it cannot, trace the necessary contract change through Rust validation, Forge inspection, preparation evidence, execution snapshots, and tests.

items.title: Change preparation
items.text:
Follow the value through:

  1. Recipe validation.
  2. Registered-input selection.
  3. Identity and specification resolution.
  4. Serialized Engine input.
  5. Preparation evidence.
  6. Execution verification.
  7. Relevant downstream consumers.

A new recipe field is complete only when its effect on the prepared work and retained evidence is defined.

items.title: Change output or registration
items.text:
Identify the producer, publication validator, registry mapping, lineage consumers, and Python readers.

For a manifest or canonical-schema change, inspect the corresponding Engine contract as well as Forge’s evidence readers.

A field can be valid in a newly written file while remaining unsupported by a discovery or inspection path. Verify the intended consumers directly.

items.title: Change pipeline behavior
items.text:
Start with PipelineRecipe and PipelineRun.

Define the stage’s accepted input, produced evidence, completion condition, and recovery behavior before adding presentation.

Use typed or otherwise explicit handoffs comparable to ArchiveSelection and RegisteredFiles. Avoid replacing a concrete handoff with a broad filesystem or registry search that can select unrelated work.

items.title: Verification at architectural boundaries
items.text:
Choose tests according to the responsibility being changed.

Boundary Existing test locations Startup, configuration, and paths forge/tests/integration/startup/, forge/tests/unit/shared/ Archive adapters and source identity forge/tests/unit/historical/archives/test_sources.py, test_source_regressions.py Discovery scans and managed-copy recovery forge/tests/integration/historical/archives/ Manual declarations and registration forge/tests/integration/catalogue/test_registration.py Profile installation and Engine integration forge/tests/unit/historical/engine/ Historical inference and family discovery forge/tests/unit/historical/metadata/ Normalization preparation and execution forge/tests/unit/historical/normalization/ Merge selection and execution evidence forge/tests/unit/historical/merge/ Conversion contracts and preparation forge/tests/unit/historical/conversion/test_conversion.py Pipeline composition forge/tests/integration/cli/test_pipeline.py Market identity and collection behavior forge/tests/unit/markets/, forge/tests/integration/markets/ Ranking publication forge/tests/integration/markets/ranking/ Dataset registration and readers forge/tests/integration/datasets/, forge/tests/unit/datasets/ Storage maintenance forge/tests/integration/storage/, forge/tests/unit/storage/ Complete registered-data workflow forge/tests/integration/forge_workflow/test_workflow.py

The Python development configuration includes pytest, pytest-asyncio, Ruff, and Pyright. Pytest declares markers for integration, database, network, Engine, and terminal-dependent checks.

Fixtures have different requirements and isolation mechanisms. Some database tests roll back a transaction; other workflow tests create committed records or disposable schemas and perform targeted cleanup. Inspect the fixture used by the test being extended.26

Verification should establish the intended boundary:

  • A model test establishes input acceptance and rejection.
  • A preparation test establishes the selected inputs and serialized contract.
  • An execution test establishes process and evidence handling.
  • A registration test establishes identities and lineage.
  • A data test establishes exact values or reconstructed state.
  • A workflow test establishes that the relevant components cooperate.

For market data, expected behavior often requires exact timestamps, decimal values, instrument identities, ordering evidence, or reconstructed book states. Explain why the fixture contains the values that make those assertions meaningful.

items.title: Related development paths
items.text:
• System architecture and operation lifecycles place Forge in the historical workflow.
  • Prepared contract and user workflow describe the public handoff.
  • Test selection and diagnostics cover verification and inspection.

items.title: Registry context for an extension
items.text:
CLI dispatch and the TUI select an environment before a registry-backed service runs. The shared resolver selects one credential key and validates the actual database name, purpose, and UUID before yielding a connection. A workflow can pin that UUID across stages. Keep numeric file and publication IDs scoped to that identity when adding a selector or a recovery path.

Use the database selection tests in the repository for purpose mismatches, and the testing guide to choose an integration fixture. Keep local artifact inspection independent of the registry where the operation already supports it.

  1. Project configuration and CLI entry point. ↩↩

  2. Application context. ↩

  3. Explicit initialization workflow. ↩

  4. Application models, settings loader, and configuration-library resolution. ↩

  5. Project path resolution. ↩

  6. Catalogue declarations, catalogue service, and historical authority schema. ↩

  7. Historical metadata service, resolution, inference policy, and Engine-assisted discovery. ↩

  8. Market collection, persistence, public providers, and capabilities. ↩

  9. Ranking service, refresh workflow, and normalization batch planning. ↩

  10. Source protocol, exchange dispatch, discovery, operation coordination, and managed acquisition. ↩

  11. Unified raw-data schema. ↩

  12. Managed registration, local copying, and registered normalization inputs. ↩

  13. Profile discovery, validation, and installation. ↩

  14. Batch preparation, archive mapping, job serialization, and execution. ↩

  15. Publication verification and registration coordination and primary-file registration. ↩

  16. Merge service and derived selection. ↩

  17. Conversion recipe, standalone job contract, preparation, discovery, and execution. ↩

  18. Pipeline recipe, planning, stage execution and recovery, and run-artifact paths. ↩

  19. Managed Engine targets and installation and asynchronous process supervision. ↩

  20. Storage maintenance, cleanup, and dependency inspection. ↩

  21. Filesystem catalogue, discovery, dataset and stream handles, and Parquet row access. ↩

  22. Dataset inspection and bounded profiling. ↩

  23. Credential resolution, testing connection guards, and migrations. ↩

  24. Workspace ownership. ↩

  25. Configured HTTP clients, HTTP request and streaming behavior, and bounded asynchronous work. ↩

  26. Python tooling and test configuration, shared integration fixture, pipeline integration, and full workflow integration. ↩

items.title: Merge Engine architecture
items.text:
flowchart TD
    J["Resolved merge job and runtime"] --> R["Verify inputs and stream declarations"]
    N["Normalized publications"] --> R
    R --> I["Build trade and depth inventories"]

    I --> O{"Timeline ordering"}
    O -->|Chronological| T["Plan time partitions"]
    O -->|Causal| C["Select reconstruction dependencies"]

    T --> L["Merge event references"]
    C --> L
    L --> V["Validate logical timeline"]

    V --> M["Materialize canonical payloads"]
    N -->|Canonical rows and event metadata| M

    M --> P["Validate physical output"]
    P --> E["Build manifest and publication evidence"]
    E --> F["Publish merged dataset"]

The merge engine turns selected canonical trade and depth publications into a materialized event dataset. It establishes an event order, retains source provenance, preserves depth reconstruction information, and publishes validated Parquet output.

The implementation lives in engine/src/historical/merge/. The diagram shows the unified executor, which supports trade-only, depth-only, and combined output.

Its central design is the separation between logical merging and physical materialization:

  • Logical merging decides which events belong in the output and their order. It writes references to canonical input rows.
  • Physical materialization resolves those references, copies the canonical values into the output schema, and preserves the established event order.

This separation lets ordering work with compact event metadata while materialization organizes reads around physical files and row groups.2

items.title: Responsibilities and boundaries
items.text:
Merge consumes completed normalization publications. Its inputs already contain canonical market data, instrument identity, source ownership, and the evidence needed to interpret their layout.

The caller supplies a resolved MergeJob. The job and submission types belong to historical::job; merge consumes their validated values and verifies the corresponding filesystem publications.

Within that boundary, merge owns:

Responsibility What merge establishes Input verification Selected files belong to the declared publications and satisfy the applicable identity, path, size, and checksum checks. Stream resolution Selected files map to compatible concrete streams with consistent declared ranks. Event selection Events satisfy the requested interval and, for causal depth, include required reconstruction dependencies. Event ordering Output follows the selected chronological or causal contract. Materialization References resolve to the expected canonical rows and become physical event payloads. Output validation Written files satisfy schema, ordering, reference, and accounting requirements. Publication Validated files and retained execution evidence are committed to a fresh destination.

Catalogue lookup, archive acquisition, raw-format decoding, profile interpretation, and database registration belong to other parts of MarketForge.

Merge also reuses infrastructure rather than implementing every mechanism locally. The event queue comes from shared::merge; canonical schemas come from shared persistence; resource accounting comes from shared historical infrastructure; scheduling and publication primitives are reused from normalization.14

items.title: Merge does not repeat normalization
items.text:
Trade merging reads canonical event positions and timestamps. It does not run normalization’s native trade-ID reconciliation again.

Depth merging consumes committed observations, initialization boundaries, and reconstruction segments. Its boundary handling has specific rules for retaining or omitting initialization events; those rules do not provide general duplicate detection for arbitrary market observations.

Combined output interleaves trade and depth events. It does not automatically associate each execution with a particular book update or join the two into paired records.6720

items.title: The data model
items.text:
Several identities and units appear throughout the implementation. Keep them distinct when extending the module.

Term Meaning Input publication A committed normalization dataset with its manifest, primary files, and auxiliary evidence. Registered file A file selected through the submitted job. Its catalogue identity is separate from the Engine publication identity. Source task The normalization task that contributed a canonical row range or depth observation sequence. Logical stream A compatible market-data stream identified by committed stream and instrument metadata. Stream rank The declared priority used to order available events from different streams when timestamps tie. Event reference A publication/task address, event ordinal, and canonical row span. Canonical row One normalized trade row or one normalized depth level-change row. Physical merge row One materialized market event. A depth row can contain multiple level changes. Logical partition A unit of work that creates part of the ordered reference timeline. Materialization partition A unit of work that turns a contiguous portion of that timeline into physical payloads.

In timeline records, dataset_id identifies the input Engine publication. It is not the registered file ID from a file-based submission.

An event ordinal also has a narrower meaning than a native exchange identifier. For trades, the reference ordinal follows the task’s canonical row position. For depth, it identifies an indexed observation. Neither should be interpreted as a native trade ID or a globally comparable exchange sequence.156

items.title: Events and canonical rows have different counts
items.text:
A trade reference addresses exactly one canonical row. A depth reference addresses zero or more canonical level-change rows.

Observation Physical merge rows Referenced canonical rows One trade 1 1 One depth observation with 20 level changes 1 20 One depth observation without level changes 1 0

An empty depth change list still represents an observation. It can carry a timestamp, sequence information, or a reconstruction boundary.

This distinction also changes the meaning of familiar metric names. In merge, events_written counts materialized event rows. It must not be interpreted as normalization’s count of emitted depth level rows.2021

items.title: Code organization
items.text:
Paths in this table are relative to engine/src/historical/merge/.

Module Responsibility core/ Event-reference abstractions, stream interfaces, merge keys, and K-way queue integration. execution/shared/ Input resolution, logical resource estimates, shared publication paths, and sequential depth-reference execution. execution/parallel/ Parallel depth-reference execution and result validation. execution/unified/ Production orchestration, concrete stream resolution, and ranked logical partition execution. partition/ Time partition planning, task selection, and logical partition workers. trades/ Trade ownership inventories, timestamp cursors, and logical trade streams. depth/ Event-index inventories, cursors, boundary relations, checkpoints, and chronological or causal depth streams. output/ Logical timeline schemas, writers, reference validation, and reference-oriented manifests. materialize/planning/ Physical work plans, whole-event windows, canonical read plans, and resource estimates. materialize/readers/ Canonical file and row-group addressing, forward readers, decoders, and alternative cache APIs. materialize/builders/ Trade, depth, and combined physical schemas, batch construction, and Parquet writing. materialize/validation/ Physical file validation, global accounting, and reconstruction metadata. materialize/publication/ Physical manifests, final layout preparation, and committed-publication validation. progress/ Phase events, partition progress, and validation progress.

Most submodules are internal. mod.rs exposes selected types and functions as the public library surface.1

items.title: Execution entry points
items.text:
The exported executors serve different purposes.

Entry point Result execute_unified_merge_job A validated physical publication containing trades, depth, or both. execute_unified_merge_job_with_progress The same execution path with phase and partition reporting. execute_merge_job A sequential depth-reference timeline. File-based submissions are rejected by this entry point. execute_parallel_merge_job A parallel depth-reference timeline with its reference-oriented manifest.

Use the unified executor as the starting point when tracing the production physical-publication workflow.

Lower-level exports such as partition workers, cursors, builders, and validators provide reusable components. Calling one of them does not establish the full publication contract by itself.3

items.title: Resolve inputs before planning work
items.text:
execution/shared/resolver.rs converts the job’s selected publications into ResolvedMergeInput values.

A resolved input contains the publication directory, parsed normalization manifest, selected canonical files, and applicable auxiliary files.

For explicit file submissions, resolution checks:

  1. The publication and manifest resolve to the expected paths.
  2. The manifest identifies the requested Engine dataset.
  3. The manifest fingerprint matches the submitted evidence.
  4. Each selected file is a primary manifest member.
  5. File size and SHA-256 match the submitted selection.
  6. File paths remain inside the publication.
  7. Duplicate references, including duplicate physical files on Unix, are rejected.
  8. Required depth auxiliaries satisfy their applicable size and checksum checks.

These checks happen before merge relies on row offsets or stream ownership.

The legacy dataset-oriented path can resolve a publication without an explicit file submission and has different verification behavior. Its fallback location must not be treated as the managed storage contract for file-based Forge workflows.4

items.title: Resolve ownership from committed evidence
items.text:
ResolvedMergeInput::selected_streams() identifies the committed stream that owns each selected canonical file.

execution/unified/stream_resolver.rs then loads the retained processing job and compares:

  • Publication and processing-job identities.
  • Source-task membership.
  • Stream identity.
  • Exchange, instrument, symbol, and instrument specification.
  • Submitted content type and stream rank.
  • Instrument namespace evidence where present.

For an explicit submission, selected files cannot silently redefine the stream to which they belong.

Compatible trade publications may share a declared stream rank. Distinct logical streams cannot share that rank. The current resolver also requires additional reconstruction guarantees before a depth stream can span publications.5

items.title: Current input restrictions
items.text:
These restrictions are part of the current execution contract.

Input Current requirement Canonical content Trade and depth publications are supported. Combined canonical inputs are rejected. Modern trade publications Protocol version 4 or later must declare event_timestamp_ns ordering. Trade ownership Modern trade inputs with disjoint source ranges or repeated source-task ownership entries are rejected. Depth file selection Every primary part belonging to the selected depth stream must be supplied. Depth across publications One depth stream cannot currently span publications without validated reconstruction across that boundary. Modern segmented depth Protocol version 4 or later requires causal ordering. Older depth layouts Replay requires one compatible concrete stream per publication.

Causal ordering does not bypass the trade ownership or native-order restrictions.

Extending one of these cases requires changes to the evidence model, inventories, replay behavior, and validators. Removing the admission check alone would leave the later stages without the guarantees they depend on.5

items.title: Output mode and timeline ordering
items.text:
Output mode and ordering are independent choices.

Output mode describes the physical payload:

  • trades
  • depth
  • combined

The unified executor derives the mode from the selected stream kinds.

Timeline ordering describes how events enter the timeline:

  • Chronological ordering.
  • Causal ordering.

The term “unified” refers to the shared execution path for trade and depth events. It does not imply that every accepted input is timestamp-sorted or that every output uses the same ordering contract.2

items.title: Chronological ordering
items.text:
Chronological execution expects its source streams to provide events in an order compatible with chronological merging.

KWayEventMerger maintains one available head per stream. It selects the next head, advances that source, and continues.

The ranked production path orders available events by timestamp and stream priority. Within a stream, the cursor preserves the established source order. Task IDs and task-local ordinals do not provide a new ordering across source boundaries.

Some lower-level constructors use a fuller MergeKey containing task and ordinal components. Preserve that distinction when modifying the shared ordering code.

The K-way merger is not a general sorting stage for arbitrary disordered input. Its correctness depends on the source stream contract.7

items.title: Causal ordering
items.text:
Causal execution preserves the supplied order of each source stream.

Only the current head of a stream is eligible for selection. A later event becomes available after its predecessor has been selected. If that later event has an earlier timestamp, the merged timeline can regress in timestamp while still preserving the required source order.

Causal output records this order explicitly through timeline_sequence.

Here, causal ordering means preserving replay dependencies and source order. It does not establish economic causation between exchanges or prove which trade caused a particular book update.78

items.title: Build inventories that preserve source positions
items.text: Inventories connect logical task ownership to physical files. They are more than lists of Parquet paths.

items.title: Trade inventories and cursors
items.text:
trades/inventory.rs builds a TradeTaskInventory for each contributing source task.

Its file contributions retain:

  • The physical file and part position.
  • The file-local starting row.
  • The number of rows owned by the task.
  • The task-local canonical row offset.
  • Observed timestamp bounds.

A shared Parquet part may contain contributions from multiple tasks. The inventory preserves those slices rather than assigning the entire file to one task.

TradeCursor projects the event timestamp column needed for logical merging. Where usable page indexes exist, it can narrow reads while retaining original row positions. Missing or unsuitable index statistics fall back to scanning; they do not justify excluding rows.

Exact event selection uses the half-open interval [start_ns, end_ns).

TradeStream maps physical positions back to task-local references and validates timestamp progression. Its ranked constructor can combine compatible contributions from multiple publications, but it rejects ambiguous task overlap. Across publications, even a shared observed timestamp boundary is rejected by the current task-range check.6

items.title: Depth inventories and cursors
items.text:
Depth requires both canonical level rows and the observation index that explains how those rows form events.

A DepthTaskInventory includes canonical file slices together with:

Artifact Role events.parquet Observation order, event metadata, and canonical row spans. segments.json Initialization points and reconstruction segments. boundary.json Source identity, coverage, and boundary-state evidence.

The inventory also retains source event ranges and the row base needed to translate stream-level canonical offsets into task-local references.

DepthEventCursor reads selected event-index ranges. For native-order histories, it cannot assume that the first timestamp beyond the requested end means every later event is outside the interval.

visit_depth_events() checks event ordinals, canonical coverage, initialization segments, bounds, and final totals. Timestamp regressions are recorded separately from those structural checks.9

items.title: Depth selection follows reconstruction dependencies
items.text: A depth update is meaningful only in the context of the preceding state.

items.title: Causal selection retains complete dependency prefixes
items.text:
For each reconstruction segment containing a requested observation, CausalDepthStream retains:

  1. The segment initialization.
  2. Every subsequent dependency.
  3. The last requested event in that segment, determined by its event-index position.

This can include observations whose timestamps lie outside the requested interval.

For example, consider this illustrative source sequence and a requested interval of [10:01:00, 10:01:30):

Source position Event timestamp Observation Included as 0 09:59:00 Initialization Reconstruction dependency 1 10:02:00 Update Reconstruction dependency 2 10:01:10 Update Requested observation

All three observations are required to preserve the source’s state progression. Sorting them by timestamp or removing the second observation changes the state seen by the third.

Out-of-interval depth events carry reconstruction_only = true. Their original timestamps remain unchanged. Initialization events inside the requested interval are ordinary selected events and do not receive that marker merely because they initialize a book.

Zero-change observations remain part of the dependency sequence.

The causal path carries initialization events through the timeline. It does not run the older timestamp-based checkpoint-selection algorithm or infer a replacement initialization when committed evidence is missing.8

items.title: Chronological boundary handling
items.text:
The chronological depth path compares adjacent source-task boundaries and classifies their relationship.

Relationship Meaning VerifiedContinuation Matching sequence, comparable coverage, and matching recorded state fingerprint establish continuation. IndependentInitialization An initialization establishes a new independently replayable history without proving continuity. SequenceGap The available sequence evidence advances without establishing the required continuation relationship. StateMismatch Boundary-state evidence is incompatible. Unverifiable Available evidence is insufficient to establish the relationship.

A verified continuation can allow the next task’s redundant initial checkpoint to be omitted. The omitted reference is retained in MergeSkippedInitialization.

Independent histories and uncertain boundaries retain their initialization evidence. State mismatch fails the chronological stream.

This is a narrowly defined initialization rule. It must not be expanded into general event deduplication based only on equal timestamps, equal books, or similar-looking records.10

items.title: Compatibility behavior differs between older executors
items.text:
The older chronological depth components do not all apply the same regression policy.

DepthStream rejects timestamp regressions and applicable sequence regressions. PartitionDepthStream counts and skips timestamp regressions while producing chronological output.

The depth-only parallel result exposes a dropped-regression count. UnifiedPartitionResult does not expose that same counter.

Modern segmented depth avoids this chronological path by requiring causal ordering. When maintaining older paths, account for their existing omission behavior explicitly; do not assume every exported executor either preserves every observation or rejects every regression.11

items.title: Plan logical work
items.text:
Chronological execution divides the requested interval into deterministic, contiguous, non-overlapping partitions.

plan_merge_partitions() derives the requested count from the worker and partitioning settings, caps it by the available nanoseconds, and distributes the remainder without gaps.

plan_unified_partition_inputs() assigns source tasks using overlap between their inclusive observed bounds and each half-open partition.

Observed bounds help select work. They do not prove continuous market coverage within the interval.12

items.title: Causal execution uses a different partition boundary
items.text:
Causal ordering uses one logical partition covering the requested interval.

This preserves one forward ordering pass while selecting depth dependencies by source position. Arbitrary timestamp partitions would break that dependency model.

Physical materialization can still run in parallel. After the logical timeline is validated, split_causal_materialization_plan() assigns contiguous logical output files to separate physical workers.

Consequently, logical partition count and materialization partition count can differ. A physical partition of causal output represents a contiguous portion of the established timeline, rather than an independent timestamp interval.213

items.title: Admit work before starting workers
items.text:
Logical partitions use the shared budgeted scheduler.

Admission estimates account for active stream readers, baseline processing memory, writer buffers, and file descriptors. Empty time partitions still reserve the resources required to create and finalize their writer.

Materialization uses a separate resource plan and budget for its phase. Requested worker count is an upper bound; resource admission determines how many partitions can run together.

These estimates are cooperative reservations. They are not operating-system RSS limits.

The current logical resource estimate requests zero scratch bytes even though merge writes staging files. Resource admission therefore must not be described as a disk-usage cap for the entire publication.

Partition failures propagate through the collected results. These interfaces do not promise immediate cancellation of every sibling worker when one partition fails.14

items.title: Write and validate the logical timeline
items.text:
A UnifiedTimelineRecord records an event address and the metadata needed to interpret it.

Fields Purpose event_timestamp_ns, stream_rank, event_kind Event time, stream priority, and trade/depth classification. dataset_id, task_id, event_ordinal Source publication, source task, and event position. canonical_row_offset, canonical_row_count The addressed canonical row span. event_boundary, source_operation Depth initialization and operation metadata. Causal position fields Timeline sequence, reconstruction marker, and retained indexed receive-time and sequence metadata.

The canonical row span is half-open:

[canonical_row_offset, canonical_row_offset + canonical_row_count)

A zero-length depth span is valid.

UnifiedTimelineWriter buffers references, writes Parquet parts, and tracks event counts and observed timestamp bounds. A writer error marks the writer failed; it cannot later finalize as a successful writer.15

items.title: Validate the files that were written
items.text:
Logical validation reopens the staged Parquet output.

It checks paths, exact schema, file sizes, footer counts, decoded counts, stream membership, event kinds, and source references.

UnifiedReferenceValidator additionally verifies that:

  • Every publication/task pair exists in the inventory.
  • Trade references contain exactly one canonical row.
  • Canonical spans remain within task bounds.
  • Event ordinals increase within each publication/task.
  • Canonical row spans do not overlap or regress.

Chronological validation checks partition membership and nondecreasing timestamp/rank order.

Causal validation checks contiguous timeline positions, correct reconstruction markers, and initialization before depth source updates. Only depth events may appear outside the requested interval.

These checks establish the consistency of the selected logical timeline. Their event counts become the expected counts for physical materialization.16

items.title: Materialize canonical payloads
items.text:
flowchart TD
    T["Validated logical references"] --> W["Whole-event windows"]
    W --> P["Canonical read planner"]
    I["File and row-group inventories"] --> P

    P --> D["Forward canonical readers"]
    D --> R["Restore event and slice order"]
    W --> R

    R --> B["Trade, depth, or combined builder"]
    E["Depth event metadata"] --> B
    B --> F["Physical Parquet parts"]

MaterializationPartitionWorker coordinates physical reading and output construction.

It owns a canonical read planner, grouped decoder, depth metadata resolver, stream identities, and registered canonical files. For each window, it resolves the referenced rows, builds the selected physical schema, and submits the resulting batch to the writer.17

items.title: Keep events whole
items.text:
MaterializationWindowBuilder groups references using an event-count limit and a canonical-row target.

A depth event remains intact even if its number of changes exceeds the ordinary row target. The target therefore controls batching but is not an absolute maximum size for an individual window.

Any resource or batching change must account for unusually large single events instead of silently splitting their identity across output rows.18

items.title: Separate read order from event order
items.text:
Canonical references can cross files and row groups.

CanonicalRowIndex maps task-local row spans to file-local slices. CanonicalRowGroupIndex maps those slices to row groups. CanonicalReadPlanner groups reads by physical location while retaining each slice’s original event position.

GroupedCanonicalDecoder reads those groups and restores the original event and slice order before batch construction.

For example, references can arrive in the order A0, B0, A1, while physical reading groups the two reads from file A. The resulting event order must still be A0, B0, A1.

Read locality is an implementation concern; it cannot redefine the timeline.19

items.title: The production decoder uses forward cursors
items.text:
The active materialization worker uses persistent forward file cursors with LRU eviction.

The decoder remembers each file’s high-water position even after eviction. Reopening an evicted cursor does not authorize reading backward through an already consumed source range.

A replacement cursor can be opened before an existing cursor is evicted, which is reflected in the file-descriptor allowance.

The module also exports CanonicalRowGroupCache and CanonicalReferenceResolver. These are separate reusable APIs. They are not the active read strategy inside MaterializationPartitionWorker.

Changes to ordering, ownership ranges, or read grouping must preserve the production decoder’s forward-position assumptions.19

items.title: Physical output schemas
items.text:
Materialization preserves canonical Arrow values and their types, including decimal values. It does not perform another economic normalization or currency conversion.

Mode Physical representation Trades One row per trade, containing canonical trade columns and provenance. Depth One row per depth observation, containing identity, provenance, event metadata, and a non-null changes list. Combined One row per event, containing shared identity, provenance, event_kind, and exactly one populated trade or depth struct.

The depth changes list contains the canonical level-change fields. An event without level changes has an empty list.

For combined output, trade-specific fields belong inside the trade struct and depth-specific fields belong inside the depth struct. Consumers must select the payload using the event kind.

Every mode retains source provenance:

  • stream_rank
  • dataset_id
  • task_id
  • event_ordinal
  • canonical_row_offset
  • canonical_row_count

Causal physical output additionally carries timeline_sequence and reconstruction_only.20

items.title: Preserve metadata for zero-row depth events
items.text:
A depth observation without level changes has no canonical level row from which to recover its metadata.

The materialization path therefore uses the validated event reference and retained source identity. Causal depth receives indexed time and sequence metadata through the logical record; chronological depth resolves the corresponding event-index metadata.

Dropping an empty change list or attempting to derive all metadata from its first level would lose valid observations.1720

items.title: Canonical schema changes affect multiple builders
items.text:
The schema helpers currently treat the first six canonical columns as shared event identity and the remaining columns as payload.

A canonical schema change must review that positional assumption alongside:

  • Specialized trade and depth builders.
  • The combined builder.
  • Reader projections.
  • Physical validators.
  • Schema-version handling.
  • Downstream consumers.

Adding a canonical field is therefore not confined to editing one Arrow schema declaration.20

items.title: Validate the physical dataset
items.text:
PhysicalParquetWriter owns row-group buffering, compression, part rotation, and writer accounting.

Row-group and file settings are targets. Flush boundaries, Arrow memory estimates, encoding, and writer behavior affect actual sizes. They do not create strict upper bounds on every physical file.

After writers finish, physical validation reads the resulting Parquet files and checks:

  • Expected filenames, file counts, and directory ownership.
  • Exact schema and required values.
  • Trade/depth payload structure.
  • Decoded row counts against footer counts.
  • Event order and interval semantics.
  • Canonical row counts and event-kind totals.
  • Agreement with partition and writer results.

Global validation then checks the combined partition inventory and the relevant ordering rules across partition boundaries.

For causal output, timeline_sequence remains contiguous across the complete physical publication.21

items.title: Accounting invariants
items.text:
The publication distinguishes event rows from referenced canonical rows:

events_written = trade_events + depth_events

canonical_rows = sum(canonical_row_count for every materialized event)

reconstruction_events <= depth_events

For causal output, depth_events includes reconstruction-only observations. The number of depth observations inside the requested market interval is:

depth_events - reconstruction_events

The unified executor also compares logical and physical totals. Materialization must preserve the selected logical event population.

These validations check structure, ordering, and accounting. They do not independently reprocess raw archives or reconstruct every order book as a second implementation.212

items.title: Reconstruction availability
items.text:
Chronological clipping can produce a physical dataset whose first selected update depends on an initialization outside the requested interval.

The chronological path therefore records both physical checkpoints and initial reconstruction availability.

Availability Meaning available A suitable physical initialization establishes state at the requested start. prior_external Initial reconstruction depends on an earlier canonical checkpoint outside the physical interval. unavailable The required starting state is not established for the requested start.

An initialization first available later inside the interval does not establish state for earlier requested observations.

Causal output handles this differently: selected initialization and dependency events are materialized within the timeline. Its manifest uses that inline reconstruction model and requires the older checkpoint, initial-reconstruction, boundary-link, and skipped-initialization collections to remain empty.

Having materialized payload values and having complete initial reconstruction state are separate properties. Consumers must follow the publication’s ordering and reconstruction contract.22

items.title: Publication lifecycle
items.text:
The unified executor creates fresh sibling staging with separate logical and physical areas.

Logical references are written first. Physical materialization writes into a separate timeline. Both stages must complete their validation before publication preparation.

stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB

    [*] --> Staging
    Staging --> Validated: Logical and physical validation
    Validated --> Prepared: Manifest and provenance
    Prepared --> Visible: No-replace rename
    Visible --> Complete: Parent synchronization

    Staging --> Failed: Processing or validation error
    Validated --> Failed: Publication preparation error
    Prepared --> Failed: Commit rejected
    Visible --> SynchronizationFailed: Parent synchronization error

items.title: Prepare the final layout
items.text:
prepare_physical_publication() moves the validated physical timeline into the publication layout, writes the physical manifest, and removes the intermediate logical timeline.

The unified executor then retains the job, runtime, input fingerprints, and partition results and writes publication checksums.

The resulting publication contains:

Path Purpose manifest.json Physical schema, ordering, streams, counts, file inventory, and reconstruction metadata. timeline/partition-…/part-….parquet Materialized event payloads in publication order. merge-job.json Submitted file-based job or the applicable resolved legacy job. merge-runtime.json Effective merge resource, partitioning, and Parquet settings. merge-input-checksums.json Retained input manifest fingerprints. merge-partitions.json Physical partition results used for subsequent verification. publication-checksums.json Checksums for publication files and retained execution evidence.

The logical reference timeline is an intermediate artifact of the unified execution path. It is removed during successful publication preparation.23

items.title: Keep protocol versions separate
items.text:
The physical manifest and the physical Arrow schema have independent versions.

The current physical publication uses:

Contract Version Physical merge manifest 1 Chronological physical schema 1 Causal physical schema 2

Reference-oriented manifests and timeline schemas have their own version constants. They must not be interpreted as the physical publication format merely because their files are also named manifest.json or contain a timeline.24

items.title: Commit and failure behavior
items.text:
MergeCommitPaths derives a sibling staging directory and delegates publication to the shared normalization commit primitive.

Commit uses a same-filesystem, no-replace directory rename followed by parent-directory synchronization. Existing output is not overwritten, and there is no copy fallback.

An error during parent synchronization can occur after the final directory becomes visible. Callers must inspect the resulting filesystem state rather than assuming every error means the destination is absent.

Failures after staging begins can leave intermediate or partially prepared output. Staging is not an operational resume checkpoint, and this module does not define a general resume-from-staging protocol.

The unified executor returns Result<UnifiedMergeExecutionResult>. It does not create a normalization-style failed-job result for every failure, and successful filesystem publication is separate from subsequent catalogue registration.252

items.title: Validate an existing publication
items.text:
validate_committed_merge() reopens the saved manifest and execution evidence, checks their identities, reruns physical validation, and compares the observed output with the retained manifest.

Depending on the saved format and ordering, it also verifies runtime or physical payload checksum evidence.

This validates the committed merge publication. It does not reopen every original raw archive or repeat normalization.

The retained output path is part of the verification contract. Moving a publication to a different directory is not transparent to this validator.23

items.title: Progress and diagnostics
items.text:
MergeProgressReporter reports named execution phases and partition outcomes without owning processing decisions.

A PartitionKey contains both the phase and partition ID. This keeps a logical partition and a materialization partition with the same numeric ID distinct.

Lifecycle events use an optional channel. Atomic partition counters and replaceable validation progress support polling without producing an event for every row.

A disconnected progress consumer does not make processing fail.

Progress metrics also retain separate units. Inputs verified, logical events, materialized events, reconstruction observations, and canonical rows are different quantities. Completing a progress phase does not substitute for output validation or publication.

When progress reporting is disabled, the unified executor can emit stage timings when MARKETFORGE_PROFILE is set. Those timings help locate expensive phases; they do not replace output verification.262

items.title: Extending merge
items.text: Choose the module that owns the behavior being changed, then follow the resulting contract through validation and publication.

items.title: Support another canonical input layout
items.text:
Start with input resolution and the appropriate inventory builder.

The new layout must establish:

  • Which committed publication owns each file.
  • Which source task owns each referenced row or observation.
  • How task-local offsets map to physical positions.
  • Which event and reconstruction metadata are authoritative.
  • Which checks bind that evidence to the selected files.

Update stream admission and reference validation alongside the reader. Avoid making an unsupported layout appear supported by substituting guessed ownership or timestamp bounds.

items.title: Support more trade overlap or ownership patterns
items.text:
Begin with trades/inventory.rs, trades/stream.rs, and the restrictions in execution/unified/stream_resolver.rs.

The current stream implementation expects unambiguous ordered task contributions. Supporting disjoint or repeated ownership requires a representation that preserves those contributions through cursors, logical references, forward materialization, and validators.

If the proposed behavior requires identifying duplicate or conflicting native trades, define that responsibility explicitly. The existing merge cursor does not possess normalization’s full trade-identity reconciliation machinery.

items.title: Extend depth replay
items.text:
Work through the complete dependency path:

  • Depth inventory and event-index validation.
  • Source stream selection.
  • Initialization and segment handling.
  • Logical timeline metadata.
  • Materialization of zero-row and nonzero-row events.
  • Physical validation and reconstruction evidence.

For a depth stream spanning publications, establish how ownership and initialization remain valid across the publication boundary. Matching a stream ID alone is insufficient.

Any new selection algorithm must preserve every dependency needed for a selected state, including dependencies whose timestamps lie outside the requested interval.

items.title: Add an event kind or physical field
items.text:
An event kind crosses several boundaries: the reference enum, stream classification, timeline schema, materialization dispatch, physical schema, counters, and validators.

A field change must preserve values in both specialized and combined output. Review nullable payload construction and the shared-column assumptions in builders/schema.rs.

Update schema compatibility deliberately. A reader should reject an unsupported representation rather than interpret it through an older schema by accident.

items.title: Improve read performance
items.text:
Start with CanonicalReadPlanner, GroupedCanonicalDecoder, and the forward readers.

An optimization must preserve:

  • Original physical row positions.
  • Task-local reference meaning.
  • Event order after grouped reads.
  • Slice order within a depth event.
  • Exact interval selection.
  • Forward-read guarantees across cursor eviction.

Evaluate cache and cursor changes with interleaved streams, references crossing files, and events crossing row groups. Faster contiguous reads alone do not establish correctness for mixed workloads.

items.title: Change concurrency or publication
items.text:
Concurrency changes belong in the phase planners, resource estimators, and scheduler integration. Account for complete events, writer buffers, retained metadata, and descriptor replacement behavior.

Publication changes must keep the manifest, retained job/runtime evidence, checksum inventory, and committed validator consistent.

Preserve the distinction between replay checkpoints and resumable execution state. The presence of depth reconstruction checkpoints does not make a partially completed merge resumable.

items.title: Testing merge changes
items.text:
Tests should verify observable contracts across stage boundaries.

The module contains focused unit tests at these locations:

Source location Existing focus core/ordering.rs Timestamp ordering and merge-key tie behavior. partition/shared/partition.rs Deterministic partitions, exact interval coverage, non-overlap, and half-open membership. execution/shared/resources.rs Resource estimates, invalid settings, overflow, and growth with stream count. output/writers/timeline.rs Reference schema and event-reference preservation. materialize/builders/schema.rs Canonical field preservation and nested depth/combined schema structure. materialize/readers/inventory.rs Cross-file spans, zero-row references, bounds, and overflow. materialize/readers/reader.rs Reader batch-size validation.

Use these as focused entry points, then exercise the public unified executor for behavior that spans planning, writing, validation, and publication.27

For new behavior, select the relevant end-to-end cases:

Change Evidence the test should establish Ordering Equal timestamps preserve declared stream priority; source-task IDs do not accidentally reorder a ranked stream. Causal replay Timestamp regressions retain source order and produce contiguous timeline positions. Interval selection Initialization and out-of-interval dependencies remain available for requested depth observations. Depth cardinality Multiple-change and zero-change observations each retain one physical event row. File selection Partial trade selections preserve original offsets; unsupported partial depth selections fail. Read planning Grouped physical reads restore the original event order across files and row groups. Materialization Specialized and combined output preserve canonical values and nullability. Reconstruction A checkpoint available later in the interval does not become proof of state at the interval start. Resource behavior Work exceeding admission limits fails predictably; cursor eviction preserves forward positions. Validation Altered schemas, invalid references, inconsistent counts, and corrupted retained evidence are rejected. Publication Existing destinations remain untouched, and failures preserve enough state to distinguish staging failure from a visible post-rename result.

Compare decoded semantics, provenance, and ordering rather than assuming two valid executions must produce byte-identical Parquet files.

The most useful integration test follows one event through the complete lifecycle: committed ownership, logical reference, physical payload, manifest accounting, and committed-publication validation.

items.text:
• System architecture and operation lifecycles place Merge Engine in the historical workflow.
  • Prepared contract and user workflow describe the public handoff.
  • Test selection and diagnostics cover verification and inspection.
