Use mf acquisition sources | cpout to see which combinations the installed archive adapters accept. Use mf --json acquisition sources | cpout for the same capability rows in JSON. These are historical archive routes. Availability depends on the exact scope, date, and upstream response. Use the acquisition guide to map a recipe.

Exchange ID Instrument type Market category Trades L2 depth Scope kind binance spot spot Yes — instrument binance perpetual, future linear, inverse Yes — instrument bybit spot spot Yes Yes instrument bybit perpetual, future linear, inverse Yes Yes instrument bybit option option Yes Yes base_coin bitget spot spot Yes Yes instrument bitget perpetual linear, inverse Yes Yes instrument bitget future inverse Yes Yes instrument okx spot spot Yes Yes instrument okx perpetual, future linear, inverse Yes Yes family okx option option Yes Yes family, base_coin gateio spot spot Yes Yes instrument gateio perpetual, future linear, inverse Yes Yes instrument

items.title: Historical scopes
items.text:
Kind Selects Example instrument One provider-native instrument Bybit BTCUSDT family An archive family used by the provider for derivatives OKX inverse dated futures BTC-USD base_coin Options grouped or resolved by their underlying coin Bybit options on BTC

Explicit historical instrument and family scopes can find delisted instruments absent from today's catalogue if their archives are still published. Use the exact identifier expected by the historical source. See scope and provider options.

items.title: Binance
items.text: The adapter lists daily trade files under the native instrument's paginated S3 prefix. It has separate spot, linear futures and inverse futures routes. Historical L2 and options are unsupported.

items.title: Bybit
items.text: Spot and non-option derivatives use instrument directory listings for trades and depth. Options use a base coin for daily archive discovery with queries of at most seven calendar days. This window bounds individual queries. Provider history and access determine which files are returned.

items.title: Bitget
items.text: Spot discovery resolves compact symbols through the historical symbol endpoint. Supply the explicit display symbol, such as BTC/USDT, if lookup is ambiguous. Availability queries use windows of up to seven UTC+8 calendar days. Options and linear dated futures are unsupported.

items.title: OKX
items.text: Spot discovery uses native symbols such as BTC-USDT. Derivatives use a family identifier. Family bundles can stay family-scoped in managed storage. Options accept an explicit family or expand a base coin using currently advertised option families. Choose an explicit historical family when the provider no longer advertises it. The adapter queries one archive day at a time, using UTC+8 for trades and UTC for the historical 5000-level depth module.

items.title: Gate.io
items.text: The adapter probes monthly trade candidates and hourly L2 candidates for existence, using separate spot, USDT derivatives and BTC derivatives routes. The L2 feed option selects incremental or snapshot archives. Dated futures use the same candidate construction as the corresponding perpetual market. Only a successful probe establishes that a candidate archive was found.

items.title: Prepared conversion job
items.text:
A version 1 prepared job describes one execution against complete physical merge publications. Forge uses read-only discovery and verified lineage to produce this job. The individual Rust job has a separate schema from the Forge collection.

Job field Meaning schema_version, operation, job_id Schema version 1, operation convert, execution identity input_merge, source Absolute path and prepared binding for the source publication conversion.reference_merge, external_reference Optional absolute path and prepared binding for an external trade-only publication catalog_sha256 Fingerprint of the preparation catalog or the historical catalog snapshot derived from committed authority conversion Target quote, price source, staleness, hop limit, path policy, instrument-kind filter, and explicit reference identities resources, parquet Effective resource caps and Parquet row group size, file size, and compression output.dataset_path Absolute destination. Its sibling with extension .staging is used for materialization

Each binding records the engine merge job ID, SHA-256 pins for manifest.json and publication-checksums.json, the originating normalized dataset IDs and evidence hashes, and a record for each stream. Each stream identifies its normalized dataset, stream ID, rank, kind, instrument ID and namespace, exchange, symbol, instrument and contract kinds, and base and quote currencies. Merged and normalized IDs have different roles. The JSON stores IDs as integers.

Forge checks the instrument metadata against committed normalized authority and checks an installed catalog against that authority when present. It retains catalog and normalization evidence fingerprints. The Engine compares the prepared bindings against the physical stream inventory, including currencies where the physical manifest carries them. Where the manifest omits currencies, the embedded assignments are statements of verified preparation evidence. A publication hash establishes source identity and integrity. It cannot independently establish omitted currency values.

Forge caps recipe resources using historical runtime settings during preparation and records the effective Parquet writer sizes in MiB and Zstandard level. The conversion runtime supplies these values. The Engine checks worker limits and admission estimates for writer row groups and open files. --workers can choose a lower worker count. Publish staged output using the same job and worker override. The committed conversion-runtime.json records the full job and effective settings.

Execution requires the job, declared physical publications and their commit metadata, and the output location. The old --catalog, --normalization-root, --config, and --project-root flags report migration errors. Re-prepare incomplete jobs with Forge. The Engine needs neither database access nor a runtime configuration file.

See the conversion workflow for commands, reference selection, and bounded verification.

items.title: Structured bindings and limits
items.text:
All listed job-level fields are required except that external_reference is nullable and can be omitted by the Rust decoder. Positive IDs and counters use unsigned 64-bit JSON integers, stream ranks use uint32, and instrument IDs use positive signed 64-bit integers. SHA-256 fields use 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Source and output paths are absolute. The external path and binding must be supplied together. Forge emits the optional values explicitly where its serializer uses nulls.

Object Serialized fields source, external_reference merge_job_id, manifest_sha256, publication_checksums_sha256, nonempty normalized_inputs, nonempty streams normalized_inputs[] dataset_id, nullable manifest_sha256, processing_job_sha256 streams[] dataset_id, stream_id, stream_rank, kind (trade or depth), instrument_id, instrument_namespace, identity, base_currency, quote_currency identity, conversion.references[] Nonblank exchange, symbol, instrument_kind (spot, perpetual, future, option, equity), nullable contract_kind (linear or inverse) conversion Required target_quote, price_source (last_trade), max_staleness_ns (positive uint64). Optional instrument_kinds and absolute reference_merge default to null. references defaults to an empty array, path_policy to all, max_hops to 3. Forge resolves and emits explicit policy fields and references resources Positive workers, memory_limit_mb in MiB and max_open_files parquet Positive row_group_target_mb and file_target_mb in MiB, with row group target no larger than file target. compression_level is 1–22 output Absolute dataset_path

Bindings reconcile the source manifest's dataset, stream identity, rank and kind with each entry. Inspect --validate diagnostics for inconsistent, duplicate, missing or unsupported evidence. Currency codes use uppercase ASCII letters or digits. Unknown wire fields are rejected. Engine model

items.title: Forge preparation and run evidence
items.text:
Forge reports coordinate the Engine handoff and recover committed output. Pass the operation's prepared job to its Engine, and use the separate retained evidence when working with Forge.

Operation Preparation Execution and recovery Normalize Batch schema 4 plus prepare-report.json with selection and job summaries submitted-batch.json, execution-intent.json, Engine result and execution-result.json. Verified committed outputs can be registered from the supported receipt Merge merge-job.json and prepare-report.json Pinned submitted job, configuration and selected inputs, execution intent and result. Registration recovery checks the same committed evidence Convert convert.json is a Forge object with version: 1, type: "forge-conversion-collection", environment, jobs, pins, sources, external_reference, and compatibility_blockers. jobs indexes standalone job files and their validation state Forge submits each job separately. The execution intent and result retain compatibility and output verification. Conversion registration is unavailable Pipeline Versioned recipe and read-only plan. Its child preparation artifacts use the corresponding operation schemas report.json and events.jsonl under the run ID. Child stage records link to prepared inputs, execution attempts, verification and registration

The pipeline's top-level report has schema_version: 1, kind: "historical_pipeline" and a state. Stage keys are acquire, normalize, merge. Each stage tracks phase and state, and processing stages may include prepared job and report pins, execution attempts, result and registered primary_file_ids. Status is a read of that report. Resume checks original input bindings and work context. It may recover a verified registration or allocate fresh output identities for a processing retry. Acquisition, preparation, submission and publication are separate transitions. Pipeline service · Resume guide

All artifact paths resolve according to their producer and contract. Treat retained inputs as immutable evidence. A preparation report can exist even if the job is blocked or generated without validation. Verify current binary compatibility before using older retained artifacts.

items.title: Prepared merge job
items.text: Forge writes one pinned job consumed by marketforge-merge. Its identity, input file references and half-open event-time interval are independent of editable recipe selectors. Workflow

items.title: Why Does Merging Use a Different Contract?
items.text:
Normalization reads registered raw archives.

Merging reads registered normalized Parquet files.

These operations require different input information.

items.title: Normalization input
items.text:
For example:

Raw ZIP Archive
    |
    v
Source Profile
    |
    v
Canonical Trades

items.title: Merge input
items.text:
For example:

Normalized Trades ──┐
                    |
                    v
                  Merge
                    ^
                    |
Normalized Depth ───┘

The merger does not need to decode the original exchange archive format again.

Instead, it needs to know:

  • Which exact normalized primary files were selected.
  • Which publications own them.
  • Which streams they represent.
  • Their content types.
  • Their retained checksums.
  • The required timeline ordering.
  • The requested interval.

items.title: Why pin files rather than only instruments?
items.text:
An instrument may have several normalized publications.

For example, the same BTCUSDT period may have been normalized more than once.

A merge must use the exact selected files rather than silently switching between publication revisions.

items.title: Merge Job Structure
items.text:
The prepared merge job contains:

Field Purpose job_id Merge job identity. operation Processing operation. inputs Exact registered normalized primary files. time_range Requested historical interval. timeline_ordering Chronological or causal timeline behavior. output Merge publication destination.

items.title: Example structure
items.text:
{
  "job_id": 123456,
  "operation": "merge",
  "timeline_ordering": "chronological",
  "inputs": [],
  "time_range": {
    "start_ns": 1793059200000000000,
    "end_ns": 1793318400000000000
  },
  "output": {
    "dataset_path": "/absolute/path/to/data/datasets/merged/123456"
  }
}

This is a structural illustration, not an executable job.

A valid merge job requires eligible registered inputs.

items.title: Why is the merge interval numeric?
items.text:
The merge contract uses integer Unix nanoseconds.

This allows precise event-time boundaries.

items.title: What Does Each Merge Input Identify?
items.text:
Each merge input represents one selected registered normalized primary file.

Important fields include:

Field Meaning dataset_id PostgreSQL primary file dataset ID. stream_id Exact concrete logical stream identity. stream_rank Merge ordering priority. content_type trades or depth. path Absolute primary Parquet file path. sha256 SHA-256 of the selected primary file. publication Owning normalized publication identity and manifest evidence.

items.title: Why is dataset_id important?
items.text:
It identifies one registered physical primary file.

It is not the same as the Engine publication ID.

items.title: Why is stream_id important?
items.text:
A merged file may combine multiple instruments and content types.

The stream identity identifies the logical source of an event.

items.title: Why is content_type required?
items.text:
Trades and depth have different event semantics.

The merger must know which kind of normalized data the selected file represents.

items.title: Merge Input Example
items.text:
A merge input has the following structure:

{
  "dataset_id": 119,
  "stream_id": "binance.linear.future.BTCUSDT_261225.trades",
  "stream_rank": 0,
  "content_type": "trades",
  "path": "/absolute/path/to/part-000000.parquet",
  "sha256": "<primary-file-sha256>",
  "publication": {
    "engine_dataset_id": "7868739277080297142",
    "manifest_path": "/absolute/path/to/manifest.json",
    "manifest_sha256": "<manifest-sha256>"
  }
}

This is a structural illustration.

Replace the paths and checksums with real Forge-generated values.

Do not submit placeholder fingerprints.

items.title: What does this input mean?
items.text:
It identifies:

Registered primary file:
119

Logical stream:
Binance BTCUSDT futures trades

Primary file:
Specific Parquet part

Owning publication:
Specific normalized Engine publication

Verification:
Pinned file and manifest checksums

items.title: Why include both file and manifest checksums?
items.text:
The file checksum identifies the selected Parquet bytes.

The manifest checksum identifies the corresponding publication metadata.

Together, they help establish that the input still matches the intended committed publication.

items.title: File Checksum Pinning
items.text:
The merge input contains:

"sha256": "<primary-file-sha256>"

items.title: What is SHA-256?
items.text:
It is a cryptographic checksum used to identify file contents.

For example, two files with different bytes should ordinarily produce different SHA-256 values.

items.title: Why pin the checksum?
items.text:
Suppose you prepare a merge today.

Tomorrow, someone modifies one of the selected Parquet files.

The prepared job should not silently process the changed content as though it were the original input.

The checksum helps detect that mismatch.

items.title: Does a matching checksum prove the market data is historically complete?
items.text:
No.

It establishes consistency with the pinned file bytes.

It does not prove that the original exchange supplied every event.

items.title: What happens if the checksum changes?
items.text:
The applicable validation or execution check can reject the input.

Prepare a new job only after investigating the reason for the change.

Do not manually replace the fingerprint merely to bypass the mismatch.

items.title: Publication Pinning
items.text:
The merge input contains:

{
  "publication": {
    "engine_dataset_id": "7868739277080297142",
    "manifest_path": "/absolute/path/to/manifest.json",
    "manifest_sha256": "<manifest-sha256>"
  }
}

items.title: What is engine_dataset_id?
items.text: It identifies the owning Engine normalization publication.

items.title: Why is it a string?
items.text:
Engine dataset identities may use unsigned 64-bit integer values.

Representing them as canonical decimal strings avoids precision loss in tools that cannot exactly represent all such integers.

items.title: What is manifest_path?
items.text: It identifies the owning publication manifest.

items.title: What is manifest_sha256?
items.text: It pins the expected manifest bytes.

items.title: Why is the manifest necessary?
items.text:
The manifest provides publication information required to interpret the selected normalized file.

For example:

  • Content type.
  • Stream membership.
  • Physical layout.
  • Ordering information.
  • Source ownership.
  • Applicable auxiliary data.

The merger cannot safely infer all these properties from the Parquet filename.

items.title: Why Independent JSON Must Be Verified
items.text:
A user can construct a JSON document with plausible field names.

However, that does not establish that its inputs are valid.

For example:

{
  "dataset_id": 119,
  "stream_id": "some-stream",
  "content_type": "trades"
}

could refer to an incorrect stream.

items.title: What does Rust check?
items.text:
The merge contract validates the selected file against its owning publication information.

This includes the applicable:

  • Registered file identity.
  • Stream ownership.
  • Content type.
  • Publication fingerprint.
  • Physical input compatibility.

items.title: Why not trust the supplied values?
items.text:
Because a JSON document is a request, not independent evidence.

A user could accidentally supply a depth file while labeling it as trades.

The Engine must reject inconsistent input contracts.

items.title: Recommended practice
items.text:
Use Forge preparation.

It resolves the registered file and publication evidence automatically.

items.title: Why Merge Inputs Need Stream Ranks
items.text:
A merged timeline may contain several logical streams.

For example:

BTCUSDT Trades
BTCUSDT Depth
ETHUSDT Trades
ETHUSDT Depth

Events can have identical timestamps.

The merger needs deterministic ordering information.

items.title: Example
items.text:
12:00:00.100 BTCUSDT Trade
12:00:00.100 ETHUSDT Trade

Both events have the same event timestamp.

Stream rank can provide the applicable tie-breaking order.

items.title: Merge Rank Rules
items.text: The prepared merge contract uses unsigned 32-bit stream ranks.

items.title: Lower ranks first
items.text:
For applicable equal-time ordering:

Rank 0

comes before:

Rank 1

items.title: Same stream
items.text:
Files representing the same concrete stream repeat its rank.

For example:

BTCUSDT Trades
    Part 1 → Rank 3
    Part 2 → Rank 3
    Part 3 → Rank 3

items.title: Different streams
items.text:
Distinct concrete streams use distinct ranks across the selected content types.

For example:

BTCUSDT Trades → Rank 3
BTCUSDT Depth  → Rank 4
ETHUSDT Trades → Rank 5

items.title: Can ranks contain gaps?
items.text:
Yes.

For example:

Rank 1
Rank 5
Rank 9

can remain valid in a filtered prepared job.

items.title: Why not require dense ranks?
items.text:
Filtering a job may remove selected streams without changing the retained ordering identities.

The merge contract allows rank gaps.

items.title: Are normalization and merge rank rules identical?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

Normalization preparation can generate dense ranks from retained ranking positions.

Merge preparation can preserve selected normalized stream ranks and applies its own distinct-stream consistency requirements.

items.title: Half-Open Merge Intervals
items.text:
A prepared merge job contains:

{
  "time_range": {
    "start_ns": 1793059200000000000,
    "end_ns": 1793318400000000000
  }
}

The start is included.

The end is excluded.

This is:

[start_ns, end_ns)

items.title: Why use nanoseconds?
items.text:
High-frequency market events can occur within microseconds or nanoseconds of one another.

Integer nanosecond boundaries preserve the requested time precision.

items.title: Does this interval prove the source contains every event?
items.text:
No.

It describes the requested processing range.

The actual input files must satisfy the applicable selection and overlap requirements.

items.title: What if an input does not overlap the interval?
items.text: Preparation can reject the selection.

items.title: Can the merger invent missing observations?
items.text:
No.

It combines available supported normalized events.

It does not recreate missing exchange history.

items.title: Why Timeline Ordering Matters
items.text:
Merging trades and order-book data is not simply concatenating files.

Consider:

Trade:
12:00:00.100

Depth:
12:00:00.050
12:00:00.150

A chronological timeline might place them as:

12:00:00.050 Depth
12:00:00.100 Trade
12:00:00.150 Depth

However, depth events can depend on earlier book state.

For example:

Snapshot
    |
    v
Update
    |
    v
Update

Arbitrarily rearranging these events can corrupt reconstruction.

items.title: Why does this require an explicit contract?
items.text:
Different normalized publications may use different physical ordering and reconstruction layouts.

The merger must apply the supported ordering semantics for the selected inputs.

items.title: Chronological Ordering
items.text:
The merge job can contain:

"timeline_ordering": "chronological"

items.title: What does this mean?
items.text: The merger constructs the supported chronological timeline using event timestamps and the applicable tie-breaking rules.

items.title: When is it appropriate?
items.text: For compatible inputs whose physical layout and event semantics support chronological merging.

items.title: Does it mean arbitrary depth sorting is permitted?
items.text:
No.

Depth dependencies remain subject to the supported input-layout and reconstruction requirements.

items.title: What if timeline_ordering is omitted?
items.text:
The prepared merge job contract defaults to chronological ordering.

However, Forge may explicitly resolve a different mode when the selected recipe and inputs require it.

items.title: Causal Ordering
items.text:
The merge job can also contain:

"timeline_ordering": "causal"

items.title: Why is causal ordering necessary?
items.text:
Some depth publications contain source-order or reconstruction dependencies that timestamp sorting alone cannot safely represent.

For example:

Initialize book
    |
    v
Apply update
    |
    v
Apply next update

The causal timeline preserves the applicable processing dependencies.

items.title: Does causal mean economic causation?
items.text:
No.

It does not prove that one trade caused another event.

Here, causal ordering describes the required event-processing dependencies.

items.title: Why is this distinction important?
items.text:
A trade occurring before a depth update does not automatically prove that the trade caused the update.

The merger preserves event order and source semantics.

Market-impact analysis remains a separate research task.

items.title: Causal Timeline Physical Schema
items.text:
The documented committed causal timeline uses physical schema version 2.

Important fields include:

timeline_sequence
reconstruction_only

items.title: What is timeline_sequence?
items.text: It records the physical ordering information required by the causal timeline representation.

items.title: What is reconstruction_only?
items.text: It identifies rows that are present for supported reconstruction purposes rather than ordinary event interpretation.

items.title: Why retain reconstruction rows?
items.text:
Some order-book histories require initialization or dependent observations to establish valid state.

Those rows may be necessary even when they are not ordinary user-visible market events.

items.title: Should they be removed manually?
items.text:
No.

Removing reconstruction dependencies can make a historical book impossible to replay correctly.

items.title: Can I sort the resulting file by timestamp?
items.text:
Do not assume that independently sorting causal timeline rows preserves the required event semantics.

Use the supported timeline sequence and reconstruction information.

items.title: Chronological vs. Causal
items.text: Property Chronological Causal Main objective Supported timestamp ordering Preserve required event dependencies Typical consideration Compatible independent events Stateful segmented depth Ordering information Timestamp and stream-rank contract Physical causal sequence and reconstruction evidence Can arbitrarily sort depth levels? No No Proves economic causation? No No

items.title: Which should I choose?
items.text:
Use the ordering mode appropriate to the selected publication layouts and processing requirements.

For ordinary workflows, allow Forge preparation to resolve the supported behavior.

items.title: Does every normalized publication support both?
items.text:
No.

The selected inputs must satisfy the merger's current compatibility rules.

items.title: Why Valid Parquet Files Can Still Be Incompatible
items.text:
A Parquet file can be structurally valid while using a physical layout that the merger does not support.

For example, a normalized depth publication may preserve native-order reconstruction segments.

A particular merger path may require additional supporting files or a specific physical ordering.

items.title: What does compatibility depend on?
items.text:
It can depend on:

  • Manifest protocol version.
  • Content type.
  • Physical timestamp ordering.
  • Stream ownership.
  • Source spans.
  • Reconstruction dependencies.
  • Selected primary file set.
  • Supporting publication evidence.

items.title: Why not merge every valid file?
items.text:
Because combining files under unsupported assumptions could create an incorrect timeline.

Rejecting an incompatible selection is safer than silently inventing ordering or reconstruction rules.

items.title: Normalization Manifest Versions
items.text:
Normalization publications use versioned manifest protocols.

The documented range includes:

3–5

These protocols can describe different publication capabilities and evidence.

items.title: Why are manifests versioned?
items.text:
As the Engine evolves, it can add information about:

  • Source ownership.
  • Reconstruction boundaries.
  • Processing quality.
  • Physical ordering.
  • Publication integrity.

items.title: Does a newer manifest automatically work with every downstream operation?
items.text:
No.

For example, a newer normalization publication may contain a valid native-order depth layout that is not supported by a particular merge reader.

items.title: What should users inspect?
items.text:
Check the actual publication manifest and the current merge compatibility report.

Use:

Supported Merge Layouts

for the detailed compatibility matrix.

items.title: Source Ownership and Merge Compatibility
items.text:
Some normalized trade publications retain information about which source records contributed to each output row.

For example, a trade publication may contain:

sources.jsonl

This provides source-ownership evidence.

items.title: Why is source ownership important?
items.text:
A publication can contain events from overlapping archives.

The merger may need to know whether a selected physical part has contiguous source ownership.

items.title: What does contiguous ownership mean?
items.text:
Conceptually, a compatible file might contain:

Source A rows
Source B rows
Source C rows

with each source represented in one contiguous span.

An interleaved layout might contain:

Source A
Source B
Source A
Source C
Source B

The latter can require different processing support.

items.title: Does the merger support every ownership layout?
items.text:
No.

The documented timestamp-first merge contract supports certain v4/v5 trade layouts with contiguous source ownership and no repeated source spans.

More complex layouts may be rejected.

items.title: What about native-order depth?
items.text:
The timestamp-first merger's supported input set is narrower than the complete set of valid depth publications.

Inspect the current supported-layout rules rather than assuming every depth publication is eligible.

items.title: Wire identity
items.text:
The public document has no schema_version. It contains operation:"merge", positive uint64 job_id, nonempty inputs, time_range, output, and optional timeline_ordering defaulting in the Engine to chronological. time_range.start_ns and end_ns are signed int64 and ordered. output.dataset_path is absolute.

Each input has positive uint64 registry dataset_id, nonempty stream_id, uint32 stream_rank, content_type of trades or depth, absolute path, lowercase SHA-256 sha256, and a publication object. The latter contains positive canonical decimal text engine_dataset_id, absolute manifest_path ending in manifest.json, and lowercase SHA-256 manifest_sha256. IDs and file paths cannot repeat in one submission. A repeated Engine publication ID must have identical manifest path and hash. Forge's editable database selectors are further constrained to signed 64-bit IDs. Unknown fields are rejected. Engine wire definition

items.title: Prepared normalization batch
items.text: Forge writes the schema-4 normalization batch. The Rust normalizer validates and resolves it; a TOML recipe remains a separate input. Workflow

items.title: Manual batch submission
items.text:
Use the recipe-first normalization workflow for ordinary runs. Use separate preparation and submission when you need to inspect and retain the exact job inputs before execution.

mf --json normalize prepare my_dataset --testing > prepare.json &&
batch=$(python3 - <<'PYTHON'
import json
from pathlib import Path

report = json.loads(Path("prepare.json").read_text())
if report["status"] != "prepared" or not report["engine_ready"]:
    raise SystemExit("Batch is not ready. Inspect prepare.json.")
print(report["batch_path"])
PYTHON
) &&
mf normalize run "$batch" --testing

The guarded command chain submits only a persisted plan with status = "prepared" and engine_ready = true. Keep normalize-batch.json, prepare-report.json, and their sibling profile and runtime copies together. Execution checks the retained batch, runtime, executable and profile hashes, verifies the registry identity and raw inputs, and validates the batch again with Rust. Reprepare from the TOML recipe if pinned evidence has changed. See execution and registration.

items.title: What Is a Normalization Batch?
items.text:
A normalization batch describes one or more concrete Rust normalization jobs.

For example:

                  Normalization Batch
                          |
              +-----------+-----------+
              |                       |
              v                       v
           Trades Job              Depth Job
              |                       |
         +----+----+              +---+---+
         |         |              |       |
         v         v              v       v
       Task 1    Task 2         Task 3  Task 4

A task identifies source work assigned to a job.

A job produces the applicable normalized publication.

items.title: Why use batches?
items.text:
One normalization recipe may select several archives and content types.

For example:

BTCUSDT Trades
BTCUSDT Depth
ETHUSDT Trades
ETHUSDT Depth

Instead of submitting each archive manually, Forge groups the resolved processing work into jobs.

items.title: Are trades and depth processed identically?
items.text:
No.

They have different processing contracts.

For example, depth normalization may require book reconstruction and sequence validation.

Trade normalization uses its own event-identity and reconciliation rules.

The batch groups these jobs without pretending they are the same content type.

items.title: Current Normalization Batch Version
items.text:
The current normalization batch protocol uses:

{
  "schema_version": 4,
  "kind": "normalization_batch",
  "status": "prepared"
}

This is an illustrative fragment.

A complete batch contains additional required information.

items.title: Why does the batch use schema version 4?
items.text:
The batch protocol has evolved independently of user-facing recipes.

For example:

Normalization recipe:
version = 1

Prepared Engine batch:
schema_version = 4

These are different contracts.

items.title: Does recipe version 1 mean batch version 1?
items.text:
No.

Forge converts the supported recipe format into the current Rust Engine contract.

items.title: Where is the implementation?
items.text:
Forge generates normalization batches in:

forge/historical/normalization/batch.py

Rust parses and validates them in:

engine/src/historical/config/batch.rs

The maintained normalization fixture is:

engine/tests/historical/fixtures/normalize.json

items.title: Why does the fixture matter?
items.text:
It provides a concrete reference for the maintained parser workload.

However, the fixture may contain environment-specific file paths and registered identities.

It should not be assumed executable in every workspace without its required dependencies.

items.title: Batch-Level Parameters
items.text:
The prepared batch contains information shared by the normalization jobs.

Parameter Purpose schema_version Prepared-batch protocol version. kind Batch document kind. status Preparation status. run_id Logical preparation run identifier. run_directory Associated run directory. batch_path Prepared batch location. ranking_snapshot Selected ranking snapshot identity, when available. ranking_policy Ranking policy used for stream-ordering resolution. requested_interval Original requested historical interval. instrument_namespace Canonical instrument identity namespace. instruments Resolved authoritative instrument definitions. families Supported family authority information. jobs Concrete normalization jobs.

items.title: Why does the batch need these fields?
items.text:
The Engine needs a complete description of the requested work.

For example, the jobs identify source processing tasks.

The instrument definitions provide the relevant economic interpretation.

The namespace establishes which canonical identity system the numeric instrument IDs belong to.

items.title: Example Batch Header
items.text:
A prepared batch can begin with:

{
  "schema_version": 4,
  "kind": "normalization_batch",
  "status": "prepared",
  "run_id": "normalize-example",
  "run_directory": "/absolute/path/to/data/runs/normalize-example",
  "batch_path": "/absolute/path/to/data/runs/normalize-example/normalize-batch.json",
  "ranking_snapshot": null,
  "ranking_policy": "turnover",
  "requested_interval": {
    "start": "2026-10-27T00:00:00Z",
    "end": "2026-10-30T00:00:00Z"
  }
}

This is a structural illustration, not a complete executable batch.

Actual prepared batches include instrument authority and job definitions.

items.title: Why preserve requested_interval?
items.text:
The requested interval describes what the user selected.

The actual raw archives can extend beyond that interval.

Preserving the original request makes the selection traceable.

items.title: Why preserve ranking_policy?
items.text:
The selected ranking policy can provide ordering evidence for the generated streams.

The prepared batch retains that policy identity.

items.title: Why can ranking_snapshot be null?
items.text:
A suitable published ranking snapshot may not exist.

Forge can use deterministic stream identity ordering when the required ranking positions are absent.

items.title: Preparation Status
items.text:
The normalization batch contains:

"status": "prepared"

The preparation system can also report a partial selection.

items.title: Prepared
items.text:
A prepared status indicates that Forge resolved the applicable complete selection and constructed the corresponding batch.

A persisted prepared plan runs the production Rust batch validator and records engine_ready = true after validation passes. Dry-run prepared describes successful Forge planning. It has engine_ready = false, skips Rust batch validation and writes neither the batch nor its report. Resolving registered external inputs may still compile profiles to verify fingerprint compatibility.

items.title: Partial
items.text:
A partial status can indicate that some selected work was resolved while other requirements remain blocked.

For example:

Requested archives: 100
Resolved archives:  95
Blocked archives:    5

These numbers are illustrative.

items.title: Does partial mean the complete workload is ready?
items.text:
No.

A partial preparation does not establish that the complete requested selection is executable.

items.title: What should users inspect?
items.text:
The preparation report distinguishes selection evidence from generated work.

Evidence Meaning requests[] One entry per source request or legacy input selection. Each source request includes its matching scope and content. matched_archives Candidate registry records returned for a source request, including records that can subsequently fail resolution. selected_archives Candidates that resolved into usable input evidence for the request. The same archive can appear in multiple requests. blockers, coverage Input or metadata issues and nominal archive interval evidence. Gaps can block the plan. Missing evidence stays unknown. prepared_job_count, prepared_task_count, prepared_stream_count Generated jobs by content type, deduplicated source work within each job, and distinct planned streams summed across jobs. Family expansion can resolve additional concrete streams in the Engine. job_summaries Per-job Engine IDs, content type, planned destinations, and task and stream counts. ranking_resolution Policy, retained snapshot and ordering or fallback evidence. batch_path, report_path Batch and preparation report destinations. These paths are prospective in dry runs.

The requested interval selects overlapping whole archives. Nominal archive bounds and gaps do not establish market-event completeness or final row bounds.

items.title: Can the batch exist without being executable?
items.text:
Yes.

A generated artifact is not automatically equivalent to a successfully validated processing request.

For executable results, use the reported preparation and Engine validation outcomes together. A persisted partial batch can be retained for diagnosis; the Rust loader accepts only prepared batches.

Runtime controls such as resource limits and Parquet writer settings come from the normalization runtime configuration. Persisted preparation retains the effective runtime file and profile copies. They are not per-recipe overrides.

items.title: What Is a Normalization Job?
items.text:
A job groups concrete source tasks belonging to one normalization operation.

For example:

Trades Job
    |
    +-- BTCUSDT October 27
    +-- BTCUSDT October 28
    +-- ETHUSDT October 27

The corresponding job contains a unique identity, output configuration, and task list.

items.title: Job parameters
items.text: Parameter Purpose operation Requested processing operation. job_id Engine job identity. dataset_id Engine dataset identity. tasks Source tasks assigned to the job. ordering.primary Primary output ordering declaration. ordering.tie_break Tie-breaking rule. output.content_type trades or depth. output.staging_path Intermediate publication destination. output.dataset_path Final publication destination.

items.title: Job Identity
items.text:
A prepared job contains:

{
  "operation": "normalize",
  "job_id": 123456,
  "dataset_id": 123457
}

These are illustrative identifiers.

items.title: What is job_id?
items.text: It identifies the normalization processing job.

items.title: What is dataset_id?
items.text: It identifies the Engine dataset produced by the job.

items.title: Why are they different?
items.text:
A job describes processing work.

A dataset identifies the publication produced by that work.

These are related, but they serve different purposes.

items.title: Are these PostgreSQL file IDs?
items.text:
No.

Engine dataset IDs are separate from PostgreSQL's registered primary file dataset IDs.

For example, one normalized publication may contain several Parquet parts.

Each primary file can receive its own PostgreSQL dataset ID after registration.

items.title: Does Forge reserve the IDs during preparation?
items.text:
The current normalization preparation allocates collision-checked testing identifiers.

The preparation report identifies them as unreserved.

They are not automatically database registrations.

items.title: Why does this matter?
items.text:
A prepared job should not be mistaken for an already published and registered dataset.

Registration occurs after successful processing and verification.

items.title: Job Ordering
items.text:
The maintained normalization fixture uses:

{
  "ordering": {
    "primary": "event_timestamp_ns",
    "tie_break": "stream_rank"
  }
}

items.title: Primary ordering
items.text:
"primary": "event_timestamp_ns"

identifies event time as the primary output-ordering field.

items.title: Tie-breaking
items.text:
"tie_break": "stream_rank"

provides an ordering rule for applicable equal-time events.

items.title: Why are tie-breakers necessary?
items.text:
Different streams can contain events with identical timestamps.

For example:

12:00:00.100 BTCUSDT Trade
12:00:00.100 ETHUSDT Trade

A deterministic tie-breaker helps establish a reproducible ordering.

items.title: Does stream rank change timestamps?
items.text:
No.

Stream ranks are ordering metadata.

They do not rewrite event timestamps.

items.title: Can the ordering fields arbitrarily sort depth events?
items.text:
No.

The Engine still applies its source-order, reconciliation, and reconstruction rules.

Stateful depth updates cannot be safely rearranged merely because the batch declares timestamp-based ordering.

The actual physical layout and required reconstruction semantics must remain valid.

items.title: Job Output Configuration
items.text:
Each job identifies its output content type and publication destinations.

Conceptually:

{
  "output": {
    "content_type": "trades",
    "staging_path": "/absolute/path/to/staging",
    "dataset_path": "/absolute/path/to/normalized-publication"
  }
}

This is an illustrative fragment.

items.title: Content type
items.text:
The supported normalization job content types are:

trades
depth

items.title: Staging path
items.text: The Engine writes intermediate publication output to its staging destination.

items.title: Dataset path
items.text: The final destination identifies where the committed publication will be stored.

items.title: Why separate staging and final output?
items.text:
Processing can fail before publication is complete.

For example:

Read Source
    |
    v
Normalize Events
    |
    v
Write Staging Files
    |
    v
Verify Publication
    |
    v
Commit Dataset

The staging directory is not automatically a valid committed publication.

items.title: Does the Engine overwrite existing datasets?
items.text:
The managed workflow uses fresh output destinations.

Existing committed publications should not be silently replaced.

items.title: Why does this matter for recovery?
items.text:
A valid committed publication can sometimes be registered without rerunning the complete normalization workload.

An incomplete staging directory cannot be treated as a completed publication.

items.title: What Is a Task?
items.text:
A task represents concrete source work assigned to a normalization job.

For example:

Task 1:
Read one registered BTCUSDT archive.

Task 2:
Read the next BTCUSDT archive.

Task 3:
Read one ETHUSDT archive.

A task identifies the source and its applicable processing metadata.

items.title: Why use tasks?
items.text:
One job may need to process many archives.

Tasks provide concrete units of source work.

items.title: Does every task correspond to one instrument?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

A concrete instrument task can identify one instrument.

A family-scoped task may refer to source data containing several concrete instruments.

Those cases require different identity-resolution information.

items.title: Task-Level Parameters
items.text:
The prepared normalization contract supports task fields including:

Parameter Meaning task_id Task identifier within the job. input_path Source archive path. exchange Execution venue. instrument_type Financial instrument type. market_category Market classification. base_asset Base asset when applicable. quote_asset Quote asset when applicable. symbol Concrete source instrument symbol when applicable. instrument Concrete economic specification. instrument_id Canonical instrument identity when applicable. stream_id Logical canonical stream identity. stream_rank Stream ordering metadata. scope Optional source-family selection. source_options Supported source interpretation options. instrument_selection Concrete instrument-selection rule.

Some task forms use additional family authority information.

Not every field has the same meaning for concrete instrument and family-scoped tasks.

items.title: Concrete Instrument Task Example
items.text:
The following example illustrates a prepared Bybit BTCUSDT depth task:

{
  "task_id": 15,
  "input_path": "/absolute/path/to/BTCUSDT-depth.zip",
  "exchange": "bybit",
  "instrument_type": "perpetual",
  "market_category": "linear",
  "base_asset": "BTC",
  "quote_asset": "USDT",
  "symbol": "BTCUSDT",
  "instrument": {
    "tick_size": "0.10",
    "contract_value": null,
    "contract_value_asset": null
  },
  "stream_id": "bybit.linear.perpetual.BTCUSDT.depth",
  "stream_rank": 5,
  "instrument_id": 9
}

This is an illustrative task fragment.

The task must still belong to a valid complete batch with the required job, runtime, profile, and authority information.

items.title: What does this identify?
items.text: Field Example Source venue Bybit Instrument BTCUSDT Product Linear perpetual Content Depth Tick size 0.10 Stream ID bybit.linear.perpetual.BTCUSDT.depth Canonical instrument ID 9 Stream rank 5

items.title: Why does this contain more information than the recipe?
items.text:
Because Forge has resolved the concrete source identity.

The recipe only needs to describe the intended market selection.

items.title: Source Paths
items.text:
The prepared task contains:

"input_path": "/absolute/path/to/BTCUSDT-depth.zip"

items.title: Why use a concrete path?
items.text: Rust needs to know which physical managed file to read.

items.title: Does Rust search the exchange archive server?
items.text:
No.

Normalization uses registered raw inputs.

Remote acquisition is handled separately.

items.title: Why not use an arbitrary filename?
items.text:
A filename alone may not identify the correct registered source.

For example, several managed archives may share similar names.

Forge resolves the applicable managed source and its registered metadata.

items.title: Can I replace the path manually?
items.text:
Do not change the path merely to point to another file with a similar name.

The selected file must agree with the registered source identity and applicable preparation evidence.

For ordinary workflows, change the selection recipe or registration and prepare a new batch.

items.title: Why Does the Batch Contain Instrument Definitions?
items.text:
A source archive may contain prices and quantities without all the economic information required to interpret them.

For example:

Price: 80,000
Quantity: 100

For a spot instrument, quantity might represent base units.

For a derivative, it might represent contracts.

The corresponding historical instrument specifications establish the correct interpretation.

items.title: Why include authority in the batch?
items.text:
Rust Engine should not need to guess the economic specifications from the source filename.

Forge resolves the applicable historical evidence and includes the required definitions.

items.title: Instrument definition example
items.text:
{
  "instrument_id": 9,
  "exchange": "bybit",
  "instrument_type": "perpetual",
  "market_category": "linear",
  "symbol": "BTCUSDT",
  "base_asset": "BTC",
  "quote_asset": "USDT",
  "instrument": {
    "tick_size": "0.10",
    "contract_value": null,
    "contract_value_asset": null
  }
}

This is an illustrative definition based on the maintained task structure.

items.title: Why is contract value nullable?
items.text:
Not every instrument requires contract-value interpretation in the same way.

For example, a base-quantity instrument may not use a separate contract multiplier in its applicable definition.

For contract-denominated quantities, the required value and denomination must be available through the supported historical specifications.

items.title: Instrument Namespace
items.text:
The batch includes:

"instrument_namespace": "marketforge:testing:historical:v1"

This identifies the canonical historical instrument namespace.

items.title: Why is a namespace necessary?
items.text:
Numeric instrument IDs are not universally meaningful.

For example:

instrument_id = 9

may identify one instrument in a particular registry namespace.

Another independently managed catalogue could assign the same number to something else.

items.title: What does the namespace establish?
items.text: It identifies the authority under which the instrument IDs were assigned.

items.title: Can I copy numeric IDs between databases?
items.text:
Do not assume numeric IDs are interchangeable between independent registries.

A concrete instrument identity must agree with its namespace and retained authority evidence.

items.title: Does the namespace replace the symbol?
items.text:
No.

The prepared contract retains the relevant instrument information and concrete identifiers.

The namespace helps interpret the authority of those IDs.

items.title: Historical Specifications
items.text:
Prepared tasks can contain the resolved economic specification.

For example:

{
  "tick_size": "0.10",
  "contract_value": "100",
  "contract_value_asset": "USD"
}

This is an illustrative specification.

items.title: Why preserve decimal values as strings?
items.text:
Financial specifications require exact decimal interpretation.

For example:

0.000001

should not be unnecessarily converted into an approximate floating-point value.

items.title: Why does contract denomination matter?
items.text:
Consider:

Contract value: 100 USD

and:

Contract value: 100 BTC

These represent very different economic quantities.

The denomination must be explicit when required.

items.title: Does the prepared batch prove historical correctness?
items.text:
It carries the resolved authority accepted by preparation.

The quality of the historical evidence depends on the applicable catalogue and specification records.

For example, operational inference should not be described as independent historical verification.

items.title: What if specifications conflict?
items.text:
Forge can block preparation when the selected instrument crosses conflicting historical authority evidence.

A processing job should not silently use incompatible specifications for the same selected instrument.

items.title: What Is a Stream?
items.text:
A stream identifies a logical sequence of market-data events.

For example:

bybit.linear.perpetual.BTCUSDT.trades

and:

bybit.linear.perpetual.BTCUSDT.depth

identify different logical content streams.

items.title: Why does this matter?
items.text:
A normalization job can contain several instruments.

The Engine needs to distinguish which stream each event belongs to.

For example:

BTCUSDT Trades
ETHUSDT Trades
SOLUSDT Trades

These should not lose their individual identities merely because they are processed in one batch.

items.title: Is stream_id the same as instrument_id?
items.text:
No.

The instrument ID identifies the financial instrument.

The stream ID identifies the logical market-data stream.

For example, BTCUSDT trades and depth can share one instrument identity while having different stream IDs.

items.title: Stream Ranks
items.text:
The prepared task includes:

"stream_rank": 5

items.title: Why use stream ranks?
items.text:
Several streams may contain events with identical timestamps.

A deterministic ordering contract can use stream ranks when resolving applicable ties.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose a batch contains:

BTCUSDT Trades
ETHUSDT Trades
SOLUSDT Trades

The prepared streams might receive:

BTCUSDT → Rank 1
ETHUSDT → Rank 2
SOLUSDT → Rank 3

items.title: Does a lower rank mean a more important instrument?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

Stream ranks are processing-order metadata.

They can be derived from persisted market ranking positions, but they are not a universal economic priority.

items.title: Do ranks change original timestamps?
items.text: No.

items.title: Do ranks override depth reconstruction?
items.text:
No.

Stateful source-event dependencies remain mandatory.

items.title: Ranking Snapshot Resolution
items.text:
Normalization preparation can use persisted market-ranking information.

For example:

{
  "ranking_policy": "turnover",
  "ranking_snapshot": null
}

items.title: Why include the policy?
items.text: The selected policy identifies the preferred source of stream-ordering evidence.

items.title: What happens when a snapshot exists?
items.text: Forge can use its stored instrument positions when ordering the selected streams.

items.title: Are the stored positions copied directly?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

Forge can assign dense stream ranks to the selected workload.

For example:

Stored ranking positions:

BTCUSDT → 1
ETHUSDT → 4
SOLUSDT → 8

A selected three-stream workload may receive:

BTCUSDT → 1
ETHUSDT → 2
SOLUSDT → 3

The stored positions provide ordering evidence.

The generated ranks describe the selected processing streams.

items.title: What if ranking positions are missing?
items.text: Forge uses deterministic stream identity ordering for the applicable fallback.

items.title: Does preparation build a new market ranking?
items.text:
No.

It uses retained ranking information.

It does not automatically refresh exchange statistics or publish new ranking snapshots.

items.title: What Is a Family Archive?
items.text:
Some providers publish historical data grouped by instrument family.

For example, an OKX futures archive may contain records for several dated contracts.

Conceptually:

BTC Futures Family
        |
        +-- Contract A
        +-- Contract B
        +-- Contract C

The archive path may identify the family rather than one concrete contract.

items.title: Why is this different from an ordinary task?
items.text:
A concrete instrument task identifies one instrument.

A family-scoped task may need to identify several instruments from the source records.

items.title: What does Rust need?
items.text:
It needs enough information to:

  • Identify the source family.
  • Read the native instrument identity.
  • Resolve the concrete instrument.
  • Apply the correct historical specification.
  • Route the event to the appropriate stream.

items.title: Why not assign one instrument ID to the family?
items.text:
Because a family is not necessarily one financial instrument.

Different futures contracts can have different expirations and other instrument-specific properties.

items.title: Family Scope
items.text:
A family-scoped task can describe a native source family.

For example:

{
  "scope": {
    "kind": "family",
    "identifier": "BTC-USD_UM"
  },
  "instrument_selection": {
    "mode": "all"
  }
}

This is a structural fragment.

items.title: What does scope.kind mean?
items.text: It identifies the source selection as a family.

items.title: What does scope.identifier mean?
items.text: It contains the provider-native family identifier.

items.title: Is the family identifier a canonical instrument ID?
items.text:
No.

It is the native source grouping.

Concrete instrument identities must still be resolved.

items.title: Instrument Selection Modes
items.text: The current normalization family-selection contract supports explicit selection behavior.

items.title: All instruments
items.text:
For example:

{
  "instrument_selection": {
    "mode": "all"
  }
}

This selects the supported concrete instruments represented by the applicable family source population.

items.title: Explicit inclusion
items.text:
The contract also supports an include form:

{
  "instrument_selection": {
    "mode": "include",
    "symbols": [
      "BTC-USD-261225"
    ]
  }
}

This illustrates the supported exact-symbol selection structure.

The actual symbol must match the source-native identity.

items.title: Are wildcards supported?
items.text:
Not by the explicit include list.

The symbols must be exact.

items.title: Can the include list be empty?
items.text:
No.

The current parser requires a nonempty list of unique symbols.

items.title: Does selection establish missing instrument metadata?
items.text:
No.

Selecting a symbol does not create its historical specifications.

The concrete authority must already be available.

items.title: Family Parameters
items.text:
The relevant family-processing contract includes information such as:

Parameter Purpose scope.kind Family or concrete source-scope type. scope.identifier Native family identifier. scope.family_id Optional family authority identity. scope.members Concrete family-member bindings where supplied. instrument_selection.mode Selection strategy. instrument_selection.symbols Exact native symbols for supported inclusion. instrument_namespace Canonical identity authority. source_priority Relevant source-precedence information. archive_member Selected archive member where applicable.

items.title: Why is source priority separate from stream rank?
items.text:
Source precedence and stream ordering describe different relationships.

For example:

  • Source precedence can affect reconciliation between overlapping archives.
  • Stream rank can affect ordering between logical streams.

One should not be treated as an automatic replacement for the other.

items.title: Does every family task contain every field?
items.text:
No.

The concrete serialized form depends on the supported family authority and task representation.

Use the current Forge-generated job rather than inventing fields.

items.title: Family Record Routing
items.text:
Rust routes records using their source-native instrument identities.

For example:

Family Archive
      |
      v
Read Native Symbol
      |
      +-- Contract A
      |       |
      |       v
      |   Stream A
      |
      +-- Contract B
      |       |
      |       v
      |   Stream B
      |
      +-- Contract C
              |
              v
          Stream C

items.title: What can happen to a record?
items.text:
A record may be:

Outcome Meaning Routed Native identity resolves to a supported selected instrument. Filtered outside scope Record belongs outside the requested family selection. Filtered unselected Instrument exists but is not selected. Rejected missing identity Native instrument identity is absent. Rejected malformed identity Native identity cannot be interpreted. Rejected missing authority Required concrete instrument metadata is unavailable. Rejected unsupported instrument Source instrument is outside the supported processing contract.

items.title: Why distinguish filtering from rejection?
items.text:
A record outside an explicit selection may be intentionally excluded.

A record whose identity is missing or malformed represents a different problem.

For example, an unknown symbol inside a supposedly selected family may indicate missing historical metadata.

The resulting diagnostics should preserve that distinction.

items.title: Why Family Authority Must Be Complete Enough
items.text:
Family routing requires authoritative concrete instrument metadata.

For example, a futures record may contain:

Symbol: BTC-USD-261225
Quantity: 100 contracts

The Engine needs the applicable contract specifications to interpret that quantity.

items.title: Can Rust infer the multiplier from the filename?
items.text:
No.

The native symbol does not automatically establish contract value.

items.title: Can current metadata always resolve expired futures?
items.text:
No.

Expired contracts may no longer appear in the provider's current catalogue.

items.title: What can MarketForge do?
items.text:
The historical metadata system can retain catalogue, explicit historical, and archive-derived identity evidence.

Where applicable, initialization can perform bounded identity discovery.

However, incomplete authority can still block preparation.

items.title: Important limitation
items.text:
Family routing cannot safely invent missing contract specifications.

This is particularly important for OKX futures-chain archives.

See Historical Metadata Inference.

items.title: Wire types and scope
items.text:
schema_version is uint32 4, kind is normalization_batch and status is prepared. Required strings are run_id, run_directory, batch_path, ranking_policy and instrument_namespace. requested_interval carries start and end strings. ranking_snapshot is optional JSON evidence. instruments and jobs are arrays, and families defaults to an empty array. A job has operation, job_id, dataset_id, tasks, ordering, and output. Job and dataset IDs are positive uint64 JSON integers, each unique within its own domain across a batch.

A task requires a positive uint64 integer task_id, unique within its job. It also requires nonempty input_path, exchange, instrument_type, market_category, nonblank stream_id and uint32 stream_rank. Optional/nullable fields are base_asset, quote_asset, symbol, instrument, instrument_id, scope, source_options, instrument_selection. instrument_id is signed 64-bit and resolves against the batch authority when supplied. source_options.feed is incremental or snapshot. instrument_selection is either {"mode":"all"} or {"mode":"include","symbols":[...]}. With a concrete symbol, omit the selector or include only that exact symbol. Family scope requires a selector and leaves concrete identity fields null. Scope carries kind:"family", identifier, optional family_id, and members defaulting to an empty array. Each explicit member has instrument_id and optional archive_member.

One stream ID maps to one rank and one rank to one stream within a job. Relative paths resolve from the Engine project root. Output destinations cannot overlap or contain parent traversal, and the configuration validation and execution perform further checks. Loader and job resolution are distinct from archive decoding. Production loader

items.title: Prepared Engine contracts
items.text:
Compare editable recipes, generated Engine jobs and retained application evidence at their own boundaries. A structural check, successful execution and committed publication are separate outcomes.

Artifact Producer and reader Normalization batch Forge or a prepared fixture → Rust --batch, schema 4 Merge job Forge or a compatible writer → Rust --job or --validate-job Conversion job Forge or a compatible writer → Rust --job, schema 1 Forge collections and run evidence Forge preparation, execution, recovery and pipeline services

items.title: Merge jobs
items.text:
See prepared merge job for the required file and publication pins.

For output and integrity evidence, use the publication reference.

items.title: Normalization profile field index
items.text: See the authoring guide for working trade and depth examples. Angle brackets mark a key you supply. Empty brackets mark an array item. An optional key is unset when omitted unless a default is listed. A field marked conditional depends on its enclosing table, target or transform. Applicability labels distinguish trade and depth fields. The compiler and reader check the whole combination.

items.title: Identity
items.text:
Schema discriminator, installed identity and inventory-only marker. Match the venue, instrument and market to the catalogue.

Use the filename <id>.toml under the matching trades/ or depth/ directory. Valid market pairs are spot/spot, perpetual or future with linear or inverse, option/option, and equity/equity. A valid identity does not establish reader support.

Field Type and presence Meaning and constraints exchange identifier · required · trades, depth Execution venue code, including manual venues. One to 32 lowercase ASCII letters, digits or underscores, starting with a letter. The reserved code external is rejected. format_code identifier · required · trades, depth Venue and content format identity used by catalogue resolution. Venue uppercase with hyphens in place of underscores. Gate.io uses GATE. Suffix T or B plus a positive decimal integer without leading zero. Must be unambiguous in its venue and market namespace. id identifier · required · trades, depth Exact installed namespace and filename stem. exchange.instrument_type.market_category.trades|depth Must agree with the three identity keys and installed trades/ or depth/ directory. instrument_type enum · required · trades, depth Instrument kind matched by the catalogue and task. "spot" — Spot instrument. "perpetual" — Perpetual contract. "future" — Dated future. "option" — Option contract. "equity" — Cash equity. kind literal · required · trades, depth Document kind. "profile" — Standalone normalization profile. market_category enum · required · trades, depth Market namespace used for matching. "spot" — Spot instruments. "linear" — Linear perpetuals or futures. "inverse" — Inverse perpetuals or futures. "option" — Options. "equity" — Cash equities. schema_version literal · required · trades, depth Authoring schema discriminator. 2 — Current self-contained TOML profile. unsupported_reason string · optional · trades, depth Mark this definition inventory-only with a nonblank reason. Rust checks structure and references but does not enable its processing rules.

items.title: Source
items.text:
Archive wrapper, record representation and source layout.

Read the format and layout rows together. Trades take CSV or JSONL with rows. Depth supports JSONL events and snapshots, specific positional CSV layouts, and a fixed XLSX snapshot layout. Archive members, headers and the selected mappings must match an implemented reader. For XLSX use one header sheet with exactly timestamp, asks and bids, Unix seconds, and common input_ordering = { order = "ascending", sort_by = "timestamp" }.

Field Type and presence Meaning and constraints source table · required · trades, depth Physical input metadata. source.archive_day_boundary enum · optional · trades, depth Descriptive calendar boundary for source packaging, independent of event time. "UTC" — UTC boundary. "UTC+8" — UTC plus eight hours. source.container enum · required · trades, depth Outer wrapper, independent of the inner record representation. "plain" — Uncompressed input. "gzip" — Gzip stream. "zip" — ZIP archive member. "tar_gzip" — Gzip-compressed tar member. source.daily_packaging literal · optional · trades, depth Descriptive daily package shape. "numbered_zip_chunks" — Numbered ZIP chunks. source.format enum · required · trades Physical format decoded after opening the wrapper. "csv" — Comma-separated records. "jsonl" — One JSON value per line. source.format enum · required · depth Physical format decoded after opening the wrapper. "csv" — Comma-separated records. "jsonl" — One JSON value per line. "xlsx" — Excel workbook with the fixed depth layout. source.granularity enum · required · trades, depth Descriptive archive packaging interval, independent of event frequency. "daily" — Daily package. "hourly" — Hourly package. "monthly" — Monthly package. source.header boolean · conditional · trades, depth Whether input has a header row. Required for CSV and XLSX. Must be true for XLSX. Forbidden in JSONL trade profiles. source.maximum_depth_per_side integer · optional · trades, depth Declared maximum levels per side. Positive unsigned 64-bit integer. A bounded_observation must declare the same value in snapshot.levels_per_side. source.ordering enum · required · trades, depth Declared source ordering. "chronological" — Source-ordered input. "timestamp_sortable" — Input that can be sorted by timestamp. "not_chronological" — Alias for timestamp_sortable. source.record_format enum · required · trades Logical grouping of records, independent of the physical format. "rows" — Trade rows. source.record_format enum · required · depth Logical grouping of records, independent of the physical format. "events" — Depth events. "snapshot_rows" — Snapshot rows. "book_rows" — Book rows. source.trade_id_reset_domain string · conditional · trades Nonblank native identifier reset domain. Required for instrument_scoped and ordered_run. Forbidden for other scopes or when scope is omitted. source.trade_id_scope enum · optional · trades Native trade identifier uniqueness policy. "global" — Globally unique native ID. "instrument_scoped" — Unique within an instrument and declared reset domain. "ordered_run" — Decimal IDs in one checked, non-reset ordered stream run. "source_local" — Unique only within a source. "unreliable" — ID has no reliable deduplication contract. Trade-only. Required for XLSX and forbidden otherwise. XLSX requires header=true, timestamp-sortable input, exactly timestamp/asks/bids, Unix seconds, and ascending timestamp sort.

items.title: Fields
items.text:
Replace with a real source column or JSON path. Use [fields."data.ts"] for a dotted raw key. Omit optional TOML keys to leave them unset unless a default is documented.

In executable mappings, field = "size" references the declared [fields.size] key. For nested JSON use a literal dotted key such as [fields."data.ts"] and field = "data.ts". Where listed, source is a compatibility spelling. Prefer field, and use only field for the event timestamp and trade instrument bindings. CSV positions start at one. Level-array indices start at zero. Precision annotations describe the source and encoding selects the decoder.

Field Type and presence Meaning and constraints fields table · required · trades, depth Nonempty map of source names to raw field declarations. fields.<name> table · conditional · trades, depth One literal source column or JSON path. Quote a dotted key in TOML. At least one field is required. fields.<name>.decode literal · optional · trades, depth Encoding of a structured source field. "json" — JSON-encoded cell or value. fields.<name>.encoding enum · conditional · trades, depth Timestamp encoding for a mapped source field. "unix_seconds" — Unix epoch seconds. "unix_milliseconds" — Unix epoch milliseconds. "unix_microseconds" — Unix epoch microseconds. "unix_nanoseconds" — Unix epoch nanoseconds. "iso8601_nanoseconds" — ISO 8601 text with nanosecond precision. Required for each effective event_timestamp field. If either timestamp uses ISO 8601, both mapped timestamps must declare ISO 8601 and type string. fields.<name>.fractional_digits TOML value · optional · trades, depth Descriptive fractional-digit evidence. The compiler does not enforce a digit cap from this key. fields.<name>.level_fields table · optional · trades, depth Object members for a depth level. Use either positional or object level mappings. A mapping-local level_fields table cannot override a raw field's layout. fields.<name>.level_fields.order_count string · optional · trades, depth Optional nonempty order count member in the same object level. fields.<name>.level_fields.price string · conditional · trades, depth Nonempty price member name in an object level. Required when the containing table is used. fields.<name>.level_fields.quantity string · conditional · trades, depth Nonempty quantity member name in an object level. Required when the containing table is used. fields.<name>.level_format array of string · optional · trades, depth Positional depth level layout. Array order defines zero-based indices. Exactly ["price", "quantity"] or ["price", "quantity", "order_count"]. fields.<name>.observed_effective_precision TOML value · optional · trades, depth Descriptive observation of effective precision. fields.<name>.ordering TOML value · optional · trades, depth Descriptive source field ordering. Does not request sorting. fields.<name>.position integer · optional · trades, depth · csv, xlsx One-based source column position. If used, all positions must be contiguous from one and distinct. Not supported for JSONL trades. fields.<name>.precision TOML value · optional · trades, depth Descriptive precision evidence. Does not select a timestamp decoder. fields.<name>.snapshot_precision TOML value · optional · trades, depth Descriptive timestamp precision for snapshots. fields.<name>.type enum · conditional · trades, depth Declared source field representation. "decimal" — Decimal value. "integer" — Integer value. "string" — Text value. "array" — Array. "boolean" — Boolean value. "integer/string" — Integer or text. "uuid/string" — UUID or text. "integer/bool" — Integer or boolean. "string/integer" — Text or integer. "signed_integer" — Signed integer. "signed_decimal" — Signed decimal. Required when the containing table is used. fields.<name>.update_precision TOML value · optional · trades, depth Descriptive timestamp precision for updates. fields.<name>.values TOML value · optional · trades, depth Descriptive observed raw values. A separate mapping defines canonical output.

items.title: Normalization
items.text:
Map raw fields to canonical operations. Use [[normalization.rules]] for multiple targets. Each item inherits common mappings and cannot override a common key.

Use one target or a nonempty [[normalization.rules]] array. Each item has its own target and inherits common mappings without overriding their keys. The tables below show the common paths. Use the same mapping keys within rules where applicable. Keep quantity_encoding, book and the trade instrument binding in common normalization. With depth, use an unsequenced path when both sequence mappings are absent, a consecutive policy with only sequence_start, or a ranged policy with both. All rules in a task must agree. See the bounded-observation exception below.

items.text: Field Type and presence Meaning and constraints normalization.quantity_encoding enum · conditional · trades, depth Select the units recorded by the vendor before canonical conversion. Compare a normalized sample to the raw price and size. "base" — The vendor measures size in units of the underlying asset. "quote" — The vendor measures size in the quote currency. "contracts" — The vendor reports a count of contracts. Requires a compatible derivative instrument. Spot and equity reject it. Required when the containing table is used. normalization.rules array of table · conditional · trades, depth Nonempty array of target-specific rules. No rule key can override a common normalization key. normalization.rules[].target enum · required · trades Canonical operation for a single target or one rule. "trade" — Canonical trade. At normalization level, choose target or a nonempty rules array. Each rule item requires its own target. items.title: Create a normalization profile
items.text: For processing budgets, integrity, and reconciliation, see Normalization runtime configuration.

items.title: What a profile does
items.text:
A profile tells the Rust Engine how to read one source layout and interpret its records as canonical trades or order-book events. Acquisition recipes select what to acquire. Normalization runtime settings control execution. The profile defines what the raw values mean.

A profile ID has four components, exchange.instrument_type.market_category.data_type. The first three match the venue and market, and the final component is trades or depth. Name the file <id>.toml. Installation places it under data/.config/engine/normalize/profiles/trades/ or depth/, according to the suffix. Use the execution venue for data supplied by an external vendor.

items.title: 1. Inspect a small source sample
items.text:
Run from the project root. For example, inspect the bundle’s headerless trade CSV.

mf normalize profiles sample --file docs/content/examples/catalogue/synthetic-trades.csv --no-header | cpout

Pass --header for named CSV columns or --no-header for positional columns. If neither is set, the preview shows the first record as data and marks header status unknown. Use --member to select a stored or deflated ZIP entry. The inspector also accepts plain and gzip-compressed CSV and JSONL. For TAR.GZ and workbook inputs, inspect a small extracted text example or use a workbook viewer.

The Source structure table shows inferred representations, up to three distinct observed examples, and missing counts. JSONL also counts explicit nulls. Arrays stay grouped. Use --fields to skip the record preview or --rows 10 to see more records. Human output defaults to five data records and accepts 1–20, within a 65,536-byte decoded prefix and a 64-field display limit. The sample covers the beginning of the input. It cannot establish total records or whole-file types.

For CSV, use the displayed one-based position when the profile declares positional fields. Resolve duplicate or empty headers before relying on name-based mappings. For nested JSONL, a row labeled data.ts maps to [fields."data.ts"] in TOML. The quotes keep the dotted path as one TOML key, and the Engine follows the nested JSON components. A literal JSON key named "data.ts" is ambiguous for this lookup and is omitted. Suggested types reflect the observed values. Choose actual field types and encodings using the source specification, then use mf normalize profiles new PROFILE_ID and mf normalize profiles validate --file PATH.

Write down the source facts before choosing mappings.

Check What to establish Packaging and layout Outer wrapper, inner file type, and how records are organized. Identify the real header, column positions, JSON paths, or worksheet columns. Time and order Confirm the timestamp unit or text encoding, and whether file order must be preserved. Price, size and side Identify the relevant fields, whether size is in base units, quote units or contracts, and what side tokens or signs mean. Depth events Find the initialization snapshot and subsequent updates. Confirm how to distinguish them, whether updates replace or change quantities, what zero means, and whether sequence numbers carry continuity guarantees.

A sample shows the shape and actual values. Use the vendor’s specification to confirm facts the sample cannot establish, such as quantity units or sequence resets. Then choose which raw fields will supply each canonical value.

items.title: 2. Create a trade profile
items.text:
The fictional source below has one execution with four columns and no header.

1730125800000000000,233.62,10,B

Save this complete definition as example_exchange.equity.equity.trades.toml, or copy the example profile.

schema_version = 2
kind = "profile"
id = "example_exchange.equity.equity.trades"
format_code = "EXAMPLE-EXCHANGE-T1"
exchange = "example_exchange"
instrument_type = "equity"
market_category = "equity"

[source]
container = "plain"
format = "csv"
record_format = "rows"
header = false
