Unreadable artifacts and unsupported versions appear in catalog.diagnostics. Bare Parquet can be discovered with missing-identity diagnostics. To include registry IDs, supply file summaries with distinct absolute storage_path values and a nonempty registry_context. Discovery does not connect to PostgreSQL. Invalid scope or registry arguments raise ValueError. datasets returns the corresponding discovery summary table.

from forge.datasets import MarketData

catalog = MarketData().discover()
print(catalog.overview())

items.title: DatasetCatalog
items.text:
A catalog supports iteration, length, integer indexing, and slicing. An integer index yields a Dataset. Slicing retains catalog context. one() -> Dataset raises ValueError unless exactly one file matches. records() -> list[dict[str, object]] returns file metadata records. summary() -> pl.DataFrame returns a display table, and overview() -> dict[str, Any] includes aggregate metadata and diagnostics.

Text = str | Sequence[str]
IDs = int | Sequence[int]
Moment = int | str | datetime
Paths = str | Path | Sequence[str | Path]

find(
    *,
    exchange: Text | None = None, symbol: Text | None = None,
    symbol_match: Literal["exact", "contains"] = "exact",
    instrument_id: IDs | None = None, instrument_namespace: Text | None = None,
    instrument_type: Text | None = None, market_category: Text | None = None,
    data_type: Text | None = None, stream_id: Text | None = None,
    fingerprint: Text | None = None, operation: Text | None = None,
    publication_id: IDs | None = None, publication_path: Paths | None = None,
    engine_publication_id: int | Text | None = None, dataset_id: IDs | None = None,
    path: Paths | None = None, min_rows: int | None = None, max_rows: int | None = None,
    min_bytes: int | None = None, max_bytes: int | None = None,
    start: Moment | None = None, end: Moment | None = None,
    interval: Literal["overlap", "envelope_contained"] = "overlap",
    status: Text | None = None, integrity: Text | None = None,
) -> DatasetCatalog

Filters compose with AND. Alternatives within one filter compose with OR. Market selectors must match the same membership inside a candidate file. File-size and row-count filters apply to complete primary files. Time filters use observed metadata envelopes with a half-open query interval. Unknown endpoints cannot establish a match. Neither interval mode establishes continuous coverage. A file can match several logical streams. Finding a file does not change which rows a Dataset reads. Registry publication, Engine publication and file dataset IDs have separate namespaces.

files = catalog.find(exchange="bybit", symbol="BTCUSDT",
                     instrument_type="perpetual", data_type="trades")

items.title: Dataset and Stream
items.text:
Dataset.info() -> dict[str, Any]
Dataset.streams() -> pl.DataFrame
Dataset.select(*, stream_id: str | None = None, exchange: str | None = None,
               symbol: str | None = None, kind: str | None = None,
               fingerprint: str | None = None, instrument_id: int | None = None,
               instrument_type: str | None = None,
               market_category: str | None = None) -> Stream
Dataset.trades(**filters: Any) -> Stream
Stream.info() -> dict[str, Any]
Stream.membership() -> dict[str, object]

info reports metadata, including observed extents and their evidence. streams lists verified memberships. select requires exactly one logical stream and raises ValueError for zero or competing matches. trades calls the trade-kind selector. Logical stream counters may be unavailable when evidence does not establish them. An observed envelope or row count does not imply source continuity.

trade_stream = files[0].trades(exchange="bybit", symbol="BTCUSDT")
print(trade_stream.info())

items.title: Record readers
items.text:
The following methods are shared by Dataset and Stream.

schema() -> pa.Schema
head(n: int = 10, *, columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
     start: Moment | None = None, end: Moment | None = None,
     time_field: str = "event_timestamp_ns",
     input_rows: int | None = None) -> pl.DataFrame
batches(*, columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, batch_size: int = 65_536,
        start: Moment | None = None, end: Moment | None = None,
        time_field: str = "event_timestamp_ns",
        input_rows: int | None = None) -> Iterator[pa.RecordBatch]
scan(*, columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, start: Moment | None = None,
     end: Moment | None = None,
     time_field: str = "event_timestamp_ns") -> pl.LazyFrame

Use Arrow batches when preserving typed Decimal256 and nanosecond values. head represents Decimal256 as exact strings, including in nested data. scan requires an explicitly compatible projection when the schema includes unsupported Decimal256 columns. Time bounds are inclusive start and exclusive end, and accept Unix nanosecond integers, ISO strings and aware datetimes. Use integer or ISO nanosecond bounds for sub-microsecond precision. Projected columns must exist. Timestamp and column constraints raise ValueError when rejected by Forge. Parquet readers can also raise I/O or backend errors.

n limits matching preview rows delivered to the caller. input_rows limits the physical prefix inspected before row predicates. batch_size is an Arrow batch row limit. These limits do not cap byte I/O. Readers traverse physical order, including causal order where applicable. Lazy collection uses Polars and follows the requested query plan. A selected stream applies its membership predicate. A plain file handle reads all member streams.

for batch in trade_stream.batches(columns=["event_timestamp_ns"], batch_size=512):
    print(batch.schema)
    break

items.title: Inspection helpers
items.text:
from forge.lab.inspection import compare, inspect
# inspect(target: Dataset | Stream | str | Path) -> Inspection
# compare(*targets: Dataset | Stream) -> dict[str, object]

Inspection.schema() returns the Arrow schema. columns(), row_groups(), and timestamps() return lists of metadata records. summary() -> dict[str, object] combines inspection evidence. profile(columns: Sequence[str], *, input_rows: int = 1000) -> dict[str, object] reads a physical prefix and reports sampled values. Sampling limits do not establish properties of unread rows. compare compares artifact metadata, including schema and time evidence, without a row-by-row diff.

view = inspect(trade_stream)
print(view.timestamps())

items.title: Managed raw registration declarations
items.text: Schemas, identity requirements and plan checks for managed raw registration. See Register external recordings for the procedure and Import, profile and registration commands for flags.

items.title: Registration Metadata Fields
items.text: Field Required Type / constraint registration.version Yes Integer 1 registration.name Yes Nonempty string

items.title: Important rules
items.text:
The version must be exactly 1.

The name must be nonempty.

The registration metadata identifies the declaration, not the source-provider product or instrument.

items.title: Source Fields
items.text: Field Required Type / constraint source.key Yes Nonempty string source.provider Yes Nonempty string source.product Yes Nonempty string source.root Yes Nonempty path string source.provenance Yes Nonempty string source.kind No recording, purchased, other; default recording

items.title: Important rules
items.text:
Relative roots resolve against the project root.

Source-key reuse requires a compatible retained source identity.

Provider, product, and provenance should describe the actual source.

The provider and execution venue are separate concepts.

items.title: Coverage Fields
items.text: Field Required Type / constraint coverage.start Yes Timezone-aware TOML datetime coverage.end Yes Timezone-aware TOML datetime later than start

items.title: Important rules
items.text:
The interval is half-open:

[start, end)

It applies to every input in the recipe.

The declared coverage is not independently inferred from all source records.

Historical specification evidence must be applicable to the interval.

items.title: Input Fields
items.text: Field Required Type / constraint inputs.instrument Yes Concrete catalogue instrument reference inputs.profile Yes Matching four-component profile ID inputs.content Yes trades or depth inputs.files Conditional List of root-relative paths inputs.patterns Conditional List of root-relative patterns inputs.max_files No Integer 1–10000; default 1000 inputs.specification No Exactly 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters inputs.native_identity No Complete native identity table

items.title: Important rules
items.text:
At least one nonempty file or pattern selection is required.

The profile must match the instrument's venue, type, category, and selected content.

The input must resolve to a registered concrete instrument.

The selected files must be valid local managed-copy candidates.

Duplicate physical files within the recipe are rejected.

items.title: Native Identity Fields
items.text: Field Required when table present Type / constraint inputs.native_identity.namespace Yes Nonempty string inputs.native_identity.publisher_field Yes Nonempty string inputs.native_identity.publisher_id Yes Nonnegative strict integer inputs.native_identity.instrument_field Yes Nonempty string inputs.native_identity.instrument_id Yes Nonnegative strict integer inputs.native_identity.provenance Yes Nonempty string

items.title: Important rules
items.text:
Publisher and instrument field names must be different.

Numeric IDs must not be negative.

The namespace identifies the source-native scope.

Native instrument IDs are not canonical MarketForge instrument IDs.

The selected source must support the corresponding bounded identity checks.

items.title: Where Registration Recipes Are Stored
items.text:
Managed registration recipes live under:

data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/import/registration/

For example:

data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/import/registration/
├── synthetic-equity.toml
├── databento-aapl.toml
├── private-recorder.toml
└── purchased-data.toml

These names are illustrative.

items.title: Create a managed recipe
items.text:
You can create one from an existing TOML declaration.

For example:

mf acquisition register new synthetic-equity \
    --from docs/content/examples/catalogue/registration.toml

This creates a managed copy of the supplied recipe.

items.title: Does new overwrite an existing recipe?
items.text:
No.

The destination must be new.

The command refuses to overwrite an existing file.

items.title: Create a starter from a directory
items.text:
You can also create an incomplete draft from an existing source directory.

For example:

mf acquisition register new private-recorder \
    --from ./recordings

The command creates a starter declaration.

You must supply the missing identity, provenance, coverage, and input information.

items.title: Edit the recipe
items.text:
Use:

nvim data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/import/registration/synthetic-equity.toml

Or use the configured editor:

mf acquisition register edit synthetic-equity

The editor command inspects the saved declaration after editing.

items.title: Can I use an explicit path?
items.text:
Yes.

Registration commands accept managed names or explicit paths.

For example:

mf acquisition register inspect \
    docs/content/examples/catalogue/registration.toml

Use a path containing a directory component when referring to an explicit file.

items.title: The Four Main Sections
items.text:
A managed registration recipe uses version 1 of its TOML contract.

The main sections are:

Section Purpose [registration] Identifies the registration declaration. [source] Describes the external source and its provenance. [coverage] Declares the historical interval represented by the inputs. [[inputs]] Binds selected files to instruments, profiles, and specification evidence.

An input can also contain an optional native identity declaration:

[inputs.native_identity]

items.title: Overall structure
items.text:
Registration Recipe
        |
        +-- Registration Identity
        |
        +-- Source Provenance
        |
        +-- Historical Coverage
        |
        +-- Input 1
        |      |
        |      +-- Instrument
        |      +-- Profile
        |      +-- Content Type
        |      +-- Files / Patterns
        |      +-- Optional Specification Fingerprint
        |      +-- Optional Native Identity
        |
        +-- Input 2
               |
               +-- Instrument
               +-- Profile
               +-- Content Type
               +-- Files / Patterns

The recipe must contain at least one input.

Each input identifies a concrete registered instrument.

items.title: The [registration] Section
items.text:
Every recipe requires:

[registration]
version = 1
name = "synthetic-equity"

items.title: Version
items.text:
The required version is:

version = 1

The current managed registration schema supports only version 1.

Unlike some other MarketForge configuration formats, this field is required.

items.title: Name
items.text:
The name identifies the registration declaration.

For example:

name = "synthetic-equity"

It must be a nonempty string.

items.title: Why does registration have its own identity?
items.text:
A source collection may participate in several operations.

The registration name describes the particular declaration used to bind its files.

This helps distinguish the managed recipe from the source collection itself.

items.title: Is the registration name the same as the source key?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

For example:

[registration]
name = "aapl-october"

[source]
key = "databento-xnas-itch-aapl-20241028"

The registration name identifies the declaration.

The source key identifies the retained source collection.

For small examples, the two values may be identical.

items.title: The [source] Section
items.text:
The source section describes where the files came from.

For example:

[source]
key = "synthetic-equity"
provider = "example_recorder"
product = "synthetic_csv_and_jsonl"
kind = "recording"
root = "docs/content/examples/catalogue"
provenance = "Two synthetic example records with explicitly assigned semantics"

items.title: Why is source provenance necessary?
items.text:
Imagine two providers supply historical trades for the same market.

For example:

Provider A:
AAPL Trades

Provider B:
AAPL Trades

Both may describe Nasdaq executions.

However, their recordings can differ in:

  • Coverage.
  • Record format.
  • Source timestamps.
  • Native identifiers.
  • Data quality.
  • Processing history.

MarketForge should preserve the distinction between the providers.

The source declaration supplies this information.

items.title: Source Key
items.text:
The required source key is:

key = "synthetic-equity"

It identifies the source collection.

items.title: Why use a stable key?
items.text:
The registry associates source information with the declared key.

Repeating registration can reuse compatible previously registered source information.

However, the same key must not silently change meaning.

items.title: What should a key identify?
items.text:
Ideally, a key identifies one stable source collection.

For example:

databento-xnas-itch-aapl-20241028

is more descriptive than:

data

items.title: Can a source key be reused?
items.text:
Yes, when the registered source identity remains compatible.

For example, repeating the same registration can reuse the source key and verified managed files.

items.title: Can the same key point to another directory?
items.text:
Not arbitrarily.

The registration service checks the source root and source kind.

It also checks retained provider, product, and provenance information.

Conflicting reuse can be rejected.

items.title: Why?
items.text:
A stable source key should not silently become an unrelated dataset.

That would make source provenance difficult to trust.

items.title: Provider
items.text:
The provider field identifies who supplied the data.

For example:

provider = "Databento"

items.title: Why is provider separate from exchange?
items.text:
Because a market-data provider is not necessarily the execution venue.

For example:

Provider:
Databento

Execution venue:
Nasdaq

Instrument:
AAPL

The provider distributes the recording.

The venue identifies where trading occurred.

items.title: What happens if I confuse them?
items.text:
You could register the recording under the wrong market identity.

For example, assigning Nasdaq executions to a fictional Databento execution venue would be incorrect.

Use the actual catalogue exchange for the instrument.

items.title: Does provider need to match a built-in acquisition adapter?
items.text:
No.

An external provider may be any appropriately identified source organization or recording system.

The registered instrument must still use the correct execution venue.

items.title: Product
items.text:
The required product field identifies the source dataset or product.

For example:

product = "XNAS.ITCH"

items.title: Why preserve the product?
items.text:
A provider may distribute several different datasets.

For example:

Trades
Order-book depth
Different market feeds
Different publishers
Different archive products

These products may use different formats and source identifiers.

Recording the product helps distinguish them.

items.title: Is product the same as a normalization profile?
items.text:
No.

The product describes the provider's source offering.

The profile describes how MarketForge interprets the source records.

For example:

Provider product:
XNAS.ITCH

Profile:
xnas.equity.equity.trades

These are related, but they are not interchangeable.

items.title: Source Kind
items.text:
The source section supports:

kind = "recording"

The accepted values are:

Value Meaning recording Data captured or recorded by a system. purchased Data obtained as a purchased dataset. other Another explicitly identified source type.

The default is:

recording

items.title: Why record source kind?
items.text:
It helps distinguish different acquisition origins.

For example, a file purchased from a vendor and a file captured by your own software may require different provenance explanations.

items.title: Does source kind change the execution venue?
items.text:
No.

It describes how the data was obtained.

The execution venue remains part of the instrument identity.

items.title: Does purchased automatically verify the data?
items.text:
No.

Source kind is provenance metadata.

It does not establish the correctness or completeness of the recording.

items.title: Source Root
items.text:
The required root field identifies the directory containing the files.

For example:

root = "docs/content/examples/catalogue"

items.title: How are relative roots resolved?
items.text:
For managed registration recipes, relative source roots resolve against the MarketForge project root.

For example, suppose the checkout is:

/home/user/projects/marketforge/

Then:

root = "docs/content/examples/catalogue"

resolves to:

/home/user/projects/marketforge/docs/content/examples/catalogue/

items.title: Does the working directory matter?
items.text:
Not for this relative-root resolution.

The registration service resolves the source root against the project root rather than using the current invocation directory.

items.title: Why is this useful?
items.text: It makes the recipe more predictable when invoked from different shell directories.

items.title: Can I use an absolute root?
items.text:
Yes.

For example:

root = "/mnt/market-data/recordings"

This identifies an absolute source location.

items.title: Should I use relative or absolute paths?
items.text:
Repository-relative roots are convenient for examples and files stored within the checkout.

Absolute roots may be appropriate for large external recordings stored on separate disks.

The choice depends on your source layout.

items.title: Important distinction
items.text:
The legacy raw-only import configuration resolves relative roots differently.

Its relative root is interpreted from the command working directory.

Do not assume that import and registration use identical path-resolution rules.

items.title: Provenance
items.text:
The required provenance field describes the origin of the source.

For example:

provenance = "User-supplied Databento XNAS.ITCH recording for 2024-10-28"

items.title: Why is a provenance description useful?
items.text:
A source key and provider name may not explain everything about a recording.

For example, you may want to preserve:

  • How the dataset was obtained.
  • Which product it came from.
  • The original recording date.
  • Whether files were manually exported.
  • Known provider-specific information.
  • Important interpretation assumptions.

items.title: What should provenance contain?
items.text:
Supply a factual description supported by the source.

For example:

provenance = "Trades and MBP-10 JSONL exports supplied by Databento for AAPL on 2024-10-28"

items.title: Does provenance prove the source is correct?
items.text:
No.

It records the declared origin information.

The correctness of the source identity remains the responsibility of the declaration and its supporting evidence.

items.title: Why not leave provenance empty?
items.text:
The schema requires a nonempty string.

A meaningful description also makes later investigation easier.

items.title: The [coverage] Section
items.text:
Every managed registration recipe requires a historical coverage interval.

For example:

[coverage]
start = 2024-10-28T00:00:00Z
end = 2024-10-29T00:00:00Z

This declares the historical period represented by the selected files.

items.title: Why is coverage required?
items.text:
MarketForge needs to know when the registered source applies.

The interval is used when resolving historical specification evidence and preparing the source for later processing.

items.title: Does the interval apply to every input?
items.text:
Yes.

The top-level coverage interval applies to all inputs in the recipe.

items.title: What if trades and depth cover different periods?
items.text:
The current managed registration recipe uses one shared interval.

If independently different coverage declarations are required, create separate recipes with the appropriate intervals.

Do not declare a misleading shared interval merely to combine unrelated recordings.

items.title: Half-Open Coverage Intervals
items.text:
Registration uses a half-open interval:

[start, end)

The start is included.

The end is excluded.

items.title: Example
items.text:
[coverage]
start = 2024-10-28T14:30:00Z
end = 2024-10-28T14:40:00Z

This declares ten minutes of source coverage.

The requested interval includes:

14:30:00

but excludes:

14:40:00

items.title: Why use half-open intervals?
items.text:
They make adjacent intervals easier to express.

For example:

Recording A:
[14:30, 14:40)

Recording B:
[14:40, 14:50)

The declared intervals meet at the same boundary.

items.title: Does the end need to be later?
items.text:
Yes.

An empty or reversed interval fails validation.

items.title: Are timezones required?
items.text:
Yes.

The timestamps must be timezone-aware TOML datetimes.

For example:

start = 2024-10-28T14:30:00Z

The Z indicates UTC.

items.title: Declared Coverage vs. Observed Events
items.text:
This is an important distinction.

The coverage section is a declaration, not a measurement of every event inside the file.

For example, a registration may declare:

14:30 ───────────────── 14:40

However, the recording might contain events only at:

14:30:01
14:35:00
14:39:58

The declaration does not prove that every possible market event exists between those timestamps.

items.title: Why not infer coverage from the filename?
items.text:
Because filenames do not necessarily describe the exact event interval.

For example:

AAPL_2024-10-28.jsonl

might contain:

  • One complete trading day.
  • Only regular trading hours.
  • A short recording.
  • A filtered subset of events.

The actual source provenance must establish the declared coverage.

items.title: Does registration verify every timestamp?
items.text:
No.

Registration performs bounded source-layout checks and the relevant metadata validation.

It does not normalize every record simply to establish observed timestamp coverage.

items.title: When are actual timestamps inspected?
items.text:
Normalization processes the source records and records the applicable observed bounds and integrity evidence.

Dataset inspection can then show the observed timestamps of the generated Parquet files.

items.title: Why Historical Specifications Must Cover the Interval
items.text:
Registration requires applicable historical instrument specifications.

For example, the AAPL source needs the relevant equity specifications covering the declared recording period.

items.title: Why?
items.text:
MarketForge must know the economic rules used to interpret the source.

For example:

  • Quantity type.
  • Tick size.
  • Base and quote assets.
  • Contract value when applicable.
  • Other required specifications.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose the registration covers:

2024-10-28 14:30 ─── 14:40

The selected historical specification evidence must cover that interval.

items.title: What happens if it covers only part?
items.text:
Registration can reject the binding.

For example:

Registration:
14:30 ───────────── 14:40

Specification:
14:35 ───────────── 14:40

The specification does not cover the complete declared interval.

items.title: Does a current specification automatically qualify?
items.text:
No.

The current registration workflow requires applicable explicit historical specification evidence.

A current catalogue observation or operationally inferred specification is not automatically an acceptable substitute.

This is stricter than merely having a current instrument record.

items.title: What kind of evidence is accepted?
items.text:
The registration preflight uses the supported explicit historical evidence categories, including:

historical_declaration
historically_verified

These must be applicable to the complete registered interval.

For ordinary catalogue preparation, follow the supported historical specification declaration workflow.

See Historical Specifications.

items.title: The [[inputs]] Array
items.text:
Each registration recipe must contain at least one input.

An input identifies a set of source files and the interpretation required for them.

For example:

[[inputs]]
instrument = "example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL"
profile = "example_exchange.equity.equity.trades"
content = "trades"
files = ["synthetic-trades.csv"]

items.title: What does this describe?
items.text:
It declares:

Instrument:
AAPL

Content:
Trades

Profile:
Example Exchange Equity Trades

Source file:
synthetic-trades.csv

items.title: Why use an array?
items.text:
A registration recipe may contain several related inputs.

For example:

AAPL Trades
AAPL Depth

Each input has its own content type, profile, and file selection.

items.title: Can one input select several files?
items.text:
Yes.

A single input may select multiple files when they share the declared instrument and interpretation.

items.title: Can one recipe contain several instruments?
items.text:
Yes.

Each input can declare a different concrete instrument, provided the applicable catalogue, profile, and historical evidence requirements are satisfied.

items.title: Instrument Reference
items.text:
Every input requires:

instrument = "example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL"

This is a concrete catalogue instrument reference.

items.title: Reference format
items.text:
The required structure is:

exchange.instrument_type.market_category.symbol

For example:

example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL

Another example:

bybit.perpetual.linear.BTCUSDT

items.title: Why use the complete reference?
items.text:
A symbol alone may be ambiguous.

For example:

BTCUSDT

might refer to spot or perpetual trading.

The complete reference preserves the market identity.

items.title: Is this the same as an acquisition scope?
items.text:
No.

Acquisition scopes use source-native archive selectors.

For example:

BTCUSDT

or:

BTC-USD

Registration uses the canonical catalogue reference.

items.title: Does the instrument need to exist?
items.text:
Yes.

Registration preflight resolves the declared instrument against the testing catalogue.

A syntactically valid reference is not sufficient.

The corresponding registered instrument must exist and agree with the historical identity authority.

items.title: Can I use a family reference?
items.text:
No.

The managed registration contract requires a concrete instrument reference.

It does not use an arbitrary family name in place of an instrument.

items.title: Profile Reference
items.text:
Every input requires:

profile = "example_exchange.equity.equity.trades"

This identifies the installed normalization profile.

items.title: Why is the profile necessary?
items.text:
The source file may use its own timestamp, quantity, and event format.

The profile describes how Rust interprets those fields.

items.title: Profile ID format
items.text:
A profile ID has exactly four components:

exchange.instrument_type.market_category.content

The content must be:

trades
depth

items.title: Why must the profile match the instrument?
items.text:
The selected profile must agree with the instrument's exchange, instrument type, and market category.

For example:

instrument = "example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL"
profile = "example_exchange.equity.equity.trades"
content = "trades"

is consistent.

items.title: Invalid example
items.text:
instrument = "example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL"
profile = "bybit.perpetual.linear.trades"
content = "trades"

The profile describes another exchange and market type.

The registration model rejects the mismatch.

items.title: Does a matching ID prove profile validity?
items.text:
No.

Registration also checks that the profile is installed and accepted by the Rust compiler.

A correctly named but invalid profile is not sufficient.

items.title: Content Type
items.text:
Every input requires:

content = "trades"

or:

content = "depth"

items.title: Trades
items.text:
Use:

content = "trades"

for executed-trade recordings.

items.title: Depth
items.text:
Use:

content = "depth"

for supported L2 order-book recordings.

items.title: Why is the name depth used here?
items.text:
Different MarketForge interfaces use related but distinct content names.

Interface Trades L2 order book Acquisition recipe trades order_book_l2 Registration recipe trades depth Profile ID trades depth Normalization recipe trades order_book_l2

Use the values accepted by the relevant schema.

items.title: Does one input support both types?
items.text:
No.

Each input declares one content type.

To register both trades and depth, use two input entries.

items.title: Profile and Specification Compatibility
items.text:
Registration does more than check profile names.

It also checks whether the profile's quantity interpretation agrees with the applicable historical specification.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose the installed trade profile declares:

[normalization]
target = "trade"
quantity_encoding = "base"

The historical instrument specification declares:

quantity_type = "base"

These interpretations agree.

items.title: Conflicting example
items.text:
The profile declares:

quantity_encoding = "contracts"

but the historical specification declares:

quantity_type = "base"

The interpretations disagree.

Registration rejects this conflict.

items.title: Why is this necessary?
items.text:
The source quantity cannot simultaneously be interpreted as base units and contract counts under the same binding.

Allowing the mismatch could produce incorrect normalized quantities.

items.title: Can I change the specification to make validation pass?
items.text:
Only when the new value is supported by actual historical evidence.

Do not alter the quantity type merely to satisfy the validator.

items.title: Can I change the profile instead?
items.text:
Only when the source format actually uses the revised quantity encoding.

The correct solution depends on the real source semantics.

items.title: Explicit File Selection
items.text:
Each input can list its source files explicitly.

For example:

files = ["synthetic-trades.csv"]

items.title: How are paths resolved?
items.text:
The filenames are relative to the declared source root.

For example:

[source]
root = "docs/content/examples/catalogue"

combined with:

files = ["synthetic-trades.csv"]

selects:

docs/content/examples/catalogue/synthetic-trades.csv

relative to the project root.

items.title: Multiple files
items.text:
For example:

files = [
    "trades-2024-10-28.csv",
    "trades-2024-10-29.csv",
    "trades-2024-10-30.csv",
]

This can be useful when several recordings share the same market identity and source interpretation.

items.title: Why use explicit filenames?
items.text:
Explicit selection is appropriate when:

  • You know the exact files.
  • The source directory contains unrelated data.
  • You want to avoid broad pattern matching.
  • You are registering a small research example.
  • You need reproducible input selection.

items.title: Pattern-Based Selection
items.text:
The registration schema also supports file patterns.

For example:

patterns = ["trades-*.csv"]

This can select several matching files beneath the source root.

items.title: Why use patterns?
items.text:
Suppose your directory contains:

recordings/
├── trades-2024-10-28.csv
├── trades-2024-10-29.csv
├── trades-2024-10-30.csv
└── notes.txt

A pattern such as:

patterns = ["trades-*.csv"]

can select the trade recordings without selecting the notes file.

items.title: Recursive selection
items.text:
The underlying source-file selection supports bounded recursive pattern matching.

For example:

patterns = ["**/*.csv"]

can select matching files in nested directories.

items.title: Why be careful with recursive patterns?
items.text:
A broad pattern may select files from several instruments or source formats.

For example:

recordings/
├── BTCUSDT/
└── ETHUSDT/

If one input declares BTCUSDT but recursively selects both directories, the source identity would be incorrect for some files.

Use appropriately narrow patterns.

items.title: Can I combine files and patterns?
items.text:
Yes.

For example:

files = ["special-recording.csv"]
patterns = ["trades-*.csv"]

The resulting selection is resolved through the supported input enumeration logic.

items.title: What if neither is supplied?
items.text:
The recipe is invalid.

Each input must supply at least one nonempty selection.

items.title: File Selection Limits
items.text:
Each input supports:

max_files = 1000

The accepted range is:

1–10000

The default is:

1000

items.title: Why limit file selection?
items.text:
A broad pattern could accidentally select thousands of files.

The limit prevents unexpectedly large registration selections.

items.title: Is the limit per recipe?
items.text:
The max_files field belongs to each input selection.

A recipe can contain several inputs with their own limits.

items.title: Does this limit file size?
items.text:
No.

It limits the number of selected files.

A single large recording can still require substantial storage.

items.title: Does the input selection have other bounds?
items.text:
Yes.

The shared source-selection implementation also bounds recursive traversal.

For example, pattern expansion stops after inspecting too many filesystem entries.

This prevents unbounded source-directory scanning.

items.title: What if the limit is exceeded?
items.text:
Registration rejects the selection.

Narrow the pattern or adjust the limit deliberately.

items.title: Deterministic Selection
items.text: MarketForge resolves selected input files into a deterministic order.

items.title: Why is this important?
items.text:
Suppose a pattern selects:

trades-2024-10-28.csv
trades-2024-10-29.csv
trades-2024-10-30.csv

The registration operation should not depend on incidental filesystem enumeration order.

Deterministic selection helps make the registered input inventory traceable.

items.title: Does deterministic enumeration mean chronological processing?
items.text:
No.

The sorted file selection is an input-inventory property.

Actual event ordering depends on the source profile and Rust normalization contract.

For example, a file with a lexically later name may contain events with earlier timestamps.

Do not use filename sorting as a substitute for source-ordering evidence.

items.title: Duplicate Physical Inputs
items.text: The registration workflow rejects duplicate physical source files within the selected recipe.

items.title: Why?
items.text:
Imagine the same file is selected twice:

files = ["trades.csv"]
patterns = ["*.csv"]

The overlapping selections may resolve to the same physical file.

Registering it twice would create ambiguous input ownership.

items.title: What does MarketForge compare?
items.text:
Registration inspection tracks the physical source identity using filesystem information.

It checks the selected files across input groups.

items.title: Why is this stronger than comparing filenames?
items.text:
Two paths can refer to the same physical file.

For example, hard links can provide different names for one underlying file.

A filename-only check would not reliably detect that situation.

items.title: What happens if a duplicate is found?
items.text:
The registration operation fails.

Remove the duplicate selection.

items.title: Can one file legitimately contain several instruments?
items.text:
Some source formats can contain multiple instrument identities.

However, the current managed registration selection still rejects duplicate physical inputs within one recipe.

For mixed-instrument sources, use the supported source-specific registration and normalization contracts rather than listing the same physical file repeatedly under different input groups.

items.title: Source Symlinks and Path Safety
items.text: Registration inherits the shared external-input path safety rules.

items.title: Root-relative selections
items.text: Individual file entries must remain beneath the declared source root.

items.title: Parent traversal
items.text:
Selections such as:

../other-recordings/trades.csv

are rejected.

items.title: Absolute file entries
items.text:
Individual file selectors must be root-relative.

Use source.root to specify an absolute source directory when necessary.

items.title: Symlinks
items.text:
Selected source symlink files are not accepted as managed-copy inputs.

Recursive enumeration does not follow symlinked source directories.

items.title: Why enforce these rules?
items.text:
The registration operation must know exactly which physical files belong to the declared source.

Unexpected path traversal or symlink resolution could select data outside the intended collection.

These checks protect the integrity of the frozen input inventory.

items.title: What Is inputs.specification?
items.text:
An input can optionally pin a particular historical specification fingerprint.

For example:

specification = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"

This is a syntactically valid illustrative fingerprint.

It is not a real specification fingerprint from the MarketForge registry.

items.title: Why use a fingerprint?
items.text:
A registered instrument may have several historical specification evidence records.

For example, different observations or historical declarations may describe different periods.

You may want to explicitly identify the evidence used for registration.

items.title: What does the fingerprint pin?
items.text: It identifies the exact applicable historical specification evidence selected for the input.

items.title: Required format
items.text:
The value must contain exactly:

64 lowercase hexadecimal characters

This corresponds to a SHA-256-style hexadecimal fingerprint.

items.title: Are uppercase hexadecimal characters accepted?
items.text:
Not by the current field pattern.

Use lowercase hexadecimal.

items.title: Does the fingerprint replace the instrument reference?
items.text:
No.

The input still requires a concrete registered instrument.

items.title: Does it replace coverage validation?
items.text:
No.

The selected specification must still be applicable to the complete declared coverage interval.

items.title: Is the field required?
items.text:
No.

It is optional.

When omitted, the registration service resolves the applicable explicit historical specification evidence through its supported authority rules.

items.title: When should I supply it?
items.text:
Use it when you need to pin a particular known historical declaration or verified evidence record.

For example, it may be useful when several specification revisions exist.

items.title: Why not invent a fingerprint?
items.text:
Because the fingerprint identifies registered evidence.

An arbitrary 64-character hexadecimal string does not create a valid specification.

items.title: How Registration Resolves Historical Specifications
items.text:
During registration validation, Forge resolves historical specification evidence for the selected instrument.

The process includes:

Registered Instrument
        |
        v
Historical Authority
        |
        v
Applicable Explicit Evidence
        |
        v
Optional Fingerprint Match
        |
        v
Historical Specification

items.title: What happens if no applicable evidence exists?
items.text: Registration fails.

items.title: What if evidence exists but does not cover the interval?
items.text: Registration fails.

items.title: What if the fingerprint does not match?
items.text: Registration fails.

items.title: What if several conflicting declarations apply?
items.text: The historical authority resolver can reject conflicting evidence.

items.title: Why not silently choose the latest observation?
items.text:
Because the latest observation is not necessarily the correct historical specification.

The declaration must apply to the actual source period.

items.title: What about inferred catalogue specifications?
items.text:
The managed registration preflight explicitly requests declared historical evidence.

It does not use arbitrary catalogue inference as a substitute for the required historical declaration.

This is an important distinction from some other MarketForge metadata-enrichment workflows.

items.title: Why Preserve Source-Native IDs?
items.text:
Some market-data providers use their own numeric identifiers for instruments.

For example, Databento records can include:

publisher_id
instrument_id

These identifiers belong to the provider's source namespace.

They are not the same as MarketForge's canonical PostgreSQL instrument IDs.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose a source record contains:

Publisher ID: 2
Instrument ID: 38

MarketForge may separately identify the corresponding canonical AAPL instrument through its catalogue.

items.title: Why keep both?
items.text:
Because the source-native IDs help trace the original recording.

For example:

Source:
Publisher 2
Instrument 38
        |
        v
Registered Interpretation
        |
        v
Canonical AAPL Instrument

The source identity and canonical identity serve different purposes.

items.title: Why not use the native instrument ID as the canonical ID?
items.text:
Source-native IDs may be scoped to:

  • A provider.
  • A publisher.
  • A product.
  • A dataset.
  • A historical period.

The same numeric ID may refer to different instruments in different namespaces.

MarketForge therefore preserves the source namespace separately.

items.title: The [inputs.native_identity] Table
items.text:
An input can declare native identity information.

For example:

[inputs.native_identity]
namespace = "databento:XNAS.ITCH:2024-10-28"

publisher_field = "hd.publisher_id"
publisher_id = 2

instrument_field = "hd.instrument_id"
instrument_id = 38

provenance = "Header identity in the supplied XNAS.ITCH exports."

This is the native identity declaration used by the repository's Databento example.

items.title: What does it describe?
items.text: Field Meaning namespace Source-native identity scope. publisher_field Source field containing the publisher ID. publisher_id Expected native publisher ID. instrument_field Source field containing the native instrument ID. instrument_id Expected native instrument ID. provenance Explanation of the identity evidence.

items.title: Why use a namespace?
items.text:
Numeric IDs are not necessarily globally unique.

The namespace records the context in which those IDs have meaning.

For example:

databento:XNAS.ITCH:2024-10-28

identifies the relevant source product and date context.

items.title: Is this namespace a MarketForge instrument namespace?
items.text:
No.

It describes the source-native identifiers.

The canonical instrument namespace is managed separately by the historical catalogue.

items.title: Native Identity Validation Rules
items.text: When [inputs.native_identity] is supplied, all required fields must be present.

items.title: String fields
items.text:
The following must be nonempty strings:

namespace
publisher_field
instrument_field
provenance

items.title: Numeric fields
items.text:
The following must be nonnegative integers:

publisher_id
instrument_id

For example:

publisher_id = 2
instrument_id = 38

is valid.

Negative values are rejected.

items.title: Can I use floating-point IDs?
items.text:
No.

These fields use strict integer validation.

For example:

instrument_id = 38.0

is not accepted as an integer identity.

items.title: Can publisher and instrument fields be identical?
items.text:
No.

For example:

publisher_field = "hd.instrument_id"
instrument_field = "hd.instrument_id"

is invalid.

The two field references must be different.

items.title: Why?
items.text:
The declaration identifies two distinct source-native concepts.

Using one field for both would make the binding ambiguous.

items.title: Does the schema verify the provider's ID assignment?
items.text:
It validates the declaration and supported source evidence.

It does not independently prove that a provider's historical identity documentation is correct.

Use the actual source contract to establish the meaning of the IDs.

items.title: Native Identity Sampling
items.text: When native identity is supplied, registration preflight can check the corresponding fields against bounded source samples.

items.title: Why is this useful?
items.text:
Suppose a recipe declares:

publisher_id = 2
instrument_id = 38

but the sampled source records contain a different publisher or instrument ID.

This may indicate that the wrong file was selected or the declaration is incorrect.

Registration can detect such mismatches during preflight.

items.title: Does sampling read the entire file?
items.text:
No.

The supported source-layout check is bounded.

It does not independently verify every record in an arbitrarily large recording.

items.title: Does every source format support native identity sampling?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

The current bounded sampler supports particular CSV and JSONL identity paths.

For example, the specialized XLSX sample path does not provide the same native identity sampling behavior.

items.title: What happens if the source format is unsupported?
items.text:
Registration reports the applicable source or sampling incompatibility.

Do not bypass the check by inventing field names.

items.title: Does successful sampling guarantee complete source validity?
items.text:
No.

A bounded sample can establish useful evidence about selected records.

Complete record processing and integrity evaluation belong to normalization.

items.title: Validation and plan review
items.text: Follow the registration workflow to validate, inspect, and apply a declaration.

items.title: Why Registration Uses the Production Profile Compiler
items.text:
The profile declaration controls how Rust interprets source records.

For example, it may describe:

Timestamp encoding
Trade-side mapping
Quantity interpretation
Order-book snapshot behavior
Sequence handling

These rules are consumed by the Rust Engine.

items.title: Why not validate only the TOML syntax?
items.text:
Because a syntactically valid declaration may contain unsupported normalization behavior.

For example, an arbitrary transformation name might be valid TOML but not supported by the Engine.

items.title: What does Forge do?
items.text:
During preflight, Forge loads the installed profile and invokes the supported production semantic validation.

The resulting compiled definition and fingerprint become part of the registration evidence.

items.title: Why preserve the fingerprint?
items.text:
It identifies the approved interpretation associated with the registered source.

This helps establish which source-format definition was used.

items.title: Does successful compilation prove all source records are valid?
items.text:
No.

It proves the declaration is accepted by the compiler.

Complete record validity belongs to normalization.

items.title: Bounded Source-Layout Checks
items.text: Registration preflight also checks representative source data.

items.title: Why?
items.text:
Suppose a profile declares:

CSV with five columns

but the selected file contains a different structure.

The mismatch may be detectable before registering the file.

items.title: What can preflight inspect?
items.text:
Depending on the source format, the bounded checks can examine:

  • Source container compatibility.
  • Physical record layout.
  • Field structure.
  • Expected instrument identity.
  • Optional native identity values.

items.title: What if the source is unsupported?
items.text:
Registration reports the applicable incompatibility.

For example, an unsupported binary format does not become a valid JSONL source merely because the profile ID is correct.

items.title: What does bounded mean?
items.text:
The preflight checks only the source evidence required by the supported sampling procedure.

They do not scan every record in an arbitrarily large source file.

items.title: Why is this distinction important?
items.text:
An early sample might be valid while later records contain malformed values.

Such failures may only become visible during full normalization.

Registration preflight checks source compatibility. Normalization checks actual processing behavior.

items.title: Engine runtime settings and policies
items.text: Use the normalization runtime reference for the normalization TOML, Rust defaults and policy semantics. This page retains the shared entry point for merge and conversion settings and pipeline inheritance.

items.title: Merge and conversion runtime
items.text:
Merge reads data/.config/engine/merge.toml. Conversion preparation reads data/.config/engine/convert.toml. Both use the shared Rust resource and Parquet types and reject unknown fields. The sample is a bounded starting point. Resource and Parquet fields without defaults are required. The merge-only partitioning table is optional and defaults to four partitions per worker.

schema_version = 1

[resources]
workers = 2
memory_limit_mb = 512
max_open_files = 64

[parquet]
row_group_target_mb = 16
file_target_mb = 64
compression_level = 3

# Omit this table for convert.toml.
[partitioning]
partitions_per_worker = 4
Field Type, units, range Effect schema_version Integer, exactly 1 Runtime document schema resources.workers Positive integer Worker ceiling. Actual admission depends on available resources and the workload. resources.memory_limit_mb Positive integer MiB, must fit in unsigned 64-bit bytes Budget for admitted work and writer buffers. resources.max_open_files Positive integer, file handles, default 64 File-handle ceiling. Conversion estimates participating source and reference handles before proceeding. parquet.row_group_target_mb Positive integer MiB, at most the file target Target size for buffered row groups. Conversion checks the target multiplied by workers against its memory limit. parquet.file_target_mb Integer MiB, at least the row-group target, must fit in unsigned 64-bit bytes File rotation size target. parquet.compression_level Integer 1–22, default 3 Zstandard level applied to Parquet output. partitioning.partitions_per_worker Positive integer, merge only, default 4 Timeline partition target. Multiplication by workers must fit in the platform size type.

The direct Rust merge command accepts --config PATH, relative to its --project-root. Forge records the original path and checksums the retained runtime file, then uses that copy for prepared-job execution. The merge monitor and merge-runtime.json show effective settings.

Conversion clamps each recipe resource request to the corresponding runtime ceiling. It transfers the clamped values and Parquet settings into prepared jobs, where the Rust converter reads them. The direct converter can lower the prepared worker count with --workers. Physical input, reference, file-handle and writer-memory prerequisites are checked separately from runtime TOML validation.

items.title: Parquet compression
items.text: parquet.compression_level controls the supported Zstandard compression level for merge output.

items.title: Does a higher number always improve compression?
items.text:
The exact outcome depends on the data and compression implementation.

Higher levels can require more computational work.

items.title: Does compression change market-data meaning?
items.text:
No.

Compression affects physical storage representation.

It does not intentionally change the canonical event values.

items.title: Is this the same as scratch codec?
items.text:
No.

Merge Parquet compression and internal scratch compression are separate settings.

For example:

scratch_codec = "zlib"

does not mean the final merged Parquet output uses zlib.

items.title: Pipeline runtime
items.text:
data/.config/engine/pipeline.toml has a required integer schema_version = 1. It accepts optional [normalize] and [merge] tables with the same nested fields as their operation documents, excluding the operation schema version. For example:

schema_version = 1

[normalize.resources]
workers = 2

[merge.parquet]
compression_level = 5

Each operation TOML is independently validated, then each override is applied recursively to its own stage. Unspecified fields inherit the operation file and its Rust defaults. Rust validates the resulting TOML before processing. Acquire uses Forge HTTP settings and the workflow request. The pipeline executes acquire, normalize and merge.

For a new run, Forge retains the effective TOMLs, their checksums, the source TOML hashes, compiled settings, profile source files and executable hashes. Resume uses the retained files. A prior pipeline snapshot with a shared general.toml remains readable through its retained report and executables.

mf engine runtime normalize
mf engine runtime merge
mf engine runtime convert
mf --json engine runtime pipeline

Runtime inspection requires the matching managed Engine builds and does not open a database connection. The pipeline workflow recipe supplies the interval, requests, ranking name and merge ordering. Pipeline recipe

items.title: Forge command index
items.text:
mf and marketforge use the same parser. Run mf or mf --help to browse the command groups. Follow a family into its nested commands, then use -h or --help at the action you want. Action help shows operands, choices, required flags, defaults and mutually exclusive options from the installed parser.

Root help group Command families and references Getting Started Interactive workspace · Initialization and diagnostics Data Engineering Acquisition · Import, profiles and registration · Normalization · Merge · Conversion · Pipeline Data & Markets Datasets · Storage · Markets and rankings · Catalogue Operations & System Runs · Engine · Database and configuration 
mf --help | cpout
mf acquisition import -h | cpout
mf markets rank --help | cpout
mf normalize prepare --help | cpout

Help works outside a workspace and exits before command execution. It uses the Tokyo Night palette when terminal and application settings permit it. Redirected output is plain text in automatic color mode. The presentation.color setting can force or disable color.

items.title: Global options
items.text:
Option Behavior -h, --help Show help for the parser at that position and exit. Running mf by itself prints root help. --version Print the installed Forge package version and exit. --project-root PATH Select a checkout containing forge/pyproject.toml and engine/. The default is MARKETFORGE_PROJECT_ROOT if set, then the nearest enclosing checkout. --config PATH Select an application TOML file relative to the caller's working directory. The workspace default is data/.config/forge/marketforge.toml. A missing workspace default uses built-in settings. An explicit missing file is an error. --json Print the command result as JSON on stdout where supported. CLI-handled errors are JSON on stderr. Argparse usage errors retain standard usage text.

Put root flags before the command. Put action flags after their command path, except where a reference explicitly documents inherited options.

mf --project-root . --json config show | cpout
mf --json datasets list --testing --limit 10 | cpout

items.title: Database environments
items.text:
Production is the default for database-backed commands. Actions that expose --testing and --production accept only one at a time. Actions that require an explicit selection show it in their usage. Some maintenance actions are restricted to testing.

mf database status | cpout
mf database status --testing | cpout
mf database status --production | cpout

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• Managed names resolve in each command's library, usually with an optional .toml suffix. Check the command reference for explicit path support. In examples, uppercase operands such as FILE_ID, NAME, or PREVIEW_PATH stand for values from your workspace or a previous command.
  • --testing selects the guarded testing database. Commands can still write records, access the network, or remove eligible managed files. A preview or dry run is available only where documented. Testing credentials and setup
  • Normalization and merge --tui require an interactive terminal and are incompatible with global --json. --silent is action-specific. It generally controls progress while preserving results. Some editor actions require an interactive session.
  • Exit 0 means the action completed under its stated policy. Check result fields for empty selections, incomplete evidence, or explicitly accepted partial normalization. Exit 1 generally means an operation-level failure, an unaccepted partial result, or a blocked apply. Exit 2 means a parser or handled setup/configuration error. Handled cancellation can return 130. Processing actions can instead return 1 with an interrupted receipt.
  • Raw archive IDs, PostgreSQL file dataset IDs, engine job IDs, and engine publication IDs serve different purposes. Committed publications retain their original manifests and paths. Inspect the reported artifacts under the configured data root. Registration-only recovery uses the committed publication, primary file or execution intent as documented for each processor. File dataset model

Handled errors in JSON mode use {"schema_version":1,"error":{"message":"…"}} on stderr. The command's successful or partial result is a separate stdout document when the handler supports JSON. Some failures return an operation report on stdout with a nonzero code. Read both channels and the process status. The command references describe result fields as implemented, subject to the explicitly versioned artifact contracts.

items.text:
The following table summarizes the exchange archive-acquisition commands.

Command Contacts exchange Writes registry Downloads archives new No No No edit No No No validate No No No list No No No sources No No No map When discovery is needed Yes No plan --cache-only No No No download When discovery or downloading is needed Yes Yes, when required

new and edit can create or modify local configuration files. The table's registry column refers specifically to PostgreSQL changes.

items.title: Configuration inventory and validation
items.text:
mf acquisition list | cpout
mf acquisition validate getting_started | cpout

The inventory reads the managed TOML files locally and shows request counts and requested periods in UTC. Malformed recipes remain visible as invalid entries. Validation checks the named file's structure and reports the failing field or TOML location when possible. These commands require no database or network access. Source support and archive availability are checked during discovery.

items.title: Mapping and download options
items.text:
Both map and download accept these options:

Option Meaning --testing, --production Choose the verified registry. Production is the default. --refresh Check the exchange again rather than reusing fresh discovery results. --requests-per-second RATE Set the requested HTTP request rate, subject to provider limits. --silent Hide progress updates while keeping the final result and failures.

Examples:

mf acquisition map getting_started --testing --refresh

mf acquisition download getting_started \
    --testing \
    --requests-per-second 0.5

mf acquisition download getting_started \
    --testing \
    --silent

items.title: Request-rate limits
items.text:
MarketForge applies request-rate limits when contacting exchanges.

This helps avoid overwhelming providers or exceeding their permitted request rates.

You can lower the requested rate using --requests-per-second.

For example:

mf acquisition map getting_started \
    --testing \
    --requests-per-second 0.5

This requests a pacing rate of half a request per second, subject to the implementation's provider controls.

The rate must be a positive, finite number.

If the requested rate exceeds a provider's configured limit, that limit still applies.

Retries, redirects, and provider cooldowns can also affect how quickly discovery or downloading proceeds.

See the HTTP configuration reference for the current limits and application settings.

items.title: Cache-only planning options
items.text:
The planning command uses:

mf acquisition plan NAME --testing --cache-only [--verify-local] [--limit N]
Option Meaning --testing Select the guarded testing registry. --cache-only Use stored information without making network requests or registry changes. --verify-local Read and hash local files in the selected sample. --limit N Set the maximum number of sampled archive entries. Default: 100.

--cache-only is required. The registry defaults to production. Pass --testing to inspect the testing registry.

Planning is a read-only inspection tool, not a saved download job or a complete estimate of future transfer size.

items.title: JSON output
items.text:
Use the global --json option when you need machine-readable results:

mf --json acquisition map getting_started --testing

mf --json acquisition download getting_started --testing

The human output summarizes request outcomes, coverage evidence, and the retained report location. JSON mode emits the full operation result for scripts. The list JSON continues to return configuration names. Validation JSON returns the structural result and parsed configuration.

mf --json acquisition list | cpout
mf --json acquisition validate getting_started | cpout
mf --json runs report RUN_ID --testing | cpout

The --json option belongs before the command name.

Interactive editing does not provide a JSON result.

items.title: Understanding Acquisition Results
items.text:
Acquisition records two different kinds of information:

Discovery information describes the archive files the exchange exposes.

Local file information describes files that MarketForge has downloaded and stored.

These are related, but they are not the same thing.

For example, mapping may find an archive even though it has never been downloaded.

Likewise, a previously downloaded file may still exist locally even when the original discovery result is no longer fresh.

items.title: Successful discovery
items.text:
A successful mapping operation means MarketForge completed discovery for the applicable request.

It may find many files, a few files, or no matching files.

It does not establish that every market event is present inside those archives.

items.title: Successful download
items.text:
A completed download means the operation finished its applicable download and reuse work.

It does not mean the files have already been normalized or that order-book continuity has been verified.

Normalization is responsible for interpreting records and evaluating the relevant processing and data-integrity conditions.

items.title: Failed or interrupted operations
items.text:
Network problems, provider errors, missing files, and local filesystem problems can interrupt an acquisition.

MarketForge keeps run information so you can investigate what happened.

A partially completed operation can leave successfully downloaded files available for later reuse.

Do not assume an unsuccessful acquisition automatically removes previously completed downloads.

For details about retained operations and recovery, see Managing acquisitions.

items.title: Command Exit Codes
items.text:
MarketForge uses exit codes to indicate whether an operation succeeded or encountered a problem.

Code Meaning 0 The command completed successfully. Inspect the result for request coverage and file outcomes. 1 One or more acquisition operations failed. Some completed files may remain available. 2 A command, configuration, filesystem, database, or setup error was reported. 130 The command was interrupted through the handled cancellation path.

A successful empty mapping result can return zero.

A zero exit code should not be interpreted as proof that the requested historical market data is complete.

When investigating an unsuccessful run, inspect the reported status, individual request outcomes, and saved run report rather than relying only on the exit code.

items.title: Storage inspection
items.text: Use raw storage commands to inspect registered archives, date filters and file coverage.

items.title: Run inspection
items.text: Use run evidence commands to inspect retained fetch and processing runs.

items.title: Cleanup reference
items.text: Use the cleanup options and effects and the managed storage workflow.

items.title: Mapping and download results
items.text:
Mapping discovers remote archive identities. The final report shows each requested scope, including family and base-coin scopes, and identifies reused discovery scans as Cached and fresh scans as Refreshed. A cached discovery does not establish that the files are present locally. A successful empty scan remains an empty result.

Download reports completed, reused, failed and cancelled file outcomes. The registered local archive count counts distinct retained local IDs. Bytes in completed downloads use recorded size evidence. Unknown measurements display as Unknown. Nominal archive intervals describe the retained objects and do not establish uninterrupted market-data coverage.

The terminal shows at most 20 request rows, with incomplete requests first. Read the retained report for all requests and the event log for individual archive outcomes. A partial acquisition remains a nonzero command outcome. Live progress is emitted separately from the final result.

mf acquisition map getting_started --testing | cpout
mf --json acquisition map getting_started --testing | cpout
mf --json runs list --testing --operation acquisition --limit 10 | cpout
mf runs report RUN_ID --testing | cpout

Use an actual ID from the acquisition result. The PostgreSQL record, retained report and event metadata use the same acquisition-<uuid> identity. Execution history and recovery

items.title: Catalogue Command Reference
items.text:
MarketForge provides the same four basic operations for exchanges, instruments, and specifications.

These commands use the mf catalog namespace.

items.title: Supported entities
items.text:
The current manual catalogue CLI supports:

Entity What it manages exchange Execution venues. instrument Individual financial instruments. specs Current and historical instrument specifications.

The general command structure is:

mf catalog ENTITY ACTION

Replace ENTITY with one of the supported entity names.

items.title: Available actions
items.text: Action Purpose validate Check a local declaration without writing to the database. add Validate and register a declaration in the testing catalogue. list List registered catalogue records. show Inspect a specific registered entry.

items.title: Validate
items.text:
mf catalog ENTITY validate --file PATH

For example:

mf catalog instrument validate \
    --file docs/content/examples/catalogue/instrument.toml

Validation reads the local TOML file.

It does not establish that the corresponding records are already present in PostgreSQL.

items.title: Add
items.text:
mf catalog ENTITY add --from PATH --testing

For example:

mf catalog instrument add \
    --from docs/content/examples/catalogue/instrument.toml \
    --testing

Adding a declaration performs database work.

The command checks the relevant existing identities and rejects conflicting information.

items.title: List
items.text:
mf catalog ENTITY list --testing

For example:

mf catalog instrument list --testing

This lists the corresponding registered records.

items.title: Show
items.text:
mf catalog ENTITY show REFERENCE --testing

For example:

mf catalog instrument show \
    example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL \
    --testing

The reference format depends on the entity.

Entity Reference Exchange Registered venue code Instrument exchange.instrument_type.market_category.symbol Specifications The corresponding instrument reference

items.title: JSON output
items.text:
All catalogue actions support the global --json option.

For example:

mf --json catalog instrument list --testing

mf --json catalog specs show \
    example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL \
    --testing

The --json option must appear before catalog.

JSON output is useful when scripting catalogue inspection or examining detailed registration evidence.

items.title: Database behavior
items.text:
Command Requires PostgreSQL Can write catalogue records validate No No add Yes Yes list Yes No show Yes No

These commands do not contact exchanges to download historical archives.

Manual catalogue registration also does not require an acquisition adapter, market-statistics refresh, or ranking snapshot.

items.title: Repeated Registration and Conflicts
items.text:
MarketForge is designed to preserve stable instrument identities.

This means repeated submissions should not silently change an existing market definition.

items.title: Registering the same exchange twice
items.text:
If an exchange declaration matches the existing registered information, MarketForge can reuse it.

A different exchange name under the same code is rejected.

items.title: Registering the same instrument twice
items.text:
If an instrument declaration matches the existing registered identity and properties, MarketForge can reuse the existing record.

Conflicting instrument properties are rejected.

items.title: Registering the same historical specifications twice
items.text:
Identical historical evidence can be reused.

Conflicting overlapping validity intervals are rejected.

An adjacent or disjoint historical interval may contain different specifications.

items.title: Why preserve these rules?
items.text:
Consider historical research performed using a particular contract specification.

If the catalogue silently replaced that specification with newer values, previously processed datasets could become difficult to explain or reproduce.

MarketForge therefore retains historical specification evidence and rejects conflicting declarations instead of silently choosing new values.

The goal is to make historical interpretation traceable.

items.title: Can I change an existing instrument's meaning?
items.text:
Do not attempt to redefine an existing instrument by submitting incompatible properties under the same identity.

If the original declaration was incorrect, investigate the existing catalogue record and the appropriate supported correction path.

A conflicting add operation is not a general-purpose migration or overwrite mechanism.

Similarly, a new historical specification should describe a genuinely applicable period rather than overwrite earlier evidence without justification.

items.title: Troubleshooting Catalogue Registration
items.text: Most catalogue errors involve invalid declarations, missing dependencies, or conflicting metadata.

items.title: Exchange not found
items.text:
Possible cause: You are trying to register an instrument before registering its exchange.

First inspect the exchange:

mf catalog exchange show example_exchange --testing

If it does not exist, register the appropriate exchange declaration.

Then retry the instrument registration.

items.title: Instrument not found
items.text:
Possible cause: You are registering specifications for an instrument that has not yet been added.

Inspect the instrument:

mf catalog instrument show \
    example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL \
    --testing

If it is absent, register the instrument declaration first.

items.title: Invalid TOML declaration
items.text:
Possible cause: The file is malformed, missing required fields, or contains unsupported values.

Run the relevant validation command:

mf catalog specs validate \
    --file docs/content/examples/catalogue/specs.toml

Review the reported validation error and correct the declaration.

Validation is useful because it does not modify the database.

items.title: Conflicting exchange or instrument definition
items.text:
Possible cause: A catalogue identity already exists with different registered properties.

Inspect the existing record before retrying.

For example:

mf catalog instrument show \
    example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL \
    --testing

Compare it with the submitted TOML file.

Do not change the symbol or market classification arbitrarily to bypass the conflict.

items.title: Conflicting historical specifications
items.text:
Possible cause: A new declaration overlaps an existing historical interval but contains incompatible values.

Inspect the existing specification evidence:

mf --json catalog specs show \
    example_exchange.equity.equity.AAPL \
    --testing

Review the validity intervals, economic values, and provenance.

If a genuine specification change occurred, declare the correct applicable periods.

Do not use a new observation timestamp as a substitute for historical validity.

items.title: Missing historical specification coverage
items.text:
Possible cause: The registered specifications do not cover the entire period represented by a raw input.

Inspect the relevant historical specification intervals.

Compare them with the declared source coverage.

Register additional applicable evidence where necessary.

Do not extend a validity interval without evidence that the values were actually valid during the additional period.

items.title: Database connection rejected
items.text:
Possible cause: The testing database is not configured, initialized, or recognized as the expected testing environment.

Check:

mf database status --testing

See Database setup for the required credentials and identity checks.

items.title: Profile installation fails after catalogue registration
items.text:
Catalogue registration and profile installation are separate operations.

If a profile fails validation, inspect its format mappings and the Rust compiler diagnostics.

If installation fails because of a missing venue or an existing conflicting profile identity, inspect the corresponding catalogue and profile records.

See Profile authoring and troubleshooting.
