items.title: Command inputs and effects
items.text:
Action Input and effects Current JSON result new A new managed name, exactly one upstream selector and an explicit target currency. Reads and fingerprints the upstream TOML. Writes a recipe and refuses an existing destination. Source selectors accept managed names or explicit paths. The parsed --testing flag is optional because creation performs no registry selection status: "template_created", path, and source with the retained declaration validate Managed recipe name, TOML path, or individual job JSON. A recipe check validates its structure, local constraints and source fingerprint. A job check runs the managed converter’s --validate; install it first. The Forge collection is not a standalone Rust job status: "valid", path, validation, and recipe for TOML prepare A recipe and the guarded testing registry. Resolves complete registered sources and references, then generates job documents and validates them with the installed converter if available. Dry run performs selection and computes job specifications without invoking the Engine or writing files prepare-report.json shape described below run Managed recipe, TOML path, retained collection or retained individual job path. A recipe is prepared first. A retained submission reuses its pinned inputs. This action can publish converted data. The documented registry remains unchanged by conversion Run status and execution results with artifact and publication evidence

--tui is an execution option and is mutually exclusive with global --json. An action report with status of blocked, failed, or interrupted returns exit 1. A generated preparation can return exit 0 even when compatibility remains unvalidated. Parse and handled configuration errors use the shared CLI rules.

items.title: Preparation result
items.text:
Read status and compatibility together. blocked identifies failed selection, evidence or metadata and lists blockers. generated identifies a successfully constructed job specification. The CLI uses status: "generated" even when the production parser passes. In that case, compatibility: "validated" records an installed binary that validated every saved job with no remaining compatibility blockers. Otherwise compatibility: "not_validated" retains the exact reasons in compatibility_blockers.

The report identifies requested and effective publication scope, the upstream TOML and digest, source and external reference publications, resolved streams and effective settings. job_path points to the Forge collection or is null on dry run. report_path identifies the saved report when written. In a persisted report jobs[] contains path and sha256, an integer job_id, destination output, selected references, source registry publication ID and string Engine publication ID, and engine_validation of not_run, passed, or failed. Successful validation can include validation_output. The dry-run job records intended_job_path in place of the saved path and digest. artifacts records file pins when persisted.

items.title: Compatibility and publication
items.text:
Current standalone conversion consumes chronological and causal physical merge publications under its validation rules. Matching depth membership does not prevent a configured trade stream from being a reference. Trade-only execution uses internal references. Depth-only requires an external trade-only merge. Combined can bind selected internal trades and supported external references. The policy can consider multiple currency paths within the configured hop limit. It still needs eligible prior observations at event execution.

Instrument metadata is embedded in the prepared job. Forge checks the workspace preparation catalogue against verified historical evidence if the file exists. The Engine does not read a fixed instrument catalogue to run a standalone job. Atomic conversion publication currently requires Linux. Committed converted files can be inspected through Arrow. Conversion registration is unavailable.

mf convert validate NAME
mf --json convert prepare NAME --testing --dry-run
mf convert run PATH_TO_CONVERT_JSON --testing

See conversion recipes, prepared Engine job, Forge collection and run evidence, conversion workflow, and converted publication format.

items.title: JSON results
items.text:
List and find return {datasets, interval_semantics, limit, offset} in JSON mode. datasets is an array, including when no files match. limit and offset are integers. interval_semantics is descriptive text. Each array member has a numeric registry file id, numeric publication_id, text engine_dataset_id and engine_job_id, and an instrument_namespace. File fields are storage_root, storage_path, storage_format, primary_file, manifest_path, manifest_sha256, and file_sha256. operation, data_type, status and summary describe the record. Inclusive observed endpoints use nullable integer start_timestamp_ns/ end_timestamp_ns and nullable text first_observed_utc/ last_observed_utc.

Action Top-level keys Show file, publication Streams id, scope, streams Schema id, columns Head id, rows Lineage id, file_contributions, publication_selection Verify a primary file id, scope, status, file_sha256, entire_publication_verified

Decimal values in head JSON use strings, including nested trade and depth values. Timestamp columns remain integers. Use a parser that preserves integers beyond the IEEE-754 exact range. Read the display-independent rules in identity and provenance.

items.title: JSON dataset inspection
items.text:
Most dataset commands support global JSON output.

For example:

mf --json datasets list --testing

Or:

mf --json datasets show FILE_ID --testing

The global --json option must appear before datasets.

items.title: Why use JSON?
items.text:
JSON is useful when:

  • Writing scripts.
  • Extracting file IDs.
  • Inspecting complete metadata.
  • Comparing processing results.
  • Building automation around registered datasets.
  • Working with other command-line tools.

items.title: JSON previews
items.text:
For datasets head, JSON output includes all stored columns by default unless you explicitly select columns.

For example:

mf --json datasets head FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --limit 5

Exact decimal values are serialized as strings.

This helps avoid losing decimal precision through ordinary JSON number handling.

items.title: Does --wide change JSON output?
items.text:
The wide and compact display modes primarily control terminal presentation.

JSON retains the underlying response structure.

For dataset previews, use --column when you want to request a smaller set of physical fields.

items.title: Does JSON ignore pagination?
items.text:
No.

List, find, and coverage still use their requested file limits and offsets.

JSON does not automatically return the entire registered dataset collection.

items.title: File-Level Contributions vs. Publication-Level Selection
items.text:
This is an important distinction.

A publication may select many input files, but one individual output part may contain records from only some of them.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose a normalization publication uses three raw archives:

Archive A
Archive B
Archive C

The Engine produces two primary files:

Publication
    |
    +-- File 1
    |      |
    |      +-- Archive A
    |      +-- Archive B
    |
    +-- File 2
           |
           +-- Archive B
           +-- Archive C

The publication-level input selection is:

A, B, C

However, File 1 does not necessarily contain data from Archive C.

Likewise, File 2 does not necessarily contain data from Archive A.

items.title: Why not attach every source to every file?
items.text:
That would incorrectly suggest that every selected source contributed records to every output part.

MarketForge therefore distinguishes:

File-level contributions

The source inputs that are proven to have contributed to the selected primary file.

Publication-level selection

The complete set of inputs selected for the overall processing publication.

items.title: Expand the publication selection
items.text:
Use:

mf datasets lineage FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --publication

This includes the shared publication-level selection information.

items.title: Why is this useful for merging?
items.text:
A merged publication may select several normalized files.

However, attributing a particular merged output part to one input file can require additional evidence.

For example, if a represented stream was selected from exactly one primary input file, the contribution may be established precisely.

If several files from the same parent publication were selected, the available evidence may only support attribution to the publication as a whole.

MarketForge preserves this distinction.

It does not invent exact file-level contributions when the evidence is insufficient.

items.title: Does --publication change the dataset?
items.text:
No.

It expands the lineage inspection.

The physical Parquet file remains unchanged.

items.title: Verification vs. Data Integrity
items.text: Dataset verification and processing integrity are different.

items.title: File verification
items.text:
File verification answers:

"Does this file still match the registered bytes?"

For example, a SHA-256 comparison can establish that the current Parquet file matches its recorded fingerprint.

items.title: Processing integrity
items.text:
Processing integrity answers different questions.

For example:

  • Were source records parsed successfully?
  • Were required order-book snapshots available?
  • Were sequence gaps detected?
  • Were timestamp regressions observed?
  • Were the applicable integrity policies satisfied?
  • Was the publication accepted with clean or degraded integrity?

These checks occur during the relevant Engine processing and publication workflow.

items.title: Historical completeness
items.text:
Historical completeness is another separate question:

"Does this dataset contain every market event that should exist for the intended period?"

Neither a matching checksum nor a successful processing result automatically proves this.

A source provider may have supplied incomplete historical data.

items.title: Three different guarantees
items.text:
Question Relevant evidence Are the registered file bytes intact? Dataset verification. Did processing satisfy its required integrity rules? Engine reports and publication evidence. Is the historical market record complete? Source coverage evidence and applicable continuity guarantees.

These distinctions matter when using historical data for backtesting and quantitative research.

For example, a file can be perfectly intact while containing a gap inherited from the original source.

items.title: How MarketForge Displays Datasets
items.text:
The dataset CLI uses MarketForge's existing terminal theme.

It is designed to present large amounts of dataset information in a compact, readable way.

For example, the dataset browser groups files by publication and instrument rather than displaying an unstructured list of filesystem paths.

items.title: Compact and wide views
items.text:
The default list uses compact file names.

For example:

mf datasets list --testing

Use:

mf datasets list --testing --wide

to display additional path information.

items.title: Precise timestamps
items.text:
The default terminal view displays timestamps to whole seconds.

Use:

mf datasets list --testing --precise

for nanosecond precision.

items.title: Terminal width
items.text:
The display adapts to the available terminal width.

Wide terminals may show tables.

Narrower terminals may use stacked records.

This changes the presentation, not the underlying dataset metadata.

items.title: Multi-stream labels
items.text:
A file representing several instruments may be displayed under a mixed-membership heading.

This helps distinguish it from files containing only one logical stream.

Each physical file retains its registered file ID.

items.title: Tokyo Night colors
items.text:
MarketForge uses its Tokyo Night-inspired terminal palette.

You can control terminal colors through the application configuration:

data/.config/forge/marketforge.toml

For example:

[presentation]
mode = "progress"
color = "auto"

items.title: Available color modes
items.text:
Mode Behavior auto Detect supported terminal color capabilities. always Enable colors for supported interactive output. never Disable colors.

Automatic mode respects the NO_COLOR environment variable.

items.title: Plain output
items.text:
If you prefer a plain terminal view:

[presentation]
color = "never"

Redirected dataset output and global JSON use plain output.

items.title: Does silent mode hide dataset inspection?
items.text:
No.

The presentation setting:

mode = "silent"

suppresses supported progress displays.

It does not prevent requested dataset inspection results from being shown.

items.title: Does color affect dataset contents?
items.text:
No.

Terminal colors only change presentation.

They do not change Parquet data, timestamp precision, dataset registration, or processing integrity.

mf datasets list --testing [FILTERS] [--wide] [--precise]

Displays registered primary files.

items.title: Supported filters
items.text:
Option Meaning --operation normalize|merge Processing operation. --data-type TYPE Trade, depth, or combined content. --status STATUS Stored file status. --publication ID Engine publication identity. --exchange VENUE Registered exchange code. --instrument VALUE Exact symbol or canonical instrument ID. --instrument-type TYPE Registered instrument type. --market-category CATEGORY Registered market category. --start TIMESTAMP Inclusive search start. --end TIMESTAMP Exclusive search end. --limit N Number of file rows per page. --offset N Starting position within the matching file rows.

The file-page limit defaults to 50 and accepts values from 1 to 1000.

The offset defaults to zero.

The default row limit is 10.

The accepted range is 1–1000.

items.title: Verify a file
items.text:
mf datasets verify FILE_ID --testing

Checks the selected primary file and its shared manifest against registered fingerprints.

items.title: Refresh metadata
items.text:
mf datasets refresh-summary FILE_ID --testing

Updates the file's derived metadata in PostgreSQL.

items.title: Preview legacy migration
items.text:
mf datasets migrate-registration --all --testing --dry-run

Verifies eligible legacy registrations and reports the proposed file-level records without applying the registration changes.

items.title: Apply legacy migration
items.text:
mf datasets migrate-registration --all --testing

Migrates eligible legacy normalization aggregates into file-level registrations.

Legacy merge aggregates currently require separate supported evidence and are reported as conflicts.

items.title: JSON Output
items.text:
The global JSON option can be used with dataset inspection commands.

For example:

mf --json datasets list --testing

mf --json datasets find \
    --testing \
    --exchange bybit \
    --instrument BTCUSDT

mf --json datasets show FILE_ID --testing

mf --json datasets lineage FILE_ID --testing

items.title: Why use JSON?
items.text:
JSON is useful for automated inspection and downstream processing.

For example, you can extract:

  • File IDs.
  • Physical paths.
  • Publication identities.
  • Stream memberships.
  • Observed timestamps.
  • Row counts.
  • Lineage information.

items.title: Important details
items.text:
Global --json must appear before datasets.

File pagination still applies.

For head, JSON includes all stored columns by default unless an explicit column selection is supplied.

Exact decimal values are represented as strings.

items.title: No datasets are listed
items.text:
Possible cause: No matching files are registered in the selected testing database.

Inspect the relevant normalization or merge result.

Check that publication registration completed.

Also verify that you are using the intended testing database.

items.title: A file ID cannot be found
items.text:
Possible cause: The ID is incorrect, belongs to another registry, or refers to a legacy registration.

List the current files:

mf datasets list --testing

If the ID is from an older aggregate registration, inspect its migration status.

items.title: The dataset belongs to an unexpected publication
items.text:
Possible cause: The file ID belongs to another processing run.

Inspect:

mf datasets show FILE_ID --testing

Review the Engine publication identity and source lineage.

items.title: A market search returns a mixed file
items.text:
Possible cause: The selected physical Parquet file contains several registered streams.

Inspect:

mf datasets streams FILE_ID --testing

The file can legitimately represent multiple instruments.

items.title: A search by time returns a file without matching rows
items.text:
Possible cause: The file's observed envelope overlaps the requested interval, but no actual event occurs inside that narrower range.

Use physical record inspection or the Python API to perform exact row-level filtering.

items.title: Coverage seems incomplete
items.text:
Possible cause: The selected page does not contain every matching file.

Check the pagination information.

Continue through the remaining file pages when a complete registry-level inventory is required.

items.title: The schema command fails
items.text:
Possible cause: PyArrow is missing, the file is unavailable, or the Parquet schema cannot be read.

Confirm the research dependency is installed.

Also inspect the registered file path and verification status.

items.title: A preview does not show a required column
items.text:
Possible cause: The compact view hides that field.

Use:

mf datasets head FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --wide \
    --limit 5

Or inspect the schema and request the column explicitly.

items.title: A requested column does not exist
items.text:
Possible cause: The selected publication uses a different physical schema.

Inspect:

mf datasets schema FILE_ID --testing

Use the actual stored field names.

items.title: Previewed timestamps lack precision
items.text:
Possible cause: The default terminal view shows whole seconds.

Use:

mf datasets head FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --precise

items.title: Unexpected row counts
items.text:
Possible cause: You are comparing different kinds of records.

For example, depth observations can produce multiple canonical price-level rows.

Inspect the publication information and relevant processing metrics.

Do not assume the number of physical Parquet rows equals the number of original source messages.

items.title: Lineage does not list every publication input as a file contribution
items.text:
Possible cause: Not every selected publication input has proven contribution to the individual primary file.

Use:

mf datasets lineage FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --publication

Review file-level contributions separately from the full publication selection.

items.title: Verification reports a checksum mismatch
items.text:
Possible cause: The file or manifest differs from its registered fingerprint.

Inspect the physical file and reported path.

Do not overwrite the stored checksum to conceal the mismatch.

Investigate the original publication and recovery options.

items.title: Verification reports a missing file
items.text:
Possible cause: The registered path no longer contains the expected primary file.

Check the configured data root and publication location.

Do not manually recreate an empty file under the expected name.

items.title: Refreshing a summary does not repair a damaged file
items.text:
Possible cause: refresh-summary updates metadata but does not verify or rewrite the Parquet contents.

Use datasets verify for the supported physical integrity check.

items.title: Registration migration reports conflicts
items.text:
Possible cause: A legacy publication cannot be verified or lacks the required supported migration evidence.

Inspect the migration report.

Legacy merge aggregates are not automatically converted through the current normalization-focused migration path.

items.title: Registration recovery fails
items.text:
Possible cause: The committed publication, manifest, or required provenance does not satisfy the applicable verification contract.

Inspect the registration error.

Recovery cannot turn incomplete staging files into valid published datasets.

mf engine build [-h] [--dry-run] [--offline] [--jobs JOBS]

items.title: Understand Cargo Build Options
items.text:
The managed Engine builder uses Cargo internally.

For the historical normalizer, the approved build configuration includes:

Setting Value Cargo package marketforge-engine Cargo binary marketforge-normalize Build profile Release Default Cargo features Disabled Approved features historical, monitor-tui Dependency lockfile Enforced with --locked

These settings are managed by Forge.

You do not need to provide the corresponding Cargo arguments manually.

items.title: Why use release builds?
items.text:
Rust supports different compilation profiles.

Debug builds prioritize development convenience, while release builds apply optimizations intended for execution performance.

Historical normalization can involve large workloads, so the managed normalizer uses the release profile.

items.title: What are Cargo features?
items.text:
Cargo features allow Rust projects to enable optional capabilities.

For example, MarketForge's historical normalizer uses features associated with historical processing and terminal monitoring.

Forge selects the approved features for the target.

This helps ensure that the installed binary includes the capabilities expected by the relevant processing workflow.

items.title: Why disable default features?
items.text:
A Rust package may contain functionality that is not required by every executable.

By disabling default features and explicitly enabling the required ones, the managed build can select a narrower configuration.

This helps avoid unintentionally including unrelated optional functionality.

items.title: Why use --locked?
items.text:
Cargo uses a lockfile to record resolved dependency versions.

The managed build uses:

--locked

This tells Cargo to use the existing dependency lockfile without updating it.

If the lockfile needs changes that the build is not permitted to make, Cargo reports an error.

This helps keep builds consistent with the repository's recorded dependencies.

However, a lockfile does not guarantee identical compiled bytes across different operating systems, compilers, or build environments.

items.title: How MarketForge Installs Compiled Engines
items.text:
Once Cargo successfully compiles an approved target, Forge installs it into the managed .bin/ directory.

This installation process includes several safeguards.

items.title: The executable is checked before installation
items.text:
Forge performs a non-processing startup check using the compiled executable's help interface.

The purpose is to verify that the selected executable can start and respond as expected.

This is sometimes called a smoke test.

For example, the managed normalizer is expected to respond to its supported non-processing help invocation.

A failed smoke check prevents the build from being accepted as a successful managed installation.

items.title: Why check the executable?
items.text:
Successful compilation proves that Cargo produced an executable.

However, it does not necessarily prove that the executable can start correctly in the current environment.

A smoke check provides an additional verification step before installation.

It is deliberately limited to non-processing behavior.

It does not execute normalization, read historical archives, or publish datasets.

items.title: Existing installations are protected
items.text:
Forge prepares and checks the new executable before replacing an existing managed binary.

The executable replacement is performed atomically.

This reduces the risk of leaving a partially copied executable as the installed binary.

If the build or pre-installation checks fail, an existing installation is preserved rather than deliberately replaced by the failed candidate.

items.title: Concurrent builds are controlled
items.text:
Forge uses a file lock to prevent competing managed installers from modifying the same installation state at the same time.

This helps protect the managed binary directory when multiple commands attempt to build or install engines concurrently.

items.title: Why not copy Cargo output manually?
items.text:
Manually copying an executable into .bin/ bypasses the managed installation process.

The copied file may not match the recorded build information.

This can cause mf engine status to report a checksum or metadata problem.

Use:

mf engine build normalize

or:

mf engine build merge

to create supported managed installations.

items.title: Build Information and the Manifest
items.text:
MarketForge keeps a record of its managed Engine installations.

This information is stored in:

.bin/manifest.json

items.title: Why does MarketForge need a manifest?
items.text:
Imagine compiling the normalizer today and then updating the Rust source code next week.

You may want to know which executable is currently installed and how it was built.

The manifest helps answer questions about the installed binary.

For example, it can record:

  • The selected build target.
  • The Rust toolchain used.
  • The enabled Cargo features.
  • The target host.
  • The installed executable.
  • The executable's file size.
  • The SHA-256 checksum.
  • The result of the startup smoke check.
  • Build-related timestamps.
  • Repository revision and dirty-state information.

These details help MarketForge verify the installed executable and provide useful information when investigating a build.

items.title: What is an executable checksum?
items.text:
A SHA-256 checksum is calculated from the executable's contents.

If the installed file changes, its checksum will normally change as well.

MarketForge records the checksum during installation.

Later, it can compare the current executable against the recorded value.

This helps detect unexpected file changes.

items.title: Does the manifest prove which source code produced the binary?
items.text:
Not completely.

The manifest retains repository revision and dirty-state information.

However, this does not represent an exact snapshot of every modified source file used during compilation.

For example, a repository may contain uncommitted changes when the engine is built.

The manifest can indicate that the working tree was dirty, but that information alone does not reconstruct the precise source contents.

For reproducible engineering investigations, retain the relevant source revision and build environment separately.

items.title: Should you edit the manifest manually?
items.text:
No.

The manifest belongs to the managed build system.

Manually changing it can make the recorded installation information inconsistent with the actual executable.

If the manifest is missing, damaged, or inconsistent, use the supported build command to recreate a valid installation.

items.title: Check Installed Engines
items.text:
After building an engine, you should verify that MarketForge recognizes the installation.

Use:

mf engine status

This command inspects the managed Engine installation state.

items.title: Why check engine status?
items.text:
An executable may exist on disk but still be unsuitable for managed execution.

For example:

  • Its manifest may be missing.
  • The recorded checksum may not match.
  • The executable may no longer have the correct permissions.
  • The path may have been replaced by an unsafe symbolic link.
  • The recorded installation information may be malformed.

MarketForge therefore checks more than the presence of a filename.

items.title: What does status inspect?
items.text:
The status command examines the installed targets and their retained build information.

It can distinguish conditions such as:

Condition Meaning Missing installation The managed executable is not installed. Missing metadata The executable or its installation record is incomplete. Invalid metadata The manifest cannot be interpreted correctly. Non-executable file The installed file cannot be executed as required. Unsafe path The installed path does not satisfy the managed-file safety checks. Checksum mismatch The current executable differs from its recorded checksum. Verified installation The applicable file and metadata checks passed.

The exact status fields should be read from the command's output.

items.title: Does status run the executable?
items.text:
No.

mf engine status is a read-only inspection command.

It does not execute the installed Engine binary.

Instead, it checks the recorded installation metadata and the relevant filesystem properties.

This makes it useful when investigating an unknown or potentially damaged installation.

items.title: Does status require PostgreSQL?
items.text:
No.

Engine status does not need database credentials or historical market-data files.

It inspects the managed installation in the project workspace.

items.title: Check after building
items.text:
A normal sequence is:

mf engine build normalize
mf engine status

Confirm that the normalizer appears as a verified managed installation.

After building the merger, run the same status command to inspect the managed targets.

items.title: What Happens When a Build Changes?
items.text:
As MarketForge evolves, the Rust source code may change.

For example, you might update:

  • Historical normalization logic.
  • Trade decoding.
  • Order-book reconstruction.
  • Merge behavior.
  • Processing integrity checks.
  • Engine command-line behavior.

These source changes are not automatically applied to an executable that was compiled earlier.

items.title: Source code and compiled binaries are different
items.text:
Consider the following:

Rust Source Code
      |
      v
   Compile
      |
      v
Installed Binary

Once compiled, the binary contains the code produced by that build.

Editing the Rust source afterward does not modify the installed executable.

items.title: Rebuild after changing Engine code
items.text:
If you change Rust code used by the normalizer, rebuild it:

mf engine build normalize

If you change code used by the merger, rebuild that target:

mf engine build merge

The managed builder compiles and installs a new executable using the supported build configuration.

items.title: Does mf engine status detect every source change?
items.text:
No.

Status verifies the installed binary against its recorded installation information.

It does not perform a complete comparison between the current Rust source tree and the exact source contents used during compilation.

For example, an installed binary may still pass its checksum verification after you edit the Rust source code.

This means:

A verified installation is not necessarily a build of the latest working-tree changes.

Rebuild after making changes that should affect the Engine.

items.title: Does Forge rebuild automatically before normalization?
items.text:
No.

Managed normalization does not automatically compile the Engine.

This is intentional.

Compilation and historical processing are separate operations.

It prevents a normalization request from unexpectedly starting a potentially expensive Rust build.

Make sure the required executable is installed before running the corresponding workflow.

items.title: Understanding Engine Compatibility
items.text:
A successful build is necessary, but it does not prove that every historical processing request will succeed.

For example, Forge prepares normalization jobs using a defined contract.

The Rust Engine must understand the prepared job format and support the requested source interpretation.

items.title: Build validity and processing compatibility are different
items.text:
Consider these checks:

Check What it establishes Cargo compilation The selected Rust target compiled successfully. Startup smoke check The executable responded to the expected non-processing invocation. Engine status The installed file matches its recorded installation information. Prepared-job validation The Engine understands the submitted processing contract. End-to-end execution The requested workload was actually processed. Output verification The produced artifacts satisfy the applicable output checks.

These checks establish different things.

For example, a normalizer can compile successfully while a particular profile or prepared batch is invalid.

Similarly, a successfully processed source does not automatically establish complete historical market-data coverage.

items.title: When should you rebuild?
items.text:
Rebuild the relevant executable when:

  • Updating Engine code.
  • Switching to a repository revision with relevant Engine changes.
  • Changing the approved build configuration.
  • Repairing a damaged installation.
  • Investigating a suspected binary mismatch.

items.title: When should you investigate the processing configuration?
items.text:
If the installed Engine is verified but normalization rejects a particular job, investigate the processing request.

For example, the issue might involve:

  • An unsupported profile.
  • Missing historical instrument specifications.
  • An invalid prepared batch.
  • Incorrect source metadata.
  • A source-data integrity failure.
  • An unsupported output or merge layout.

Rebuilding the Engine does not automatically correct these problems.

Use the relevant normalization or merge diagnostics to identify the actual failure.

items.title: Repair an Engine Installation
items.text:
Sometimes an installation becomes inconsistent.

For example, the executable might have been modified after installation or the manifest may no longer match the file.

MarketForge is designed to detect these situations.

items.title: Step 1: Inspect the installation
items.text:
Run:

mf engine status

Review the reported state of the affected target.

items.title: Step 2: Identify the problem
items.text:
Common conditions include:

Problem What it means Missing binary The executable was not installed or is no longer present. Missing manifest The recorded installation metadata is unavailable. Checksum mismatch The executable contents differ from the recorded version. Non-executable file The file does not satisfy executable-file requirements. Unsafe symbolic link The managed path fails the safety checks. Invalid manifest The installation metadata is malformed or inconsistent.

items.title: Step 3: Rebuild the target
items.text:
For the normalizer:

mf engine build normalize

For the merger:

mf engine build merge

The managed builder creates a new executable and installation record.

items.title: Step 4: Verify the repaired installation
items.text:
Run:

mf engine status

Confirm that the affected target is now verified.

items.title: Why not manually repair the manifest?
items.text:
The executable and manifest describe one managed installation.

Changing only one can create another mismatch.

Use the build command so that compilation, executable verification, installation, and metadata recording follow the supported process.

items.title: What if installation was interrupted?
items.text:
Although the executable replacement itself is atomic, the binary and manifest are installed as separate filesystem updates.

An interruption between those updates can leave an executable and manifest that do not match.

MarketForge can detect this condition during status inspection.

A new managed build is the supported repair path.

items.title: Troubleshooting Engine Builds
items.text:
Build problems can occur because of missing tools, unavailable dependencies, compiler errors, or installation inconsistencies.

The appropriate solution depends on where the build fails.

items.title: Rust compiler not found
items.text:
Possible cause: Rust is not installed or the compiler is unavailable in your terminal environment.

Check:

rustc --version

And:

cargo --version

Install or configure a compatible Rust toolchain before retrying.

items.title: Unsupported Rust edition
items.text:
Possible cause: The installed Rust compiler is too old to support edition 2024.

MarketForge Engine uses Rust edition 2024.

Inspect the installed version:

rustc --version

Update the toolchain to a compatible version.

items.title: Cargo dependencies cannot be downloaded
items.text:
Possible cause: Network access is unavailable, a dependency source cannot be reached, or required dependencies are missing from the local cache.

Inspect the Cargo error.

If you intentionally require an offline build, use:

mf engine build normalize --offline

However, this succeeds only when the required dependencies are already available locally.

items.title: Offline build fails
items.text:
Possible cause: Cargo cannot find a required dependency in its local sources.

Offline mode does not download missing packages.

You may need to prepare the dependency cache in an environment with network access before attempting the offline build again.

items.title: Cargo reports a lockfile problem
items.text:
Possible cause: The current dependency declarations and lockfile are inconsistent.

Managed builds use --locked.

This prevents the build from silently updating the dependency lockfile.

Inspect the reported dependency or lockfile problem.

Do not remove --locked from the managed build simply to hide an unresolved repository inconsistency.

items.title: Compilation runs out of memory
items.text:
Possible cause: The selected compiler parallelism exceeds available system resources.

Try a smaller job count:

mf engine build normalize --jobs 2

Or:

mf engine build normalize --jobs 1

Reducing parallel compiler jobs can lower memory pressure.

It does not guarantee that every compilation will fit on a resource-constrained machine.

items.title: A custom Cargo target directory is configured
items.text:
MarketForge respects the applicable Cargo build artifact paths.

The managed builder resolves the compiled executable rather than assuming it always appears in one fixed Cargo directory.

The installed executable still goes into the project-local .bin/ directory.

If the build cannot locate the expected output, inspect the selected target and Cargo configuration.

items.title: Cargo is configured for another platform
items.text:
The managed build checks the configured compilation target.

A foreign target is rejected.

This prevents an executable compiled for another platform from being installed as though it were a native MarketForge Engine.

Use a supported native target for the current system.

items.title: The build succeeds but installation fails
items.text:
Possible cause: The startup smoke check, executable installation, workspace permissions, or another managed installation safeguard failed.

Inspect the reported error.

The installer checks the candidate executable before accepting it.

Do not assume that successful Cargo compilation alone means the managed installation succeeded.

items.title: The executable is missing
items.text:
Inspect:

mf engine status

If the normalizer is missing, build it:

mf engine build normalize

For the merger:

mf engine build merge

items.title: Engine status reports a checksum mismatch
items.text:
Possible cause: The installed executable changed after its installation record was written.

Rebuild the affected target using the managed builder.

For example:

mf engine build normalize

Then check the installation again.

items.title: Engine status reports missing metadata
items.text:
Possible cause: The installation manifest is missing or inconsistent.

Use the supported build command to recreate the managed installation.

Do not manually invent checksum values or metadata entries.

items.title: The Engine is verified but normalization fails
items.text:
A verified Engine installation does not guarantee that every processing request is valid.

Inspect the normalization result and the relevant Engine diagnostics.

Possible causes include invalid profiles, missing instrument specifications, unsupported source formats, or data-integrity failures.

See Historical Normalization.

items.title: The merger is installed but rejects a dataset
items.text:
The merger only supports compatible input formats and layouts.

Inspect the merge preparation result and supported compatibility rules.

The presence of a verified merger executable does not make an unsupported input layout eligible.

See Historical Merge.

items.title: Interactive Forge workspace
items.text:
mf tui --testing

The Textual workspace starts in the selected Forge project. It requires interactive stdin, stdout and stderr, and rejects global --json. Production is the default. Use --production to select it explicitly or --testing to select testing. Operations launched inside the UI use the selected verified registry and can write the same managed data and registry state as their CLI counterparts. See Forge workspace for screens and interaction. CLI index

items.title: Configuration and maintenance commands
items.text: Inspect configuration, initialize workspace services, migrate and back up or restore registry state. Workflow and prerequisites · Shared CLI behavior

items.title: mf init
items.text:
mf init [-h] [--testing | --production] [--silent]
Argument or option Parser contract --testing, --production Mutually exclusive. Defaults to production. --silent Default false.

items.title: mf doctor
items.text:
mf doctor [-h] [--testing | --production]
Argument or option Parser contract --testing, --production Mutually exclusive. Defaults to production.

Doctor is a read-only readiness assessment. It checks these areas together and expands the findings that need attention.

Area What Doctor checks Environment Supported Python, workspace root, and application TOML parsed with the Forge settings schema. Omitted configuration uses built-in defaults. Database PostgreSQL connection, expected database name and Forge UUID/purpose, registry metadata, required schemas, migration checksum history, and pending migrations. The inspection uses a read-only transaction with a 10-second connection timeout and 5-second statement and lock timeouts. Rust Engines Managed normalize, merge and convert binaries, installation checksums, and recorded smoke-test evidence when available. Doctor uses the installation inventory without launching a binary. Storage Resolved data root, directory and mount access, and filesystem capacity. A missing directory can report capacity from its nearest existing parent while writability remains unverified. Less than 1 GiB free is a warning. PostgreSQL Tools pg_dump and pg_restore on PATH. Missing tools warn about backup and recovery.

A green ✓ indicates a passed check. Yellow ! indicates a warning, red ✗ indicates a failed check, and ? indicates an unknown result. Dependent database checks remain unknown when an earlier prerequisite blocks inspection. Recommendations use the selected environment and include migration commands only when local history permits them or the registry is cleanly uninitialized.

Readiness Meaning Exit Ready Required checks passed 0 Ready with warnings Required checks passed with nonblocking findings 0 Not ready A required check failed 1 Indeterminate A required check could not be established 1

Invalid CLI usage exits 2. The default environment is production. Use --testing to inspect the testing registry explicitly.

mf doctor | cpout
mf doctor --testing | cpout
mf --json doctor | cpout
mf --json doctor --testing | cpout

JSON retains checked_at, Python and database fields, migration lists, storage observations, PostgreSQL tool availability, and the Engine inventory. It adds environment, project_root, readiness, summary, and the individual checks with stable IDs and status values. Unavailable storage observations use null. Use the individual database checks to interpret an empty migration list when inspection was blocked.

Review Forge application settings, database prerequisites, and managed Engine setup as directed by the report.

items.text: mf config show [-h]

mf database migrate [-h] (--production | --testing)

mf database status [-h] [--testing | --production]
Argument or option Parser contract --testing, --production Mutually exclusive. Defaults to production.

items.title: Application configuration
items.text:
You do not have to use the default application configuration path.

MarketForge supports selecting a configuration file explicitly through the global --config option.

For example:

mf --config ./workspace-settings.toml config show

This loads the application settings from:

./workspace-settings.toml

The option must appear before the main command.

items.title: Why use a separate configuration?
items.text:
You may want different settings for different environments.

For example:

  • A development environment with a small data root.
  • A workstation with a larger local storage directory.
  • A separate research environment with different HTTP limits.

Instead of repeatedly editing one file, you can keep separate application configurations and select the appropriate one when invoking MarketForge.

items.title: JSON output
items.text:
You can inspect the selected configuration in JSON:

mf --config ./workspace-settings.toml --json config show

The result includes the selected public settings and their resolved paths.

Sensitive database credentials are not included.

items.title: Application settings are not acquisition recipes
items.text:
The global --config option selects application settings.

It does not select an acquisition recipe.

For example:

mf acquisition map bybit-btc-20261027 --testing

uses a named acquisition recipe.

Meanwhile:

mf --config ./workspace-settings.toml \
    acquisition map bybit-btc-20261027 \
    --testing

uses the specified application settings while still selecting the named acquisition recipe.

These are two different configuration responsibilities.

items.title: Database
items.text:
Database-backed commands require a valid PostgreSQL connection.

MarketForge keeps database credentials separate from its public application configuration.

This means you should not put PostgreSQL passwords into:

data/.config/forge/marketforge.toml

items.title: Database credentials
items.text:
Production is the default and uses PRODUCTION_DATABASE_KEY. Pass --testing for TEST_DATABASE_KEY, or --production for explicit production selection. The two flags are mutually exclusive.

MarketForge resolves this setting from the environment or the project's supported credentials file:

.secrets/postgres.env

The credential loader checks for a nonempty environment value first.

If that is unavailable, it can read the corresponding value from the credentials file.

If neither supplies a usable value, the command reports a configuration error.

The testing and production connection settings are separate.

MarketForge does not silently replace a missing testing connection with the production database.

items.title: Database identity protection
items.text:
The current testing database is expected to be named:

marketforge_test

MarketForge also checks the recorded database identity when accessing the testing registry.

This protects against accidentally using a database that does not belong to the expected testing environment.

For complete credential setup, see PostgreSQL credentials.

items.title: Check the Database Status
items.text:
Before performing database operations, it is useful to know whether the database is initialized and up to date.

Use:

mf database status --testing

MarketForge connects to the configured testing database and inspects its current state.

items.title: What does the status command check?
items.text:
The result includes information such as:

Information Meaning Database name The PostgreSQL database being inspected. Database identity The recorded MarketForge database identifier. Purpose Whether the database has the expected testing identity. Initialization state Whether the required application metadata exists. Applied migrations Database schema updates already recorded as applied. Pending migrations Schema updates that have not yet been applied.

This helps you determine whether the database is ready for operations that require current registry tables.

items.title: Does checking status modify anything?
items.text:
No.

mf database status inspects the database without applying migrations.

This makes it the appropriate command when you want to understand the database state before changing anything.

items.title: What if the database has pending migrations?
items.text:
Pending migrations mean the database has not yet received all the schema updates required by the current application code.

For example, a newer MarketForge version may introduce additional tables or columns.

The database must be updated before features depending on those changes can work correctly.

Review the pending versions, then use mf database migrate --production or mf database migrate --testing to apply them to the intended registry.

items.title: Update the Database Schema
items.text:
As MarketForge evolves, its database structure may change.

For example, a new feature may require a table for dataset lineage or additional information about historical instrument specifications.

These changes are introduced through database migrations.

items.title: What is a migration?
items.text:
A migration is a controlled update to the database structure.

Instead of requiring users to manually create or modify tables, MarketForge provides migration scripts that are applied in the correct order.

The database records which migrations have already been applied.

This allows MarketForge to identify which updates are still needed.

items.title: Apply pending migrations
items.text:
Run:

mf database migrate --testing

MarketForge checks the existing migration history and applies the required pending core migrations.

The migration process uses database locking and a transaction to protect the schema update.

It also checks migration names and recorded checksums.

items.title: Why are migration checksums important?
items.text:
Suppose a migration was applied previously.

Later, someone changes the original migration file.

If MarketForge silently accepted the modified file as the same migration, the recorded database history might no longer match the source code.

Checksums help detect this kind of inconsistency.

MarketForge checks the migration history before proceeding.

This helps ensure that the database structure is consistent with the expected migration sequence.

items.title: What if the database is already up to date?
items.text:
If all current migrations are already applied, the command reports that there are no pending updates.

You do not need to manually recreate tables.

items.title: Verify the migration result
items.text:
After applying migrations, run:

mf database status --testing

Confirm that there are no pending migrations.

You can also use:

mf doctor --testing | cpout

to inspect additional environment requirements.

items.title: When should I run migrations?
items.text:
Run migrations when:

  • Setting up the MarketForge database for the first time.
  • Updating to a version that introduces schema changes.
  • A command reports missing or outdated database structures.
  • You need to confirm that the registry matches the current code.

For ordinary database preparation, migrations are sufficient.

You do not need to run the complete mf init workflow solely to create or update the database schema.

items.title: What does initialization do?
items.text:
MarketForge provides a command that performs several setup and market-information tasks together:

mf init --testing

This is more than a database initialization command.

items.title: Why does MarketForge collect market information?
items.text:
Suppose you want to work with historical BTCUSDT perpetual data from Bybit.

MarketForge needs information about the instrument, including its market identity and economic specifications.

Supported exchanges provide current instrument information through their APIs.

MarketForge can collect this information and store it in its catalogue.

It also maintains additional evidence used to prepare historical normalization jobs.

The full initialization workflow combines these tasks with database setup and standard ranking updates.

items.title: What happens during initialization?
items.text:
The current initialization workflow performs several stages.

Stage What happens Application directories Creates missing directories required by the application. Database migrations Testing initialization applies pending migrations. Production initialization requires a verified, up-to-date registry. Catalogue collection Retrieves current market metadata from supported exchange APIs. Historical metadata enrichment Adds or updates the supported historical instrument evidence. Rankings Refreshes and publishes standard turnover and volume rankings.

These stages are related, but they solve different problems.

For example, database migrations prepare the registry structure.

Catalogue collection gathers information about markets.

Historical metadata enrichment helps establish the information required for historical processing.

Ranking updates produce market-selection results based on their supported inputs and policies.

items.title: Initialization can contact external exchanges
items.text:
Because initialization collects current market information, it can make network requests.

It requires access to the supported provider endpoints involved in that collection.

It may also take longer than a simple database migration because it performs multiple operations.

Do not use mf init when you only need to inspect the configuration or apply database migrations.

Use the narrower command for the task you actually need.

items.title: Initialization does not download historical archives
items.text:
The initialization workflow is concerned with application setup, market metadata, historical instrument evidence, and rankings.

It is not a replacement for historical archive acquisition.

If you want to download BTCUSDT trades and order-book archives, use the acquisition commands.

For example:

mf acquisition download bybit-btc-20261027 --testing

This assumes the named acquisition recipe already exists.

See Historical Data Acquisition for the full workflow.

items.title: What If Initialization Is Incomplete?
items.text:
Initialization involves several independent operations.

For example, database migrations may succeed while a later exchange metadata request fails.

MarketForge can retain successfully completed work even when the overall initialization result is incomplete.

items.title: A failed stage does not undo everything
items.text:
Suppose initialization performs:

Application directories       Complete
Database migrations           Complete
Catalogue collection          Complete
Historical metadata           Failed
Rankings                      Not completed

This is an illustrative sequence, not a reproduced run result.

The earlier successful stages may have already changed the application state.

You should not assume that an unsuccessful initialization automatically rolls back every completed operation.

items.title: Inspect the failing stage
items.text:
Review the initialization result.

Identify the stage that failed and read its reported error.

For example, the problem might involve:

  • Database permissions.
  • Network access to an exchange.
  • Missing or conflicting market metadata.
  • Incomplete historical specification evidence.
  • Ranking prerequisites.

The appropriate next step depends on the actual failure.

items.title: Should you run initialization again?
items.text:
You can repeat initialization, but understand what it does.

A repeated run may collect newer market observations and publish new ranking snapshots.

It is not necessarily a no-op.

If only the database schema needs updating, use mf database migrate --production or mf database migrate --testing.

If only a particular market needs a metadata refresh, inspect the supported market-management commands rather than assuming the full initialization workflow is necessary.

items.title: Initialization exit codes
items.text:
The current initialization command uses these outcomes:

Exit code Meaning 0 The overall initialization completed successfully. 1 Initialization was unsuccessful or incomplete. 130 The operation was cancelled through the handled interruption path.

For an incomplete result, inspect the individual stage information before retrying.

items.title: Why Is Database Restoration Restricted?
items.text:
Restoring a database is potentially destructive.

A careless restore could overwrite existing registry information or cause a database to refer to the wrong filesystem artifacts.

MarketForge therefore restricts the current restore workflow to a new, explicitly disposable testing database.

It does not overwrite your existing testing database.

This is useful when you want to:

  • Verify that a backup can be restored.
  • Inspect an older registry state.
  • Test database migrations against restored information.
  • Investigate a problem without changing the original registry.

items.title: What does disposable mean?
items.text:
A disposable database is a separate database created for temporary or controlled testing.

For example:

marketforge_test

may be your existing testing registry.

A restored copy might use a different name:

marketforge_restore_a1b2c3d4

These are separate PostgreSQL databases.

The restore command requires the destination to be new.

It refuses to overwrite an existing destination.

items.title: What Happens During Restoration?
items.text:
MarketForge checks the supplied backup before restoring it.

The workflow includes several important safeguards.

items.title: Verify the backup
items.text:
MarketForge checks that the backup is complete and that the expected backup files and configuration checksums are valid.

A damaged or incomplete backup is not treated as a valid restore source.

items.title: Check the destination
items.text:
MarketForge requires a fresh destination database.

If the destination already exists, the operation refuses to overwrite it.

This protects existing databases from accidental replacement.

items.title: Restore the registry
items.text:
MarketForge creates the disposable destination and restores the registry data using PostgreSQL restore functionality.

The registry restoration is performed within the supported restore transaction.

items.title: Establish a new database identity
items.text:
After restoration, MarketForge checks the restored testing identity and assigns a fresh database UUID.

This allows the restored database to be distinguished from the original source database.

items.title: What happens to configuration files?
items.text:
The backup's configuration snapshot remains in the backup directory.

It is not automatically copied into the active application configuration.

Review the backed-up settings before choosing whether to reuse them.

This prevents an old configuration from silently replacing your current workspace settings.

items.title: What happens to raw archives and datasets?
items.text:
They are not recreated by the database restore.

The restored registry may contain references to files from the original workspace.

Those files must exist and remain consistent with the restored metadata before the corresponding data operations can work as expected.

items.title: What if restoration fails?
items.text:
A failed restore can leave the new disposable database available for inspection.

Do not assume that every unsuccessful restore automatically removes all created resources.

Review the reported error and inspect the destination before deciding whether to retry.

For a new clean attempt, choose another unused destination name.

items.title: Which Commands Change State?
items.text:
Not every maintenance command performs the same type of work.

Command Database access Network access Can change state config show No No No database status Yes No No database migrate Yes No Yes doctor Yes No No init Yes Yes Yes database backup Yes No Writes backup files database restore Yes No Creates and restores a new database engine status No No No

The table describes the main external-service and state-changing behavior of these commands.

For example, init may contact supported providers for metadata collection, while database migrate operates on PostgreSQL without performing exchange discovery.

Similarly, database backup does not change the source registry but creates real files on disk.

items.title: JSON output
items.text:
The relevant maintenance commands support global JSON output.

For example:

mf --json database status --testing

mf --json init --testing

mf --json config show

The global --json option must appear before the command name.

JSON output can be useful for diagnostics and automation.

Do not include credentials or private database connection strings in published logs.

items.title: The application cannot find PostgreSQL credentials
items.text:
Possible cause: The required testing database URL is missing or empty.

Check that the supported testing credential key is configured:

TEST_DATABASE_KEY

Review the environment and the project's private credentials file.

Do not paste the connection string into public issue reports or documentation.

See PostgreSQL credentials.

items.title: The testing database identity is rejected
items.text:
Possible cause: The selected database does not have the required name or recorded testing identity.

Inspect:

mf database status --testing

Confirm that the configured connection points to the intended testing database.

Do not bypass the identity check by modifying database metadata manually.

items.title: The database has pending migrations
items.text:
Possible cause: The current application expects schema updates that have not yet been applied.

Run:

mf database migrate --testing

Then inspect:

mf database status --testing

items.title: A migration fails
items.text:
Possible cause: Database permissions, a conflicting schema state, or an inconsistent migration history.

Inspect the reported migration error.

MarketForge validates migration names and checksums.

Do not rewrite previously applied migration files or remove migration-history records merely to make the command succeed.

Investigate the mismatch before retrying.

items.title: Doctor reports an unwritable storage location
items.text:
Possible cause: The current user cannot write to the inspected storage directory or its nearest existing parent.

Inspect the configured data root:

mf config show

Check the filesystem permissions and available space.

If necessary, configure an appropriate data root.

items.title: Doctor reports missing PostgreSQL tools
items.text:
Possible cause: pg_dump or pg_restore is not available in the environment.

These tools are required for the corresponding backup and restore operations.

Install the appropriate PostgreSQL client utilities for your environment and rerun Doctor.

items.title: Initialization cannot contact an exchange
items.text:
Possible cause: Network access, provider availability, rate limits, or another provider-specific failure.

Review the initialization stage results.

Check which exchange or scope failed rather than assuming the entire catalogue is unavailable.

Completed stages may have retained useful information.

items.title: Initialization reports incomplete historical metadata
items.text:
Possible cause: The required historical instrument evidence could not be established for one or more scopes.

Inspect the enrichment result and its recorded reasons.

Do not invent historical contract values or extend specification validity without evidence.

Where appropriate, supply verified historical declarations through the catalogue workflow.

items.title: Initialization rankings fail
items.text:
Possible cause: Required market observations, conversion information, or ranking-policy conditions were not satisfied.

Inspect the ranking results independently from database migration and catalogue collection.

A ranking failure does not automatically mean earlier initialization stages failed.

See Markets and Rankings.

items.title: Backup destination already exists
items.text:
Possible cause: The backup command requires a new destination directory.

Choose an unused backup location.

Do not overwrite an existing backup without first reviewing and preserving it.

items.title: Backup is incomplete
items.text:
Possible cause: The backup process was interrupted or failed.

Do not assume that the presence of registry.dump alone means the backup is valid.

Review the completion result and manifest.

Use a new destination for a clean retry.

items.title: Restore destination is rejected
items.text:
Possible cause: The destination already exists or does not follow the required disposable testing naming format.

Choose a fresh name such as:

marketforge_restore_a1b2c3d4

The suffix must contain 8–32 lowercase hexadecimal characters.

items.title: Restore fails after creating a database
items.text:
Possible cause: A restore or verification step failed after the destination database was created.

The disposable database may remain available for inspection.

Review the error and destination state before retrying.

Do not assume an unsuccessful restore automatically removes every created resource.
