items.title: Supported Exchanges
items.text:
The current market-discovery workflow supports five cryptocurrency exchanges.

Exchange CLI identifier Binance binance Bybit bybit OKX okx Gate.io gateio Bitget bitget

MarketForge supports several market categories within these exchanges.

items.title: Supported market categories
items.text:
Category Description spot Direct trading of supported assets. linear Derivative markets using the applicable linear contract conventions. inverse Derivative markets using the applicable inverse contract conventions.

These categories describe market structure.

They are not identical to instrument types.

For example, a linear market can contain perpetual contracts and dated futures.

items.title: Current collection coverage
items.text:
Exchange Spot Linear Inverse Binance Spot Perpetuals and dated futures Perpetuals and dated futures Bybit Spot Perpetuals and dated futures Perpetuals and dated futures OKX Spot Swaps and futures Swaps and futures Gate.io Spot Perpetuals and delivery contracts Perpetuals only Bitget Spot Perpetuals and delivery contracts when listed Not collected

When no filters are provided, MarketForge collects all 14 currently supported exchange/market scopes.

There are five exchanges and three market categories, but Bitget inverse is excluded.

items.title: What about options?
items.text:
Options are not currently collected through this market-discovery workflow.

This does not mean MarketForge's broader catalogue has no concept of options.

It means the current automatic markets sync and markets refresh adapters do not include options collection.

items.title: What about expired futures?
items.text:
The current exchange endpoints do not necessarily provide a complete history of every expired contract.

MarketForge retains known historical instrument records rather than assuming that an instrument has ceased to exist simply because it is absent from a current API response.

However, the current market API does not establish an exhaustive historical futures catalogue.

Additional historical evidence may be required for old contracts.

See Instrument Discovery.

items.title: Exchange-Specific Statistic Differences
items.text:
The following examples illustrate why MarketForge preserves native measurement units.

Exchange / market Interpretation Binance spot and linear Reported quote volume provides monetary turnover; base volume remains separate. Binance inverse Uses native quote turnover when available, otherwise supported contract-value calculations. Bybit spot and linear turnover24h is quote-denominated; volume24h is base-denominated. Bybit inverse volume24h supplies quote turnover, while turnover24h supplies base quantity. OKX spot volCcy24h and vol24h are interpreted according to the spot mapping. OKX linear Base quantity multiplied by last price can provide an explicitly estimated turnover. OKX inverse Contract count and verified quote face value can establish monetary turnover. Gate.io Uses the supported spot or derivative turnover fields and retains native volume units. Bitget Uses the applicable product-specific turnover fields, including Reality-market distinctions.

These mappings describe the current supported statistic interpretation.

They should not be generalized to every possible endpoint or instrument offered by a provider.

items.title: Why not normalize all statistics immediately?
items.text:
Some conversions require additional evidence.

For example, turning contract volume into BTC quantity requires the appropriate contract specification.

Comparing USDC turnover with USDT turnover requires an explicit currency-conversion rule.

MarketForge therefore retains native measurements and their interpretation information.

Ranking policies perform the supported comparison using explicitly defined rules.

items.title: Open interest and funding
items.text:
Open interest can be reported in:

Base units
Quote units
Contracts

depending on the provider and market.

Funding rates are optional and apply to relevant perpetual products.

MarketForge does not invent missing funding values for dated futures.

A missing statistic remains missing.

items.title: What Happens During a Partial Standard Update?
items.text:
A standard update can contain several independent outcomes.

For example:

Statistics Refresh     Partial

Turnover Ranking       Published
Volume Ranking         Failed

This is an illustrative result.

items.title: Does one ranking failure undo the other?
items.text:
No.

The standard policies are published independently.

A successful ranking publication can remain available even when another policy fails.

items.title: What happens to older snapshots?
items.text:
Existing published snapshots are not rewritten.

A failed new build does not delete an older successful snapshot.

items.title: Why can the overall command return a failure code?
items.text:
The update operation reports the completeness of the combined workflow.

If statistics refresh or ranking publication is incomplete, the overall result can be partial.

This may return a nonzero exit code even when one ranking was successfully published.

items.title: How should I inspect the result?
items.text:
Look at:

  • Overall update status.
  • Statistics refresh result.
  • Failed exchange scopes.
  • Turnover publication outcome.
  • Volume publication outcome.
  • Returned snapshot UUIDs.

Do not assume a nonzero exit means every independent operation was rolled back.

items.title: Snapshot deletion
items.text:
MarketForge preserves published rankings because they represent historical observations evaluated under specific policies.

However, you may eventually want to remove snapshots.

For example:

  • You created a ranking while testing a policy.
  • A snapshot is no longer needed.
  • A temporary research ranking should be cleaned up.
  • You want to remove obsolete stored ranking evidence.

MarketForge provides an explicit deletion workflow.

items.title: Why is deletion guarded?
items.text:
A ranking snapshot may be referenced by another managed operation.

For example, a historical processing job might record the ranking UUID used to select or order streams.

Deleting that snapshot could remove information needed to explain the processing decision.

MarketForge therefore checks concrete dependencies before allowing removal.

items.title: What can block deletion?
items.text:
A snapshot may be protected by:

  • Registered historical jobs.
  • Dataset references.
  • Retained managed job artifacts.
  • Other supported concrete dependencies.

A referenced snapshot is not silently deleted.

items.title: Preview Snapshot Deletion
items.text: Before applying deletion, inspect the selected snapshots.

items.title: Preview one snapshot
items.text:
Use its UUID:

mf markets rank delete SNAPSHOT_UUID --testing

Replace SNAPSHOT_UUID with an actual snapshot identifier.

items.title: Preview snapshots for one policy
items.text:
For example:

mf markets rank delete activity --testing

This selects the published snapshots belonging to the policy named activity.

items.title: Preview all ranking snapshots
items.text:
Use:

mf markets rank delete --all --testing

This selects all ranking snapshots, including drafts.

items.title: Important: the selectors mean different things
items.text:
Selector What it selects Snapshot UUID Exactly one matching snapshot, including a draft. Policy name All published snapshots belonging to that policy. --all All snapshots, including drafts.

Exactly one selector is required.

items.title: Does preview delete anything?
items.text:
No.

Without --apply, the command performs a nondeleting preview.

The result reports the selected snapshots and whether they are eligible for deletion.

items.title: Why inspect exact UUIDs?
items.text:
A policy name can refer to several published snapshots.

If you only intend to remove one, use its UUID.

This avoids accidentally selecting an entire policy's snapshot history.

items.title: Apply Snapshot Deletion
items.text:
Once you have reviewed the selection, you can explicitly apply deletion.

For one snapshot:

mf markets rank delete SNAPSHOT_UUID \
    --testing \
    --apply

For all published snapshots of a policy:

mf markets rank delete activity \
    --testing \
    --apply

items.title: Does MarketForge ask for confirmation?
items.text:
The current ranking deletion command does not use an interactive confirmation prompt.

The explicit --apply option authorizes the operation.

Review the selected targets carefully before using it.

items.title: Does apply use a saved preview file?
items.text:
No.

Unlike managed raw-storage deletion, ranking snapshot deletion does not require a saved preview artifact.

The command resolves the selected snapshots again when applying deletion.

items.title: Why does this matter?
items.text:
Suppose you preview all snapshots of a policy.

Then another process publishes a new snapshot before you run --apply.

When you apply deletion by policy name, the selection is resolved again.

That new snapshot may now be included.

items.title: How can I avoid this?
items.text:
Use exact snapshot UUIDs when you want to remove specific known entries.

For example:

mf markets rank delete SNAPSHOT_UUID --testing --apply

This is more precise than deleting by policy name or using --all.

items.title: What happens if some snapshots are protected?
items.text:
A mixed selection may contain eligible and blocked snapshots.

MarketForge can delete eligible snapshots while retaining protected ones.

The result reports the blocked entries.

The overall command may return a nonzero exit code.

items.title: Does deletion remove the policy TOML?
items.text:
No.

Deleting ranking snapshots does not delete the corresponding policy file.

It also does not remove:

  • The instrument catalogue.
  • Retained market observations.
  • Raw acquisition files.
  • Registered datasets.
  • Historical archive records.

The operation targets the selected ranking snapshots and their owned ranking evidence.

items.title: Market Command Options
items.text: Option Meaning --testing Select the guarded testing database. --exchange Restrict to supported exchange codes; repeatable. --market Restrict to spot, linear, or inverse categories; repeatable. --instrument Select an exact native symbol. --base-asset Exact case-insensitive base-asset filter for list. --quote-asset Exact case-insensitive quote-asset filter for list. --match Case-insensitive full-symbol glob for list. --sort Select list ordering by identity, turnover, or freshness. --limit Maximum number of stored list results. --silent Suppress supported progress displays while retaining final output.

items.title: Important scope differences
items.text:
sync and refresh use exchange, market, and exact-symbol selection.

They do not support the same asset and glob filters as list.

markets list does not provide an --instrument-type option.

Use the returned instrument type information and supported identity filters.

items.title: Collection limits
items.text:
The parser accepts hidden --limit and --sort options on some collection commands.

However, these do not limit or sort the actual network collection.

Do not rely on them for controlling the number of instruments collected.

items.title: Ranking Limits and Options
items.text:
Every ranking subcommand accepts the supported --silent and --limit options.

The default limit is:

50

The accepted range is:

1–10000

However, the limit has different meanings for different commands.

Command Meaning of limit rank list Number of returned snapshot entries. rank show Maximum human-displayed included or excluded rows. rank build Does not narrow the evaluated universe. rank update Does not narrow the statistics refresh or policy evaluation. rank delete Does not narrow the deletion target selection.

items.title: Important: --all depends on the command
items.text:
For rank show:

--all

removes human row limits.

For rank delete:

--all

selects all ranking snapshots, including drafts.

These are different operations.

Do not confuse them.

items.title: JSON Output
items.text:
The global JSON option is available for market and ranking operations.

For example:

mf --json markets list --testing

mf --json markets show bybit.spot.BTCUSDT --testing

mf --json markets rank list --testing

mf --json markets rank show activity --testing

items.title: Why use JSON?
items.text:
JSON can be useful for:

  • Inspecting full instrument metadata.
  • Saving market collection results.
  • Examining observation timestamps.
  • Extracting ranking UUIDs.
  • Inspecting conversion evidence.
  • Comparing published snapshots.
  • Automating diagnostics.

items.title: Important details
items.text:
Global --json must appear before markets.

For market lists, the configured result limit still applies.

For ranking inspection, JSON returns all matching entries regardless of the human show limit.

Decimal quantities are represented as strings where required to preserve precision.

Missing values remain null rather than being converted into zero.

items.title: Global application options
items.text:
The relevant global options include:

--json
--project-root PATH
--config PATH

These appear before the main command.

For example:

mf --config ./workspace-settings.toml \
    --json markets list --testing

The global --config selects application settings.

It does not select a ranking policy.

Ranking policies are selected by their managed names.

items.title: Which Commands Change State?
items.text:
The market commands have different effects.

Command Contacts exchanges Writes database records markets sync Yes Yes markets refresh Yes Yes markets list No No markets show No No markets rank new No Creates a local TOML file markets rank validate No No markets rank build No Yes markets rank list No No markets rank show No No markets rank update Yes Yes markets rank delete preview No No markets rank delete --apply No Yes

The table describes the main state-changing behavior.

For example, rank build reads retained observations and publishes a new snapshot without contacting providers.

Meanwhile, rank update includes a new global statistics refresh.

items.title: Exit Codes
items.text:
The market and ranking commands use the common MarketForge CLI exit behavior.

Code Meaning 0 The operation or inspection completed successfully. 1 Partial collection, incomplete standard update, or blocked snapshot deletion. 2 Command, configuration, database, identity, validation, or setup error handled by the CLI. 130 Handled cancellation or interruption.

items.title: Important: partial results may contain successful work
items.text:
For example, a statistics refresh can fail on one scope while successfully updating another.

Similarly, a standard ranking update can publish one policy while another fails.

Inspect the structured result before retrying.

items.title: JSON errors
items.text:
When global JSON output is enabled, handled CLI errors are reported through stderr.

Partial collection results can be returned as structured JSON on stdout with a nonzero exit code.

For scripts, preserve the command's exit status when piping output.

items.title: Depth Layout Compatibility
items.text:
Order-book data has additional requirements.

A depth event may depend on a previously reconstructed book state.

For example:

Snapshot
   |
   v
Update
   |
   v
Update
   |
   v
Update

If the merger starts reading from the middle without the required initialization state, the resulting book history may not be interpretable.

items.title: Why does a snapshot matter?
items.text:
A snapshot establishes a known book state.

Later incremental updates modify that state.

Without the required snapshot or another supported initialization boundary, the updates may not provide enough information to reconstruct the book.

items.title: Why does a depth publication have auxiliary files?
items.text:
Normalized depth publications may contain information such as:

Artifact Purpose Event index Connects observations to canonical row ranges. Boundary information Records initialization and source-boundary states. Reconstruction segments Identifies portions of the history and their ordering requirements. Source information Preserves the relevant input and contribution details.

The merger may need this information to preserve valid depth interpretation.

items.title: What is segmented depth?
items.text:
Some depth publications contain multiple reconstruction segments.

For example, a recording may require a new snapshot after a discontinuity or source transition.

These segments cannot always be treated as one uninterrupted book history.

The merge ordering must preserve the relevant segment dependencies.

This is one reason prepared merges containing segmented depth may use causal timeline ordering.

items.title: Can I merge only one depth Parquet part?
items.text:
Not necessarily.

A particular depth layout may require all its primary parts or additional publication-level information.

Selecting one file without its dependencies can make reconstruction impossible.

The merger checks these requirements before processing.

items.title: Does merging repair missing order-book updates?
items.text:
No.

A merge does not create missing source events or prove continuity that the source did not establish.

If a normalized depth publication contains independently initialized histories, the merged output must preserve the relevant limitations rather than present them as one verified continuous book.

items.title: What Does Merge Preparation Verify?
items.text:
Before processing, Forge and Rust perform checks against the selected files and publication evidence.

These checks can include:

  • Active registered file identities.
  • File paths and checksums.
  • Owning publication manifests.
  • Publication fingerprints.
  • Stream identities.
  • Content types.
  • Instrument namespace.
  • Requested time interval.
  • Supported physical layout.
  • Required depth reconstruction information.
  • Prepared job compatibility.

These checks help prevent an invalid selection from reaching execution.

items.title: What preparation does not prove
items.text:
Preparation cannot establish that every historical market event exists in the source data.

For example, two files may overlap the requested interval and pass all applicable structural checks while still containing an independently unverified historical gap.

Merge compatibility and historical completeness are different questions.

The first determines whether the files can be processed together.

The second concerns whether the source data contains the full intended market history.

items.title: How Forge Verifies a Merge
items.text: After Rust Engine commits the merge publication, Forge verifies the result before registering it.

items.title: Why is verification necessary?
items.text:
A file existing on disk does not automatically mean it is a completed, valid merge output.

For example, an interrupted process may leave incomplete artifacts.

Similarly, a publication may be inconsistent with its recorded job or source checksums.

Forge therefore checks the committed output and its retained evidence.

items.title: What does verification establish?
items.text:
The supported verification includes the committed physical Parquet output and relevant byte fingerprints.

It also checks the applicable publication and input evidence required by the merge registration contract.

items.title: Does verification rerun normalization?
items.text:
No.

The merge verification works with the selected normalized publications and their recorded evidence.

It does not decode the original exchange archives again.

items.title: Does verification prove historical completeness?
items.text:
No.

It verifies the applicable merge output.

It does not independently establish that the source exchanges supplied every market event during the requested interval.

items.title: What Happens When a Merge Fails?
items.text:
A merge can fail at different stages.

For example:

  • File selection may be ambiguous.
  • A required input may be missing.
  • Rust may reject an unsupported publication layout.
  • Processing may fail because of resource limits.
  • Publication verification may fail.
  • PostgreSQL registration may fail after Engine commits the output.

These problems require different responses.

items.title: Preparation failure
items.text:
A preparation failure means Forge could not create an eligible executable job.

Inspect the preparation report.

The issue may involve missing inputs, source provenance, publication selection, or compatibility.

items.title: Execution failure
items.text:
An execution failure occurs while Engine is processing the selected files.

Inspect the execution report and Rust diagnostics.

A failed job may leave temporary or incomplete output artifacts.

Do not treat them as completed datasets.

items.title: Registration failure
items.text:
A registration failure can occur after Engine successfully commits a valid publication.

The output may remain available for registration-only recovery.

This is an important distinction because the merge itself may not need to be repeated.

items.title: Find Merge Execution Reports
items.text:
MarketForge retains reports for managed merge operations.

A merge execution report is stored under the configured run directory.

For example:

data/runs/merge-execute-*/execution-result.json

The actual path is reported by the operation.

items.title: What does the report contain?
items.text:
The report distinguishes the relevant stages:

Stage What it describes Execution Whether Rust Engine completed the merge. Verification Whether the committed output passed the required checks. Registration Whether the verified output was recorded in PostgreSQL.

It can also include output file locations, registered IDs, and failure information.

items.title: Why inspect the report before retrying?
items.text:
Imagine that Engine successfully processed a large dataset but PostgreSQL registration failed.

Rerunning the entire merge may be unnecessary.

The report helps determine whether the committed publication can be recovered directly.

Similarly, if Engine rejected the input layout before processing, retrying without changing the selection is unlikely to help.

Use the reported failed stage to decide what needs to be corrected.

items.title: Recover a Completed Merge Without Rerunning
items.text:
MarketForge separates Engine publication from PostgreSQL registration.

This means a merge can successfully publish its files even when a later database operation fails.

For example, a power interruption could occur after the output was committed but before its registration completed.

items.title: Why is registration-only recovery useful?
items.text:
Merging large datasets can require substantial processing time.

If the output already exists and remains valid, repeating the full operation may waste resources.

MarketForge therefore provides a command for verifying and registering an existing committed merge publication.

items.title: Recover from an execution intent
items.text:
Use:

mf merge register \
    data/runs/MERGE_EXECUTION_ID/execution-intent.json \
    --testing

Replace the placeholder with the actual execution directory reported by your run.

The intent records information about the submitted operation and its output.

MarketForge uses that information to locate and verify eligible committed files.

items.title: Recover from a publication directory
items.text:
You can also provide a committed publication directory:

mf merge register \
    data/datasets/merged/ENGINE_JOB_ID \
    --testing

Replace ENGINE_JOB_ID with the actual output identity.

items.title: Recover from a manifest
items.text:
A committed manifest can also be used:

mf merge register \
    /absolute/path/to/merged-publication/manifest.json \
    --testing

items.title: Recover one primary file
items.text:
If you need to register one specific committed primary file, provide its path:

mf merge register /absolute/path/to/part-000000.parquet --testing

items.title: Does recovery rerun the merger?
items.text:
No.

Registration-only recovery verifies and registers existing committed output.

It does not repeat the Rust merge workload.

items.title: What does recovery verify?
items.text:
The operation rechecks the relevant committed output and required input lineage.

This prevents an incomplete or inconsistent publication from being registered merely because its files exist.

items.title: What if the publication is already registered?
items.text:
An identical registration retry can reuse the existing database identity.

Conflicting evidence or identity information is not silently overwritten.

items.title: What if the merge never completed publication?
items.text:
Registration-only recovery cannot convert an incomplete staging directory into a valid committed publication.

If Engine failed before committing the output, investigate the failure and prepare or execute new work as appropriate.

items.title: Recipe Names and Paths
items.text:
Managed merge recipes are stored under:

data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/merge/

You can use their names directly:

mf merge validate manual_merge

Or:

mf merge run manual_merge --testing

You can also use an explicit TOML path for supported recipe actions other than new.

For example:

mf merge validate ./my-merge.toml

And:

mf merge run ./my-merge.toml --testing

items.title: Why does new require a managed name?
items.text:
The new command creates a recipe inside the managed merge configuration library.

It is not an arbitrary-file writing command.

This keeps managed recipe creation predictable.

items.title: What about prepared JSON?
items.text:
A prepared JSON job can be submitted directly through run.

It must satisfy the current job contract, including its concrete selected-file and stream information.

For example, prepared file entries must contain the applicable stream_id, stream_rank, and content_type information required by the current contract.

They must also match active registered inputs and their pinned publications.

Older prepared submissions may need to be regenerated.

For ordinary workflows, use mf merge prepare to create the current job format.

items.title: JSON Output
items.text:
Merge commands support global JSON output.

For example:

mf --json merge validate manual_merge

mf --json merge prepare manual_merge --testing

mf --json merge run manual_merge --testing

The global --json option must appear before merge.

items.title: Why use JSON?
items.text:
JSON output is useful when:

  • Inspecting detailed preparation results.
  • Saving merge execution reports.
  • Working with scripts.
  • Extracting registered file IDs.
  • Investigating failures.
  • Building repeatable research workflows.

items.title: Save a merge result
items.text:
For example:

mf --json merge run manual_merge --testing > merge-result.json

This saves the structured result to a local file.

Do not combine global JSON output with the interactive TUI.

items.title: Which Commands Change State?
items.text:
The merge commands have different effects.

Command Uses PostgreSQL Executes merging Writes files merge new NAME No No Creates a recipe merge new --from-normalize Yes No Creates a recipe and may retain selection information merge validate No No No normal processing output merge prepare Yes No Writes a prepared job and report merge run Yes Yes Writes a merge publication and reports merge register Yes No Can update registration records and recovery evidence

The table describes the main effects of each operation.

For example, prepare can read and verify selected input files without executing the merge.

Similarly, register performs verification and database registration but does not rerun the Rust merger.

items.title: Normalization commands
items.text: Start with Normalize historical data. Use this reference for command effects and options. See recipe fields and the prepared batch contract for input formats.

items.title: Synopsis and arguments
items.text:
Commands below follow mf normalize. NAME is a managed recipe name with an optional .toml suffix. Where a TOML path is accepted, use an absolute or directory-qualified path such as ./recipe.toml.

Command Arguments and options PostgreSQL Main effect new NAME [--from-acquisition SOURCE] No Create a draft or copy, open the editor, and validate the saved TOML. edit NAME No Open the saved recipe and validate after editing. list None No Read the local recipe inventory and structural status. show NAME No Show the parsed configuration and declared inputs. validate NAME_OR_TOML No Check TOML and recipe constraints. delete NAME [--apply [--force]] No Preview or unlink a managed recipe. prepare NAME_OR_TOML [--dry-run] [--from-acquisition SOURCE] Yes Resolve registered inputs. A persisted plan writes artifacts and validates executable plans with Rust. execute NAME_OR_TOML [--dry-run] [--tui] [--allow-partial] Yes Prepare, execute, verify, and register. Dry run stops at planning. run REFERENCE [--tui] [--allow-partial] Yes Execute a recipe or submit prepared batch JSON. register REFERENCE Yes Verify committed output and register its primary files. config show\|get\|schema\|validate\|set\|unset\|edit No Inspect, validate, or change the Engine runtime. profiles Subcommand and arguments Varies Inspect, author, compile, or install normalization profiles.

For registry-backed commands, choose --testing or --production (the default). Keep the same registry for selection, execution, registration, and inspection. Recipe and processing commands use local files and registered evidence with no upstream archive or market API calls. Profile operations have their own requirements.

items.title: mf normalize new
items.text:
Create and open a new managed recipe. The command refuses to overwrite an existing recipe. --from-acquisition SOURCE copies a managed acquisition recipe's TOML into the normalization library. This is an independent copy. Post-edit validation checks only the saved structure. If validation fails, fix the saved draft with edit.

mf normalize new my_dataset

items.title: List, show, edit, and validate
items.text:
mf normalize list | cpout
mf normalize show my_dataset | cpout
mf normalize edit my_dataset
mf normalize validate my_dataset | cpout

list reports invalid entries alongside valid recipes. show displays declared source requests or explicit inputs. edit uses the configured editor and rechecks the file when the editor exits successfully. validate accepts a managed name or explicit TOML path and checks local fields and constraints. Registered file availability, identity resolution, and Rust batch validation belong to preparation.

items.title: Delete a recipe
items.text:
mf normalize delete my_dataset | cpout

Preview inspects the managed file and checks live references from source-derived merge and conversion recipes. It lists recipes it could not inspect. Detected references block deletion by default. To remove the TOML after reviewing the preview, use mf normalize delete my_dataset --apply. To deliberately break the listed references, use --apply --force. The command accepts only a regular, single-link managed recipe file and rechecks its identity before unlinking. Raw archives, normalized and merged datasets, registered publications, historical runs, reports, and installed profiles are outside the deletion scope.

items.title: Engine runtime configuration
items.text:
mf normalize config manages data/.config/engine/normalize.toml. Recipes select data and profiles specify how to decode it. The runtime controls Engine behavior.

mf normalize config show --section resources | cpout
mf normalize config schema --field resources.workers | cpout
mf normalize config set resources.workers 12 | cpout

set and unset preview by default and require --apply to save. edit validates a draft before asking for confirmation. See Normalization runtime configuration for field semantics, defaults, and integrity acknowledgement.

items.title: mf normalize prepare
items.text:
mf normalize prepare my_dataset --testing --dry-run | cpout
mf normalize prepare my_dataset --testing | cpout

A dry run resolves registry and local-file evidence and previews job, task and stream counts. It can use the Engine to check an external source's profile fingerprint. It skips Rust batch validation and returns prospective batch and report locations. Persisted preparation writes the batch and report and, for a prepared plan, runs the production Rust batch validator. A saved partial plan is diagnostic and cannot be submitted. See preparation results.

prepare NAME --from-acquisition SOURCE first creates a managed copy and opens the editor, then prepares the saved recipe. Even with --dry-run, this shortcut still creates and edits that recipe. Use a new managed name for this mode.

items.title: mf normalize execute
items.text:
mf normalize execute my_dataset --testing

Accepts a managed recipe name or explicit TOML path. It performs persisted preparation and starts execution only after a fully prepared result. Use --dry-run for planning only. Use --tui on a terminal to show Engine progress. TUI requires interactive stdin, stdout and stderr and is incompatible with global --json.

items.title: mf normalize run
items.text: run can execute a recipe like execute, or submit a prepared JSON batch without repeating recipe selection. Submitted JSON still goes through Rust batch validation, raw-input checks, execution, verification and registration. Use a directory-qualified path to resolve an ambiguity between a local file and a managed recipe name. Existing explicit files are identified as JSON from their opening content, rather than by filename suffix alone. See manual batch submission for a complete example.

items.title: Execution status and partial results
items.text:
Engine completion, output commit, verification, and registry registration are separate stages. Use normalization, verification, registration, and per-job outcomes in the retained execution result. status = "complete" means the managed execution verified and registered the eligible outputs for the completed batch. Manifest integrity describes processing quality, including degraded evidence, and is separate from successful registration or historical coverage.

For execute and run, the default withholds automatic registration when any job fails, even if other jobs committed valid outputs. --allow-partial permits automatic registration of successful jobs only when the Engine returns definitive outcomes for the whole batch, at least one output is verified, and registration succeeds. A verification failure still blocks registration. The resulting overall status is partial. This flag does not permit partial preparation or incomplete staging output.

The result points to the retained execution report, Engine outcome and execution intent. Use the run history for the logical run ID, publication evidence for integrity and lineage, and dataset inspection for registered file IDs.

items.title: mf normalize register
items.text:
Use the original registry. Registration verifies existing committed output and writes registration receipts. It uses the Engine's output validator and does not run normalization jobs.

Reference Result Retained execution-intent.json Recheck the submitted batch fingerprint and registry identity, verify eligible committed job outputs against the retained evidence, and register them. Keep the sibling submitted-batch.json and execution evidence. Publication directory or its manifest.json Verify the committed publication and register its eligible primary files. Canonical primary Parquet path Resolve and verify its owning publication, then register the selected primary file. 
mf normalize register PATH_TO_EXECUTION_INTENT --testing | cpout

Replace the path with the retained execution-intent.json shown by the result. An explicit registration retry can register a verified subset of committed jobs. Inspect which outputs survived before recovery. When no usable publication was committed, fix the execution problem and prepare a fresh attempt. Registration recovery can reuse existing matching registrations. See publication recovery.

items.title: Profile commands
items.text:
A normalization profile describes source interpretation. A normalization recipe selects registered inputs. Use the profile authoring guide and profile reference for authoring, validation, and installation. Run mf normalize profiles --help for the full subcommand inventory.

mf normalize profiles list | cpout
mf normalize profiles schema --type trades | cpout
mf normalize profiles guide trades | cpout

items.title: JSON and exit status
items.text:
Place global --json before normalize. It emits the command's structured result on stdout where supported. new still opens the editor. edit rejects JSON mode, as does --tui. See shared CLI behavior for global options.

Code Meaning 0 Successful local action, preview, preparation, complete execution, registered partial execution, or successful registration. A deletion preview can return zero while reporting a live reference. 1 Reported operation failure, blocked or partial preparation, interrupted execution returned as a report, unsuccessful registration, or deletion blocked during apply. 2 Usage, configuration, setup, or preflight error, including rejected Rust batch validation raised as a command error. 130 A keyboard interruption handled by the top-level CLI.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom First check Missing inputs or a gap Compare recipe scope, archive dates and statuses in managed storage. Missing specification or incompatible profile Read the archive's preparation diagnostics and check specification applicability and installed profiles. Invalid or changed batch Review the Rust diagnostics and reprepare against the intended registry and runtime. Failed Engine job or unexpected output Compare the retained execution report and publication integrity evidence. For Engine setup and resource configuration, see runtime settings. Verified output with pending registration Recover from the retained intent against the original registry.

items.title: Pipeline commands
items.text: Apply one historical recipe through acquisition, normalization and merge. Plan and validate before starting. Use the pipeline workflow for acquisition and reconciliation prerequisites and the recipe contract for accepted settings.

mf pipeline validate [-h] NAME
Argument or option Parser contract NAME Required.

items.title: mf pipeline plan
items.text:

Argument or option Parser contract NAME Required. --testing, --production Mutually exclusive. Defaults to production.

items.title: mf pipeline run
items.text:
mf pipeline run [-h] [--testing | --production] [--tui]
                                [--stop-after {normalize.prepare}]
                                NAME
Argument or option Parser contract NAME Required. --testing, --production Mutually exclusive. Defaults to production. --tui Default false. --stop-after Optional. Accepted normalize.prepare.

items.title: mf pipeline resume
items.text:
mf pipeline resume [-h] [--testing | --production] [--tui] RUN_ID
Argument or option Parser contract RUN_ID Required. --testing, --production Mutually exclusive. Defaults to production. --tui Default false.

items.title: mf pipeline status
items.text:
mf pipeline status [-h] RUN_ID
Argument or option Parser contract RUN_ID Required.

items.title: Results and effects
items.text:
• validate resolves the managed recipe and returns schema_version: 1, kind: "historical_pipeline_validation", state: "valid", the source path and normalized recipe.
  • plan reads registered evidence and reports deferred work. It starts no provider requests and writes no processing artifacts or registry rows. JSON contains schema_version: 1, kind: "historical_pipeline_plan", state, source, recipe, environment, inventory, stages and blockers.
  • run creates a retained run, can download data, executes processing children, and registers verified outputs. --stop-after normalize.prepare retains a validated batch before normalization execution. resume verifies the original run context and pins before moving to the next eligible step.
  • status reads the retained report and returns zero when it can read it, even for an interrupted or failed run. Inspect the report's state. run and resume return 1 for failed, 2 for blocked, 130 for interrupted, and 0 for successful or deliberately stopped runs.
  • --tui and global --json are mutually exclusive. The dashboard needs interactive input and stderr. Redirected terminal output uses a plain summary. Global JSON returns the report object.

For the persisted run, stage, phase and receipt relationships, see Forge preparation and run evidence.

items.title: How Profiles Are Identified
items.text:
MarketForge uses a consistent naming convention for normalization profiles.

A profile ID has four components:

exchange.instrument_type.market_category.content_type

For example:

bybit.perpetual.linear.trades

This describes the trade profile for Bybit linear perpetual data.

The corresponding depth profile is:

bybit.perpetual.linear.depth

items.title: Understanding the components
items.text:
Component Example Meaning Exchange bybit The execution venue. Instrument type perpetual The financial product type. Market category linear The market or contract category. Content type trades The type of source data the profile interprets.

The final component must be:

trades

or:

depth

items.title: Why do profiles use this naming convention?
items.text:
The naming convention helps MarketForge associate a profile with the corresponding market and data type.

It also makes installed profiles easier to discover.

For example:

bitget.perpetual.linear.trades
bitget.perpetual.linear.depth

describe different source interpretations for the same market classification.

One handles trades.

The other handles order-book data.

items.title: Profile filenames
items.text:
The filename must match the profile ID exactly, followed by .toml.

For example:

bitget.perpetual.linear.depth.toml

The profile's internal id field must agree with its declared identity.

This prevents a profile from being installed under a misleading filename.

items.title: Where are profiles installed?
items.text:
MarketForge manages installed profiles under:

data/.config/engine/normalize/profiles/

The relevant content-type directories are:

data/.config/engine/normalize/profiles/
├── trades/
└── depth/

These installed files form the profile catalogue used by the historical normalizer.

You can keep your original profile declarations elsewhere and install them through the supported CLI.

items.title: Validate Registration
items.text:
Once the recipe is complete, validate it.

Use:

mf acquisition register validate synthetic-equity --testing

This performs registration preflight checks against the relevant testing catalogue and source information.

items.title: Why is registration validation necessary?
items.text:
A valid TOML file is not enough.

For example, a recipe might contain a correctly formatted instrument reference that does not exist in PostgreSQL.

Or it might select a historical interval for which the required specifications are unavailable.

Similarly, a source file may refer to a profile that has not been installed.

Registration validation checks these relationships before managed copies are created.

items.title: What does validation check?
items.text:
The supported validation includes checks involving:

  • The registration declaration.
  • Selected source files.
  • Registered catalogue identities.
  • Applicable historical specifications.
  • Installed profiles.
  • Relevant source preflight requirements.

The exact checks depend on the supplied inputs and current implementation.

items.title: Does validation copy the files?
items.text:
No.

Registration validation checks the inputs and required bindings.

It does not perform the final managed raw-copy operation.

items.title: Does validation prove the data is correct?
items.text:
Not completely.

For example, the registration may correctly associate a file with the installed profile while the file contains unexpected records later in the recording.

Complete decoding and processing checks happen during normalization.

Similarly, a declared interval does not independently prove complete event coverage.

Registration validation establishes that the selected source is ready for the supported registration workflow, not that every market-data event has already been verified.

items.title: Prepare a Registration Plan
items.text:
Before copying files into managed storage, you can ask MarketForge to prepare a registration plan.

Use:

mf acquisition register plan synthetic-equity --testing

items.title: Why use a registration plan?
items.text:
Suppose your recipe selects hundreds of files.

Before registering them, you may want to know:

  • Which files MarketForge selected.
  • Which instrument each file belongs to.
  • Which profile will interpret it.
  • Whether the required historical specifications are available.
  • Whether any inputs are duplicated or invalid.
  • Which registration work is ready to proceed.

Planning helps you review the operation before the managed-copy stage.

items.title: What happens during planning?
items.text:
MarketForge performs the relevant preflight checks and writes a retained operation plan.

The plan records the resolved registration work.

It does not create managed raw-file copies or final registration rows.

items.title: Is planning completely read-only?
items.text:
Not in the same sense as simple inspection.

The registration planning command can write its retained operation-plan artifacts.

However, it does not publish the selected raw files into managed storage.

This is different from the acquisition cache-only planning command.

For example:

mf acquisition plan NAME --testing --cache-only

is a read-only inspection of cached acquisition information.

Meanwhile:

mf acquisition register plan NAME --testing

performs registration preflight and retains an operation plan.

These commands solve different problems.

items.title: Why are selected inputs frozen?
items.text:
A registration operation needs a stable selection of source files.

Imagine that a directory contains ten files when registration begins.

While the operation is running, another process creates an eleventh file.

MarketForge should not silently change the operation's selected inputs halfway through.

Registration therefore resolves and freezes the selected files for the operation.

Files that appear afterward require a new registration operation.

This helps make each registration traceable and reproducible.

items.title: Verify the Registered Files
items.text:
After registration, you should confirm that the expected files are now available through MarketForge's managed storage.

For the synthetic example, you expect two raw inputs:

File Content synthetic-trades.csv Executed trades synthetic-depth.jsonl Order-book observations

These files belong to the same registered AAPL instrument but use different profiles.

items.title: Inspect managed storage
items.text:
You can inspect the registered raw-file collection through the storage commands.

For example:

mf storage list \
    --testing \
    --exchange example_exchange \
    --instrument AAPL \
    --wide

Look for the expected synthetic trade and depth files.

The storage records provide the local IDs needed for more detailed inspection.

items.title: Inspect one file
items.text:
Use the returned ID:

mf storage show LOCAL_ID --testing

Replace LOCAL_ID with the actual local archive ID.

This lets you inspect the registered source identity, location, status, and retained evidence.

items.title: Registration is not the final correctness check
items.text:
At this point, MarketForge knows which managed raw files belong to the selected instrument and which profiles should be used.

However, you have not yet established that the complete normalized output matches the source's intended meaning.

For example, you should still check that:

  • Trade timestamps are interpreted correctly.
  • Prices retain the intended precision.
  • Quantities use the correct units.
  • Trade sides are mapped correctly.
  • Depth observations produce the expected book states.
  • Processing integrity results are acceptable.

Those checks belong to normalization and dataset inspection.

See Raw Data Storage for detailed storage inspection and verification.

items.title: Working with Multiple Files
items.text:
Real datasets often contain many files rather than one recording.

For example:

recordings/
├── trades-2024-10-28.csv
├── trades-2024-10-29.csv
├── trades-2024-10-30.csv
└── trades-2024-10-31.csv

MarketForge supports selecting multiple local files in a registration recipe.

items.title: Explicit file selections
items.text:
A registration input can name specific files.

For example:

files = [
    "trades-2024-10-28.csv",
    "trades-2024-10-29.csv",
    "trades-2024-10-30.csv",
]

These filenames are illustrative.

The paths are relative to the declared source root.

items.title: File patterns
items.text:
Registration also supports file patterns where appropriate.

This can be useful when a directory contains a larger collection of consistently named recordings.

However, patterns should be chosen carefully.

For example, a broad pattern might accidentally include unrelated files or a different source format.

Before running registration, inspect the resolved selection.

items.title: Why does MarketForge limit file selection?
items.text:
A misconfigured pattern could select thousands of files unintentionally.

For this reason, input enumeration is bounded.

The default max_files value is:

1000

The maximum supported value is:

10000

These limits help prevent unexpectedly broad registration operations.

items.title: Can the same physical file appear twice?
items.text:
Duplicate physical inputs within a registration selection are rejected.

This prevents one source file from being accidentally registered multiple times through overlapping selections in the same operation.

items.title: What happens if new files arrive later?
items.text:
A registration freezes the selected files for that operation.

Files created after the selection is frozen are not silently added.

To register newly arrived recordings, perform another registration using the appropriate selection.

This makes the input set of each operation explicit.

items.title: Source Identity and Provenance
items.text:
Historical data may come from many different providers.

A single instrument can also appear in recordings from multiple sources.

For example, AAPL trades may be distributed by a market-data vendor while the actual trading venue is Nasdaq.

MarketForge therefore keeps source identity separate from instrument identity.

items.title: Provider and venue are different
items.text:
Consider the following:

Property Example Provider Databento Product XNAS.ITCH Venue Nasdaq Instrument AAPL

The provider supplies the recording.

The venue identifies where trading occurred.

The registered catalogue instrument should describe the execution venue, not the vendor.

items.title: Source keys
items.text:
The registration recipe uses a source key to identify a particular source collection.

For example:

[source]
key = "synthetic-equity"

This identifier helps associate registered files with the declared source.

It is also useful when selecting those files later during normalization.

items.title: Native instrument identifiers
items.text:
Some providers use their own numeric IDs for instruments.

For example, a source record might contain:

publisher_id = 2
instrument_id = 38

These are source-native identifiers.

They are not interchangeable with PostgreSQL's canonical instrument IDs.

Registration can retain native identity information, including publisher and instrument IDs, within the appropriate source namespace.

items.title: Why preserve native identities?
items.text:
Source-native identities can be important when:

  • A provider distributes data for several instruments.
  • Symbols change over time.
  • Different publishers use overlapping numeric ID ranges.
  • Historical records must be traced back to their original source.
  • Multiple providers supply recordings of the same venue.

Preserving this information helps keep the interpretation of the data auditable.

items.title: Historical specification fingerprints
items.text:
Registration declarations can also include supported specification fingerprints.

These allow an input to be tied to particular historical specification evidence.

This is useful when exact economic interpretation matters and the catalogue contains multiple observations or historical revisions.

A fingerprint should refer to actual registered evidence.

Do not invent one or use it as a substitute for verifying the applicable specification.

items.title: What Does Successful Registration Mean?
items.text:
A successful registration means MarketForge accepted the selected source files into its managed raw-data workflow with the applicable bindings.

It establishes information about:

  • The source files.
  • Their origin and provider.
  • The registered instrument.
  • The selected profiles.
  • Their declared historical coverage.
  • Their managed copies and verification evidence.

However, registration does not prove that every record inside those files is correct.

items.title: Three different checks
items.text:
Stage What it establishes Profile validation The declared interpretation is accepted by the supported Rust compiler. Registration validation The files have the required catalogue, profile, and source bindings. Normalization The source records can be decoded and processed under the applicable rules.

These checks are complementary.

For example, a profile can be valid while a recording contains malformed rows.

Similarly, a registration can succeed while a later normalization job identifies a sequence gap.

Do not treat registration success as a substitute for processing and integrity verification.

items.title: What should you inspect after registration?
items.text:
Inspect the operation result and retained evidence.

Confirm that the expected files were accepted or reused.

Then inspect the managed storage records.

Finally, normalize a representative sample and compare its output with independently known source values.

For depth data, checking reconstructed states is more informative than merely checking the number of generated Parquet rows.

items.title: Profile file not found
items.text:
Possible cause: The supplied path is incorrect or the profile is not installed.

Check the exact filename and location.

For an installed definition:

mf normalize profiles list

For a manually authored file, validate the actual path:

mf normalize profiles validate --file PATH

items.title: Profile ID does not match the filename
items.text:
Possible cause: The file is named differently from its declared four-component profile ID.

Check the filename and the internal id field.

Use the required naming convention:

exchange.instrument_type.market_category.trades|depth

items.title: Profile semantic validation fails
items.text:
Possible cause: The profile contains an unsupported field mapping, transformation, source format, or combination of rules.

Inspect the Rust validation diagnostics.

Compare the declaration with the supported profile reference.

Do not remove important interpretation rules simply to make validation pass.

items.title: Profile installation reports a conflict
items.text:
Possible cause: Another definition with the same ID is already installed and has a different interpretation.

Inspect the existing profile:

mf normalize profiles inspect PROFILE_ID

Compare it with the new declaration.

Resolve the identity and interpretation conflict explicitly.

items.title: The profile validates, but the output is wrong
items.text:
Possible cause: The profile follows the supported schema but does not match the real source semantics.

For example:

  • Timestamps use the wrong unit.
  • Trade sides are reversed.
  • Quantities use the wrong denomination.
  • The source contains unexpected values.
  • Depth messages were interpreted as the wrong kind of observation.

Compare representative source records with the normalized result.

Use provider documentation to establish the correct meaning.

items.title: Registration cannot find the source files
items.text:
Possible cause: The declared source root or file selection is incorrect.

Inspect the recipe:

mf acquisition register inspect NAME

Check that the files exist beneath the declared source root.

Remember that relative source roots are resolved against the project root.

items.title: Registration reports a missing exchange
items.text:
Possible cause: The declared instrument belongs to a venue that is not registered.

Inspect the exchange through mf catalog.

Register the correct venue before continuing.

items.title: Registration reports a missing instrument
items.text:
Possible cause: The selected catalogue instrument has not been registered.

Inspect the instrument reference:

mf catalog instrument show REFERENCE --testing

Register the required instrument with correct identity information.

items.title: Historical specifications do not cover the recording
items.text:
Possible cause: The relevant specification evidence does not apply to the complete required interval.

Inspect the declared coverage and the registered specification validity periods.

Supply historically applicable evidence.

Do not extend validity intervals without support.

items.title: Registration reports a missing profile
items.text:
Possible cause: The recipe references a profile that is not installed.

Inspect the installed profile list and validate the required definition.

Install the correct profile before retrying.

items.title: Registration selects the same physical file twice
items.text:
Possible cause: Two explicit selections or patterns resolve to the same source file.

Review the selected inputs.

Remove the duplicate selection rather than attempting to register it twice.

items.title: Registration exceeds the file limit
items.text:
Possible cause: A file pattern selects more inputs than the configured bound.

Inspect the pattern and its intended scope.

Use a narrower selection when possible.

Increase max_files only when the larger selection is intentional and remains within the supported limit.

items.title: Registration fails after copying some files
items.text:
Possible cause: A source file changed, a copy or verification step failed, or the operation was interrupted.

Inspect the registration report and retained copy receipts.

Previously completed files may be reusable.

Do not manually overwrite managed files or alter registry statuses.

items.title: Registration succeeds, but normalization cannot prepare
items.text:
Possible cause: Registration and normalization have different readiness requirements.

For example, normalization may reject an invalid prepared source contract, missing specification applicability, or unsupported profile interpretation.

Inspect the normalization preparation report.

Do not assume that successful registration guarantees executable normalization.

items.title: Execution history and retained evidence
items.text:
New historical operations use <operation>-<uuid> logical run IDs. The five operations are acquisition, normalize, merge, convert, and pipeline. Acquisition mapping and downloading both use acquisition-. Their action records which activity ran.

PostgreSQL stores bounded execution metadata, timestamps, ordered attempts and typed resource references. Complete reports, events, submitted jobs and pinned Engine evidence remain on disk. A logical run under data/runs/ can point to separate Engine preparation and execution directories. Engine job, publication, registered file and attempt identifiers each retain their own meaning.

items.title: Browse the selected registry
items.text:
Production is the default. Add --testing to select the testing registry. Filter runs list by --operation, --action, --status, --recipe, --start or --end. Time bounds are timezone-aware ISO 8601 start-time bounds. The start is inclusive and the end is exclusive. Filters are exact. Use --limit and --offset to page the newest runs. Exchange and instrument filters require indexed associations and are not exposed by this interface.

mf --json runs list --testing --operation acquisition --action map --limit 20 | cpout
mf runs show RUN_ID --testing | cpout
mf runs report RUN_ID --testing | cpout
mf runs logs RUN_ID --testing --limit 50 | cpout

Replace RUN_ID with a recorded identifier. List and indexed show use schema version 2. Show includes a duration when the run has finished, and bounded attempt, resource and child-run lists. Report and logs use the retained sources and their original contracts. Running records have unknown liveness when no terminal evidence has been reconciled.

items.title: Attempts and recovery
items.text:
Forge verifies the selected database UUID and purpose before starting expensive work. A single invocation that prepares and executes retains one logical run with references to both preparation and execution evidence. A pipeline resume keeps the original run ID and starts a new attempt. The pipeline report retains stage order and outcomes. Independently retained acquisition executions link to their owning pipeline. HTTP retries and individual Engine tasks do not create logical attempts.

The searchable state distinguishes prepared, completed, partial, failed, blocked, interrupted, cancelled, stopped, and unknown. An in-flight attempt is running. The registry retains the operation's domain status and available execution, verification and registration outcomes separately. A committed publication can still have a pending or failed registration.

PostgreSQL and the filesystem commit separately. Forge writes a bounded outcome beneath the attempt directory before finalizing the index. If index finalization fails, the outcome remains available for reconciliation. This replays only index updates and leaves processing and registration evidence intact.

items.title: Historical evidence and index maintenance
items.text:
Anonymous UUIDs and recognized historical Engine execution directory IDs work for explicit inspection. Historical IDs and original report bytes are preserved. Legacy indexing requires evidence of the operation, timestamps and the exact selected registry UUID and environment. Missing, ambiguous or conflicting evidence stays available for local review.

mf runs index-legacy --dry-run --testing --limit 50 | cpout
mf runs index-legacy --apply --testing --limit 50 | cpout
mf runs reconcile --dry-run --testing --limit 50 | cpout
mf runs reconcile --apply --testing --limit 50 | cpout

Review the preview and use --offset for subsequent pages. Reconciliation checks the workspace and registry identity, attempt and retained outcome before applying metadata. A running row without a retained outcome needs review. Unindexed local evidence is reported and needs explicit review before assignment. Neither command launches processing or rewrites historical reports. Production indexing is an explicit administrative action.

See the pipeline reference for resume and the publication reference for retained Engine evidence.

items.title: Check Historical Coverage
items.text:
One of the most useful storage features is the ability to inspect which historical periods are represented by your downloaded files.

Imagine you want to research BTCUSDT trading activity over an entire month.

You have downloaded many archives, but you are not sure whether every day is represented.

You could manually compare filenames.

However, this becomes difficult when working with several exchanges, different archive intervals, and multiple data types.

MarketForge provides coverage inspection to help with this.

items.title: View coverage for an instrument
items.text:
Use:

mf storage coverage \
    --testing \
    --exchange bybit \
    --instrument BTCUSDT \
    --data-type trades

MarketForge examines the registered historical intervals of the matching completed files.

It combines overlapping or adjacent intervals to summarize the periods represented by those files.

For example, suppose the registry contains:

October 25    Complete
October 26    Complete
October 27    Complete

The combined nominal coverage may be represented as:

October 25 ───────────────── October 28

The end boundary is exclusive.

If the same period is represented by more than one matching copy, overlapping intervals do not create extra covered time.

items.title: Find missing periods
items.text:
Suppose one day is missing:

October 25    Complete
October 26    Missing
October 27    Complete

MarketForge can identify the gap between the registered intervals.

Use:

mf storage coverage \
    --testing \
    --exchange bybit \
    --instrument BTCUSDT \
    --data-type trades \
    --gaps

The --gaps option includes missing periods in the coverage result.

This helps you identify dates that may need another acquisition.

items.title: Check a specific date range
items.text:
You can restrict the coverage inspection to a historical interval.

For example:

mf storage coverage \
    --testing \
    --exchange bybit \
    --instrument BTCUSDT \
    --data-type trades \
    --start 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z \
    --end 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z \
    --gaps

This requests a coverage view for October 2026.

When both date boundaries are provided, the gap calculation can include missing periods at the beginning or end of the requested interval.

Without explicit boundaries, MarketForge can only report gaps within the observed coverage envelope.

For example, if your earliest recorded archive starts on October 10, MarketForge cannot assume that October 1–9 was part of your intended collection unless you specify that period.

items.title: Understanding nominal coverage
items.text:
An important limitation: archive coverage is not the same as complete market-data coverage.

Suppose an archive is registered as covering October 27.

This means the archive's recorded period represents that day.

It does not prove that every trade or order-book update from that day is present.

A file might:

  • Contain missing events.
  • Have gaps in its source sequence.
  • Start later than its declared interval.
  • End before its declared interval.
  • Contain invalid records.
  • Lack the snapshots required for continuous order-book reconstruction.

Storage coverage does not inspect these details.

Those questions belong to source processing and integrity analysis.

Similarly, missing or unknown interval information must not be interpreted as proof of complete coverage.

items.title: Coverage and completeness
items.text:
Keep these three ideas separate:

Question Where to check Do I have registered archives for this period? mf storage coverage Are the local file bytes still intact? mf storage verify Does the data contain valid, complete market events? Normalization and relevant integrity evidence

A collection can have no nominal coverage gaps while still containing incomplete market data.

items.title: Understand File Statuses
items.text:
Every managed archive has a recorded status.

These statuses describe the current known state of the local record.

Some common statuses are:

Status Meaning pending The file has been selected or reserved for acquisition. downloading A download or managed-copy operation is in progress or has an unfinished reservation. complete The managed copy was accepted as complete. missing A previously expected local file could not be found during an applicable check. corrupt A file failed an applicable integrity check. failed The acquisition or managed-copy attempt failed. deleted The managed copy has been removed through the supported lifecycle.

A recorded complete status is useful, but it should not be confused with a fresh verification of the file.

If a file was accepted yesterday and deleted manually today, its registry status may remain unchanged until an operation checks the actual file.

items.title: Filter by status
items.text:
To list completed archives:

mf storage list \
    --testing \
    --status complete

To find failed records:

mf storage list \
    --testing \
    --status failed

To inspect missing files:

mf storage list \
    --testing \
    --status missing

These filters are useful for browsing known outcomes.

They do not perform new verification.

items.title: Understand Cleanup Safety
items.text:
Both pruning and deletion use safeguards to prevent unsafe removal.

These safeguards matter because MarketForge may have active operations, registered dependencies, and files whose recorded state has changed since the last inspection.

items.title: Previews are not deletion commands
items.text:
Commands without --apply normally perform the review stage.

They do not remove the selected archive bytes.

However, they may write the managed preview and lock files needed for a later operation.

items.title: Pagination does not limit deletion targets
items.text:
This is especially important.

A display limit only controls how many results are shown.

It does not necessarily restrict the underlying cleanup selection.

For example, displaying the first twenty matching records does not mean only those twenty records will be affected by a later approved operation.

Always review the complete selection before applying cleanup.

Use --all or the full JSON preview for that review.

items.title: Applying a preview checks the selection again
items.text:
MarketForge does not blindly trust an old preview.

Before applying cleanup, it checks whether the saved target selection and relevant safety conditions are still valid.

This can prevent removal when files or dependencies have changed.

items.title: Some targets cannot be removed
items.text:
A target may be blocked because of:

  • A dependency on the managed file.
  • An active operation.
  • Missing or changed ownership information.
  • An unsafe or changed filesystem path.
  • An incomplete or unverifiable operation.
  • Another safety condition enforced by the cleanup service.

Do not bypass these protections through manual database edits or direct filesystem deletion.

Investigate the blocker first.

items.title: Keep recovery information
items.text:
Cleanup operations retain registry history and can produce receipts that help explain or recover interrupted work.

Keep preview and receipt files while recovery is still pending.

A partially completed cleanup should be investigated through its reported outcomes rather than repeated blindly.

items.title: Understanding Storage Errors
items.text:
When a storage operation fails, the most useful next step depends on the type of problem.

Problem What to investigate Archive not found Check the local ID, selected data root, and registry. File marked missing Inspect the registered path and run verification if appropriate. Checksum mismatch Check whether the file was changed or corrupted; consider reacquisition. Coverage gap Review the selected interval and map the missing period through acquisition. Unknown coverage Check whether the source has reliable historical interval metadata. Interrupted download Inspect the run report and retained reservation information. Reconciliation unsuccessful Check whether the required durable verification evidence exists. Cleanup blocked Inspect dependencies, ownership, paths, and changed target state. Database rejected Verify the testing database URL, identity, and migrations.

Avoid manually changing database statuses or moving managed files to make a failing operation appear successful.

Use the supported inspection and recovery commands so that the registry and filesystem remain consistent.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Storage and cleanup commands use the common MarketForge CLI error handling.

Code Meaning 0 The operation or preview completed successfully. A successful preview does not mean deletion was applied. 1 An applicable verification, recovery, or cleanup operation was unsuccessful or incomplete. 2 A command, configuration, database, filesystem, ownership, or setup error was reported. 130 The command was interrupted through the handled cancellation path.

Inspect detailed outcomes rather than relying only on the exit code.

For example, a cleanup preview with no eligible targets can complete successfully without deleting anything.

items.title: Guides
items.text:
Start with the outcome you need. The Bybit quick start shows the full route from provider archive to inspected Parquet.

Task Guide Find a market or compare eligibility, volume, and turnover Market discovery, statistics, and rankings Preview source coverage and download provider archives Historical acquisition Check managed copies, verify bytes, or review cleanup Raw storage Describe venue and instrument identity and attach applicable terms Catalogue and specifications Bring existing bytes into the managed workflow External recordings Map supported raw formats into canonical trades or book observations Profile authoring Turn managed inputs into canonical output Normalization Build an ordered timeline from normalized files Merge Express price or notional in another quote currency Conversion Orchestrate acquisition, normalization, and merge Historical pipeline Inspect file contents, coverage, or lineage CLI dataset inspection and Python notebooks Browse or launch operations interactively Forge workspace

For an interrupted run or environment problem, go to troubleshooting and recovery. For exact fields and output contracts, use the reference.

items.title: Prepare historical conversion
items.text: Forge converts the quote currency of a committed merge. The recipe describes source intent and references. The generated Rust job points to a complete publication directory, including its manifest and all primary files.

items.title: Select a source
items.text:
Create a recipe from one source TOML. Forge uses a merge recipe's retained submission and registered normalized parents. For a normalization recipe, it matches the recorded requests and retained normalization submission before following the merge lineage. For an acquisition recipe, it checks the raw scope, archive interval and digest against the normalized file's registered raw contributions, then follows the merge lineage. These routes reuse existing outputs. Legacy normalization requests based on archive IDs are unsupported as source recipes.

set -o pipefail
mf convert new example --from-merge upstream_merge --target-quote USDT --testing
mf convert new from_normalization --from-normalize upstream_normalization --target-quote USDT --testing
mf convert new from_acquisition --from-acquisition upstream_acquisition --target-quote USDT --testing
nvim data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/conversion/example.toml

The managed recipe records version = 1, a [source] table with kind, reference, path and SHA-256, and a half-open [interval] with integer start_ns and end_ns. Edit the recipe to choose references and review settings. If the source TOML changes, review the changes and create a new conversion recipe.

Use file IDs when you started from registered primary files and publication IDs when you already know the owning merge. Forge expands the selected files to their complete publications. If your requested interval is narrower than a source publication, approve whole-publication processing deliberately. Confirm the approved publication’s stream and row scope before submitting it.

Choose reference trade streams that can support the target quote at the event times you need. A separate trade-only merge can supply references for combined and depth inputs. Check staleness limits and any currency route gaps before accepting the result. The recipe reference lists exact selector names, defaults, and constraints. The prepared job reference describes the resolved bindings Forge hands to the Engine.

If verified outputs overlap and compete for a stream scope, prepare reports the candidate publication IDs. Pin the intended revision explicitly. Distinct noncompeting publications get separate jobs in one Forge collection. Each job needs its configured reference trades to resolve in the source or the specified external publication. File, stream, and interval selections never trim the physical input. Causal reconstruction rows remain part of the effective publication.

items.title: Recorded case: Bybit combined merge to USDT
items.text:
This recorded case uses an existing registered three-day Bybit spot merge. The recipe name and numeric IDs were assigned in that workspace. For a new run, normalize and merge the markets you need, then obtain your file IDs with dataset inspection. Use a whole publication with the required trade streams.

set -o pipefail
mf convert new engine_test_conversion --from-merge engine_test_conversation --target-quote USDT --testing
nvim data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/conversion/engine_test_conversion.toml

Keep the generated source fingerprint and interval. Set these top-level references and update the corresponding tables.

reference_stream_ids = ["bybit.spot.spot.BTCUSDT.trades", "bybit.spot.spot.BTCUSDC.trades"]

[selection]
file_dataset_ids = [360]
expected_engine_publication_ids = ["2079541492669036539"]
whole_publication = true

[conversion]
target_quote = "USDT"
price_source = "last_trade"
max_staleness_ns = 60000000000
max_hops = 2
path_policy = "all"

The 60-second staleness limit is a walkthrough setting. The JSON report can be saved for inspection without mixing stderr into the document.

set -o pipefail
mf engine build convert
mf convert validate engine_test_conversion
mf convert prepare engine_test_conversion --testing --dry-run
mf --json convert prepare engine_test_conversion --testing > conversion-prepare.json
jq '{status, compatibility, job_path, report_path, compatibility_blockers}' conversion-prepare.json

On the verified registry, file 360 belongs to registry publication 60, engine publication 2079541492669036539. Its complete inventory contains one primary file with 12,477,919 events, including 5,233,312 trades and 7,244,607 depth events. The requested interval is [2026-10-27T00:00:00Z, 2026-10-30T00:00:00Z). Inclusive observed endpoints are 2026-10-27T00:00:00.197000000Z and 2026-10-29T23:59:59.991000000Z. Endpoints describe observed extent only.

Bybit spot instrument Instrument ID Native quote Metadata route BTCUSDT 1 USDT Identity ETHUSDT 2 USDT Identity ETHBTC 4 BTC BTC → USDT through BTCUSDT trades BTCUSDC 65 USDC USDC → BTC through inverse BTCUSDC trades, then BTC → USDT through BTCUSDT trades

All four instruments have trades and depth in this publication. The reference trades are a separate selection from the eight source streams. Reachability establishes a currency route from historical base and quote metadata. The engine evaluates prior observations and staleness during event execution.

items.title: Inspect the prepared job
items.text:
Forge saves a collection named convert.json, a prepare-report.json, and one job-*.json per physical publication. The collection indexes jobs and evidence. The report distinguishes job generation from successful production Engine validation. A dry run reports intended paths without creating files or running the Engine.
