The retained catalog and TOML snapshots document preparation.

The individual job includes the stream bindings, scoped instrument metadata, publication pins, and effective runtime. See the prepared conversion job for the fields and their authority. Re-prepare older jobs from their Forge recipes. Forge accepts retained job and collection paths for run. Conversion registration is unavailable.

set -o pipefail
mf convert validate /absolute/path/to/job-123.json
mf convert run /absolute/path/to/convert.json --testing

items.title: Run a single prepared job
items.text:
The Engine needs the declared physical merge publications and their regular commit metadata. The paths in the job are absolute, so it can run from any working directory.

set -o pipefail
cargo build --release --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --features historical,monitor-tui --bin marketforge-convert
./engine/target/release/marketforge-convert --job /absolute/path/to/job-123.json --validate
./engine/target/release/marketforge-convert --job /absolute/path/to/job-123.json --run --tui

--validate checks the schema, publication IDs and hashes, Parquet inventory, stream bindings, references, and plan. It reads input bytes for checksums without executing conversion or creating staging or output. The same checks precede materialization and publication.

Combined conversion prefers configured internal trade streams and uses external trades for configured instruments absent from the internal trades. Matching depth streams remain sources. Depth-only conversion uses a trade-only external merge. Trade-only conversion uses internal trades. all tries planned routes in deterministic order and emits one valuation from the first successful route. primary tries the first planned route.

Causal conversion preserves physical order, timestamps, and reconstruction markers. Internal references must precede the event in causal traversal and have a strictly earlier event-time key. At equal timestamps, stream rank, task ID, and ordinal break ties. External trades require a strictly earlier timestamp. Reference age equal to the staleness limit is eligible.

--materialize writes staged Parquet and execution evidence. --publish checks the job and effective settings against the staged specification, validates the output, and commits it. The dashboard shows physical rows and throughput for the active phase. The conversion ETA covers the physical work only. The partition table retains completed and failed partitions, and unavailable valuations have their own counts and reasons.

Use D for details, arrows or Page Up and Page Down to navigate, and ? for help. Ctrl+C requests interruption. The Engine joins the worker and restores the terminal before returning. MARKETFORGE_TUI_HOLD=1 keeps the final screen open for review. Press Q to close it.

To preview the dashboard without accessing recorded inputs, generate a complete 12-row job in a fresh temporary directory after building the release binary.

set -o pipefail
preview=$(mktemp -d)
MARKETFORGE_CONVERSION_PREVIEW_DIR="$preview" \
  cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --features historical \
  --test historical_convert portable::export_conversion_dashboard_preview \
  -- --ignored --exact --nocapture &&
  job=$(find "$preview" -name job.json -print -quit) &&
  MARKETFORGE_TUI_HOLD=1 ./engine/target/release/marketforge-convert --job "$job" --run --tui

For recorded and portable regression checks, see conversion verification.

items.title: Verify the portable result without a terminal UI
items.text:
Run from the checkout with Rust and the converter built as above. After exporting the preview job into a fresh directory, run these commands in place of the dashboard command.

./engine/target/release/marketforge-convert --job "$job" --validate
./engine/target/release/marketforge-convert --job "$job" --run
jq '{statistics, integrity}' "$(dirname "$job")/converted/manifest.json"

The synthetic fixture has 12 physical rows, including one reconstruction-only input. The published counts are six identity, five converted, and one unavailable. The report records source_preservation = true and conversion_validation = true. An unavailable valuation is retained when the conversion policy cannot use a reference. See the conversion publication contract for the output schema.

items.title: Inspect registered datasets
items.text:
For local Python discovery, previews and schema inspection, see the Jupyter workflow.

Run from the checkout with the testing registry and Arrow inspection tools. Start with the file IDs returned by normalization or merge. To discover them later, use mf datasets find --testing --exchange bybit --instrument BTCUSDT --instrument-type perpetual --market-category linear.

For each ID, run mf datasets show ID --testing to identify the owning publication, mf datasets schema ID --testing for physical types, and mf datasets head ID --testing --limit 5 --precise for stored records. mf datasets verify ID --testing checks the selected file and shared manifest fingerprints. mf datasets streams ID --testing reports stream membership and observed bounds. mf datasets lineage ID --testing --publication includes the publication's input selections.

An observed envelope gives the earliest and latest timestamps. For depth, inspect the publication's indexed observations and reconstruction boundaries before treating rows as a usable book. Preserve the shared manifest and auxiliary files. To merge, first check layout, stream namespace and required parts in the merge guide.

items.title: Migrate existing registrations
items.text: See registry migration and recovery.

items.title: Tokyo Night colors
items.text: See terminal presentation settings.

items.title: Inspect from Python
items.text:
Use a primary file path returned by normalization, or its path shown by datasets show. With the lab dependencies installed, open the physical file through the checkout's dataset API:

from forge.datasets.discovery import open_dataset

dataset = open_dataset(path)
print(dataset.schema())
print(dataset.head(5, columns=["event_timestamp_ns", "price"]))

Substitute the returned primary path for path. Use batches(columns=..., start=..., end=...) for bounded Arrow iteration with optional half-open timestamp filtering. To interpret depth observations, use the publication's event index and boundary metadata. Bybit example

items.title: Inspect File-Level Lineage
items.text:
To inspect the registered contributions to a particular primary file, use:

mf datasets lineage FILE_ID --testing

items.title: What does the command show?
items.text:
The lineage view distinguishes between raw archive inputs and parent dataset inputs.

For example:

Normalization output

A normalized file may have proven contributions from registered raw archives.

Merge output

A merged file may have contributions from registered normalized dataset files.

items.title: Raw archive lineage
items.text:
For a normalized trade dataset, the lineage may identify:

Raw Archive 101
Raw Archive 102
Raw Archive 103

These are illustrative local archive IDs.

The records can include information about the exchange, source filename, archive scope, and recorded interval.

items.title: Parent dataset lineage
items.text:
For a merged file, the lineage may identify:

Normalized Dataset 301
Normalized Dataset 302

These are illustrative PostgreSQL file dataset IDs.

This helps trace the merged result back to its registered normalized inputs.

items.title: Why distinguish the two?
items.text:
Raw archives and normalized datasets are different types of inputs.

A normalization publication normally derives from raw market-data recordings.

A merge publication derives from compatible normalized datasets.

Separating these relationships makes the processing history easier to understand.

items.title: Inspect Source Checksums
items.text:
Lineage can also display retained raw-input checksums.

Use:

mf datasets lineage FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --checksums

items.title: Why are checksums useful?
items.text:
A checksum helps identify the exact file contents associated with a registered source.

For example, two archives may have identical filenames but different contents.

Their SHA-256 checksums can distinguish them.

This is useful when investigating:

  • Source-file changes.
  • Duplicate or conflicting recordings.
  • Reproducibility.
  • Historical processing evidence.
  • Unexpected data differences.

items.title: Does displaying a checksum verify the current raw file?
items.text:
No.

The lineage command displays retained checksum evidence.

It does not automatically rehash every original raw archive during ordinary lineage inspection.

For current raw-file integrity, use the applicable storage verification command.

items.title: Combine publication and checksum inspection
items.text:
You can request both:

mf datasets lineage FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --publication \
    --checksums \
    --limit 10

This displays a bounded set of lineage entries together with the expanded publication selection.

items.title: Lineage display limits
items.text:
The terminal lineage view defaults to:

25 rows per section

The accepted limit is:

1–1000

For example:

mf datasets lineage FILE_ID \
    --testing \
    --limit 100

The limit affects displayed lineage entries, not the underlying registered relationships.

items.title: Full JSON lineage
items.text:
For machine-readable lineage:

mf --json datasets lineage FILE_ID --testing

JSON returns the underlying file-contribution and publication-selection information.

This is useful when performing more detailed provenance analysis.

items.title: Preview a Registration Migration
items.text:
Before changing the registry, inspect which legacy registrations need migration.

First, ensure the database schema is current:

mf database migrate --testing

Then run:

mf datasets migrate-registration \
    --all \
    --testing \
    --dry-run

items.title: Why use dry-run?
items.text:
The migration may involve existing publication records and file relationships.

A dry-run allows you to inspect the proposed work before applying database changes.

items.title: What does the preview inspect?
items.text:
The migration workflow examines eligible legacy aggregate registrations.

It verifies the corresponding committed publication evidence.

This can include reading existing files and checking their SHA-256 fingerprints.

items.title: Does dry-run read Parquet files?
items.text:
It can read existing publication file bytes to perform the required verification.

Therefore, dry-run should not be interpreted as a metadata-only operation.

However, it does not apply the final file-level registration changes.

items.title: What does the preview report?
items.text:
The result can include:

  • Legacy dataset IDs.
  • Corresponding publication identities.
  • Primary files eligible for registration.
  • Existing matching file registrations.
  • Retained raw-input relationships.
  • Potential conflicts.
  • The number of primary files involved.

items.title: Why is --all required?
items.text:
The migration is an explicit registry-wide operation for the supported legacy aggregate selection.

MarketForge requires:

--all

to make that scope explicit.

Both preview and apply use the selected registry. The examples pass --testing to keep them in the testing workspace.

items.title: Can I preview one arbitrary legacy ID?
items.text:
The documented migration command requires --all.

It does not expose a separate single-ID migration action through this CLI.

Inspect the preview result to understand the individual legacy registrations included in the operation.

items.title: Apply the Registration Migration
items.text:
Once you have reviewed the preview, apply the migration:

mf datasets migrate-registration \
    --all \
    --testing

items.title: What happens during migration?
items.text:
For eligible legacy normalization registrations, MarketForge:

  1. Verifies the committed publication.
  2. Checks the retained publication fingerprints.
  3. Resolves the primary files.
  4. Reuses the existing registered raw-input relationships.
  5. Creates or reuses the corresponding file-level records.
  6. Preserves the legacy aggregate reference and its historical relationships.

items.title: Does migration rewrite the Parquet files?
items.text:
No.

The migration updates database registration information.

It leaves the published Parquet files and their manifests in place.

items.title: Does migration rerun normalization?
items.text:
No.

It uses the existing committed publication and its retained evidence.

It does not decode the original exchange archives again.

items.title: What happens to source lineage?
items.text:
The migration reuses the relevant registered raw-input relationships.

This helps preserve the historical relationship between the existing publication and its original sources.

items.title: Can the migration be repeated?
items.text:
Yes.

The supported migration is designed to reuse compatible existing file-level registrations.

Repeated application should not create duplicate primary file identities for identical evidence.

items.title: What if some registrations fail?
items.text:
The migration can report conflicts for individual legacy aggregates.

Independent successful conversions may already have been applied before a later conflict is reported.

A nonzero exit code does not necessarily mean no changes were made.

Inspect the result carefully.

items.title: What about legacy merge registrations?
items.text:
The current migration path does not automatically convert legacy merge aggregates.

These are reported as conflicts because the required historical merge input evidence cannot always be established through the supported migration procedure.

Do not invent missing lineage to make them pass.

items.title: How do I inspect an old ID afterward?
items.text:
Use:

mf datasets show LEGACY_ID --testing

Replace LEGACY_ID with an actual legacy aggregate ID.

When the migration mapping exists, MarketForge can report the replacement file IDs.

Use those file IDs for subsequent inspection.

items.title: Recover Missing File Registrations
items.text:
Sometimes Engine has committed a valid publication, but Forge could not complete the database registration.

For example, PostgreSQL might become unavailable after normalization finishes.

In this situation, you may already have a valid committed publication on disk.

Rerunning the entire processing workload could be unnecessary.

MarketForge provides registration-only recovery through the relevant processing command.

items.title: Recover a normalized publication
items.text:
Use:

mf normalize register \
    /path/to/normalized-publication/manifest.json \
    --testing

Replace the path with an actual committed manifest.

items.title: Recover one normalized primary file
items.text:
You can also specify one primary Parquet file:

mf normalize register \
    /path/to/publication/streams/STREAM/trades/part-000000.parquet \
    --testing

items.title: Recover a merged publication
items.text:
For a committed merge manifest:

mf merge register \
    /path/to/merged-publication/manifest.json \
    --testing

Or one merged primary file:

mf merge register \
    /path/to/publication/timeline/partition-000000/part-000000.parquet \
    --testing

items.title: Why use the processing-specific registration command?
items.text:
Normalization and merging have different publication contracts.

The corresponding registration services understand their applicable output structures and evidence.

Use the command associated with the operation that created the publication.

items.title: Can I recover using an execution intent?
items.text:
Yes.

The supported registration-only workflows can accept retained execution-intent receipts.

These help locate and verify the committed outputs associated with a previous processing attempt.

See the normalization and merge guides for the appropriate recovery procedures.

items.title: Does registration-only recovery reprocess data?
items.text:
No.

It verifies existing committed output and registers eligible files.

It does not repeat normalization or merging.

items.title: What if the output is incomplete?
items.text:
An incomplete staging directory is not automatically a valid committed publication.

Registration requires the applicable committed files and verification evidence.

If Engine never completed publication, investigate the processing failure rather than trying to register incomplete files.

items.title: Interactive Forge workspace
items.text:
Forge provides a Textual application alongside the direct CLI. Install Forge with Python 3.12 or newer on Linux or macOS. Textual is included in the Forge lockfile. Use an interactive terminal. Forge defaults to production and its workspace header shows the selected environment and verified connectivity. The application resolves the same project root, settings, and credentials as the CLI.

mf tui
mf tui --production
mf tui --testing

A separate workspace or settings file can be selected with the global options.

mf --project-root /path/to/marketforge --config /path/to/settings.toml tui --testing

Startup reads local workspace evidence. Network acquisition, market refresh, processing, verification, and storage mutation are explicit actions.

items.title: Navigation
items.text:
Area Contents Overview Data inventory, workspace status, current operation, attention, and recent results Workflows Pipeline, acquisition, normalization, merge, conversion, and import Data Merged, Converted, Normalized, and Raw Markets Instruments, observations, policies, and ranking snapshots Catalog Manual exchange, instrument, and specification declarations Recipes & Profiles Saved TOML recipes, declarations, and installed normalization profiles Runs Retained reports and operations owned by this application System Engine installations, the testing registry, and application settings

Press Ctrl+P to find actions. Registration commands remain in the palette, including raw registration and supported recovery. Workflows has no separate Registration tab.

Arrow keys change selection. Enter opens the selected object. For an editable recipe, Enter or a click on its name opens the configured editor. The table uses the full width. Escape returns from explicit details while retaining the list state. Right-click a row, use F2, or press Shift+F10 to open its actions. F3 in details opens raw evidence. Tab and Shift+Tab move focus. Use / for search, Ctrl+R to reload, Page Up and Page Down to change pages, and Ctrl+N to toggle navigation.

Use Filters for structured constraints and Reset to clear them. Click a supported heading or choose a sort in the filter form. The arrow indicates direction, and a second click reverses it. Registry sorting and filtering happen before pagination. Turnover ordering keeps native denominations separate. Missing numeric and time values sort last. The result strip displays the current page and applied criteria.

Inventory Structured filters Merged and Normalized Publication ID, exchange, instrument identity, instrument type, market, trade or depth content, observed interval Raw Archive ID, origin and raw source, exchange, type and market, instrument or scope, feed, assets, status, and interval Markets instruments Exchange and market lists, exact symbol and symbol pattern, base, quote and settlement, instrument type, status, observation availability Ranking snapshots Comparison currency and complete or partial universe, with policy and snapshot search Converted Manifest availability and recorded stream kinds Catalog instruments Exchange, symbol, type, market, assets, status Retained runs Run ID, operation, recipe, recorded state, exchange, scope, started interval, minimum duration, recorded outputs

Publication member constraints match the same constituent. Retained run context comes from retained reports and plans. Older records can lack scope or duration. A recorded running state has unconfirmed liveness.

Forms include selectors and optional Advanced fields. Copy command displays the equivalent quoted CLI invocation for use outside the app. Copy value requests clipboard transfer through the terminal. If terminal or tmux clipboard forwarding is disabled, the displayed text remains selectable.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Overview puts registered data ahead of run history. Its headline statistics cover completed primary files of registered normalized and merged publications. Instrument identities include their canonical namespace and venue. Logical stream IDs retain feed distinctions and are deduplicated across stages. Publication IDs and primary files are counted separately. Recorded primary-file size excludes sidecars and shows how many file sizes are missing. It is distinct from free filesystem capacity. F2 → Inventory evidence shows the exact recorded bytes, the check time, and missing size or stream evidence counts.

The stage table counts raw archives recorded complete for this workspace's raw root, registered normalizations and merges, and known local conversion outputs from the latest eight converter execution receipts. Conversion receipts can establish committed outputs and physical rows. They do not provide recorded file sizes or an exhaustive inventory. Overview does not reverify files. Physical rows describe stored representations, which can overlap.

Select a stage or market with Enter. The market list shows trade and depth membership and the latest recorded observed event time in UTC. Presence does not establish continuous interval coverage or current market freshness. Use Markets in the footer to page through the complete matching registry inventory. Each market opens publications for its exact canonical identity. Recent runs are limited to three on narrow screens and five otherwise. F2 opens the full Runs area.

The status strip shows the observed testing registry connection, verified managed installations, and filesystem free space. Use F2 → Workspace status details for each source’s check time. Ctrl+R refreshes these read-only checks as well as inventory and recent history. Returning to Overview reloads inventory and history and rechecks expired observations. Registry outages leave local history and owned operations usable.

The current operation shows the latest reported phase and any measured work. The completion summary stays until dismissed through F2 or replaced by another operation. A requested validation, preparation, or stop-after boundary can succeed without producing a publication. Results show publishing and registration evidence separately. Recent run times are shown in UTC. A recorded running state in retained history has unconfirmed liveness.

Use Enter to inspect the selected run and F2 to open its report, outputs, or available recovery actions. Attention highlights current blockers and interrupted pipelines with retained evidence. Resume opens the exact pipeline run, and registration recovery opens the retained execution intent. These actions use the existing review and verification flows.

items.title: Pipeline and standalone workflows
items.text:
Choose a saved pipeline recipe under Workflows. Validate checks its structure. Plan reads retained evidence in the testing registry. Run begins acquisition and continues through publication and registration. Choose Stop after normalize.prepare to inspect validated jobs before execution. Open the run report and use Pipeline Resume to continue with its retained inputs, ranking, settings, and jobs. Pipeline Resume and Status select retained run IDs.

Standalone workflows accept the same saved recipes and applicable submitted paths as their CLI counterparts. Preparation, execution, verification, registration, and recovery have separate service outcomes. The converter reports physical publication and verification. Conversion registration remains unavailable.

Editable source TOML can be opened with Edit TOML. Forge uses the configured editor or nvim, suspends terminal drawing for the editor, then restores the workspace and revalidates the saved source. Operation supervision continues during the edit. Retained submissions remain read-only evidence.

To edit a recipe directly from a shell, use nvim.

nvim data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/pipeline/bybit_spot.toml

items.title: Author recipes
items.text:
New recipe uses the workflow tab's creator and opens the new source in the configured editor. The pipeline creator also supports mf pipeline new NAME. Review draft fields before planning or running. A successful editor exit triggers a reload and local validation. Removing or invalidating the source produces an error. Retained submissions remain immutable.

From a Markets or Catalog instrument, choose Add to acquisition… or Add to pipeline…. Select an existing recipe or supply a name and explicit UTC interval for a new one, then choose trades, depth, or both. The review identifies the exact file and interval. Apply writes the supported TOML requests while preserving unrelated settings and comments. An exact duplicate is a no-op. Forge coordinates its writers and editor sessions, and changes observed after review require a reload. Pipeline requests are embedded in the selected pipeline TOML.

Acquisition recipes can seed normalization and conversion. Normalization recipes can seed merge or conversion, or replace the single source of a compatible derived merge that has no pinned publication IDs. Merge recipes can seed conversion. Conversion source routes still resolve committed merge inputs during preparation. Creating or editing a recipe does not execute it.

items.title: Data and maintenance
items.text:
Merged and Normalized each list registered publications once. It retains the engine publication ID, registry publication ID, full published stream membership, and a separate page of primary-file identities. Open registered files to inspect lineage, schema, or a bounded Parquet sample. The publication view provides publication lineage and complete stream membership. File verification checks the named primary file and shared manifest checksum. Its result explicitly identifies the scope and whether the whole publication was verified. Execution and verification evidence retain original timestamps and units. Observed event endpoints are inclusive and do not establish continuity for the requested half-open interval.

Converted browses known commits from the newest 100 converter execution receipts. Forge reads metadata from their known managed manifests. Missing or invalid manifests remain identifiable from the retained receipt. This source does not enumerate every local conversion and does not infer registry registration. The Overview keeps its separate shorter evidence window.

Raw uses local archive registry identities. Reloading reads retained metadata. Archive verification and reconciliation can update registry state, and dataset verification hashes the requested file and shared manifest. These actions run only when selected.

Review and apply storage cleanup using the saved preview. Forge binds apply to the displayed preview and revalidates targets before deleting anything. Ranking deletion also checks reviewed snapshot identities. Database restore accepts a verified backup and an explicitly named fresh disposable testing database. Existing storage and database safeguards remain in force.

items.title: Active work and shutdown
items.text:
Ctrl+O opens the owned operation and its current activity. Pipeline and acquisition progress comes from their typed snapshots. Processing shows phases and retained results. Inner-engine throughput, ETA, and row progress are unavailable in Forge. An open operation gains report, output, and recovery actions as evidence becomes available. When the operation finishes while you browse elsewhere, Forge shows a notification and keeps your current view.

Changing screens leaves owned work running. Workspace ownership lasts for the mutation, including child and reader cleanup. Ctrl+C opens interruption confirmation. Ctrl+Q with work active offers Back to keep the application open, or cancellation and graceful exit.

Retained external reports show the last recorded state. They carry no promise of process liveness, and Forge only cancels operations that it owns. Pipeline Resume and normalization or merge registration recovery use the existing service paths. For work that should survive leaving a terminal, launch Forge inside tmux and detach from the session.

See the CLI and TUI action inventory for action classes, service boundaries, and verification coverage.

items.title: Merge registered normalized files
items.text:
Check supported layouts before choosing inputs. Use dataset inspection to confirm concrete stream ownership, publication identities, and required primary parts.

Install the managed merge binary with mf engine build merge. Use the configured testing PostgreSQL registry for discovery and preparation.

items.title: Start from a normalization recipe
items.text:
mf merge new first_merge --from-normalize engine_test --testing
mf merge validate first_merge
mf merge prepare first_merge --testing

new reads the existing managed normalization recipe and creates data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/merge/first_merge.toml. A TOML path also works as the source. Creation is exclusive and reports matching registered files and known blockers. validate checks recipe structure without a database connection. prepare resolves the live registry and validates the resulting job with Rust. Both creation and preparation stop before processing.

version = 1

[interval]
start = 2026-10-27T00:00:00Z
end = 2026-10-30T00:00:00Z

[selection]
source = "engine_test"
operation = "normalize"
mode = "all"

The source determines the eligible requests. mode = "all" considers all eligible files for those requests. Narrow the interval or add filters under [selection]. All filters must match the same stream membership.

data_types = ["trades"]
instruments = ["bybit.spot.spot.BTCUSDT"]
Selection field Contract source Required normalization recipe. operation, mode Default to normalize and all. These are the only accepted values. data_types Optional nonempty subset of trades and order_book_l2. exchanges, instruments Optional nonempty lists of lowercase registered venue codes and canonical exchange.instrument_type.market_category.symbol identities. instrument_types Optional nonempty subset of spot, perpetual, future, option, equity. market_categories Optional nonempty subset of spot, linear, inverse, option, equity. publication_ids Optional nonempty list of distinct positive PostgreSQL publication IDs. Get these from the discovery report or mf --json datasets show FILE_ID --testing under publication.publication_id.

Omitting data_types keeps the types requested by the source. The resolver uses resolved normalization tasks to establish historical family membership and checks the applicable Gate.io feed and registered source key.

Forge discovers eligible files in historical.datasets and their shared evidence in historical.dataset_publications. A retained execution intent links a source configuration to a submission when the prepared requests and interval agree with the current source and the submitted batch fingerprint agrees with the recorded publication. A single matching verified submission can supply multiple publications. If multiple verified submissions match, or the matching files lack a verified submission link, add publication_ids = [ID] to approve specific registry publications. Use the publication IDs in the preparation report, which differ from file dataset IDs and engine IDs. Approval still requires a matching stream and interval. For legacy normalization requests with explicitly listed archive IDs, use explicit file selection.

The interval is half-open and must fit the engine’s signed 64-bit nanosecond range. Forge converts the recipe's timezone-aware datetime values to integer Unix nanoseconds. The observed maximum timestamp of a file is inclusive, so a file with a maximum equal to the merge start is eligible, while a file starting at the merge end is outside the range. The report lists observed envelopes, uncovered parts of the requested interval and files extending beyond it. Observed envelopes provide no proof of continuity inside the interval. Use explicit nanosecond bounds for precision finer than the datetime parser's microsecond resolution.

Missing requests, incomplete inputs and unresolved publication choices can block registry preparation. A blocked preparation returns exit 1 and retains prepare-report.json. If registry preparation can resolve the selection but the engine rejects it, the job and report are retained with status generated and compatibility not_validated. Execution requires validation of the exact submitted job.

items.title: Select file dataset IDs explicitly
items.text:
mf merge new manual_merge

Edit data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/merge/manual_merge.toml. Use either this explicit format or the source-derived format for each recipe. Replace the illustrative IDs with file dataset IDs returned by normalization registration or mf datasets list --testing and set the requested half-open interval in integer nanoseconds.

dataset_ids = [1, 2]
start_ns = 1727683200000000000
end_ns = 1727769600000000000

mf merge validate manual_merge
mf merge prepare manual_merge --testing
mf merge run manual_merge --testing
mf merge run manual_merge --testing --tui

Choose one run command. Both modes prepare one MergeJob, submit it, verify the committed physical timeline and register the output in PostgreSQL. TUI mode requires an interactive terminal. For machine output, use mf --json merge run manual_merge --testing.

items.title: Selection and runtime
items.text:
Explicit-file recipes assign priority in order of the first file listed for each stream. Source-derived recipes use the first matching normalization request, with expanded members ordered by canonical stream ID. Streams without a matching request use ascending canonical stream ID. The preparation report shows stream IDs, content types, ranks, and file counts alongside separate totals for files, streams, and publications.

Either recipe may override selected priorities using a top-level TOML table. Quote canonical IDs to keep punctuation literal. Unspecified streams take the lowest unused ranks in their default order.

[stream_ranks]
"binance.inverse.perpetual.BTCUSD_PERP.trades" = 3
"binance.linear.future.BTCUSDT_261225.trades" = 7

Forge uses the committed manifest's file ownership and content type. Older task-layout publications supply their single stream through the checksummed processing job. The public JSON carries each selected file's stream_id, stream_rank, and content_type with its existing file ID, SHA-256, path, and publication pin. Depth appears as depth in the job and as order_book_l2 in recipe discovery filters. Use the exact reported stream ID in overrides. For the full schema, see the prepared job reference.

Rust verifies every selected primary and its owning stream against the pinned publication. Files in one stream repeat its assigned rank. Lower ranks receive priority at equal timestamps across streams. This priority expresses a merge policy. Original source order and task-local row references are preserved within a stream. Removing files to run a trades-only or depth-only selection can leave gaps in the ranks. Preserve those ranks when preparing a filtered job under a new output path.

Merge reads data/.config/engine/merge.toml. The direct Rust merge command accepts --config PATH relative to --project-root. Forge copies and checksums the runtime at preparation and uses the retained copy at execution. A direct job-file run without a preparation report pins the current runtime at launch. Prepare a new job to apply a runtime edit. The committed merge-runtime.json records effective settings and its SHA-256 is in publication-checksums.json. Runtime fields

items.title: Supported layouts
items.text:
A timestamp-ordered v4/v5 trade publication may contribute multiple concrete streams and multiple parts per stream. Each selected stream must have contiguous source spans with no repeated task spans. Compatible consecutive trade publications can share one rank when the exact stream ID and instrument namespace agree and the committed task metadata describes the same instrument. Publications without a verified namespace remain distinct. Equal or overlapping timestamps at a cross-publication boundary for the same stream are ambiguous and rejected. Each row retains its original publication, task, and task-local offset.

Depth-only and combined execution support complete concrete streams from segmented v4/v5 depth publications in causal mode. Select all primary parts of each requested depth stream. A single publication may supply several independently ranked streams. Merge verifies the pinned event index, source boundaries and segments for those streams, then replays their committed event sequences. Each initialization, reset, update and zero-row event retains its original meaning. Independent source tasks start at their committed initialization. Depth streams spanning multiple publications require a supported continuity contract and are currently rejected.

items.title: Timeline ordering
items.text:
Forge prepares an explicit timeline_ordering for each job. Set timeline_ordering = "chronological" or timeline_ordering = "causal" at the top level of an explicit or source-derived recipe to override the resolved mode. Forge defaults segmented depth selections to causal and other selections to chronological. Older prepared jobs that omit the field use chronological ordering. The resolved field participates in the prepared job fingerprint and is recorded in the committed manifest.

  • Chronological emits nondecreasing event timestamps and uses the submitted rank at equal timestamps. This retains timestamp partitions and the existing physical schema. Segmented depth requires the causal contract.
  • Causal chooses the next available stream head by original timestamp, then submitted rank at equality. Only that stream advances. A timestamp regression is retained in source order. This deterministic policy establishes a replay sequence across independent streams.

Causal physical schema version 2 stores a zero-based timeline_sequence across all output files. Read files in manifest order and rows in sequence order, including any timestamp regressions. A single forward logical merge produces contiguous sequence partitions for budgeted physical materialization. Timestamp statistics report the actual minimum and maximum written timestamps. The timestamp-based conversion workflow still requires chronological input.

The half-open request interval selects observations. If a depth event needs earlier initialization or intervening updates outside the interval, merge includes the necessary committed segment prefix and marks those events reconstruction_only. These rows are replay dependencies and are excluded from ordinary observation membership in Forge. The manifest records their count separately. Missing primary parts, missing initialization and corrupt metadata produce dependency or integrity errors before commit.

items.title: Merge tests
items.text:
The ordinary historical_merge target runs under the historical feature using source-controlled and generated fixtures. It requires no local datasets, PostgreSQL, or prior normalization.

cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --features historical --test historical_merge -- --list
cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --features historical --test historical_merge -- --nocapture

Reference bounds, event kinds, duplicate identities and zero-change events use typed inventories. Stream metadata, provenance, partitioning, checkpoint reconstruction, publication and corruption cases use test-owned fixtures. Their primary files use production Arrow schemas and their processing-job checksums are local to each temporary directory. The production combined rotation case uses four primary files and 16,390 total events to cross one materialization window and rotate at the minimum configured 1 MiB file target.

items.title: Optional recording compatibility
items.text:
Opt-in tests derive their selections from engine/tests/historical/fixtures/merge.json. They require the pinned normalized manifests, selected Parquet files, and applicable processing provenance and sidecars. To use an identical relocated copy, set MARKETFORGE_MERGE_FIXTURE_FROM and MARKETFORGE_MERGE_FIXTURE_TO to absolute path prefixes. Both primary and manifest paths relocate together. The tests verify the existing checksums and require no PostgreSQL connection.

cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --features historical --test historical_merge bounded_recorded:: -- --ignored --nocapture
cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --features historical --test historical_merge validates_real_ -- --ignored --nocapture
cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --features historical --test historical_merge merges_two_bounded_recorded_trade_streams -- --ignored --nocapture

Explicit requests fail with the missing prerequisite when a pinned artifact is absent. The checks select their inputs before opening primary Parquet or resolving the runtime job.

The workload guard caps runtime resolution at four selected files. Trade compatibility reads primaries of up to 256 rows and 1 MiB each. The K-way case compares trades from two concrete streams. The v5 trade commit case compares physical values with the selected source Parquet using one and two workers. The depth reference check compares 16 index events starting at an initialization. It caps the selected primary at 8 MiB and also caps sidecar bytes, row-group size and snapshot levels. The miniature fixtures exercise depth reconstruction and combined publication.

The bounded trade probe commits two ranks from one v5 publication. The recorded depth-only and mixed probes commit a Gate.io segment with a real timestamp regression and compare every emitted reference and depth payload to the normalized data. The ordinary suite exercises sparse ranks, multiple depth streams in one publication, dependencies, zero-row events, input permutations and sequence rotation across worker counts. The cursor performance comparison remains opt-in.

Launch a validated prepared job with the TUI by substituting its path for PATH_TO_VALIDATED_JOB. The direct Rust command publishes files. Forge is responsible for PostgreSQL registration.

cargo run --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --locked --features historical,monitor-tui --bin marketforge-merge -- --job PATH_TO_VALIDATED_JOB --project-root . --tui

items.title: Reading the merge dashboard
items.text:
Run with --tui in an interactive terminal. The header shows the requested selection, UTC interval with an exclusive end, and timeline ordering. The center shows the active phase, elapsed time, current rate when sampled, partition work, and recent activity. Press D for details, use the arrow keys to scroll, and press Ctrl+C to interrupt. Details include exact nanoseconds, the full job ID, configuration paths and SHA-256, effective runtime limits, the output path, and the report location.

  • Checking inputs counts selected primary files whose integrity was verified.
  • Building timeline counts logical event references. Its total is unknown until the timeline has been built. Individual partitions can process many references before any partition finishes.
  • Writing Parquet counts written output events against the completed timeline reference count. Checking timeline validates the logical references. Verifying output counts physical output events against the expected output and reports checked files. Each check remains pending until it starts.
  • Active / worker cap compares current running partitions with the effective configured maximum. A causal timeline uses one forward logical pass. Parquet work can use multiple admitted workers. Queued work counts planned partitions that have yet to start. The dashboard shows a queue of work, with live memory and open-file consumption unavailable.
  • The output breakdown distinguishes trade and depth observations from reconstruction context events. Canonical payload rows are a separate count available in Details. Throughput uses samples from the current phase. ETA is omitted because these samples lack a stable estimate of remaining work.

The default runtime is data/.config/engine/merge.toml under the project root. The direct Rust --config override resolves relative paths from the same root. Forge pins a copy for validation and execution, records both its original location and loaded copy in the execution intent, and checks the retained fingerprint before launching. The dashboard shows the effective values already handed to the engine. The source TOML SHA-256 identifies the loaded configuration bytes. The separately checksummed merge-runtime.json records the effective values used for the committed publication.

Engine committed indicates the Rust publication is ready for Forge verification. The persistent Forge summary distinguishes execution, verification, and registration and lists the registered file IDs when available. Direct Rust execution prints the engine outcome and manifest path after restoring the terminal.

items.title: Publication and recovery
items.text:
A recipe uses a fresh output under data/datasets/merged/<engine-job-id> relative to the configured data root. Rust publishes the validated physical timeline, manifest, resolved job, effective runtime, input manifest checksums and physical validation evidence atomically. Forge revalidates the committed physical Parquet and byte fingerprints and registers each primary output in historical.datasets under one shared publication. Selected input file IDs are retained as publication-scope lineage.

The report under data/runs/merge-execute-*/execution-result.json distinguishes execution, verification and database registration. A complete report includes each file dataset ID and its path. Failed or interrupted runs return nonzero. One merge job publishes one output.

After a power loss or database error, retry registration by passing the execution intent, committed directory, its manifest.json, or a particular primary file path.

mf merge register data/runs/MERGE_EXECUTION_ID/execution-intent.json --testing
mf merge register data/datasets/merged/ENGINE_JOB_ID --testing

Registration-only recovery checks the output and required input lineage again. Identical retries reuse the database ID.

items.title: Normalize historical data
items.text:
Normalization converts acquired or registered historical archives into canonical trade and order-book datasets. MarketForge resolves the registered files, applies source-format profiles, runs the Rust Engine, and verifies and registers the resulting Parquet files.

Input or result Role Raw archive Preserves the original bytes selected through acquisition or external registration. Normalization profile Describes the file format, timestamps, raw fields, and trade or order-book operations. Normalization recipe Selects registered inputs and a time interval. Canonical dataset Contains normalized Parquet and the evidence needed to inspect it or use it in later processing.

items.title: 1. Check prerequisites
items.text:
• Acquire historical archives or register external data, then check the managed copies. A file on disk becomes eligible for managed selection through its registry record.
  • Check your installed normalization profiles and the instrument and historical specifications applicable over the full archive intervals. Preparation and Engine validation check the evidence and the selected source interpretation.
  • Use a configured normalization Engine and the database that owns the raw records. The commands below use --testing throughout.

For the example below, look for a complete Bybit BTCUSDT linear perpetual trades archive for 27 October 2026 in testing storage. If the source format has no applicable profile, use the profile authoring guide before preparing the recipe.

items.title: 2. Create a normalization recipe
items.text:
mf normalize new my_dataset

This creates a managed TOML draft, opens your editor, and checks the saved recipe when the editor exits successfully. Choose an unused recipe name. For an independent copy of an existing acquisition recipe, use the following command in place of plain new. The copy can be edited without affecting the acquisition recipe, and later changes to the original do not propagate.

mf normalize new my_dataset --from-acquisition getting_started

For this walkthrough, save one UTC day of Bybit BTCUSDT linear perpetual trades:

version = 1

[interval]
start = 2026-10-27T00:00:00Z
end = 2026-10-28T00:00:00Z

[[requests]]
exchange = "bybit"
instrument_type = "perpetual"
market_category = "linear"
data_type = "trades"
scope = { kind = "instrument", identifier = "BTCUSDT" }

The interval includes its start and excludes its end. It selects whole overlapping archives, which can contain records outside the requested dates. See the configuration reference for source selection and the older explicit archive-ID recipe format.

items.title: 3. Validate the recipe
items.text:
mf normalize validate my_dataset | cpout

Validation checks TOML syntax, required fields, and local recipe constraints. Use preparation to resolve registered archives and instrument metadata, and persisted preparation to check the batch with Rust.

items.title: 4. Preview preparation
items.text:
mf normalize prepare my_dataset --testing --dry-run | cpout

Check the selected archives, job, task and stream counts, ranking resolution, and any input, specification, profile, or coverage diagnostics. A dry run showing prepared means Forge resolved the plan. The displayed artifact paths are prospective, and compiled batch validation happens during persisted preparation. Resolve blockers before continuing. If an archive appears among the matches but is missing from the selected inputs, look for its local archive ID in the blockers. Nominal archive intervals describe file boundaries and leave event-level completeness unknown.

items.title: 5. Execute normalization
items.text:
mf normalize execute my_dataset --testing

This resolves inputs, writes and validates the prepared batch, runs the Rust Engine, verifies committed output, and registers eligible primary files. Check the final execution, verification, and registration statuses. A run can commit Parquet and still need registration recovery before those files appear in the dataset list. For the same workflow with an interactive progress monitor, run:

mf normalize execute my_dataset --testing --tui

items.title: 6. Inspect normalized datasets
items.text:
mf datasets list --testing | cpout
mf datasets show DATASET_ID --testing | cpout
mf datasets verify DATASET_ID --testing | cpout

Use a registry primary-file ID from the list or the normalization result. Engine dataset IDs identify Engine output, publication IDs identify registered groups of files, and execution IDs identify retained attempts. See the dataset guide for schema, row previews, and lineage.

items.title: Optional advanced execution
items.text: Use manual batch submission when preparation and execution need to happen separately. The CLI reference compares the execution modes.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Problem First check No selected inputs Recipe scope, interval, and registered archive status. Missing specification or incompatible profile Applicability across the archive and the registered source interpretation. Rust validation or execution failed Preparation diagnostics or retained execution report. Output committed but registration failed Retained execution intent and registration recovery.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: Use registered primary files in dataset inspection or merge. See runtime configuration for resource and integrity settings. See the publication reference for manifests and integrity evidence.

items.title: Explore datasets in Jupyter
items.text:
The research API reads local Parquet manifests and footers. It can discover files without PostgreSQL, inspect their stored metadata, and read explicitly selected rows.

From the repository root, install the research group and launch JupyterLab.

uv sync --project forge --group lab
uv run --project forge --group lab --with jupyterlab jupyter lab

Open the example notebook with its adjacent fixture builder. The notebook creates tiny synthetic normalized and combined files in a temporary directory. It needs no database, credentials, network access, or processing engine once the environment is installed.

items.title: Discover files and narrow the catalog
items.text:
from forge.datasets import MarketData
from forge.lab.inspection import inspect

market = MarketData()
catalog = market.discover(scope="committed")
display(catalog)

matches = catalog.find(
    exchange=["bybit", "binance", "okx"],
    instrument_type="perpetual",
    market_category="linear",
    symbol="BTCUSDT",
    data_type=["trades", "depth"],
    start="2026-10-27T00:00:00Z",
    end="2026-10-30T00:00:00Z",
)
display(matches)
matches.summary()

Set MarketData(root=..., data_root=...) when working outside the repository or with a separate data directory. With an omitted root, Forge uses MARKETFORGE_PROJECT_ROOT or searches upward from the working directory. Discover the test trees with scope="tests", or include them alongside production output with scope="all". Add include_staging=True to see recognized staging directories as uncommitted. Standalone Parquet encountered in a search tree appears as unverified with unknown market identity. Discover again to refresh the filesystem metadata.

Catalog search returns a collection for every result size. Use iteration or indexing for several matches, if not matches for an empty result, and matches.one() when exactly one file is expected. Symbol matching is exact and case-sensitive. Use catalog.find(symbol="BTC", symbol_match="contains") to search for a substring. Filters on venue, symbol, instrument type, and category apply to the same concrete stream within each file.

Catalog diagnostics preserve affected paths and reasons while successful files remain available. Inspect catalog.diagnostics for unreadable files, malformed manifests, unknown versions, conflicts, or incomplete identity.

items.title: Inspect one file or concrete stream
items.text:
if matches:
    dataset = matches[0]
    display(dataset)
    display(dataset.streams())

    report = inspect(dataset)
    display(report)
    print(report.schema())
    display(report.columns(), report.row_groups(), report.timestamps())

Choose a stream in a mixed file using dataset.select(exchange="okx", kind="depth") when it matches exactly one available membership. If the file contains Binance ETH and OKX BTC, one file appears in the catalog. A query for OKX ETH has no match. A matching view keeps all known file memberships as context and highlights the matching memberships. File totals always describe the physical file. Stream selections use actual row predicates, including rank and the combined event-kind discriminator when present.

Timestamps in the catalog are observed envelopes. The maximum is inclusive. Search uses overlap with [start, end); the envelope can overlap when no row in the range exists, and says nothing about continuity. Use interval="envelope_contained" to require the entire known file envelope inside the query range. Inspection separates recorded requested bounds, observed file or stream bounds, and physical footer statistics. Footer statistics for a selected stream may include other streams in the same file.

items.title: Read records explicitly
items.text:
if matches:
    dataset = matches[0]
    display(dataset.head(5, columns=["event_timestamp_ns", "symbol"], input_rows=10_000))
    for batch in dataset.batches(columns=["event_timestamp_ns", "symbol"], input_rows=1000):
        print(batch.num_rows)
    query = dataset.scan(columns=["event_timestamp_ns", "symbol"], start="2026-10-27T00:00:00Z")
    display(query.limit(5).collect())

These methods also work on a selected stream. Set time_field="system_timestamp_ns" explicitly to filter on the stored system time instead of event time. Its meaning depends on the source profile. A preview preserves physical order and may read more than its returned row limit, especially when filtering sparse streams. input_rows limits the physical prefix evaluated before predicates. Parquet readers may still decode whole pages or dictionaries.

Arrow batches retain exact Decimal256 prices and quantities. Previews represent Decimal256 as exact strings, including nested combined payloads. A Polars lazy query requires a supported projection. Exclude Decimal256 fields or use Arrow batches for those fields. Inspection applies no scaling or contract multipliers.

Use report.profile(["event_timestamp_ns"], input_rows=1000) to summarize a bounded physical prefix and compare(file_a, file_b) to compare stored schemas, envelopes and sizes. These operations report their evidence and scope. See the Python API reference.

items.title: Inspect causal streams and bounded reads
AND and OR Semantics
items.text: This is one of the most important properties of the search API.

items.title: OR within one filter
items.text:
For example:

exchange=["bybit", "okx"]

means:

Bybit OR OKX

items.title: AND between filters
items.text:
For example:

catalog.find(
    exchange="bybit",
    symbol="BTCUSDT",
    data_type="trades",
)

means:

Exchange is Bybit
AND
Symbol is BTCUSDT
AND
Content is trades

items.title: Why does membership consistency matter?
items.text:
Suppose one merged file contains:

Bybit BTCUSDT Trades
OKX ETHUSDT Trades

Now consider:

catalog.find(
    exchange="bybit",
    symbol="ETHUSDT",
)

The file should not match merely because it contains:

Bybit

somewhere and:

ETHUSDT

somewhere else.

The conditions must identify the same established stream membership.

items.title: Why is this important?
items.text:
Otherwise, a combined file could produce false matches for markets it does not actually represent.

MarketForge preserves this relationship.

items.title: Composable Searches
items.text:
A search returns another DatasetCatalog.

This means you can apply additional filters later.

For example:

bybit = catalog.find(
    exchange="bybit",
)

perpetuals = bybit.find(
    instrument_type="perpetual",
)

trades = perpetuals.find(
    data_type="trades",
)

display(trades.summary())

items.title: Why is this useful?
items.text:
You can build reusable research selections.

For example:

btc = catalog.find(
    symbol="BTCUSDT",
)

btc_trades = btc.find(
    data_type="trades",
)

items.title: Does each search start from every original file?
items.text:
No.

The next search operates on the current matching collection.

items.title: Are previous membership filters retained?
items.text:
Yes.

Composable searches retain matching memberships.

This prevents later filters from unexpectedly switching to unrelated streams in the same physical file.

items.title: Does filtering modify the underlying datasets?
items.text:
No.

The searches return new metadata collections.

They do not alter Parquet files.

items.title: Search by Processing Operation
items.text:
The API supports an operation filter.

For example:

normalized = catalog.find(
    operation="normalize",
)

Or:

merged = catalog.find(
    operation="merge",
)

items.title: Why distinguish operations?
items.text:
Normalization and merging produce different physical publication formats.

For example:

Normalization

Raw Archives
    |
    v
Canonical Trades / Depth

Merge

Normalized Streams
    |
    v
Combined Timeline

The appropriate inspection strategy can depend on the selected operation.

items.title: Troubleshoot and recover
items.text:
From the checkout, use mf config show to confirm the effective data root and mf engine status to check the managed binaries. Run mf database status --testing before registry work and mf database migrate --testing to apply pending migrations. Database maintenance documents backup scope, restore destinations and privileges.

Use storage inspection and run reports to trace an acquisition or verify its raw copy. For normalization and merge, retain the operation-specific reports, committed manifest and auxiliary files. When a publication succeeds and registration fails, use the registration command with the retained execution intent and the original registry. When storage reconciliation reports a partial copy, inspect its status before any cleanup.

Keep the database backup and filesystem artifacts together for recovery. Validate configuration snapshots before activation and use a disposable destination to exercise a restore.

items.title: Find the failing boundary
items.text: Symptom First check Where to go next Installer reports partial initialization Check which catalogue, enrichment, or ranking stage failed, then retry the selected initialization command Installer results Registry unavailable or identity rejected Run mf database status with the intended environment Connection setup Recipe validates but no raw input is selected Compare requested scope and interval with local status, origin, and feed Raw storage Engine command or option is unavailable Compare Forge and the managed target installed under .bin/ Engine builds and runtime inspection Prepared run cannot resume Check retained registry identity, input digests, and executable evidence Pipeline resume Output exists but has no registry rows Check whether the execution report verified the publication before attempting registration recovery Publication and registration

items.title: Back up and restore the registry
Create a Database Backup
items.text:
MarketForge provides:

mf database backup BACKUP_DIR --testing

BACKUP_DIR is the destination directory for the new backup.

For example:

mf database backup ./metadata-backup --testing

This creates a backup under:

./metadata-backup/

The destination must be a new directory.

Choose a location outside MarketForge's managed configuration, raw-data, and dataset roots.

Do not use an existing directory containing unrelated files.

items.title: What files are created?
items.text:
A completed backup has the following main structure:

metadata-backup/
├── registry.dump
├── configuration/
└── manifest.json

Each part serves a different purpose.

items.title: registry.dump
items.text:
This contains the PostgreSQL registry backup.

MarketForge uses PostgreSQL's custom-format dump support to create it.

The backup contains the selected registry schemas, not the full historical data files stored on disk.

items.title: configuration/
items.text:
This contains a snapshot of the managed TOML configuration files included in the backup.

It helps preserve the configuration associated with the backed-up registry state.

However, restoring the database does not automatically activate these configuration files.

They remain available for deliberate review.

items.title: manifest.json
items.text:
This records information about the completed backup, including SHA-256 checksums used to verify its files.

Before restoring, MarketForge checks the completed backup and relevant configuration checksums.

items.title: PostgreSQL backup utility
items.text:
The backup command requires:

pg_dump

You can check whether the utility is available with:

mf doctor --testing | cpout

Doctor reports PostgreSQL backup and restore tool availability along with workspace and registry readiness. Missing backup tools are nonblocking for ordinary processing. Doctor reference

items.title: Does backup modify the source database?
items.text:
The backup operation reads the registry and writes backup files to the selected destination.

It does not perform a schema migration or replace the source database.

However, it creates real filesystem artifacts, so the destination must be chosen carefully.

items.title: What happens if backup is interrupted?
items.text:
An interrupted backup may leave an incomplete destination directory.

Do not treat that directory as a successful backup.

Review the operation result and the retained files.

For a clean retry, use a new destination rather than assuming an incomplete directory can safely be overwritten.

items.title: Backing Up the Complete MarketForge Workspace
items.text:
A database backup protects the registry.

However, a complete MarketForge recovery may also require its managed filesystem artifacts.

This matters because the registry contains references to files that exist outside PostgreSQL.

For example:

PostgreSQL Registry
        |
        v
Registered Dataset
        |
        v
Filesystem Path
        |
        v
Canonical Parquet File

If the Parquet file is missing, restoring the registry record alone does not recreate the dataset.

Similarly, restoring a raw archive registration does not recreate the archive bytes.

items.title: What should be preserved?
items.text:
For a complete recovery strategy, consider the following components:

Component Why it matters PostgreSQL backup Preserves registered identities and metadata. Managed raw archives Preserves original acquired or imported data. Normalized datasets Preserves canonical processing outputs. Merged datasets Preserves completed merge outputs. Publication manifests Preserves publication structure and processing evidence. Run receipts Preserves operation and recovery information. Managed configuration Preserves the settings and recipes used to operate MarketForge.

The appropriate backup strategy depends on the value of your data and whether the original sources can be obtained again.

For example, some public exchange archives may still be downloadable later.

However, purchased recordings or privately collected data may not be replaceable.

Do not assume that every historical source will remain available indefinitely.

Keep independent copies of data that would be difficult or impossible to obtain again.

items.title: Keep metadata and files consistent
items.text:
Ideally, a recovery set should contain registry information and filesystem artifacts representing a consistent application state.

For example, the restored registry should not refer to dataset files that were created later but were never included in the filesystem backup.

Similarly, copied dataset files should retain their associated manifests and verification information.

The current mf database backup command audits representative artifact references, but it is not a complete snapshot of the entire MarketForge filesystem.

A full workspace recovery procedure must account for the external files separately.

items.title: Restore a Database Backup
items.text:
The restore command has this form:

mf database restore BACKUP_DIR \
    --testing \
    --destination NAME \
    --disposable-testing

For example, after creating and verifying a backup at ./metadata-backup, a restore invocation could be:

mf database restore ./metadata-backup \
    --testing \
    --destination marketforge_restore_a1b2c3d4 \
    --disposable-testing

The destination name is illustrative.

Choose a fresh, unused name that follows the required format.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
The restore operation requires:

  • A completed MarketForge database backup.
  • A correctly configured source testing database.
  • The pg_restore PostgreSQL utility.
  • PostgreSQL permission to create a new database.
  • An unused disposable destination name.

The PostgreSQL role must have the required CREATEDB permission.

items.title: How are destination names restricted?
items.text:
Restore destinations must follow this pattern:

marketforge_restore_<hex>

The suffix must contain between 8 and 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters.

For example:

marketforge_restore_a1b2c3d4

is structurally valid.

A destination outside the accepted naming scheme is rejected.

This restriction helps distinguish disposable restore targets from ordinary application databases.

items.title: What does --disposable-testing mean?
items.text:
The flag explicitly confirms that the restore destination is intended to be a disposable testing database.

It is required by the current restore command.

The flag does not make restoration a dry run.

MarketForge actually creates and restores the new PostgreSQL database when the operation succeeds.

items.title: Historical pipeline
items.text: A single Forge recipe acquires and registers raw archives, prepares and runs normalization, then publishes and registers a merged dataset. Conversion is a separate workflow.

items.title: Recipe
items.text:
Save named recipes under data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/pipeline/. The version 1 recipe uses the acquisition request schema and one half-open UTC interval [start, end). Use the existing scopes and feed options for each exchange. Forge resolves archive, instrument, job, dataset, and registry identities.

The example is checked in at data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/pipeline/bybit_spot.toml. To inspect or edit it, run nvim data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/pipeline/bybit_spot.toml.

Use the maintained sample recipe as the complete example. See the recipe reference for field definitions.

[normalize] and [merge] are optional. Normalization defaults to turnover ranking. Merge accepts causal and chronological. When omitted, the existing merge planner picks the ordering required by the selected inputs. It derives trade, depth, or mixed processing from registered files.

items.title: Inspect and run
items.text:
Use a configured marketforge_test database with the testing identity and current migrations. Install the managed normalize and merge engines and use the operation runtime files, pipeline runtime and normalization profiles. The catalogue must supply instrument identity and applicable historical specifications for the requested archives. Forge reads its ordinary application and HTTP configuration.

set -o pipefail
mf engine build normalize
mf engine build merge
mf pipeline validate bybit_spot
mf pipeline plan bybit_spot --testing

Validation checks recipe structure and options. Planning reads existing registered evidence and identifies deferred work. It issues no HTTP requests, allocates no output identities, and writes no recipe, job, or registry rows. Local archive readiness is confirmed on run.

mf pipeline run bybit_spot --testing --tui

Forge runs processing stages sequentially to preserve their configured engine budgets. Acquisition uses the usual HTTP concurrency and source rate limits. Preparation and validation are distinct phases. A processing stage completes only after engine execution, committed publication verification, and registration succeed. Archive discovery, nominal archive intervals, verified local files, and observed event extents describe different evidence.

Acquisition passes its exact verified local archive IDs, paths, checksums, and source revision evidence to normalization. Normalization keeps its existing coverage and readiness checks, and uses only those inputs. After normalization registers every required publication, merge takes the exact registered primary-file dataset IDs in that receipt. Engine job and publication IDs stay distinct from registry publication and primary-file IDs.

items.title: Inspect a preparation and resume
items.text:
mf pipeline run bybit_spot --testing --stop-after normalize.prepare --tui

This stops with validated normalization jobs before execution. The command prints the retained run ID and the resume command.

set -o pipefail
mf pipeline status RUN_ID
mf --json pipeline status RUN_ID

mf pipeline resume RUN_ID --testing --tui

Resume uses the original workspace, storage root and testing registry. It checks retained TOML, settings, profile and executable hashes, prepared jobs, and acquisition evidence. Retained jobs preserve the ranking and stream ordering selected during preparation. Completed acquisition scans and verified archives from an interrupted acquisition are retained. A request whose discovery never finished may still need discovery. Changed or missing pinned inputs require investigation. A new selection belongs to a fresh run.

If processing committed a valid publication but registration failed, resume verifies that publication and retries registration through the existing registration service. It keeps failed attempts and any published outputs. A processing retry allocates fresh output identities. A fresh pipeline run also allocates fresh outputs and may reuse verified raw archives.

items.title: Progress and reports
items.text:
The Rich dashboard owns the terminal for the entire run. Ctrl+C requests cancellation. Forge signals and joins the engine, retains diagnostic logs and writes an interrupted report. Redirected output uses a plain summary. Acquisition exposes typed request and file counts, with provisional discovery totals identified during discovery. Processing exposes stage and job lifecycle counts. It has no live row throughput, ETA, or partition counters from Rust.

Run artifacts live under <storage>/runs/<run-id>/. Start with report.json and events.jsonl. The run also retains submitted.toml, resolved-plan.json, frozen engines, and historical settings and profiles. steps/ links execution attempts and stores the exact acquisition selection. The report points to the existing child preparation, execution, verification, and registration receipts. Each engine attempt retains separate diagnostic logs and its structured result when available.

Read the reported child error before retrying. Build missing managed engines, verify access to the testing registry, and supply missing catalogue or profile evidence as indicated. Preserve existing outputs and staging when inspecting interrupted attempts. Use a fresh run when the recipe, data selection, or interpretation needs to change.

items.title: Historical data acquisition
items.text:
Acquisition discovers provider archives, records their identities, and downloads verified local copies. It does not normalize market events. Register external recordings and purchased files through the BYOD workflow to preserve their declared origin and bytes.

Start with the historical-data workflow, use the supported historical sources and configuration reference to select inputs, then inspect and manage acquisitions. The CLI reference lists exact arguments and effects.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Install Forge using the installation guide and run commands from the repository root. Registry-backed commands default to production. Pass --testing for the dedicated marketforge_test database with a verified testing identity.

Forge reads PRODUCTION_DATABASE_KEY or TEST_DATABASE_KEY for the selected environment, first from the process environment and then from the workspace's literal .secrets/postgres.env file. Do not source shell expressions or put credentials into shared recipes. Ask the workspace administrator to provision the database, testing identity and current schema. mf database status --testing inspects migration status. mf doctor --testing checks the initialized environment using the guarded testing loader. These commands connect to PostgreSQL; neither downloads archives.

If the provisioned testing database needs pending migrations, the explicit mf database migrate --testing command applies them and writes schema/identity state. Coordinate schema migration with other testing database users.

Application settings default to data/.config/forge/marketforge.toml. Raw copies live beneath the configured data root's raw/; recipes remain in the workspace's data/.config/workflows/data_engineering/acquisition/. A different storage root does not relocate the recipe library. Configuration, database access, writable storage and internet access are distinct prerequisites.

items.title: Understand command effects
items.text:
Operation Effects acquisition list, validate Read local configuration with no provider or database access. acquisition sources Read historical capabilities from the installed adapters. acquisition new, edit Write a saved TOML recipe; do not acquire data. acquisition plan ... --testing --cache-only Read registry/cache; optional read-only local hashing. No HTTP or writes. acquisition map ... --testing May contact providers; writes discovery/cache records and run artifacts, without downloading archive bodies. acquisition download ... --testing Maps as needed, downloads/reuses files, and updates registry and run artifacts. storage list, show, coverage Read registry records without rehashing files. Use --testing to select the testing registry. storage verify, reconcile Maintenance: can update records and recover reserved files, without HTTP.

Testing is a destination guard, not a dry run. Mapping, downloading, importing, synchronization, and publication perform real work when passed --testing.

items.title: Bring external data
items.text:
See the BYOD guide for the complete workflow and a real recording example.

Register the venue, instrument, historical specifications, and Rust profiles first. Archive recipes refer to those existing entities and record separate source provider and product information.

The complete synthetic archive example registers one trade file and one L2 depth file. Each input gives its canonical instrument, profile ID, content type, and file selection. The declared half-open coverage interval applies to every file in the recipe. Add an optional specification fingerprint to an input to pin its applicable historical evidence.

recipe="$PWD/docs/content/examples/catalogue/registration.toml"
mf acquisition register inspect "$recipe"
mf acquisition register validate "$recipe" --testing
mf acquisition register plan "$recipe" --testing
mf acquisition register run "$recipe" --testing
mf storage list --testing --origin external --exchange example_exchange --instrument-type equity

Validation requires the previously registered catalogue identity, one applicable historical declaration covering the interval, and an installed profile whose Rust fingerprint can be verified. Registration rejects mismatched profiles, conflicting source identities, and inconsistent sampled layouts before publishing managed copies. It retains the declaration and profile fingerprints beside the input checksum. The sample is bounded. Complete event validity belongs to normalization.

Repeating registration can reuse an existing managed copy after checksum verification. Provider, product, source root, and source key describe acquisition provenance. Supply the real execution venue separately. Native publisher and instrument identifiers can be recorded as provenance when available and remain scoped to the source.

items.title: Raw-only preservation
items.text: Use mf acquisition import to preserve local bytes whose interpretation is still incomplete. For example, create a draft with mf acquisition import new recorder --from ./recordings/trades.csv, edit its explicit venue and source identity, and run mf acquisition import run recorder --testing. The legacy import configuration describes its fields. Raw-only import can retain declarations and reuse managed copies. Use acquisition register to bind a source to a verified catalogue and profile interpretation.

items.title: Creating Historical Normalization Profiles
items.text:
